### Introductory.

## I.
### General Preliminary Remarks.

### a. The Task of the Work.

“To have representations <note>original: "Vorstellungen." In 19th-century philosophy, this term refers to any mental image, idea, or perception—the "content" of the mind.</note>, and yet not be conscious of them; in this there seems to lie a contradiction, for how can we know that we have them if we are not conscious of them? — Yet we can nonetheless be indirectly conscious of having a representation, even if we are not immediately conscious of it.” (Kant, <term>Anthropology<note>In the 18th and 19th centuries, "Anthropology" was the study of human nature and the soul, functioning as a precursor to modern psychology.</note></term> § 5. “On the representations that we have without being conscious of them.”)

These clear words of the great thinker from Königsberg <note>A reference to Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), who lived and taught in the Prussian city of Königsberg.</note> contain the starting point of our investigations, as well as the field assigned for our cultivation.

The domain of consciousness is a vineyard so thoroughly plowed in all directions that the pursuit of such works has almost become a weariness to the public; and yet, the sought-after treasure has still not been found, even if unexpected and rich harvests have sprouted from the well-worked soil. That one began with the philosophical consideration of what consciousness found directly within itself was very natural; but should it not now be enticing for the sake of novelty, and hopeful in regard to the gain, to seek the golden treasure in the depths of the mountain—in the noble ores of its bedrock—instead of on the surface of the fertile soil? To be sure, this requires the drill and the chisel and long, arduous labor until one strikes the golden veins, and finally long...

v. Hartmann, Philosophy of the Unconscious.

<summary>In this opening passage, Eduard von Hartmann introduces the central theme of his work: the existence of unconscious mental processes. He uses a quote from Immanuel Kant to justify the study of the "Unconscious" and uses a mining metaphor to suggest that while the surface of the human mind (consciousness) has been well-studied, the true "golden treasure" lies in its deeper, hidden layers.</summary>

<keywords>Immanuel Kant, Anthropology, consciousness, the unconscious, representations, philosophical method, psychology, 19th-century philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory section, moving from the metaphorical "plowing" of consciousness to the "mining" of the unconscious. It addresses the logical paradox of the "unconscious representation" and outlines the methodology for the first two sections of the book.</meta>

...soil? The processing of the ores until the treasure is raised—whoever does not shy away from the effort, let him follow me; for in the work itself lies the highest pleasure! — The concept of an "unconscious representation" <note>original: "unbewusste Vorstellung." As noted previously, this refers to mental content—ideas, images, or perceptions—that exists without the subject's immediate awareness.</note> indeed has something paradoxical for the natural understanding; however, the contradiction contained therein is, as Kant also says, only apparent. For if we can only know of that which we have in consciousness, and thus can know nothing of that which we do not have in consciousness, what right do we then have to claim that that whose existence we know in our consciousness should not also be able to exist outside of our consciousness?

Certainly, in this case, we would be able to claim neither existence nor non-existence, and for this reason we would have to remain with the assumption of non-existence until we receive a right to the positive claim of existence from elsewhere. This was, in general, the previous standpoint. However, the more philosophy left the dogmatic standpoint of instinctive sensuality and instinctive intellectual conviction, and recognized the only highly indirect knowability of everything previously held as immediate content of consciousness, the more value an indirect proof of the existence of a thing naturally had to receive. Thus, it could not fail that here and there in thinking minds, the need arose—for the sake of explaining certain phenomena in the realm of the spirit that were otherwise impossible to explain—to go back to the existence of unconscious representations as their cause. 

To grasp all these phenomena together, to make the existence of unconscious representations and an <term>unconscious will<note>The "Will" here refers to a driving force or impulse that operates below the level of conscious intent, a concept famously explored by Arthur Schopenhauer.</note></term> probable from each individual instance, and through their sum to raise the principle consistent in all of them to the level of a probability bordering on certainty, is the task of the first two sections of this work. The first of these considers phenomena of a physiological and <term>zoopsychological<note>A 19th-century term for animal psychology or the study of the "animal soul."</note></term> nature; the second moves within the realm of the human mind. 

Through this principle of the Unconscious, the considered phenomena simultaneously receive their only correct explanation—which in part had not yet been expressed, but in part could find no recognition simply because the principle itself can only be established through the compilation of all relevant phenomena. Furthermore, there open up from the application of this principle—which has hitherto existed in an embryonic state...

<summary>The author justifies the study of the "Unconscious" by arguing that while it seems paradoxical, its existence can be proven indirectly by its effects. He outlines the work's first two sections: one focused on biology and animal psychology, and the other on the human mind.</summary>
<keywords>unconscious representation, unconscious will, Immanuel Kant, zoopsychology, epistemology, philosophy of mind, physiological phenomena</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page follows the introduction of the "unconscious representation," transitioning from the logical possibility of the concept to its practical application as a unifying principle across various philosophical schools and scientific fields.</meta>

...principles previously established, the most significant perspectives on new ways of treating seemingly familiar subjects emerge; a multitude of contrasts and contradictions from earlier systems and views find their comprehensive solution through the establishment of a higher standpoint that encompasses both sides as incomplete truths. In a word, the principle proves to be highly fruitful for specialized questions. Far more important than this, however, is the way in which the principle of the Unconscious imperceptibly expands from the physical and psychological realms toward views and solutions of tasks that, according to common usage, would be designated as belonging to the **metaphysical** realm. Within our principle, however, these results spin themselves out so simply and naturally from scientific and psychological considerations that one would not notice the transition into another realm at all if the content of these questions were not already known from elsewhere. Everything pushes and pulls toward **the One**; in each new chapter, a piece more of the world crystallizes, so to speak, around this **core**, until, having grown into **All-Unity** <note>original: "All-Einheit." A philosophical concept where all of reality is viewed as a single, unified whole.</note>, it encompasses the universe and finally suddenly presents itself as that which has formed the core of all great philosophies: Spinoza’s substance, Fichte’s absolute I, Schelling’s absolute Subject-Object, Plato’s and Hegel’s absolute Idea, Schopenhauer’s Will, and so on.

I ask, therefore, that you do not take offense for the time being at the concept of "unconscious representation" <note>original: "unbewusste Vorstellung." In German philosophy, "Vorstellung" refers to the mental image, idea, or "representation" of an object in the mind.</note>, even if it initially has little positive meaning; the positive content of the concept can only form in the course of the investigation. For now, let it suffice that it refers to an unknown cause of certain processes falling outside of consciousness, which has received the name "representation" because it shares with what we know in consciousness as a representation the fact that it, like the latter, possesses an **ideal** content that itself has no reality, but can at most resemble an external reality in an ideal image. Analogously, I use the collective term "the Unconscious" to designate not the negative predicate of "being unconscious," but the unknown positive subject to which this predicate belongs—specifically for "unconscious will and unconscious representation" captured as one.

**Vocabulary:** Unconscious, Metaphysics, All-Unity, Spinoza, Fichte, Schelling, Plato, Hegel, Schopenhauer, Will, Representation

<summary>The author explains how the "Unconscious" serves as a unifying principle that bridges the gap between science and metaphysics, harmonizing the systems of major philosophers. He defines "the Unconscious" not as a lack of awareness, but as a positive underlying force combining will and mental representation.</summary>
<keywords>The Unconscious, Metaphysics, All-Unity, History of Philosophy, Will and Representation, Ideal Content</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's introductory argument. Having previously suggested that his principle of the "Unconscious" serves as a unifying "All-Unity" for past systems (like those of Spinoza, Hegel, and Schopenhauer), he now addresses the relationship between new philosophical discovery and historical tradition using an organic metaphor of a tree.</meta>

->“Philosophy is the history of philosophy”—this<-
statement is one I subscribe to with all my heart. However, anyone who understands this word as if truth lay only behind us might be caught in deep error, for there is a dead and a living part in the history of philosophy, and life exists only in the present. Just as in a tree, the solid trunk that braves the storms is formed of dead wood—of the growth of earlier years—and only a thin layer contains the life of the mighty plant, until it too is counted among the dead in the following year. It was not the ornament of leaves and blossoms, which most captivated the observers of previous summers, that gave the tree its prosperity—at most, they helped fertilize its roots once they had fallen and decayed—but rather the unnoticed small ring of growth on the trunk, and the inconspicuous new branches; it was these that increased its expansion, height, and stability. And the fresh, living ring owes not just its stability to its dead ancestors, but also the greatness of its circumference by encompassing them; therefore, as with a tree, the first law for a newly emerging ring is that it must truly encompass and enclose all its predecessors within itself, while the second is that it must grow independently from the roots upward. The task of uniting both of these in philosophy is almost paradoxical, because someone who stands at the height of the current situation usually tends to have lost the impartiality <note>original: "Unbefangenheit." This implies a freedom from preconceived notions or the ability to approach a subject with a fresh, unbiased perspective.</note> to be able to start from the beginning, and whoever attempts an independent start usually delivers an amateurishly immature product because they do not possess the previous historical development.

I believe that the principle of the **Unconscious**, which forms the focal point of this investigation—uniting all rays within itself—may well be considered a new standpoint when grasped in this generality. How far I have succeeded in penetrating the spirit of the previous development of philosophy, I must leave to the readers' judgment; I only note that, with regard to the plan of the work, the proof that almost everything which can be considered "true heartwood" <note>original: "Kernholz." In forestry, heartwood is the dense, inner part of a trunk; here it refers to the essential, enduring truths of previous philosophies.</note> in the history of philosophy is encompassed in these final results must be limited to brief hints—which will certainly suffice for the expert.

<summary>The author uses the metaphor of a tree's growth to argue that true philosophy must both encompass all historical knowledge and grow independently as a new "living layer." He introduces his principle of the Unconscious as a new focal point that synthesizes the "heartwood" of past philosophical truths.</summary>
<keywords>Philosophy of the Unconscious, History of Philosophy, organic growth, heartwood, philosophical synthesis, historical development, Eduard von Hartmann</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's introductory discussion on philosophical methodology. The previous page ended with a reflection on the need for a new philosophy to encompass historical tradition while remaining independent and unbiased. Here, the author shifts to the specific scientific methods he will employ.</meta>

## b. Method of Inquiry and Manner of Presentation.

One can distinguish three main methods in research science: the dialectical (*Hegelian*), the deductive (from the top down), and the inductive (from the bottom up). I must exclude the dialectical method—without being able to engage here in considerations for or against it *)—purely because, at least in its current form, it lacks the general intelligibility <note>original: "Gemeinverständlichkeit." The author is emphasizing that his work is intended for a broad, educated public, not just specialized academic philosophers.</note> that is intended here. The representatives of this method, who are obligated more than anyone else to recognize the relative truth in everything, will hopefully not condemn this work because of its scientific character, especially since it should meet their tendencies in many respects through a certain positive contrast to common opponents and through its propaedeutic <note>A "propaedeutic" value refers to introductory knowledge or a preliminary branch of study that prepares a student for more advanced work.</note> value for non-philosophers. We must therefore still consider the relationship between the deductive or descending method, and the inductive or ascending method.

Man comes to science by attempting to comprehend and explain the sum of the phenomena surrounding him. These phenomena are effects, for which he wishes to know the causes. Since different causes can produce the same effect (e.g., friction, galvanic current <note>An early term for an electric current produced by chemical action.</note>, and chemical processes all produce heat), a single effect can also have various causes; the cause assumed for an effect is therefore only a hypothesis, which can by no means possess certainty, but only a probability determined by other factors.

Let the probability that U₁ is the cause of phenomenon E be = u₁, and the probability that U₂ is the cause of U₁ be = u₂, then the probability that U₂ is the more distant cause of E is = u₁ · u₂; from which one sees that at every step backward in the chain of causes, the probability coefficients of the individual causes in relation to their nearest effect multiply—that is, they become ever smaller (e.g., ⁸⁄₁₀ multiplied by itself nine times yields approximately ¹⁄₁₀). If the probability values of the causes did not grow again as one progresses, due to the fact that the causes to be assumed become fewer and fewer while more and more effects [originate] from...

*) My views on this matter have been set down in a special publication: "On the Dialectical Method" (Berlin 1868, published by C. Duncker).

<summary>The author outlines three scientific methods—dialectical, deductive, and inductive—ultimately choosing to focus on the latter two to ensure his work remains accessible. He provides a mathematical argument showing how the probability of a specific cause decreases as the chain of causality grows longer.</summary>
<keywords>methodology, Hegel, dialectics, deduction, induction, causality, probability, scientific inquiry, philosophy of science</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on scientific methodology, specifically contrasting the "ascending" (inductive) and "descending" (deductive) approaches. The author is justifying why he chooses to build his argument from observable facts upward to universal principles rather than starting with abstract ideas.</meta>

...be explained by a single cause,*) then probabilities would soon reach uselessly small values through constant multiplication. If the causes of all phenomena in the world were recognized back far enough until they were reduced to one or a few ultimate causes or principles, then science—which is one, just as the world is one—would be complete in an **inductive** <term>Inductive: A method of reasoning that moves from specific, observable observations to broader generalizations and theories.</term> manner. 

Suppose someone has solved this task in a more or less perfect form. The question then remains open whether that person, in order to communicate their conviction to others, would do better to lead them on the path from the phenomena backward and upward to the ultimate causes, or to **deduce** <term>Deductive: A "top-down" approach that starts with a general theory or principle and works down to specific conclusions or observations.</term> the world as it is for them from these principles from the top down. 

We are dealing here with a simple alternative. Even if Friedrich Schelling <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), a central figure in German Idealism. The author is referencing Schelling's later "Positive Philosophy," which attempted to move beyond pure logic to explain actual existence.</note> in his final system claims the necessity of a combination of both paths—by beginning (see *Works*, Section II, Vol. 3, p. 151, note) with a **negative philosophy** that ascends from below and ending with a **positive philosophy** that descends from above—this duality is only possible because he separates their domains. Specifically, he keeps the former in the purely logical realm; that is, he bases its inductive method only on the facts of the "inner experience of thinking" (compare *Works* II, 1, p. 321 and 326). Meanwhile, in his positive philosophy, he seeks to prove the "highest idea" gained as a result to be the "actually existing" and the "principle of all being" (compare II, 3, p. 150), by attempting to derive the facts of "outer experience" from it using a deductive method.

Even if the results of this latter deduction somehow satisfied the demands of science, such an arbitrary separation of inner and outer experience would not be scientifically justifiable. In any case, for this latter domain, our previous alternative would repeat itself: whether the ascending or descending method of presentation is to be preferred.

The decision undoubtedly falls in favor of the **ascending** or **inductive** method; because:

1) The "other person" <note>The author is referring to the reader or the student to whom the philosopher is presenting his work.</note> is still standing at the "bottom." The bottom is therefore the natural starting point for them. On the path from below to above, they always move from the known to the unknown, whereas...

*) The growth <note>original: "Das Wachsen." Referring to the mathematical accumulation of probability values.</note> occurs according to the formula developed on page 33.

And if he then arrives at the mouth of this river and finds himself in a strange land instead of his homeland, the sorcerer might even make him believe that this *is* his home—and many a person believes him for the sake of the beautiful journey. —

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of the deductive method in philosophy. On the previous page, the author argued that deduction requires a "leap of faith" and fails to convince the listener because it starts from the unknown. This page elaborates on why deductive systems are often based on "mystical" intuition rather than scientific proof.</meta>

and should use the deductive method to prove them; in fact, this never actually occurs. Rather, all philosophers who deduce their system (whether the method is clearly stated or in a veiled form) have, in fact, arrived at their principles through the only means remaining besides induction: through a leap of a mystical nature, as is discussed in Chapter B. IX. **Deduction** is then the attempt to descend from this mystically acquired result down to the reality that needs to be explained. They do so on a path that—through an impermissible analogy with the completely different science of mathematics and through the dazzling evidence of the results achieved in the latter—has always held something alluring for all systematic minds. For those philosophers, **deduction** is indeed the natural way, since "the Above" is their given starting point. 

Aside from the fact that both the deduction itself and the principles to be proven must always be deficient in the human way, and that accordingly **deduction** always leaves a wide chasm open between itself and the reality to be explained, the trouble with the matter is that **deduction**—as even Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) argued in his *Posterior Analytics* that the primary principles of a science cannot themselves be demonstrated by that science; they must be known by other means.</note> knew—cannot *prove* its own principles at all. This is because, in the best-case scenario, it only secures their possibility, but not a specific probability. Therefore, the principles may gain somewhat in *clarity* <note>original: *Verständlichkeit*, meaning the degree to which something can be grasped by the intellect.</note> through deduction, but not in *persuasive power*. Gaining a conviction of their correctness remains exclusively left to *mystical reproduction*, just as their discovery consisted of *mystical production*. 

This is the greatest drawback in philosophy, so far as it uses this method: that the conviction of the truth of its results is not communicable <note>In this context, "communicable" means the ability to transfer a logical proof from one mind to another so that both must agree on the truth.</note> like inductive scientific findings. Even the understanding of its content is, as is well known, subject to great difficulties, because it is infinitely hard to cast a <term>mystical conception: An idea or insight gained through direct intuition or "feeling" rather than through step-by-step logical reasoning.</term> into an adequate scientific form. Only too often, however, philosophers deceive both themselves and the reader regarding the mystical origin of their principles. In the absence of good evidence, they seek to give these principles a scientific grounding through subtle, sham proofs. They are blinded to the worthlessness of these proofs only by their own firm conviction in the truth of the result.

Here lies the explanation for that phenomenon where one feels—with the rare exceptions of a chance intellectual affinity—unpleasantly repelled by the reading of philosophers when looking at their proofs and deductions, but, on the contrary, highly attracted and captivated when looking at the imposing coherence of their systems, their grand worldviews, their brilliant flashes of insight that illuminate the most hidden things, their deep conceptions, their witty observations <note>original: *Aperçus*, a French term often used in German to denote a sudden, intuitive insight or a pithy observation.</note>, and their psychological sharp-sightedness. Furthermore, from the deductive method of the philosophers, it follows that individual points can only be debated insofar as they concern the consequences of principles agreed upon from the outset, and that every system stands more or less independent of the others. No such collective bond exists between them as in inductive science, where every step taken in a strictly scientific manner benefits all further steps, and even the smallest contribution is gratefully accepted as a building block for the whole. Finally, it follows from this why deductive philosophy has never yet succeeded in expanding its narrow audience to include the majority of educated people, and why it has been equally unable to fill the great chasm that ***separates*** it from the reality it seeks to explain.

That part of philosophy, however, which has adopted the inductive process, along with the natural sciences in the broadest sense of the word, has indeed provided valuable results of a subordinate kind and a foundation for successors; yet they are still a world apart from ultimate principles and a unified system of science.

Thus, a chasm yawns for both sides: induction does not reach ultimate principles and a system, while speculation does not reach an explanation of reality or communicability. One can conclude from this that the whole cannot be grasped from one side alone, but that one must grasp the matter from both sides at once, and move from both here and there toward the...

...must look around at the most projecting points where a bridge can be built. For the matter is not entirely hopeless. We have reached that point in the history of science where the first pioneers meet, like two miners in underground tunnels who hear each other knocking through the wall that still separates them. But indeed, along with these advancements, the world has also become clearer about the polar opposition between the two fields, which previously escaped our consciousness; hence, every researcher now tends to decide much more decisively for one of the two directions than was formerly the case. Therefore, what the present day chiefly lacks is a personality who grasps both sides with equal love and devotion—someone capable, if not of mystical production <note>The author uses "mystical" here to refer to the intuitive, creative leap of faith used to form philosophical systems, as discussed on the previous page.</note>, then at least of reproduction, while simultaneously mastering a precise overview of exact knowledge and the rigor of the inductive method. This person must clearly recognize the task at hand: to connect speculative principles (those acquired through intuition) with the highest results of inductive science using the inductive method itself. By doing so, they might build a generally accessible bridge to these principles and elevate these previously subjective convictions to the level of objective truth. In view of this great and timely task, I chose the motto: **“Speculative results according to the inductive natural-scientific method!”** Not as if I believed myself to possess such a comprehensive mind as is required for the solution of this task, or even believed...

### c. Predecessors in relation to the concept of the Unconscious.

How long did it take in the history of philosophy for the contrast between <term>Spirit: In this context, "Geist," referring to the mind or the non-material principle of thought.</term> and Nature, between Thinking and Being, between Subject and Object to reach clear consciousness—that contrast which now dominates our entire thinking. For the natural human being, as a creature of nature, felt body and soul within himself as one; he instinctively anticipated this identity, and his conscious intellectual work had to be far advanced before he could distance himself from this instinct enough to recognize the full scope of that opposition. In all of Greek philosophy, we nowhere find this contrast presented with full clarity, much less its significance recognized, and least of all during its classical period. If this is already true of the contrast between the Real and the Ideal, why should we wonder that the contrast between the Unconscious and the Conscious occurs even less to the natural understanding, and therefore appears even later...

<meta>This page continues the historical introduction to the concept of the Unconscious. ...comes to a breakthrough in the history of philosophy; indeed, even today, the vast majority of educated people consider one to be foolish if one speaks of unconscious thinking. For the Unconscious is so much an <term>unknown territory: original: "terra incognita"</term> to the natural consciousness that it considers the identity of having a representation and being conscious of a thing to be completely self-evident and beyond doubt. This naive standpoint is already expressed in <term>Descartes: Latin: "Cartesius"</term> (<note>original: "princ. phil. I, 9," referring to *Principles of Philosophy*, Part 1, Article 9</note>) and even more extensively in Locke: *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* <note>original: "Versuche üb. d. menschlichen Verstand"</note>, Book II, Chapter 1, Section 9: “For to have ideas and to be conscious of something is one and the same,” or Section 19: “for an extended body without parts is as conceivable as thinking without consciousness. They may, if their hypothesis requires it, say with just as much reason: Man is always hungry, but he does not always have a feeling of it. And yet hunger consists in this very feeling, just as thinking consists in the consciousness that one is thinking.” One sees that Locke postulates these sentences with utter simplicity; it is therefore quite incorrect when one still hears the claim from certain quarters today that Locke proved the possibility of unconscious representations. He only proves, from this postulated premise, that the soul can have no representation without the man being conscious of it—because otherwise the consciousness of the soul and that of the man would constitute two different persons—and that consequently the <term>Cartesians: Followers of the philosopher René Descartes</term> are wrong in their claim that the soul, as a thinking being, must think incessantly. 

Locke is therefore the first and only one who brings this implicit assumption of the natural understanding to a scientific and detailed expression; with this step, however, the knowledge of its one-sidedness and untruth, and the discovery of unconscious representations by Locke’s great opponent Leibniz, was naturally inevitable. Meanwhile, all earlier philosophers likely leaned silently more toward one side or the other, but they did not bring the problem to their consciousness at all. Leibniz was led to his discovery by the effort to save the <term>innate ideas: Concepts or knowledge present in the mind from birth, rather than learned through experience.</term> and the incessant activity of the power of representation. For if Locke had proven that the soul cannot think consciously if the man is not conscious of it, and yet it was still supposed to think constantly, then nothing remained but an unconscious thinking.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leibniz’s philosophy, specifically how his concept of the Unconscious bridges the gap between empirical experience and innate knowledge. It transitions from Leibniz’s mathematical influence to how Immanuel Kant later adopted these ideas.</meta>

— However, the weak side of Leibniz’s unconscious representation follows, which is already inherent in its common name, “*little perception*” <note>original: "petite perception"</note>. Because Leibniz introduced the concept of the (mathematically speaking) infinitely small with brilliant success in his invention of calculus <term>Infinitesimalrechnung: the mathematical study of continuous change, co-invented by Leibniz and Newton</term> and in many parts of his observation of nature—such as in mechanics (rest and motion), in the law of continuity, and so on—he also sought to conceive of these *little perceptions* in this way: as representations of such low intensity that they escape consciousness.

In doing so, he destroyed on one hand what he seemed to have built on the other: the true concept of the Unconscious as a domain opposed to consciousness, and its significance for feeling and action. For if, as Leibniz himself claims, a person’s nature, instinct, passions—in short, the most powerful influences in human life—originate from the realm of the Unconscious, how can they be caused by representations that are so weak that they escape consciousness? How could the more powerful conscious representations not prevail in the decisive moment? This, however, interests <term>Leibniz: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716)</term> less; for his main focus, innate ideas and the constant activity of the soul, his assumption of an infinitely small consciousness is indeed sufficient. Accordingly, most of his examples of *little perceptions* focus on representations with a low degree of consciousness, such as sensory perceptions during sleep. Despite all this, Leibniz retains the glory of being the first to assert the existence of representations of which we are not conscious and to have assigned them great importance.

It shows a sharp gaze that <term>Kant: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), a central figure in modern philosophy</term> was the first to seek the essence of sexual love in the Unconscious. In the essence of the concept, however, he too seems to have progressed little beyond the Leibnizian standpoint of weakened consciousness, as the phrase "obscure representation" <note>original: "dunkle Vorstellung" — Kant used this to describe mental contents that influence us without being consciously perceived</note> suggests, although he must have stood much closer to a higher conception also in this point by virtue of his entire philosophy, as is already proven by the fact that he nowhere explicitly brings forward the Leibnizian theory of infinitely small consciousness. To him also, the subject lay too far off to devote more than three pages to it, half of which do not belong to the matter. The concept of the Unconscious lay much closer to the <term>Philosophy of Faith: a movement represented by Hamann, Herder, and Jacobi that emphasized feeling and belief over pure rationalism</term> (Hamann, Herder, and Jacobi), which actually rests upon it, but is so unclear about itself and so incapable of rationally grasping its own foundation that it never manages to find the keyword of its party.

In full purity, clarity, and depth, on the other hand, we find the concept of the Unconscious in Schelling; it is therefore worth taking a side glance at the way he arrived at it. The following passage gives the best information on this (Schelling’s Works, Div. I, Vol. 10, pp. 92–93): "The opinion of this (Fichte’s) subjective idealism could not be that the I <note>original: "Ich" — in the context of German Idealism, often translated as the "Ego" or "Self," representing the active, thinking subject</note> set things outside itself freely and with volition, for all too much is the case that the I would want things quite differently if external being depended upon it . . . . Fichte showed himself unconcerned about all this . . . . Now instructed to take up philosophy where <term>Fichte: Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814)</term> had placed it, I had to see above all how that undeniable and inescapable necessity" (with which the representations of the external world confront the I), "which Fichte seeks, as it were, to scold away only with words, could be reconciled with Fichte’s concepts, thus with the asserted absolute substance of the I. Here it immediately became apparent that, while the external world is only there for me insofar as I am simultaneously there and conscious of myself (this goes without saying), conversely, just as I for...

### DISCOURSE IV.

->18<-

As <term>Fichtean Idealism: the philosophy of J.G. Fichte, which emphasizes the "I" as the source of all reality</term> receded in its own developmental history, the concept of the Unconscious met the same fate. While this concept played a leading role in <term>Transcendental Idealism: a school of thought exploring how our minds shape our experience of the world</term>, it was hardly mentioned in the writings that appeared shortly thereafter, and later it vanished almost entirely. Even the mystical natural philosophy of the <term>Schelling</term> school—which (especially <term>Schubert: Gotthilf Heinrich von Schubert (1780–1860), a physician and philosopher who explored the "night side" of natural science</term>) dealt so extensively with the realm of the Unconscious—has, to my knowledge, nowhere concerned itself with a formal development or examination of this specific concept.

In <term>Hegel: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831), whose system focused on the evolution of "Spirit" through history</term>, as in the later works of <term>Schelling</term>, the concept of the Unconscious does not emerge clearly, except in the introduction to his lectures on the "<term>Philosophy of History</term>." There, he reproduces <term>Schelling</term>’s ideas on this subject (which are to be cited in Chapter B. X.). Nevertheless, <term>Hegel</term>’s <term>Absolute Idea: the ultimate reality in Hegel’s system, representing pure thought or reason</term> has much in common with what I call the Unconscious. This is true of the Idea in its "being-in-itself" <note>original: "Ansichsein" — a state of potentiality before it becomes conscious</note> before its release into Nature, and thus before its return to itself as Spirit. In that state, where it is truth without a veil—likened to the Godhead in its eternal essence before the creation of the world and of a finite mind—it mirrors the Unconscious, even if it represents only one side of it: namely, the logical side, or the side of "presentation" <note>original: "Vorstellung" — the mental image or concept</note>. For in <term>Hegel</term>’s view, thought only attains consciousness when, through the mediation of its externalization into Nature, it has completed the journey from mere "being-in-itself" to "being-for-itself" <note>original: "Fürsichsein" — self-aware existence</note>, and has come to itself as Spirit, having become its own object. The <term>Hegel</term>ian God as a starting point is initially only "in itself" and unconscious; only God as a result is "for itself" and conscious—is Spirit. That this "attaining of being-for-itself" or "becoming an object to oneself" is truly a <term>coming-to-consciousness</term> is clearly stated by <term>Hegel</term> in his Works, Vol. XIII, pp. 33 and 46.

<term>Schopenhauer: Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), who argued that a blind, irrational "Will" is the fundamental reality of the world</term> recognizes only the "Will" as a metaphysical principle, whereas for him, "presentation" <note>original: "Vorstellung"</note> is a product of the brain in a materialistic sense. Accordingly, he cannot speak of an unconscious presentation, but only of an unconscious Will. In doing so, however, he strangely fails to notice that the unconscious Will by that very fact <note>original: "eo ipso"</note> presupposes an unconscious presentation as its own goal, object, or content. (Compare Chapter A. IV.) In any case, given the sharp psychological gift for observation he possesses, his reflections are mostly highly instructive—for example, on instinct, on sexual love, and the life of the species.

In modern natural science, the concept of the Unconscious has as yet found little entry; a laudable exception is made by the well-known physiologist <term>Carus: Carl Gustav Carus (1789–1869), a physician and painter who argued that the key to conscious life lies in the realm of the unconscious</term>, whose works *Psyche* and *Physis* essentially contain an investigation of the Unconscious in its relations to bodily and mental life. How far he has succeeded in this attempt, and how much I may have borrowed from him in my own, I leave to the judgment of the reader. However, I will add that the concept of the Unconscious is presented here in its purity, clearly set apart from any "infinitely small" consciousness. Aside from Carus, the concept of the Unconscious has also forced its way into recognition in a few specialized investigations, which have, however, rarely been extended beyond the specific field in question. Thus, for example, <term>Perty: Maximilian Perty (1804–1884), a naturalist who studied the intelligence and "soul-life" of animals</term>, in his book *On the Soul-Life of Animals* (Leipzig and Heidelberg, 1865), is led to derive instinct from unconscious factors; and likewise <term>Wundt: Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), often called the father of experimental psychology</term> (in his "Contributions to the Theory of Sensory Perception" in Henle and Pfeuffer’s *Journal of Rational Medicine*, 1858 and 59) recognizes the necessity of tracing the origin of sensory perception back to unconscious mental processes—for example, unconscious inferences—an exposition which has been approved by <term>Helmholtz: Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894), a massive figure in physics and physiology known for his work on the mathematics of the eye and ear</term>.

<term>Herbart: Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841), a philosopher who pioneered the use of mathematics in psychology</term> understands by "unconscious representations" those "which are in **consciousness** without one being conscious of them" (*Works*, Vol. V, p. 342), that is, without one "observing them as one's own and linking them to the 'I'," or in other words, without connecting them with **self-consciousness**. This concept offers no danger of confusion with the truly Unconscious; on the other hand, for the sake of the applications made by <term>Fechner: Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801–1887), the founder of psychophysics, who studied the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations</term>, another concept treated by Herbart must be taken into account: namely, that of "representations below the threshold of consciousness." These represent only a striving toward a representation—a striving more or less distant from being realized—but are themselves "by no means an actual representing"; rather, for consciousness, they do not even mean nothing, but "an impossible magnitude" (Herbart’s *Works*, Vol. V, pp. 339–342). Herbart arrives at this difficult-to-grasp concept because, following the way of thinking of <term>Leibniz: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), who first proposed that the mind is full of "tiny perceptions" of which we are unaware</term>, he assumes a continuity of increase and decrease in the transition from actual representations of consciousness to those that are in the mi-

...slumber in memory, and conversely, to hold fast, also did not want to give up the possibility of an interaction between these slumbering <term>memory-ideas: *Gedächtnissvorstellungen*; the mental representations or images stored in one's memory</term>; notwithstanding this, however, he could not bring himself to a materialistic way of explaining these processes, in such a way that he would have seen in them only material brain processes of a strength insufficient for the stirring of consciousness. Now, however, from the current standpoint of science, it is easy to see that the so-called slumbering memory-ideas are by no means ideas **in action** <note>original Latin: *in actu*</note>, in activity, but merely **dispositions** of the brain for the easier emergence of these ideas. Just as a string resonates to the note A or C, depending on whether it is tuned to A or C, so too one idea or another arises more easily in the brain, depending on whether the distribution and tension of the brain molecules is such that it responds more easily to one or the other kind of vibrations upon a corresponding stimulus. What tuning is for the string, for the brain is the lasting change which a vivid idea leaves behind in the distribution and tension of the molecules after its disappearance. But that every idea really fades away completely in a finite and indeed rather short time is already evident **from the outset** <note>original Latin: *a priori*; referring to knowledge that is independent of experience or purely theoretical.</note>, since only a movement which meets no resistance can continue indefinitely, but in the brain the resistances that oppose every movement are very strong. Accordingly, <term>Herbart’s: Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841), a philosopher and educator who attempted to apply mathematics to the study of the mind</term> unconscious state of an idea can only remain within the limits given, on the one hand, by the cessation of movement, and on the other, by the cessation of the conscious idea while the movement of brain vibrations still continues—provided that both limits do not coincide. The question is therefore:

1) whether every intensity of brain vibrations awakens an idea, or whether the idea only begins at a certain intensity of the same, and
2) whether a conscious idea is excited by every intensity of brain vibrations, or only from a certain intensity onwards.

...sounding bell is only heard from a certain distance. If several similar stimuli, which are individually unperceivable, are added together, conscious sensations arise; for example, through several distant bells ringing at the same time, each of which would not be heard individually, or the rustling of leaves in a forest. Now, one could certainly explain this by saying that a stimulus below the <term>threshold: *Schwelle*; the boundary between unconscious and conscious perception</term> fails to cause a sensation only because it is not strong enough to overcome the resistance to conduction in the sense organ and nerves up to the <term>central organ: *Centralorgan*; in 19th-century physiology, this refers to the brain or spinal cord where sensory information is processed</term>, but that the soul reacts with a corresponding sensation to even the smallest stimulus that reaches the center itself. 

This assumption alone is not sufficient, however, because it does not apply to differences in sensation. For stimuli of different strengths of the same type cause different sensations; yet even here, the difference between the stimuli must exceed a certain measure (the <term>difference threshold: *Unterschiedsreizschwelle*; the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected by a person</term>) if the sensations are to be perceived as distinct. Here, the resistance to conduction cannot obviously be held responsible for the phenomenon, since each of the sensations is already large enough to overcome them. On the other hand, different principles cannot be applied to the stimulus threshold and the difference threshold, since the first case can be reduced to the second case if, in the latter, one stimulus is set to zero. Consequently, the only remaining assumption is that the vibrations at the center must exceed a certain degree before the sensation occurs. 

What applies here to sensory perception applies, of course, to every other <term>mental representation: *Vorstellung*; any idea, image, or concept present in the mind</term>, and thus the second question is decided. It remains to be determined whether stimuli below the threshold cause the soul to react at all—which would then be an unconscious sensation or idea—or whether the soul’s reaction only begins at the threshold.

Let us listen further to <term>Fechner: Gustav Fechner (1801–1887), a founder of psychophysics who sought to mathematically link the physical and mental worlds</term>. The so-called <term>Weber’s Law: named after Ernst Heinrich Weber, a principle describing how we perceive changes in stimulus intensity</term> states: “Two similar differences in sensation are proportional to the two quotients of the corresponding stimuli,” and the formula most ingeniously derived from this by Fechner is:
γ = k log β/b

It is intended to mean that the sensation *γ* removes itself further from reality the further *γ* sinks below 0; that is, an ever-greater increase of the stimulus is required just to bring the value of *γ* back to zero and recall it to the threshold of reality. The negative sign before *γ* thus signifies here (as the "imaginary" often does elsewhere in mathematics) the unsolvability of the task of calculating a sensation from the given stimulus size.

Regarding the physical meaning of the negative sign, Fechner very rightly says that only a reasonable comparison of the calculation's starting point with the facts of experience can provide an explanation. III.; then these reactions can no longer remain unconscious. If one were to return here to the theory of "infinitely small consciousness," it is simply refuted by experiment, which shows that conscious sensation steadily decreases until it reaches a <term>zero value</term>, which corresponds to the <term>stimulus threshold</term>. Thus, the sensation actually passes through those infinitely small values *above* the threshold (where an infinitely small consciousness truly still exists), but becomes zero—that is, ceases absolutely—at the threshold itself. I refer the reader to <term>Fechner</term>'s work on this matter.

# II.
## How Do We Arrive at the Assumption of Purposes in Nature?

One of the most important and well-known forms of expression of the **Unconscious** is **instinct**, and this rests upon the **concept of purpose** <note>original: *Zweckbegriff*; the idea that things in nature happen for a specific reason or goal, often called teleology.</note>; therefore, an investigation of the latter is unavoidable for our task. Since this investigation does not fit well into Section A, I have placed it here in the introduction. To be sure, the following treatment of the subject will easily face the reproach of dryness, and anyone who shrinks from wading through investigations of probability <note>The author intends to use mathematical probability to prove that the complex designs of nature cannot be accidental.</note> may—if they are already convinced of the justification for assuming purposes in nature—leave this chapter unread. Yet I must add that the manner in which this highly important question is brought to a hypothetical decision here is, to my knowledge, both new and the only one possible.

In the work of many great thinkers, the **concept of purpose** has played a highly important role and formed the basis of a large part of their systems—for example, in **Aristotle** and **Leibniz**. **Kant** <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804). The author refers to Kant's view that "purpose" is a subjective lens through which humans view nature, rather than a proven objective fact of the world itself.</note> naturally had to deny its reality outside of conscious thought, since he did not grant it for time (cf. **Trendelenburg**: *Logical Investigations* Cap. VIII. 5); modern **materialism** likewise denies it, because it denies the existence of **Mind** <note>original: *Geist*; in this context, it refers to a non-physical intelligence or spirit.</note> outside of the animal brain. In modern natural science, the **concept of purpose** has rightly fallen into discredit through **Bacon** <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), an early advocate for the scientific method, who argued that looking for "purposes" in physics distracted scientists from finding the actual physical causes of things.</note>, because it has so often served as a convenient means for "lazy reason" to spare itself the search for efficient causes <note>The mechanical "how" behind an event, as opposed to the "why" or purpose.</note>, and in that part of natural science concerned purely with **matter**, **purpose**, as a spiritual cause,

He acknowledges that while many modern scientists and philosophers like Bacon or Kant are skeptical of "purpose," he will offer a new proof based on probability.</summary>
<keywords>teleology, instinct, the Unconscious, efficient causes, probability, Aristotle, Leibniz, Kant, Francis Bacon, materialism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on teleology (the study of purpose in nature) by contrasting philosophical views on whether "purpose" is a real force or a human illusion, and then provides a psychological definition of how we experience purposeful action ourselves.</meta>

must remain excluded; **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher who believed everything happens by necessity from the nature of God/Substance, leaving no room for "purpose" or "goals" in the traditional sense.</note> denied purpose completely because it could not be derived from his concept of Substance. If, however, on one hand a spirit as great and honest as Spinoza is able to deny purpose in the face of the facts, while on the other hand purpose plays such a large role for others—and even the free-thinker **Voltaire** <note>François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778). Despite his skepticism toward religion, Voltaire argued that the complexity of nature (like the eye) proved the existence of a "Great Designer."</note> does not dare to deny purposes in nature, however inconvenient and incompatible they may be with his other convictions—then there must be something quite peculiar about the matter.

The concept of **purpose** <note>original: *Zweck*</note> is formed primarily from the experiences one makes in one's own conscious mental activity. A purpose, for me, is a future event that I have imagined and willed, the realization of which I am able to bring about not directly, but only through causal intermediate steps (the **means** <note>original: *Mittel*</note>). If I do not imagine the future event, then for me it does not currently exist; if I do not will it, I do not "purpose" it—instead, it is indifferent or even repugnant to me. If I can realize it directly, the causal intermediate step (the means) disappears, and with it the concept of "purpose" vanishes, as it only exists in relation to the concept of "means," for the action then follows immediately upon the will.

By realizing that I am unable to fulfill my will directly, and by recognizing the "means" as the **efficient cause** <note>original: *wirkende Ursache*; the physical force or action that brings something about, as opposed to the "final cause" or goal.</note> of the purpose, the *willing of the purpose* becomes the **motive**—that is, the efficient cause for the *willing of the means*. This willing, in turn, becomes the efficient cause for the realization of the means through my action, and the realized means becomes the efficient cause of the realization of the purpose. Thus, we have a threefold causality among four members: 

1. Willing the purpose 
2. Willing the means 
3. Realization of the means 
4. Realization of the purpose. 

Only in rare cases does all of this remain in the purely subjective, mental realm—for example, when composing a poem in one's head, the mental elaboration of some other artistic conception, or other "head-work." Most of the time, however, we find three of the four types of causality represented directly: namely, causality between mental and mental processes (willing the purpose → willing the means), mental and material processes (willing → realization of the means), and between material and material processes (means → purpose). Also

the fourth type of causality—the interaction between material and mental processes—frequently occurs here; however, it lies prior to the start of our analysis, within the motivation of the will toward a purpose through sensory impressions. From this, one can see that the connection between a willed purpose and a realized purpose (or **finality** <note>The principle that an end goal or "final cause" directs a process.</note>) is by no means something that exists alongside or even in spite of **causality** <note>The relationship between cause and effect.</note>. Rather, it is merely a specific combination of the various types of causality, such that the starting point and the end point are the same—the only difference being that one is "ideal" (mental) and the other is "real" (physical); the former exists as a willed mental representation, the latter in reality.

Far from destroying the universal, exceptionless nature of the law of causality, finality actually presupposes it. This applies not only to how matter affects matter, but also to the interaction between mind and matter, and mind and mind. It follows from this that finality negates "freedom" in any individual, empirical mental act, and instead places even the mind under the necessity of the law of causality. This should be the first point of agreement with those who oppose the concept of finality.

Now, let us assume that **M** <note>Standing for the "Means" or intermediate step.</note> has been observed as the efficient cause of **Z** <note>Standing for the "Ziel" or goal/result.</note>, and that all material circumstances prevailing at the moment **M** occurs are established as **n. n.** <note>Likely an abbreviation for "noted" or "given" conditions.</note>. Furthermore, let the premise stand that **M** must have a sufficient efficient cause. In this case, three scenarios are possible: either the sufficient cause of **M** is contained within the material circumstances **n. n.**; or it is completed by other material circumstances that escaped observation; or, finally, the sufficient cause of **M** cannot be found in the material realm at all and must therefore be sought in the mental realm. The second case contradicts our assumption that all material circumstances immediately preceding the emergence of **M** are already contained in **n. n.** 

Even if this condition is strictly speaking impossible to fulfill—since it would technically involve the state of the entire world-system—it is nevertheless easy to see that cases are very rare where essential conditions for a process lie outside of a narrow local circle. All insignificant circumstances do not need to be considered. For example, no one will look for the essential reasons why a **spider** spins its web outside of the spider itself—on the **moon**, for instance. Here, an almost infinite number of causes work together to ensure this total effect—the existence of organisms. Insofar as these causes lie within the organisms themselves, they divide into those that bring about the preservation of the individual and those that bring about the preservation of the species. 

These two points, as well, have rarely been misidentified as natural purposes. If we now call such a purpose, recognized with the greatest possible certainty, **Z** <note>original: "Zweck" (Purpose/Goal)</note>, then we know that none of its many causes may be missing if it is to be achieved—including, for example, **M** <note>original: "Mittel" (Means)</note>. Since I now know that **Z** and **M** were both willed and represented <note>In 19th-century psychology, "represented" (vorgestellt) means to have a mental idea or image of something before it physically exists.</note> prior to their real existence, and I see that for the realization of **M**, among other things, the external cause **M₁** is required, the assumption that **M₁** was also willed and represented before its real existence gains a certain probability through this inference. 

For whether **M** is realized through the direct influence of a spiritual cause <note>The term "spiritual cause" (geistige Ursache) refers to a conscious or intelligent force, as opposed to a blind mechanical force.</note>, or indirectly, by following from material causes of which some or several are spiritually caused—in both cases **M₁** can be willed and represented as a means for the purpose **M** before its real existence. In the latter case, this is immediately clear; but even in the former case, the direct influence of a spiritual cause in the realization of **M** does not exclude the possibility that the material causes of **M**—and thus also **M₁**—have again, to a greater or lesser extent, originated from spiritual causes that aimed at **M** and **Z**; this is even in the organic

### I.

# **The Unconscious Will in the Independent Functions of the Spinal Cord and Ganglia.**

---

The time is past when people contrasted free humans with animals as if the latter were merely walking machines—automata without souls. A closer examination of animal life, along with the earnest effort to understand their communication and the motives behind their actions, has shown that humans differ from the higher animals (just as animals differ from one another) only in degree, and not in the essential nature of their mental capabilities. It has shown that, by virtue of this higher capability, humanity has created a more perfect language, and through this, has acquired a "perfectibility" <note>This refers to the Enlightenment-era concept of *Perfectibilität*—the capacity of a species to improve itself over generations through culture and education.</note> across generations; something animals lack precisely because they lack such advanced means of communication. 

We know now, therefore, that we cannot compare the educated person of today with animals without being unfair to the animals. Instead, we should only compare them to those peoples who have moved little from the state in which they were first released from the hand of nature. For we know that even our own race—now privileged through higher predispositions—was once what those peoples still are today. We know that our current higher cerebral and mental faculties have only gradually reached this height through the law of inheritance, including the inheritance of acquired traits. <note>The author is writing in a pre-Darwinian or early Darwinian context where the "inheritance of acquired characteristics" (Lamarckism) was a common explanation for how species evolved their mental capacities over time.</note> 

Thus, the animal kingdom stands before us as a unified series of stages, characterized by a continuous analogy. The fundamental mental powers must be essentially the same in all beings; what appears in higher beings as "newly added" powers are merely secondary faculties that develop in certain directions through the higher refinement of common fundamental abilities. These fundamental or primal activities of the spirit in all...

Essences consist of <term>willing</term> <note>German: *Wollen*. In this chapter, we speak only of the will. It is the same thing that we find in our own consciousness as the immediate cause of our actions and call "will." That this very same thing lives in the consciousness of animals as the causal driver of their actions, and must also be called "will" here, is hardly a matter of doubt—unless one wishes to be so pretentious as to use different names for the same thing in animals (such as "gorging," "swilling," and "dropping young" <note>The author is highlighting a quirk of the German language where specific verbs are used for animals (*fressen*, *saufen*, *werfen*) versus humans (*essen*, *trinken*, *gebären*). The dog does not want to be separated from his master; he wants to save the child who has fallen into the water from a death he knows all too well; the bird does not want to let its young be harmed; the male does not want to share possession of his female with another, and so on.

I am well aware that there are many who believe they are elevating humanity by explaining as much as possible in animals—especially the lower ones—as a mere <term>reflex action</term> <note>A "reflex action" was understood then, as now, as a purely mechanical response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought.</note>. If these people have in mind the usual physiological scope of the term "reflex action" as an involuntary reaction to an external stimulus, then one could say they must never have observed animals, or they must be blind while their eyes are wide open. If, however, they extend the concept of reflex action beyond its usual physiological meaning to its true underlying concept, then they are indeed right; but they merely forget two things: first, that man also lives and moves in nothing but reflex actions, and that every act of will is a reflex action; and second, that every reflex action is itself an act of will, as will be shown in Chapter V.

Let us, therefore, provisionally retain the usual, narrower meaning of "reflex" and speak only of those acts of will which are *not* reflexes in this sense—that is, not involuntary reactions of the organism to external stimuli. There are two main characteristics by which one can distinguish the will from reflex actions: first, the presence of **affect**, and second, the **consistency** in carrying out a purpose. Reflexes take place mechanically and without emotion, but it does not require much study of <term>physiognomy</term> <note>Physiognomy was the 19th-century practice of reading an individual's character or internal emotional state through their outward physical features, especially the face.</note> to clearly perceive the presence of affects even in lower animals. ...while here the **worm** <note>Referring to "vermicular" or worm-like movement (peristalsis) in the intestines.</note> is fixed, and the (inner) base, the food masses, and the feces are pushed along—should one of these be called "will" and the other not? — **Muscle tone** (tonus) is a gentle **muscle contraction** that occurs incessantly during life in all muscles, even during sleep and unconsciousness. The frogs with a spared medulla oblongata still ate and digested their earthworms after twenty-six days, while the **secretion of urine** also proceeded regularly.

The **spinal cord** (including the **medulla oblongata**) presides over—in addition to the already mentioned **tone** of the voluntary muscles—all **involuntary movements** of the voluntary muscles (**reflex movements**, see Chapter V) and the **breathing movements**.

If pushed, she continued to walk straight ahead; if thrown into the air, she flew. She did not eat on her own, but only swallowed food pushed into her palate. Rabbits and guinea pigs, from which the cerebrum has been removed, run around freely after the operation; the behavior of a decapitated frog was already mentioned above. All these movements, such as the shaking and preening of the hen, or the running around of the rabbits and frogs, occur without noticeable external stimulus, and are so completely identical to the same movements in healthy animals that it is impossible to assume a difference in the underlying principle in both cases; here, just as there, it is an **expression of will**. Now we know, however, that higher animal consciousness is dependent on the integrity of the **cerebrum** (see Chapter C. II.), and since this is destroyed, those animals are, as they say, without consciousness—acting unconsciously and willing unconsciously. However, brain-consciousness is by no means the only consciousness in the animal, but only the highest, and the only one that reaches **self-consciousness**, the ***I***, in higher animals and humans; therefore, it is also the only one which I can call *my consciousness*.

— But that the subordinate **nerve centers** must also have a consciousness, even if of lesser clarity, follows simply from a comparison of the gradually descending animal series and the **ganglion-consciousness** of invertebrate animals with the independent ganglia and **spinal cord centers** of higher animals.

It seems necessary to add a remark here at the conclusion regarding the meaning in which the word "will" is understood here. We began by understanding this word as a "conscious intention," which is the sense in which it is commonly understood. However, in the course of our observation, we have found that within a single individual, but in different nerve centers, consciousnesses can exist that are more or less independent of one another, and **wills** can exist that are more or less independent of one another, each of which can, at most, be conscious for the nerve center through which it expresses itself. With this, the common, restricted meaning of "will" has been overturned; for I must now acknowledge a will in me other than that which has passed through my brain and thereby become conscious to me. Once this barrier of meaning has fallen, we cannot help but grasp the **will** henceforth as the **immanent cause** <note>An "immanent cause" (original: *immanente Ursache*) is a cause that originates and remains within the acting subject, rather than being triggered by an outside force.</note> of every movement in animals that is not produced by reflex. This may also be the only characteristic and infallible mark for the will conscious to us: that it is the **cause of the represented action** <note>That is, the cause of an action that the mind has first "represented" or pictured to itself.</note>. One sees now that it is something **incidental** for the will whether it passes through the brain-consciousness or not; its essence remains unchanged. What is designated here by the word "will" is nothing but the principle that is essentially the same in both cases. ## II.

## The Unconscious Idea in the Execution of Voluntary Movement.

I want to lift my little finger, and the lifting of it occurs. Does my **will** move the finger directly? No; for if the nerve in the arm is severed, the will can no longer move it. Experience teaches us that for every movement there is only one single location—namely, the central ending of the relevant **nerve fibers**—which is capable of receiving the **will-impulse** for a specific movement of a specific limb and bringing it to execution. If this single location is damaged, the will is just as powerless over the limb as if the nerve conduction from this point to the relevant muscles were interrupted. 

We cannot reasonably imagine the movement impulse itself—aside from its intensity—to be different for various nerves being stimulated. Since the excitation in all **motor nerves** is to be viewed as identical in nature, so too is the excitation at the center from which the current originates. Consequently, movements differ only because the central endings of different motor fibers are struck by the will-impulse, thereby forcing different muscle groups into **contraction**. We can thus think of the central ending points of the motor nerve fibers as a kind of **keyboard in the brain** <note>original: *Claviatur im Gehirn*; Hartmann uses this metaphor to explain how the mind "plays" the body like a musical instrument.</note>; the "keystroke" is, aside from its strength, always the same—only the keys being struck are different. 

Therefore, when I intend a very specific movement—for example, the lifting of the little finger—the key factor is that I compel those muscles to contract which, in their combined activity, [produce] this movement...

<sig>v. Hartmann, *Philosophy of the Unconscious*, p. 4</sig>

He posits that since all nerve impulses are essentially the same, the variety of our movements depends entirely on which specific nerve centers the will targets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the "keyboard of the brain." Hartmann is explaining why a conscious intention to move a limb cannot directly trigger the correct nerves without some form of unconscious mediation.</meta>

to produce, and that for this purpose I strike that **chord** on the **keyboard of the brain** with the will, whose individual keys set the relevant muscles in motion. If one or more wrong keys are struck in the chord, a movement arises that does not correspond to the intended one—for example, in slips of the tongue <note>original: *Versprechen*</note>, slips of the pen <note>original: *Verschreiben*</note>, missteps, the clumsy grasping of children, and so on. To be sure, the number of **central fiber endings** in the brain is significantly smaller than the number of **motor fibers** in the nerves, because through unique mechanisms to be discussed in Chapter V, care is taken for the simultaneous excitation of many **peripheral fibers** by ***one central fiber***; nevertheless, the number of different movements subject to the conscious will—and thus to be directed by the brain—is already large enough for each individual limb through thousands of small modifications of direction and combination, and for the whole body, it is virtually immeasurable. Thus, the probability would be infinitely small that the conscious idea of lifting the little finger would coincide with the actual lifting without ***causal mediation***.

Clearly, the purely mental idea of lifting the little finger cannot act directly on the central nerve endings, since the two have absolutely nothing to do with one another; the mere ***will*** as a ***movement impulse*** <note>term: *Bewegungsimpuls*; the initial spark of energy required to start a physical action.</note>, however, would be absolutely blind, and would therefore have to leave hitting the correct keys to ***pure chance***. If there were no ***causal connection*** at all, then ***practice*** <note>term: *Uebung*; the process of repeating an action to gain proficiency, which Hartmann argues requires an underlying mechanism to "learn" from.</note> could not do the slightest thing to help; for no one finds an idea or a feeling of this infinite quantity of central endings in their consciousness. Therefore, if by chance the conscious idea of finger-lifting had coincided once or twice with the executed movement, no point of reference for human experience would result from this; and the third time he wants to lift the finger, the ***striking*** of the correct keys would remain just as much left to ***chance*** as in the earlier cases.

One sees, therefore, that ***practice*** can only do something for the linking of ***intention*** and ***execution*** if a ***causal mediation*** between the two is present, through which the transition from one link to the other is facilitated by the repetition of the process. It remains our task, therefore, to find this ***causal mediation***; without this—

Furthermore, the fact that the idea of the intended movement can very well exist without the movement occurring speaks against this; an error in movement would then be even more incomprehensible, as would the influence that practice should be able to exert on such a mechanical arrangement.

# III.

## The Unconscious in Instinct.

---

**Instinct** is purposive action <note>original: *zweckmässiges Handeln*; behavior directed toward a specific goal or "end," even if the actor isn't aware of it.</note> without consciousness of the purpose. — A purposive action with consciousness of the purpose, where the action is thus a result of reflection, no one would call instinct; just as little would one call a purposeless, blind action instinct, such as the outbursts of rage in mad animals or those provoked to fury. — I do not believe that the definition placed at the head of this discussion should meet with challenges from those who assume the existence of instinct at all; however, whoever believes they can trace all so-called instinctive actions of animals back to conscious reflection effectively denies every instinct, and must consequently strike the word "instinct" from the dictionary. More on this later.

Let us first assume the existence of instinctive actions in the sense of our definition; they might then be explained as: 1) a mere consequence of physical organization, 2) a brain- or **mental mechanism** <term>mental mechanism: *Geistesmechanismus*; the idea that the mind has "pre-programmed" software that runs automatically without active thought.</term> established by nature, or 3) a consequence of **unconscious mental activity**. In the first two cases, the idea of the purpose lies far in the past <note>That is, the "purpose" was decided by evolution or a creator when the body or mind was first designed, not by the individual performing the act.</note>; in the last, it lies immediately before the action. In the first two, an arrangement given once and for all is used as a means, and the purpose is thought of only once during the creation of this arrangement; in the last, the purpose is thought of in every individual case. Let us consider the three cases in order.

Instinct is not a mere consequence of physical organization, for a) instincts are entirely different despite identical physical makeup. All spiders have the— <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with a comparison of different web-building techniques among similar spider species.</note>

One must acknowledge from this that instinct is to a high degree independent of physical organization <note>In 19th-century philosophy, "organization" refers to the biological structure or "hardware" of a living being.</note>. That a certain measure of physical organization is an indispensable condition <note>original: *conditio sine qua non*</note> for the execution [of an act] goes without saying; for example, without sex organs, no mating is possible; without certain skilled organs, no artful construction; without silk glands, no spinning. Nevertheless, one cannot say that instinct is a result of organization. The mere presence of an organ does not yet provide the slightest motive for exercising a corresponding activity; at the very least, a feeling of well-being <note>original: *Wohlgefühl*</note> in the use of the organ must be added; only this can then act as a motive for activity. But even when this feeling of well-being provides the impulse for activity, the organization only determines the **that**, not the **how** of this activity; however, it is precisely the **how** of the activity that contains the problem to be solved. No one would call it instinct if the spider allowed the fluid to run out of its overfilled silk gland simply to provide itself with the pleasant feeling of relief, or if the fish, for the same reason, simply discharged its seed into the water; instinct and the miraculous only begin when the spider spins threads, and from those threads a web, and when the fish discharges its seed only over the eggs of its own species. Finally, the feeling of well-being in the use of organs is a completely insufficient motive for the activity itself; for that is precisely the greatness and awe-inspiring nature of instinct: that its commands are fulfilled with the disregard of all personal well-being, indeed with the sacrifice of life itself. If the mere feeling of well-being from emptying the silk gland were the motive for why the caterpillar spins at all, it would only spin until its gland reservoir was empty, but it would not repair the repeatedly destroyed web over and over again until it dies of exhaustion. It is the same with all other instincts that are apparently motivated by one’s own well-being; as soon as circumstances are arranged such that individual sacrifice takes the place of individual welfare, their higher origin <note>The author implies that instincts come from a source beyond mere mechanical biology, likely the "Unconscious."</note> reveals itself unmistakably.
