For the sexual drive persists; as soon as an egg is removed from the nest, they mate anew and the female adds an egg, or, if they belong to the cleverer birds, they abandon the nest and start a new brood. A female <term>wryneck (*Jynx torquilla*)<note>The OCR reads "ignex torquilla," a misspelling of the scientific name for the wryneck, a type of woodpecker.</note></term>, from which the newly laid egg was repeatedly removed from the nest, continued to lay an egg after mating again and again; these eggs became progressively smaller until she was found dead on the nest at the twenty-ninth egg. If an instinct cannot withstand the test of a demanded sacrifice of individual well-being—if it truly arises merely from the pursuit of physical pleasure—then it is not an instinct and can only be mistakenly regarded as such.

**Instinct is not a brain or mental mechanism implanted by nature**, such that the instinctive action would be performed mechanically without the individual's own (albeit unconscious) individual mental activity and without a representation of the purpose of the action. If it were a mere mechanism, the purpose would have been thought out once and for all by nature or a providence, which had then so psychologically organized the individual that it merely carried out the means like a machine. 

We are dealing here, then, with a psychic organization as the cause of instinct, just as we previously dealt with a physical one. This explanation would be conceivable if every instinct belonging to an animal functioned incessantly; but none do. Instead, each waits until a motive approaches perception, which signifies to us that the appropriate external circumstances have arisen which make achieving the purpose through this means—which the instinct desires—possible at this very moment. Only then does the instinct function as an **actualized will** <note>original: *actueller Wille*—in this philosophical context, it refers to a potential drive being put into active motion.</note>, which the action follows immediately; until the motive appears, the instinct remains, as it were, latent and does not function. The motive appears in the mind in the form of a sensory representation, and there is a constant connection between the functioning instinct and all sensory representations which indicate that the opportunity to achieve the purpose of the instinct has arrived. The "psychic mechanism" would therefore be found in this constant connection. Here again, one might imagine something like a **keyboard** <note>original: *Claviatur*</note>; the keys struck are the motives, and the sounding notes are the functioning instincts.

<meta>This page continues the argument against the "mechanical" view of instinct. The author argues that because animals adapt their behavior to achieve a goal (like a bird brooding less in a greenhouse), instinct must involve an unconscious "representation of purpose" rather than a rigid, pre-programmed machine.</meta>

One could perhaps even tolerate this idea, even if the oddity occurs where completely different keys produce the same tone—if only instincts were truly comparable to **specific** tones, i.e., if one and the same instinct always functioned in exactly the same way in response to its associated motives. However, this is simply not the case; instead, it is only the unconscious purpose of the instinct that remains constant. The instinct itself, as the will toward a specific means, varies just as the most practical means to be applied varies according to external circumstances. 

With this, judgment is passed on the assumption that rejects the unconscious representation of purpose in every individual case. For if one still wished to hold fast to the idea of a mental mechanism, then for every variation and modification of the instinct according to external circumstances, a special constant device—a new key with a tone of a different timbre—would have to be inserted, causing the mechanism to fall into an utterly infinite complexity. But the fact that the purpose remains constant despite all variation in the means chosen by instinct should be a sufficiently clear hint that such an infinite complexity of the mind is not needed at all; instead, one simply needs to assume the unconscious representation of purpose. 

For example, the constant purpose for a bird that has laid eggs is to bring the chicks to maturity. If the external temperature is insufficient for this, the bird broods over them; only in the warmest regions of the world does brooding cease, because the animal sees the instinctive purpose fulfilled without its intervention. In warm countries, many birds brood only at night. Even when small birds happen to nest in warm greenhouses here at home, they sit on the eggs little or not at all. How repulsive is the assumption of a mechanism here, which forces the bird to brood as soon as the temperature drops below a certain degree! How simple and clear is the assumption of an unconscious purpose, which is necessary for the willing of the appropriate means—though of this process, only the final link, the will immediately preceding the action, enters into consciousness. 

In southern Africa, the sparrow fences its nest with thorns for protection against snakes and monkeys. The eggs laid by the cuckoo always resemble the eggs in the nest where it lays them in size, color, and pattern; for example, in the case of the <term>*sylvia*<note>original: *sylvia*. This refers to the genus of Old World warblers.</note></term>

In contrast, it is precisely characteristic of instinctive actions that they are carried out just as perfectly by animals raised in isolation as by those who have enjoyed the instruction of their parents, and that the first attempt, prior to any experience or practice, succeeds just as well as subsequent ones. Here, too, the difference in the underlying principle is unmistakable. 

Next, experience teaches that the more narrow and weak an intellect is, the more slowly ideas succeed one another within it; that is, the slower and more ponderous its conscious thinking becomes. This is confirmed both in humans of varying intellectual capacity and in animals, insofar as instinct does not come into play. Instinct, however, has the peculiar quality that it never hesitates or wavers, but occurs instantaneously as soon as the motive for its action enters consciousness. This rapidity of decision in instinctive actions is the same in the lowest and the highest animal; this circumstance also points to a difference of principle between instinct and conscious reflection.

<meta>This page continues Eduard von Hartmann's exploration of "unconscious knowledge" in the animal kingdom. The flight of young pigeons is shy and they scatter when a bird of prey approaches, even without an older leader; oxen and horses coming from regions where there are no lions become restless and anxious in the night as soon as they scent one sneaking near; a young chimpanzee, as the explorer Grant observed, fell into the highest state of terror at the first sight of a giant snake; and even among us humans, it is not so rare for a "Gretchen" to instinctively sense a "Mephistopheles." <note>A reference to Goethe’s *Faust*, in which the innocent character Gretchen instinctively feels a profound, inexplicable dread in the presence of the devilish Mephistopheles, despite his civilized disguise.</note> It is very remarkable that an insect, the *Bembix* <note>original: Bombex; likely referring to the sand wasp</note>, attacks and kills another, the *Parnopes* <note>original: Parnope; a genus of cuckoo wasp</note>, wherever it finds it, without making any use of the carcass; yet we know that the latter preys upon the eggs of the former and is thus the natural enemy of its species. 

The phenomenon known to herders of cattle and sheep as the "gadding of livestock" <term>das Biesen des Viehes; a state of frantic running or agitation in herds caused by the presence of parasitic flies</term> also provides evidence. When a botfly or gadfly <term>Dassel- oder Biesfliege; parasitic flies of the family Oestridae</term> approaches a herd, the animals become quite wild and run about as if mad, because the larvae that hatch from the eggs laid on their fur later burrow into their skin and cause painful inflammation. Since the fly looks very similar to other horseflies, and the painful consequences only occur much later, one cannot assume the animal has made a conscious deduction regarding the connection. The caution shown by ferrets and buzzards toward adders has already been mentioned; similarly, it was observed that a young honey buzzard <term>Wespenbussard; *Pernis apivorus*, a bird of prey that feeds on the larvae of social insects</term>, when presented with its first wasp, only consumed it after it had squeezed the stinger out of its body.

No animal whose instinct has not been deadened by unnatural habit eats poisonous plants; even an ape pampered by living among humans can still be reliably used in the primeval forests as a "taster" of fruits, where he rejects the poisonous ones offered to him with loud cries. Every animal selects precisely those plant or animal substances for its food which correspond to its digestive system, without receiving any instruction on the matter, and even without previously making use of its organ of taste. While one must certainly assume that smell, and not sight, is the determining factor for distinguishing substances, it is nonetheless just as mysterious how the animal recognizes what suits its digestion through a scent impression as it would through a visual impression. <meta>This page continues Eduard von Hartmann’s discussion of innate animal instincts, moving from the recognition of predators to the unconscious knowledge of diet, medicine, and navigation. The *hawfinch* splits the cherry pit by turning it so that the beak meets the seam, and does this with its first cherry pit in life just as it does with its last; *polecats*, *martens*, and *weasels* make small holes on the opposite sides of the egg to be sucked out, so that the air can flow in while they suck. Animals do not merely know their appropriate food; they also frequently seek out appropriate remedies with correct *self-diagnosis* and unacquired *therapeutic knowledge*. Thus, dogs often eat a great deal of grass, especially that of *couch grass* <term>Quecken; a common weed (Elymus repens) often consumed by domestic animals for its medicinal properties</term>, when they are unwell—among other things, according to *Lenz* <note>Harald Othmar Lenz (1798–1870), a German naturalist and pioneer in the history of biology.</note>, when they have worms, which are then supposed to be passed while wrapped in the undigested grass, or when they want to remove bone shards from the stomach. As a laxative, they use *prickly herbs*. Chickens and pigeons peck lime from walls and roofs when their food does not offer enough lime for the formation of eggshells. Small children eat chalk when they have stomach acid, and pieces of coal when they suffer from flatulence. We also find these particular *nutritional instincts* or *medicinal instincts* in adult humans under circumstances where unconscious nature gains power—for example, in pregnant women, whose capricious appetites presumably appear when a particular condition of the fetus makes a peculiar blood composition desirable. *Field mice* bite the sprouts off the gathered grains so that they do not grow during the winter. A few days before the onset of cold, the *squirrel* gathers most diligently and then seals its dwelling. *Migratory birds* depart our regions for warmer countries at times when they still have no lack of food here, and at a significantly higher temperature than that at which they return; the same applies to the time when animals enter their winter quarters, which *beetles* often do precisely on the warmest autumn days. When swallows and storks find their home again from hundreds of miles away, even with the completely changed appearance of the landscapes, this is attributed to the sharpness of their *sense of place* <term>Ortssinn; the instinctive ability to navigate back to a specific location</term>; but when pigeons and dogs are transported in a sack, turned around twenty times, and yet run the straightest path home through unknown terrain, then one no longer knows how to

<meta>This page continues Eduard von Hartmann’s exploration of animal instinct, specifically focusing on the "clairvoyance" animals appear to possess regarding future weather events. It transitions from the previous discussion on medicinal instincts to the prophetic behaviors of birds, mammals, and insects.</meta>

...say, rather: their instinct has guided them, i.e., the clairvoyance of the unconscious has allowed them to sense the right path. In years where an early winter is set to occur, most migratory birds gather earlier than usual to depart; when a very mild winter is imminent, some species do not migrate at all, or only a short distance to the south; if a severe winter is coming, the turtle makes its winter quarters deeper. When gray geese, cranes, and so forth soon depart again from the regions where they had appeared at the start of spring, a hot and dry summer is in prospect, where the resulting lack of water in these areas would make breeding impossible for marsh and water birds. In years when floods occur, the beaver builds its lodge higher, and when a flood in Kamchatka is imminent, the field mice suddenly migrate away in swarms. If a dry summer is imminent, one sees in April and May the hanging spiders <note>original: "Hängespinnen"; likely referring to species of orb-weavers or spiders that produce long draglines</note> spinning threads several feet long from up high. If in winter one sees funnel-web spiders <term>Winkelspinnen; a family of spiders (Agelenidae) known for their funnel-shaped webs</term> or winter spiders running back and forth a lot, fighting boldly with one another, or crafting new and multiple webs on top of each other, then cold weather will set in within 9–12 days; if, on the other hand, they hide, then a thaw follows.

I do not doubt in the least that many of these precautionary measures against future weather conditions are conditioned by sensory perceptions of current atmospheric states that escape us; yet these perceptions always refer only to **present** weather conditions, and what can the affection of the general sense <term>Gemeingefühl; a 19th-century psychological term referring to the inner physical sensation of one's own body, often called coenesthesia</term> produced by the current weather have to do in the animal's consciousness with the representation of the future weather? One surely would not want to expect animals to **calculate** the weather months in advance through meteorological conclusions, or even to foresee floods. Rather, such a sensory perception of present atmospheric influences is nothing more than the sensible perception which acts as a motive, and a motive must **after all always** be present if an instinct is to function. It thus remains established that the foreseeing of the weather is an unconscious clairvoyance, of which the stork, departing for the south four weeks earlier, knows as little as the deer that [grows] a thicker coat than usual before a cold winter...

<meta>This page continues the philosopher Eduard von Hartmann’s argument that animal instincts are guided by an "unconscious representation." He moves from discussing how animals predict the weather to how they navigate complex reproductive cycles, arguing that these actions cannot be explained by simple sensory experience or logic alone.</meta>

...usually allows to grow. Animals possess, on one hand, a conscious feeling of the current weather; from this, on the other hand, their actions follow exactly as if they had a representation of the future weather. However, they do not have this representation in their consciousness. Thus, the only natural connecting link is the unconscious representation, which is always a form of *clairvoyance* <note>original: "Hellsehen"; used here to mean an innate, non-sensory knowledge of future events</note>, because it contains something that is neither directly given to the animal through sensory perception nor can be deduced from perception through its intellectual faculties.

The most wonderful of all are the *instincts* <term>Instincte; innate, complex patterns of behavior triggered by specific stimuli</term> related to reproduction. Every male finds the female of its species to complete the act of mating—but certainly not merely by their similarity to himself. In many animal species, such as parasitic crustaceans <term>Schmarotzerkrebse; a diverse group of crustaceans that live off other organisms, often showing extreme physical differences between males and females</term>, the sexes are so fundamentally different in form that the male would more likely be led to mate with females of thousands of other species than with those of his own. In the insect order of Strepsiptera <term>Strepsipteren; often called "twisted-wing parasites," these insects are known for their extreme sexual dimorphism</term>, the female is a shapeless worm that lives its entire life in the abdomen of a wasp, with only its lens-shaped head shield protruding between two of the wasp's abdominal rings. The male, which lives for only a few hours and resembles a moth, recognizes his female by this stunted protrusion and completes the mating through an opening that appears just below her mouth.

Before any experience of what *giving birth* might be, the pregnant mammal is driven into solitude to prepare a bed for her young in a cave or some other protected place; the bird builds its nest as soon as the eggs ripen in its ovary. Land-dwelling snails, crabs, tree frogs, and toads go into the water; sea turtles come onto land; many sea fish swim up rivers to lay their eggs where they alone find the conditions necessary for their development. Insects lay their eggs in the most diverse places: in the sand, on leaves, under the skin and nails of other animals—often in places where the future food for the larva will only emerge much later. For example, they may lay eggs in autumn on trees that will not sprout until spring, or in spring on blossoms that will not bear fruit until autumn, or in caterpillars that will only serve as food and protection for the parasitic larvae once they have reached the pupa stage. Through this, the eggs reach the animals' intestines—their proper place of development—and once grown, they are expelled with the manure. The warble flies <note>original: "Rinderbremsen"</note> know how to select the strongest and healthiest animals with such certainty that cattle dealers and tanners rely entirely on them, preferring to take the animals and hides that show the most traces of grub-damage <term>Engerlingsfrass; the tracks or holes left in a hide by larvae feeding under the skin</term>. The mason wasp <term>Mauerwespe; a solitary wasp known for building or digging nests for its young</term> digs a hole several inches deep into the sand, lays an egg inside, and stacks legless green maggots—which are near pupation <term>Verpuppung; the process of turning into a chrysalis or cocoon</term> and thus well-fed and able to live a long time without food—so tightly around it that they can neither move nor pupate. It captures these by lying in wait for them just as they emerge from their pupation; it kills them while they are still weak, but at the same time appears to inject them with a fluid that keeps them fresh and suitable for food. 

Many species of wasps open the cells of their larvae exactly when they have consumed their food in order to provide more, and then close them again; in a similar way, ants always find the right moment when their larvae are ready to crawl out to open the cocoon for them, from which the larvae could not free themselves. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of animal instinct, specifically the concept of "unconscious clairvoyance." It must be equally beyond doubt that it is clairvoyance which, in certain animals, awakens the will at the exact moment to open the cells or the web <note>original: "Gespinnst"</note> when the larvae have finished their food supply or are ready to emerge.

The cuckoo—whose eggs do not take one or two days to mature in the ovary like those of other birds, but rather seven to eleven days—cannot incubate its own eggs because the first ones would rot before the last one is laid. For this reason, it places them in the nests of other birds, naturally placing each egg in a different nest. To ensure that the host birds do not recognize and discard the foreign egg, it is not only much smaller than one would expect given the size of the cuckoo (since it only finds opportunities among small birds), but it is also, as mentioned, deceptively similar to the other eggs in the nest in color and pattern. 

Now, since the cuckoo selects the nest it wishes to use a few days in advance, one might imagine—in the case of open nests—that the maturing egg takes on the color of the existing nest eggs because the pregnant cuckoo "marks" <note>original: "sich an denselben versieht"; referring to the historical folk belief of "maternal impression," where a mother's visual experiences were thought to physically influence her offspring</note> itself by looking at them. However, this explanation does not fit nests hidden in hollow trees (e.g., the Common Redstart <note>original: "sylvia phoenicurus"</note>) or those with an oven-like shape and a narrow entrance (e.g., the Whitethroat <note>original: "sylvia rufa"</note>). In these cases, the cuckoo can neither slip inside nor see inside; it must even lay its egg outside and carry it in with its beak. Therefore, it cannot perceive through its senses what the existing eggs look like. If, despite this, its egg exactly resembles the others, this is only possible through unconscious clairvoyance, which regulates the process in the ovary according to color and pattern.

A significant support and confirmation for the existence of clairvoyance in animal instincts lies in the facts that also document clairvoyance in humans in various states; the healing instincts of children and pregnant women have already been mentioned. For the most part, however, given the higher level of human consciousness, a stronger resonance of consciousness with unconscious clairvoyance emerges here, which presents itself as a more or less distinct premonition <term>Ahnung; a gut feeling or intuitive inkling of the future</term>. <meta>This page continues the investigation into "unconscious clairvoyance" (Hellsehen). Having previously established that insects and birds act on an unconscious knowledge of the future to provide for their young, the author now transitions to how this faculty manifests in humans and other animals as a form of "presentiment" or "foreboding" (Ahnung) regarding health and death.</meta>

...performance of an action occurs, but sometimes also shows itself independently of the condition of a deed to be performed at the moment as a mere representation without conscious will, if only the condition is met that the object of this foreboding <term>Ahnung; a sense of intuitive knowing or presentiment</term> interests the *will* of the foreboding person in general to a high degree. After the suppression of an intermittent fever <note>original: "Wechselfieber"; likely referring to malaria or similar recurring fevers common in the 19th century</note> or another illness, it is not uncommon for the sick to predict exactly the time at which a fit of convulsions will occur and end; the same takes place almost regularly in spontaneous somnambulism <note>a state of "sleep-waking" or trance occurring naturally</note>, and frequently in artificially induced ones; even the Pythia <note>the high priestess and oracle at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi</note>, as is well known, determined each time the hour of her next ecstasy <term>Ekstase; here meaning a trance-like state of prophetic inspiration</term>. Likewise, in somnambulistic states, healing instincts often express themselves in presentiments of the appropriate medicines, which have just as often led to brilliant results as they seem to contradict the current standpoint of science. The determination of remedies is also certainly the only use which decent magnetizers <term>Magnetiseure; practitioners of "animal magnetism" or mesmerism, a 19th-century precursor to hypnotism</term> make of the half-awake sleep of their somnambulists. 

"It also happens occasionally that quite healthy persons, before giving birth or at the very beginning of an illness, have a certain premonition of their approaching death; the fulfillment of this can hardly be explained as mere chance, for otherwise it would have to occur much less frequently than non-fulfillment, which is exactly the opposite; also, many of these persons show neither a longing for death nor a fear of it, and it can therefore not be explained as an effect of the imagination" (Words of the famous physiologist Burdach <note>Karl Friedrich Burdach (1776–1847), a pioneer in neuroanatomy and physiology</note>, from his work: "Glances into Life," <note>original: "Blicke in's Leben"</note> Chapter 'Presentiment,' from which a large part of the relevant examples are borrowed). This premonition of death, which occurs exceptionally in humans, is something quite common in animals, even in those that do not know or understand death; they crawl away, when they feel their end approaching, to the most remote, lonely, and hidden places possible; this is, for example, the reason why even in cities one so rarely finds the corpse or the skeleton of a cat. It is only to be assumed that the unconscious clairvoyance <term>Hellsehen; the author's term for an unconscious, intuitive perception of facts or future events</term>, which is identical in essence in humans and animals, evokes presentiments of varying clarity: thus, for example, it merely drives the cat instinctively to crawl away without its knowing why, but in humans, it awakens the clear consciousness of their approaching death.

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of "unconscious clairvoyance" (Hellsehen). Having previously discussed how animals and somnambulists can sense future events regarding their own health, the text now shifts to "second sight" and presentiments concerning the deaths and fates of others.</meta>

But presentiments exist not only regarding one’s own death, but also concerning the deaths of dear persons close to the heart, as evidenced by the many accounts where a dying person appeared to a friend or spouse in a dream or vision at the hour of death. Such stories span all peoples and eras and, in part, undoubtedly include true facts. Closely related to this is the faculty of "second sight," which was formerly common in Scotland and still occurs on the Danish islands today. In these cases, certain individuals—without being in an ecstatic state and while in full possession of their senses—foresee future or distant events that are of interest to them, such as deaths, battles, or great fires (for instance, Swedenborg’s vision of the fire of Stockholm <note>Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772) was a renowned Swedish scientist and mystic who famously claimed to have seen a fire in Stockholm in great detail while he was 300 miles away in Gothenburg.</note>), as well as the arrival or fates of distant friends, and so on (cf. Ennemoser: *History of Magic*, 2nd Ed. § 86 <note>Joseph Ennemoser (1787–1854) was a physician and historian whose work on "animal magnetism" and magic was a standard 19th-century reference for paranormal phenomena.</note>).

In some persons, this clairvoyance is restricted only to the deaths of their acquaintances or fellow locals; examples of such corpse-seers <term>Leichenseherinnen; literally "female corpse-seers," referring to women in folklore who claim to see funeral processions or omens before a death occurs</term> are numerous and documented in the best possible way, in some cases even by legal testimony. This ability of second sight appears temporarily in ecstatic states, in spontaneous or artificially induced <term>Somnambulismus; a state of "sleep-waking" or trance where the subject is unconscious of their surroundings but can perform actions or speak</term> of the higher degrees of waking-dreams, as well as in lucid moments shortly before death.

Often, these presentiments—in which the clairvoyance of the Unconscious reveals itself to the consciousness—are dark, incomprehensible, and symbolic. This is because they must take on a sensory form in the brain, whereas the unconscious representation can have no part in the form of sensibility <note>In 19th-century philosophy, "sensibility" refers to the way our mind organizes raw data into space and time; the author argues the unconscious doesn't use these categories, so the brain "translates" its messages into symbols</note> (see Chapter C. I.); for this reason, one can so easily mistake accidental moods, dreams, or morbid images for something meaningful. The resulting high probability of error and self-deception, the ease of intentionally deceiving others, and the predominant disadvantage that knowledge of the future generally brings to mankind, place the practical harmfulness of all efforts to know the future beyond any doubt. However, this cannot diminish the theoretical importance of this field of phenomena, and must in no way hinder the recognition of the true facts of clairvoyance, even if they are buried under a heap of nonsense and fraud. To be sure, the predominantly rationalistic and materialistic tendency of our age finds it convenient to deny or ignore all facts in this field, because they...

I am convinced that many deniers of all human **divination** <term>divination; the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural or instinctive means</term> would judge differently, or at least more cautiously, if they considered it worth the effort to familiarize themselves with the reports of the relevant facts. As little as I would consider this field of phenomena suitable to serve as the sole basis for scientific proofs, I find it just as noteworthy as a completion and continuation of the series of phenomena that confronts us in the **clairvoyance** <term>Hellsehen; literally "clear-seeing," used here to describe instinctive or prophetic knowledge</term> of animal and human **instincts**. Precisely because it continues this series only with a heightened resonance of consciousness, it supports those testimonies of instinctive actions regarding their own nature just as much as its own probability finds support in those analogies with the clairvoyance of instinct. This, as well as the desire not to leave unused an opportunity for an explanation against a modern prejudice, is the reason why I have permitted myself to mention this field—which is so discredited today—in a scientific work, even if only in passing.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on instinct, moving from individual manifestations to collective behavior. The previous page concluded with a mention of Goethe's personal experience with second sight; here, the author transitions into how instincts can serve a collective or "solidarity" rather than just the individual or their immediate offspring.</meta>

benefits them—namely, his children; now we have yet to consider the cases where a **solidarity of instincts** <term>solidarity of instincts; a shared, innate drive where individual actions coordinate perfectly toward a group goal without conscious planning</term> exists among several individuals, such that, on the one hand, the performance of each individual benefits everyone, and on the other hand, a useful result can only be achieved through the unanimous cooperation of many. Among higher animals, this interaction of instincts also occurs, yet here it is much more difficult to separate from agreements made through conscious will, as language makes a more perfect communication of mutual plans and intentions possible. We will nevertheless clearly recognize this collective effect of a **mass instinct** in the origin of language and the great political and social movements of world history; here, however, we are concerned with examples that are as simple and clear as possible. Therefore, we turn to lower animals, where the means of communicating thoughts—due to the lack of voice, mimicry, and physiognomy—are so imperfect that the harmony and the interlocking of individual performances in the most essential matters cannot possibly be attributed to conscious communication through language. 

According to the observations of Huber <note>François Huber (1750–1831) was a Swiss naturalist who, despite being blind, made groundbreaking observations on honeybees with the help of his assistant.</note> in his *New Observations on Bees* <note>original: "Nouvelles observations sur les abeilles"</note>, during the construction of new honeycombs, a portion of the larger worker bees, which had gorged themselves with honey, took no part in the usual occupations of the others but remained completely still. After twenty-four hours, small plates of wax had formed under their abdominal scales. The bee pulled these out with her hind leg, chewed them, and shaped them into the form of a band. The wax plates prepared in this way were then stuck onto each other on the ceiling of the hive. When one bee had used up her wax plates in this manner, another followed her, continuing the same work in the same way. In this way, a small, rough wall, fixed to the beehive and half a line <note>A "line" is an archaic unit of measurement, approximately 2.25 millimeters or 1/12th of an inch.</note> thick, was formed in a vertical direction. 

Now came one of the smaller worker bees, which had an empty abdomen, examined the wall, and made a shallow, semi-oval hollow in the middle of one of its sides; she piled the bitten-off wax at the edge of the hollow. After a short time, she was relieved by another similar bee, and so more than twenty followed one after another. During this time, on the opposite side of the wall, another bee began to make a similar hollow there,

Just imagine now how beings, who were supposed to agree on their mutual intentions and plans through sensory means of communication, would fall into a thousandfold differences of opinion, into bickering and strife; how often something would be done incorrectly and have to be destroyed and done over again; how too many would crowd into one task, while too few would be found for another; what a running back and forth there would be before everyone had found their right place; how often several would now push to take over a shift, while others would then be missing—just as we find in the collective labors of humans, who stand so much higher. 

We see none of this with the bees; rather, the whole thing gives the impression as if an invisible, supreme master builder <note>The "master builder" (Baumeister) is a common 19th-century metaphor for a divine or natural intelligence that directs the biological world.</note> had presented the plan for the whole to the assembly and imprinted it on each individual; as if each type of worker had learned by heart their specific job, position, and shift number, and were notified by secret signals of the moment when their turn came. All this, however, is precisely the achievement of instinct; and just as the plan of the entire hive dwells within each individual bee through instinct in a state of unconscious clairvoyance <note>original: "unbewusstem Hellsehen"; the author suggests that instinct allows the bee to "see" the finished result and its part in it without conscious thought.</note>, so a common instinct drives each individual to the work to which they are called at the right moment; only through this is that wonderful peace and order possible. As to how this common instinct is to be understood,

In the bee colony, working activity and sexual activity, which are otherwise united in one body, are personified in three types of individuals; and just as organs exist within a single individual, here the separate individuals exist in an inner, unconscious, spiritual-organic unity.

We have thus obtained the following results in this chapter: instinct is not the result of conscious reflection, not a mere consequence of physical organization, not the result of a mechanism located in the structure of the brain, and not the effect of a dead mechanism attached to the mind from the outside—alien to its innermost essence. Rather, it is the individual's own achievement, springing from their innermost essence and character. The purpose served by a specific type of instinctive action is not conceived once and for all by a mind standing outside the individual, such as Providence <note>original: "Vorsehung"</note>, with the necessity of acting according to it being grafted onto the individual as something external and foreign; rather, the purpose of instinct...

Up to this point, clairvoyance still stands as an incomprehensible empirical fact, and one might object: "then I would rather simply stick with *instinct* as an incomprehensible fact." But this is countered by three points: first, we find clairvoyance even outside of instinct (especially in humans); second, clairvoyance does not necessarily need to occur in all instincts, meaning that instinct and clairvoyance are already given empirically as two separate facts, of which clairvoyance may well contribute to the explanation of instinct, but not the other way around; and third, finally, the clairvoyance of the individual will not remain such an incomprehensible fact, but will find its explanation quite well in the later course of this investigation, whereas one would have to renounce the understanding of instinct in any other way.

Only the view presented here makes it possible to understand **instinct** as the **innermost core of every being**; that it is indeed this is already shown by the drive for **self-preservation** and **preservation of the species** <note>original: "Selbsterhaltung und Gattungserhaltung"</note> which permeates all of creation. It is further shown by the heroic **sacrificial courage** with which individual well-being, indeed even life itself, is sacrificed to instinct. One thinks of the caterpillar that repeatedly repairs its web until it succumbs to exhaustion; of the bird that dies of exhaustion from egg-laying; of the restlessness and grief of all migratory animals when they are prevented from wandering. A captive cuckoo dies every winter from the despair of not being able to migrate; the vineyard snail, from which the winter sleep...

# IV.

## **The Connection Between Will and Representation.**

---

Every act of willing desires the transition from a present state into another. — A present state is always given, even if it were merely a state of rest; however, the will could never and would never arise from this present state alone if the possibility—at least the ideal <note>Here, "ideal" refers to the realm of ideas or thought rather than perfection.</note> possibility—of something else were not present. A single state that allowed for nothing else, either in reality or in thought <note>original: "ideal"</note>, would be locked within itself, without ever moving beyond itself—not even conceptually <note>original: "idealiter"</note>—for this act of stepping outside itself would then already be its "other." Even that will which desires the persistence <note>The desire for things to stay as they are.</note> of the present state is only possible through the representation <term>Representation (Vorstellung); in German philosophy, this refers to the mental image, idea, or "presentation" of something in the mind.</term> of that state's cessation, which is then loathed; it exists, therefore, through a double negation. Without the representation of cessation, a willing of persistence would be impossible.

It is therefore established that two things are primarily necessary for willing: the first is the present state, specifically as the starting point <term>Starting point (Ausgangspunct); the initial condition from which an action or process begins.</term>. The other—the endpoint or the goal of the willing—cannot be the state currently present, for one already fully possesses the present. Therefore, it would be nonsensical to still "will" it; the present can, at most, produce satisfaction or dissatisfaction, but not the will itself. Consequently, what is willed cannot be a state that is <note>original: "seiender"</note>, but only a state that is not, which is willed *to be*. From non-being into being, a state can only arrive through *becoming*; and once it has reached being through *becoming*, the moment previously called the "present" is *over*, and a new present has arrived, which from the previous moment—

I have lingered so long on this self-evident observation because the neglect of it gives rise to the entire peculiarity and inconsistency of Schopenhauer’s <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a philosopher famous for his work *The World as Will and Representation*.</note> philosophy. For in the Will, there is always Representation; and if the Representation also possessed outward causality, then the distinction between Will and Representation would indeed be abolished. We would find both different moments within **each one of them** and would have to name them all over again. Therefore, we prefer to retain the words "Will" and "Representation" for these polar moments and assume a connection between the two wherever we find these moments combined. We have already done this with the Will; it remains for us in the future to recognize a Will everywhere within a Representation where that representation shows an outward causality. # V.

## The Unconscious in Reflex Actions.

---

> "Reflex movements are currently defined as those in which the exciting stimulus directly hits neither a contractile structure nor a motor nerve, but rather a nerve which communicates its state of excitement to a central organ, whereupon, through the mediation of the latter, the stimulus jumps over to motor nerves and only then exerts its influence through muscle movements."

(Wagner's *Handbook of Physiology* <note>original: "Handwörterbuch der Physiologie"</note> Vol. II. p. 542. Article "Nerve Physiology" by Volkmann. Compare also, regarding the historical development of the concept of reflex movement and as an appreciation of the views of earlier researchers who often came close to the truth, the recommendable writing of J. W. Arnold: "The Doctrine of Reflex Function" <note>original: "Die Lehre von der Reflexfunction"</note>.) — This explanation seems to me as good as physiology is capable of providing, and no restriction of it can be found that would not exclude certain classes of movements generally recognized as reflex actions from this name; yet, it is easy to see that it is much broader than physiology intends, since all movements and actions find a place in it whose motive is not a thought originating of itself in the brain, but rather, directly or indirectly, a sensory impression. To follow this steady transition from the lowest reflex movements into conscious activities of the will more closely, we must examine specific examples.

If one stimulates a freshly excised frog heart, which is pulsing slowly, with a needle prick, a **systole** <term>systole; the phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle contracts and pumps blood from the chambers into the arteries</term> (contraction) occurs independently of the rhythm of the beat in the normal sequence of the parts. Before the complete cessation

If the heart is dissected while still vigorous, but in such a way that bridges of connection remain between the parts, then stimulating a part that contains a **ganglion node** <term>ganglion node; a cluster of nerve cell bodies that acts as a local control center</term> within the muscle tissue causes both parts to contract. In contrast, stimulating a part that contains no node results only in a local contraction. From this, it is evident that the normal **systole** <note>the phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle contracts</note> occurring upon stimulation is not a simple phenomenon of contractile tissue, but rather a reflex movement mediated by the embedded ganglion nodes. Other experiments—for example, dividing the spinal cord into small cross-sections, etc.—make it probable that every nerve center can act as a mediator for reflex movements. The more highly developed the nerve center, the higher the degree of purposefulness and skill shown in the complexity of its reflex effects. Volkmann says (*Handbook* <note>original: "Hwb." referring to Wagner's Handwörterbuch der Physiologie</note> II. 545):

> “If various muscles combine for a reflex movement, whether simultaneously or in sequence, the combination is always mechanically purposeful. I mean that muscles acting simultaneously support one another—for example, in producing a **flexion** <note>the action of bending a limb or joint</note>—and those acting in sequence unite in the purposeful continuation and completion of the movement already begun.

If one stimulates a decapitated frog lying in a stretched position with sufficient force on the hind thigh, the **flexors** <note>muscles that bend a limb</note> and **adductors** <note>muscles that pull a limb toward the body's midline</note> of both thighs first combine; only after the thighs are drawn toward the body do the **extensors** <note>muscles that straighten a limb</note> combine for a joint extension, and the total result is a more or less regular locomotion for swimming or jumping. — In many cases, reflex movements possess not only the character of purposefulness but even a certain air of intention. **Eye centers** <term>Augencentra; the neurological centers in the brain that coordinate eye movements and focus</term> adjust according to the point of greatest stimulation; there is the **accommodation** of the lens for distance and of the iris for light intensity. All these movements can also be performed voluntarily, but only through the mental image of the changed sensory impression; they are achieved only with difficulty or not at all through a direct mental image of the movements themselves. For example, the examining eye doctor holds his finger where the patient should look, because if he tells him to turn his eye to the upper right, the most distorted movements often occur in the eyes and lids, except the one requested. Furthermore, movements in the **vocal organs** <term>Sprachwerkzeuge; the anatomical parts involved in speech, such as the larynx, tongue, and lips</term> are reflected through the ear, for as is well known, all learning of speech in children and animals rests on the fact that an involuntary drive compels them to reproduce what they have heard; the same takes place with melodies, where it is more easily observed even in adults. Without this reflex, it would be impossible to train birds to whistle melodies. One can also observe the reflexive compulsion to pronounce heard words within oneself while thinking. Here, in a manner similar to (though to a higher degree) the formation of dream images and hallucinations, the as-yet non-sensory thought of the word first evokes a **centrifugal innervation stream** <term>innervation stream; the flow of nervous energy from the center to the periphery</term> toward the auditory nerve. As a reflexive consequence, a centripetal stream brings back the auditory sensation of the word, and this evokes the reflex movements of loud or quiet pronunciation in the vocal organs. The natural human—for instance, the uneducated or the passionately excited—thinks aloud; it already requires the constraint of education to think quietly, and even here, if one pays attention, one will almost always catch oneself in a muscle sensation in the vocal organs. This sensation is the same, though to a weaker degree, as that which would arise through the actual pronunciation of the words; it thus clearly contains the beginning of that activity. It is quite similar when reading.

For conscious deliberation always brings doubt with it, doubt brings hesitation, and hesitation frequently leads to being too late. The **unconscious intelligence**, by contrast, is always doubtlessly sure of seizing the right thing; or rather, doubt never occurs to it, and therefore it almost always seizes the right thing at the right moment.

But more important than everything considered so far is the consideration that there is no, or almost no, voluntary movement that should not also be understood as a combination of **reflex actions**. I mean it this way: Anatomical examinations show that in the upper part of the **spinal cord**, the total number of **primary nerve fibers** <term>primary nerve fibers; a 19th-century term for the individual thread-like structures that make up a nerve</term> is only a very small fraction of the fibers of all the nerves intended to trigger movements through the conscious will—that is, starting from the **brain**. Since the transmission from the brain to the muscle nerves can, with few exceptions, only occur through the upper spinal cord, it follows that one fiber in the upper spinal cord must be intended to **innervate** <term>innervate; to supply an organ or body part with nerves or nerve impulses</term> a large quantity of associated muscle nerve fibers. 

A direct **anastomosis** <term>anastomosis; from the Greek, meaning a cross-connection or "interlocking" between vessels or nerves</term> (an interlocking or linkage) of these fibers could be imagined, yet this assumption appears highly unlikely based on anatomical observations. Furthermore, we are forced to discard this idea because the very same movements are sometimes stimulated from the brain and sometimes performed independently by the central organs of the spinal cord as a result of some other stimulation; these movements allow for a myriad of the finest modifications in their complexity, whereas a direct physical linkage would always have to result in the exact same, unchanging movements. 

Added to this is the fact that the brain, which gives the command for the execution of a complicated sequence of movements, has no conception at all of this complexity itself, but only a general idea of the result—as seen in speaking, singing, walking, dancing, running, jumping, gymnastics, fencing, riding, or ice skating. Thus, all the details of execution required for the intended overall result are left to the spinal cord. (One need only ask oneself whether one knows anything about the muscle combinations needed to pronounce a word or to sing a **coloratura** <term>coloratura; elaborate ornamentation in vocal music, featuring rapid runs and trills</term>.) 

Accordingly, the only remaining way of understanding this seems to be that the **nerve impulse** <note>original: "Innervationsstrom"</note>—which conducts the conscious will for the overall result of the movement from the brain to the movement's central organ in the spinal cord—is an **outward-flowing** <term>centrifugal; moving away from a center, here referring to the signal leaving the brain</term> one for the brain, but an **inward-flowing** <term>centripetal; moving toward a center, here referring to the signal arriving at the spinal cord's control center</term> one for the nerve center of the movement...

The next thing we have to investigate is the question of whether the phenomena under consideration can be viewed as the effects of a dead mechanism, or whether we are not rather forced to understand them as consequences of an intelligence inherent in the <term>central organs; the primary processing units of the nervous system, such as the brain or spinal cord</term>—leaving the aforementioned alternative unresolved for the time being. Let us turn first to physiology. We see that upon a needle prick to the skin of a frog's thigh, both thighs twitch, provided only that the small portion of the spinal cord from which the thigh nerves originate remains intact. The needle prick obviously affects only *one* <term>primitive nerve fiber; an individual nerve cell axon or thread-like structure</term>, since within a circle of a certain size, the exact location of the pricked spot cannot be distinguished; however, the number of motor fibers set into action by this is immense, for it can encompass the entire body. By this alone, a direct <term>anastomosis; a connection or junction between two anatomical structures, in this context specifically a direct link between sensory and motor nerves</term> is highly improbable. This becomes even more improbable because the same motor fibers react regardless of which spot on the frog's thigh skin is pricked—that is, when different sensory nerve fibers conduct the stimulus to the center. 

Furthermore, microscopic examinations provide no support for this assumption; rather, <note>Albert von Kölliker (1817–1905) was a Swiss anatomist and physiologist who was among the first to show that nerve fibers are continuous with nerve cells.</note> Kölliker has already directly observed the emergence of motor fibers from globules of gray nerve substance (the central organ), and it is now generally assumed that the central origin of all nerve fibers is to be found in <term>ganglion cells; large nerve cells found in the brain and spinal cord that process and relay information</term>, i.e., the characteristic spherical or radiating cells of the gray nerve substance. Reflex actions are entirely impossible to explain through a peculiar mechanism of conduction conditions alone; for one can no longer conceive of any laws or arrangements that could cause the very same current to jump sometimes to nearby parts and sometimes to distant ones, or allow reactions to follow one another in one sequence and then another. It could even, in response to a simple stimulus, trigger an alternating play of **antagonists** <term>muscles that act in opposition to one another, such as those that extend versus those that flex a limb</term> (as seen when rubbing a pinched spot). 

The impossibility of a **pre-established** <note>original: "prästablirten"</note> mechanism can be demonstrated even more strikingly through physiology. If one divides the spinal cord along its entire length with a cut from front to back, the capacity for reflex movements does not suffer, except that they are then restricted to the specific side of the body being stimulated. If, however, one leaves a connecting bridge at any point between the two separated halves, or if one makes transverse cuts through the left half and then the right half of the spinal cord at some distance from each other—so that all its longitudinal fibers are severed—one can still excite general reflex movements by stimulating any point on the skin. 

This is perhaps the clearest proof that the motor reaction is not a consequence of **pre-drawn** <note>original: "vorgezeichneten"; referring to fixed, "hard-wired" biological paths</note> paths of stimulus conduction. Instead, in order to bring about **purposeful** reflex movements, the current creates new paths for itself after the destruction of the usual conduction paths, provided that the parts have not been completely isolated. There must, therefore, be a **principle standing above the material laws of nerve current conduction** which creates the change in circumstances, by virtue of which the paths of those currents are altered; and this principle can only be an **immaterial** one. This is also documented by the fact that the **connection of reflex movements is, for the most part, breakable through conscious will and practice.**

As striking as these anatomical-physiological reasons are, they are still not the strongest. For if the purposiveness appearing in reflex actions were externally predetermined—staged by a material mechanism—then the ability of movements to accommodate themselves to the nature of circumstances, this **inexhaustible wealth of combinations**, each of which for its particular...

# VI.

## The Unconscious in the Healing Power of Nature.

---

If one damages a bird's nest, a spider's web, a caterpillar's cocoon, or a snail's shell, or if one takes a piece of a bird’s plumage, they all repair the damage that endangers or at least hinders their future existence. We have seen that the first of these expressions must be attributed to **instinct**, and should we be unable to recognize the striking parallelism of the last two phenomena with those? We have recognized that it is an **unconscious representation** <note>original: "unbewusste Vorstellung"; in this philosophical context, a "representation" is a mental image or idea that exists in the mind even without active, conscious awareness</note> of the **purpose** <term>Zweck: the goal or "final cause" toward which a biological process is directed</term> which, combined with the will to achieve it, dictates the conscious willing of the means; and should we doubt that we are dealing with the same thing when the object of the action is no longer something external, but rather one's own body itself? Especially since we are not capable of fixing the boundary where one's own body begins and ends—as with the caterpillar’s cocoon, the snail’s shell, or the bird’s plumage—or between excretions and secretions?

If one takes from a polyp its tentacles or from a worm its head, the animal must die for lack of food; and if the animal replaces the tentacles or the head and lives on, should anything other than the unconscious representation of this indispensability be the fundamental cause of the replacement? One should not object that the difference between **instinct** and **healing power** <note>original: "Heilkraft"; refers to the innate biological capacity of an organism to restore its health or physical integrity</note> lies in the fact that, in the former case, the representation and willing of at least the *means* are conscious, while in the latter case, these too are unconscious. For after the discussions regarding the independence of the lower **nerve centers**, one will not doubt that the willing of the means could very well occur in some way and somewhere in

Let us now consider the effects of the **healing power** somewhat more closely:

In the **Hydrae** <note>freshwater polyps</note>, every part of their mass is replaced, so that a new animal forms from every piece, whether they have been cut crosswise or lengthwise, or even divided into several strips. In **Planarians** <note>a type of flatworm</note>, every segment, even if it amounts to only 1/10–1/8 of the entire animal, becomes a new creature. In **Annelids** or worms, replacement only occurs in crosswise divisions; the head or tail is always regenerated; in some, one can cut the animal into several pieces, and each individual piece completes itself into a perfect specimen of its genus. It seems clear enough here that if—among an infinitely large number of possible ways to cut—the separated part always yields a specimen expressing the **typical idea** <term>Gattungstypus: the "blueprint" or ideal form of a species</term> of its genus, then dead causality <note>the mechanical laws of cause and effect</note> cannot produce this effect; rather, this typical idea must be present in every piece of the animal. 

An idea can only be present, however, either *really* <note>original: *realiter*; physically manifest in the world</note> in its external representation as a realized idea, or *ideally* <note>original: *idealiter*; existing as a concept or thought</note>, insofar as it is represented in and through the act of representation. Every fragment of the animal must therefore possess the **unconscious representation** <note>original: *unbewusste Vorstellung*; a mental image or plan that exists without the creature's conscious awareness</note> of the species type, according to which it undertakes the regeneration. This is just as the bee, before building its first cell and without ever having seen one, carries within itself the unconscious representation of the six-sided cell—accurate to within half an angular minute—or as every bird must unconsciously represent the form of nest-building or the manner of song belonging to its species-idea even before it has experienced them from others or itself. 

If one observes the act of regeneration, for example, in a bisected **earthworm**, one sees a small white bud sprout from the cut wound. This gradually grows larger, soon acquiring narrow rings standing close together, which then expand in all directions, as well as extensions of the **digestive canal**, the blood vessel system...

In addition, there are various secondary circumstances which confirm most clearly that the mental representation of what must be achieved according to the species-idea in a specific case is the original determining factor in these processes. If the animal is not yet fully grown and a part is torn away, the regenerated part does not correspond to the old, smaller state, but is formed as that part *ought* to be if it had already undergone the **process according to the species-idea**. Furthermore, a greater force is directed toward the replacement of a part the more important it is for the animal's survival; for example, according to Spallanzani <note>Lazzaro Spallanzani (1729–1799), an Italian biologist who performed pioneering experiments on animal regeneration</note>, worms replace the head sooner than the tail, and in fish, the replacement of cut-off fins occurs in the order of their importance for movement: first the tail fin, then the pectoral and pelvic fins, and finally the dorsal fin. If the strength—or more clearly, the power of the unconscious will—is insufficient to master the material and external circumstances for the regeneration of a part in the normal way, the "type" of the species still shines through the resulting malformations.

And the casting off of the damaged limb is, after all, merely the first act of the replacement process.

The higher we now climb in the animal scale, the more the power of the healing force generally decreases, reaching its lowest degree in humans. Therefore, if one practices physiology <term>Physiologie: the study of how living organisms and their parts function</term> exclusively on humans, the error could more easily arise that a mere material mechanism produces the healing effects; but just as anatomy only yielded significant results from the moment it was practiced comparatively, and psychology will only bring true enlightenment from that point forward, so too in physiology can only comparative investigation provide the right understanding. But once we have been set on the right path by the clearly presented conditions in the lower animals, it will not be difficult to recognize this view as the only possible one, even at the highest levels of organization.

Let us now consider some other remarkable phenomena of the healing power in humans and mammals.

In mammals where the lens had been removed from the eye, a complete replacement of the lens was frequently observed; even in humans operated on for cataracts <term>Staar: an old medical term for cataracts, the clouding of the eye's lens</term>, an incomplete regeneration of the lens sometimes occurs. When a bone fracture cannot heal back together, the organism seeks to help itself in another way. The broken ends close and round off; they are then held together either by a fibrous cord—into which the callus clamp <term>Calluszwinge: the temporary bridge of new bone that forms around a fracture</term> has transformed—acting like a cylindrical ligament, or they are united by a so-called **false joint** <term>Pseudarthrosis: a "false joint" that forms when a bone fails to knit together, creating a new, unintended point of motion</term>. In this instance, one end forms a cavity that receives the other spherical end. Both ends are enclosed by a fibrous capsule and, like other points where parts rub against each other, they receive the necessary lubrication through a newly formed synovial bursa <term>Synovialblase: a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between tissues of the body</term>. A similar process occurs in uncorrected dislocations; the abandoned joint socket fills in, and at the location where the joint head now rests, a new socket forms along with all the other necessary components of a joint.

The first question is: what then is disease? Disease is not an abnormality of formation, for there are abnormal forms, such as giants, dwarfs, extra fingers, or an irregular course of veins, which no one counts among diseases. Disease is not a state that endangers the existence of the organism, for many diseases do not do this; it is not a state that causes pain and hardship to the consciousness of the individual, for even this is not the case with many diseases. Disease is an **abnormality in the organic functions**, which can certainly have abnormalities of formation as both a cause and a consequence. In the former case, the abnormality of formation is also usually designated as a disease. Strictly speaking, however, this abnormal formation must have been preceded by another abnormality of functions as its cause, for as long as all functions proceed normally, the emergence of abnormal formations is impossible. Thus, when we ask for the cause of a disease, we must in any case ultimately return to an abnormality of functions within the normal formation of the functioning organs; for as long as abnormalities of formation are still involved, we have not followed the series of disease causes to the end.

If we now ask how the primary cause of all diseases—abnormality of function with normal formation—is possible, experience and speculation answer in unison: only through disturbance from the outside, but not from within through a spontaneous psychic act <note>original: "psychischen Act"; referring to the internal vital force or "unconscious will" of the organism</note> of the organism. # VII.

## The Indirect Influence of Conscious Mental Activity on Organic Functions.

---

### 1. The Influence of the Conscious Will.

**a. Muscle Contraction.**

Muscle contraction is evidently by far the most important organic function dependent on the conscious will, for it is through this that we move and act upon the external world, and through which we communicate via speech and writing. It occurs through the influence of the motor nerves, by means of an <term>innervation current</term> <note>original: "Innervationsstrom"; the flow of nervous energy or "impulses" from the brain to the muscles.</note> running from the center to the periphery. This is a current that is clearly related to electrical and chemical currents, as we see that they can be mutually converted into one another. We must not form too low an estimation of its intensity when we see an athlete’s muscles—contracted by this current—play with <term>hundredweights</term> <note>original: "Centner"; a traditional German unit of weight equivalent to approximately 50 kilograms or 110 pounds.</note>, especially when acting through the long lever-arms of the limbs; we need only think of what colossal galvanic currents are necessary to lift hundredweight loads with an electromagnet.

We have already seen that every muscle movement can only be conceived through the multiple mediation of <term>unconscious willing and representation</term> <note>original: "unbewusstem Wollen und Vorstellen"; the theory that the mind performs "hidden" calculations to translate a conscious thought (like "lift my arm") into the specific mechanical nerve signals required to do so.</note>. Otherwise, it would be impossible to understand how the impulse of movement could hit the specific <term>nerve center</term> <note>original: "Nervencentralstelle"</note> corresponding to the conscious idea of the movement, rather than any other point. 

Furthermore, we have seen that the immediate centers for the vast majority of movements lie in the <term>spinal cord</term> <note>original: "Rückenmark"</note> and the <term>medulla oblongata</term> <note>original: "verlängerten Mark"; the base of the brainstem which connects to the spinal cord and controls vital automatic functions.</note>. It is from these locations that movements are determined and ordered in their details. They are to be regarded as <term>reflex movements</term> of these centers, which are triggered by the stimulus...

The question now arises as to how the will is capable of generating the innervation current. We can only rely on the analogies of related, physically better-known currents and on the *a priori* <note>Latin: "from the former"; a term for reasoning that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note> suspicion that the entire apparatus of the motor nervous system must be integrated into the organism for the purpose of enabling the will to produce the necessary mechanical results through the smallest possible mechanical effort. In other words, the motor nervous system is a power-engine <note>original: "Kraftmaschine"; a machine that converts energy into work, like a motor.</note>, like a winch or—to use a more fitting comparison—like a wall-shattering cannon <note>original: "Geschütz"</note>, which a person only needs to fire. To produce mechanical movement without mechanical force is impossible, but the force initiating the movement can be reduced to a minimum, and the remaining part of the work can be transferred to forces previously stored for use. In a cannon, this is the chemical power of the gunpowder; in an animal, it is the power of the food consumed, which must therefore stand in the same proportion to the performance of muscle power <note>original: "Muskelkraft"</note> as the amount of powder stands to the power of the projectile.

### b. Currents of Will in Sensory Nerves.

We have previously encountered a type of **innervation current** <note>The flow of nervous energy or "will" from the brain to the body</note> as a reflex effect of **attention**. This can, however, be voluntarily evoked or intensified just as well. Attention directed intensely toward the genital sphere can result in the greatest sexual excitement, and **hypochondriacs** <note>In the 19th century, this referred to people with excessive anxiety about their health, often manifesting as real physical sensations</note> sometimes feel pain in every part of the body upon which they focus their attention. It is said to happen not infrequently that those about to undergo surgery believe they feel the pain of the incision even before the surgeon’s instrument has actually touched them. If one slowly moves their finger toward the tip of the nose with eyes closed, and approaches very gradually before contact, one feels the touch in advance as a clearly perceptible tingling in the tip of the nose; if I focus my attention strenuously on my fingertips, I feel them distinctly, also as a kind of tingling.

In all these cases, the mental representation in the brain of the expected sensation, combined with the attention directed toward these nerves, evidently causes a **peripheral current** <note>A current traveling from the brain out toward the surface/limbs</note>, which returns from the periphery to the center as a **sensation current**. This occurs whether—as in the first examples—the sensation is essentially first generated by the centrifugal <note>Moving away from the center (brain)</note> current, or whether—as in the last example—it only intensifies the stimuli that are always present but usually imperceptibly weak.

The first case also occurs with every sensory representation without an actual sensory impression; the vividness of the representation depends on the strength of the peripheral nerve current, and this in turn depends partly on the interest (**participation of the will**) in the representation, and partly on individual disposition. There are individuals who, through voluntary effort, can evoke visual images—for instance, of a friend—almost to the clarity of a **vision**. In others, the images always remain pale. If the current of will arose unconsciously, then with sufficient intensity, the returning sensation current manifests as a vision, exactly as in every dream. I believe, therefore, that there is no sensory mental representation in the brain that is not connected to an innervation current toward the relevant sensory organ, even if it usually does not extend far beyond the central endings of the organ’s nerves.

### c. The Magnetic Nerve Current.

The fundamental phenomena of **Mesmerism** or **animal magnetism** <note>A theory popularized by Franz Mesmer in the 18th century involving the transfer of an invisible "fluid" or energy between people for healing</note> are now to be regarded as recognized by science. The electrical discharges of the **electric ray** and **eel** were already known for a long time, and the realization that these effects originated from the **gray nerve matter** <note>The parts of the central nervous system responsible for processing information</note> provided the occasion to view these as the central parts of the nervous system in general. Nevertheless, people long resisted admitting the completely analogous effects of the **magnetizers** <note>Practitioners who used Mesmer's techniques to induce a trance or heal patients</note>, because they were, on the whole, too weak to be directly perceptible to the physicist. However, I have attended this experiment several times and secured myself against any deception through the most careful examination of the location as well as the person of the magnetizer. Specifically, if one places a person on an iron bed frame with a wire mattress, but in such a way that they are insulated from the metal by a woolen blanket, one creates, in a sense, a **Leyden jar** <note>The earliest form of a capacitor, used to store static electricity between two layers of conductive material</note>, where one "coating" is the bed frame and the other is the person lying upon it. Through the gathering (**influence** <note>The term for electrostatic induction</note>) of the electricity from the bed toward the insulating surface, the electrical effect of the "magnetizing" is significantly **potentiated** <note>Increased in power or effectiveness</note>. I have allowed myself to be magnetized in this way and clearly felt a perceptible, tingling spray of sparks from the lightly guided hand of the magnetizer to my skin,

Thus, here as there and everywhere, the mediation of an **unconscious will** intervenes, which ensures that precisely a magnetic current and no other arises, and that this current concentrates precisely toward the hands and not toward any other part of the body. All **vegetative functions** <note>Basic physiological processes like digestion, growth, and circulation that occur without conscious thought</note> of the organism are likely governed by sympathetic nerve fibers. The conscious will has no direct influence on them, but we have seen that this is also not the case with motor and sensory fibers; rather, that which acts directly is always an unconscious will

I possess the power to momentarily silence the strongest **hiccups** <note>original: "Schlucken"</note> through my mere will, whereas it previously inconvenienced me greatly and often would not yield to any usual means. Likewise, one can permanently suppress a **coughing fit** that has no mechanical cause through the will. There have always been people who exercised a wonderful power over their bodies: partly entertainers, partly those who had highly developed their will in other directions, such as **philosophers, magicians, and penitents** <note>Individuals who perform acts of self-discipline or asceticism for religious or spiritual reasons</note>. Based on these phenomena, I believe that one would possess a far greater voluntary power over one's **bodily functions** if only one had as much occasion from childhood to conduct experiments and exercises in them as one is forced to do with muscle movements and mental imagery.

## 2. The Influence of Conscious Representation.

The conscious **representation** <term>German "Vorstellung"; the mental image, idea, or concept of something</term> of a certain effect can often, without the conscious will for it, call forth the **unconscious will** to employ the means, so that the realization of the conscious representation then appears involuntary. **Physiology**, which must take these facts into account but does not know the concept of the unconscious will, finds itself prompted to make the absurd claim that the mere representation, without will, could become the cause of an external process. But if one reflects on this, one finds that in fact nothing is being said here other than that the concept of "representation" has been imperceptibly expanded in these cases to include the concept of the "unconscious will," as discussed in Chapter IV, pages 86–87. I am therefore doing nothing more than calling this imperceptible expansion of the concept of representation by its right name and establishing it as an independent link in the process, since it must appear inadmissible to nestle the characteristics of another likewise fixed concept into one that is already fixed.

In the first rank stand all gestures and facial expressions in the broadest sense. Here, the representation that calls forth the expression does not even include the effect, let alone the means to it; instead, the gestures appear entirely as **reflex actions**, occurring so necessarily and consistently in all individuals. How purposeful they are is quite obvious, for without the necessity and universality of gestures, no one would understand them, and without prior understanding through gestures, a **spoken language** <note>original: "Wortsprache"</note> would never have become possible, and mute animals would [lack] all understan—

It simply depends on which faith is stronger: the faith in the occurrence of the effect, or the faith in one's own power of resistance; according to this, the unconscious will leans to one side or the other. The art of such cures is therefore merely to instill faith in the success; and because people do not know this connection—and the faith resulting from such knowledge might be too weak to be effective—superstition must create the faith, and for this purpose all sorts of **hocus pocus** serve. Of the unconscious will, the saying literally applies: "The more will, the more power," and that is the key to **magic**.
