# VIII.

## The Unconscious in Organic Formation.

In the previous two sections, we have already found ourselves occasionally unable to avoid anticipating the contents of this chapter. This is because the subjects treated one after the other are so intimately entwined with the **formative drive** <term>German "Bildungstrieb"; the innate biological impulse that directs the growth, development, and shaping of a living organism</term>—indeed, they are one and the same—that in an attempt to keep them seemingly separate, a large portion of the most striking phenomena would have had to remain entirely disregarded. 

We have seen that the most general conceptual expression under which all these areas can be grouped is that of **instinct**; but one can just as easily view almost all of them as **reflex actions** <term>German "Reflexwirkungen"; automatic physical responses to stimuli</term>, for an external motive for action must always be present, and the action follows this motive by necessity—that is, reflexively—even if it is only mediated indirectly through various reflections. 

Equally, however, one can also view all these phenomena as effects of **nature’s healing power** <term>German "Naturheilkraft"; the inherent ability of a living body to restore itself to health without external medical intervention</term>; for only where the external motive is a foreign, resisting substance can it act as a motive; otherwise, it leaves things *indifferent* <note>In this context, "indifferent" means the stimulus fails to provoke a reaction because it does not threaten or change the organism's state</note>. The mastering of the material, however, is an act of nature’s healing power. 

The unique quality of the formative drive would be found in the realization of the **typical idea of the species** <note>The "typical idea" refers to the biological blueprint or archetype that determines what a specific animal or plant should look like and how it should function</note> at the stage appropriate to it at every age of life, whereas nature’s healing power would consist in the self-preservation of that realized idea. One sees, however, that on the one hand, the warding off of a disturbance is only possible through new formation—that is, that the self-preservation of the realized idea is not possible except through simultaneous development, and thus the realization of a new stage of the idea. On the other hand, the realization of a new stage of the idea consists only in a series of struggles and acts of self-preservation, since all...

Chapter C. XIII.). Now, one could certainly imagine the producer and consumer united in a single being, where one vegetative half of the organism creates the substances from whose consumption the other animal half develops its consciousness. It is, in fact, evident that an animal bound to the soil <note>original: "an die Scholle... gebunden"; a phrase suggesting being tied to a specific piece of land</note> on which it grows (as the transitional forms of lower aquatic animals into the plant kingdom show) is capable of no extensive experience and thus no higher mental development; one must therefore demand **locomobility** <term>Locomobility; the ability to move spontaneously from one place to another</term> as a condition for a higher level of consciousness. If, however, the substances from which organic matter (i.e., the only matter capable of supporting higher consciousness) can be formed must essentially be drawn from the water permeating the soil, and if this requires the expansion of a large surface area beneath the earth (**root fibers**), then it is clear that no beings of higher levels of consciousness can form directly from inorganic nature, since locomotion is impossible with such underground dispersal. This dictates the locomobility of animals and the stability of plants, and thus the separation of both kingdoms.

The animals must therefore seek out their food, and for this they require not only organs of movement, but also organs to distinguish between substances suitable and unsuitable for their nourishment, and to be able to carry out their movements with certainty. These are the **sensory tools**. Furthermore, the organism can only assimilate matter through resorption <term>Resorption; the process of absorbing or "soaking up" nutrients into the body's systems</term>; therefore, this matter must be in liquid form. Plants find their food already in this state, but animals find it mostly in solid form; they must therefore [have] organs...

<meta>This page continues the functional analysis of the animal organism as distinct from plants, focusing on the five physiological systems necessary to support consciousness and movement.</meta>

...[animals must] have [organs] in order to first return this solid food into a liquid form; the **digestive system** serves this purpose with its grinding organs (mouth and stomach), its dissolving juices (saliva, gastric juice, intestinal mucus, bile), its long channels, and finally the outlet for undigested materials. The chyle vessels <note>vessels that transport fatty lymph, or chyle, from the intestines to the blood</note>, which absorb the food pulp, are the root fibers of the animal. Since the animal consumes far more matter than the plant due to its incomparably greater dynamic achievements, a more rapid replacement must be ensured; the system of **blood circulation** serves this purpose, constantly offering new materials in the most suitable form for assimilation <term>German "Assimilation"; the process of absorbing nutrients into the body's cells</term> to all parts of the organism. Since the chemical **process** in the animal is essentially one of regression—that is, an **oxidation process**—care must be taken to provide the necessary oxygen. Plants require no special organs for interaction with the atmosphere because their surface area, which is exceptionally large relative to their internal volume, sufficiently facilitates diffusion; in the animal, however, whose surface area must be many thousands of times smaller than that of plants for other reasons, the necessary amount of oxygen must be introduced into the body through special organs with a large internal surface area (**branching of the trachea** <term>German "Luftröhrenverästelung"; the network of tubes in the respiratory system, such as the bronchi</term>), with vigorous ventilation and through a rapid exchange of the adjacent air layers by means of **ciliary movement** <note>the rhythmic beating of microscopic hair-like structures to move fluids or air</note>, as well as through a composition of the separating membranes favorable to diffusion. This oxidation process simultaneously produces animal heat, which is a condition for the more subtle changes of organic matter, or at least spares the psychic influence a large portion of the expenditure of force.

Thus, from consciousness as the purpose of animal life, we have already derived the necessity of five systems: those of movement, sense organs, digestion, blood circulation, and respiration. What determines the overall external form of the body is primarily the first of these: the system of movement. Its fundamental principle is **contraction**, as we already see in **ciliary movement** and the movements of lower aquatic animals. However, as soon as the other systems have reached a certain degree of development, the contractile mass requires support points <note>or "anchor points," implying the development of a skeletal structure</note> within its own body in order to be able to undertake more partial movements in more diverse directions; this need arises immediately for land animals (and even among the

<meta>This page transitions from the physical description of biological systems to a philosophical defense of teleology (purposeful design) in nature. It addresses common criticisms regarding "poor design" in the natural world by introducing the principle of biological economy and the concept of a "formative drive" that anticipates future needs.</meta>

A common error is to doubt the purposeful design <term>German "Zweckmässigkeit"; the idea that nature's structures are perfectly suited to their functions</term> of organisms simply because they do not fulfill certain requirements of suitability that we take the liberty of demanding of them. It should be obvious to everyone that perfect suitability in every detail is impossible; for if it were, no disease or weakness could ever overcome the body, and it would thus be immortal. If one demands that the human skull should be able to withstand the blow of a hailstone the size of a fist, and declares it poorly designed because it does not, this is clearly foolish; for its construction for such exceptional cases would bring other and much greater drawbacks in its wake. Most cases where it is claimed that organisms are poorly designed are of this nature; it boils down to the fact that they lack features which would be useful in certain instances, but useless or harmful in most other cases or relationships. Another type of criticism regarding a lack of purpose is made possible by the constancy of basic morphological types <note>the fundamental structural patterns shared by different species, such as the similar bone structure in a human hand and a bat's wing</note>, which constitutes a pervasive law of nature and only places the unity of all organic forms—the unity of the entire plan of creation—in an even brighter light. This is the **law of parsimony** <note>original: "lex parsimoniae"; the principle that nature tends to take the simplest or most economical path</note>, which also proves true in the invention of organic forms; it is easier for nature to leave harmless, superfluous parts standing here and there than to constantly undertake changes and devise new ideas. Rather, nature adheres to the greatest possible unity of the idea, and makes only as many changes to it as are absolutely necessary. Of this kind are the rudimentary nipples in male mammals, the eyes of the blind mole-rat <note>German "Blindmoll"</note>, the tail vertebrae in tailless animals, the swim bladders in fish that always live on the seabed, the limbs of bats and whales <note>original: "Cetaceen"</note>, and the like.

Finally, it must be noted that in the purposeful action of the formative drive <term>German "Bildungstrieb"; a hypothesized inner force that directs the growth and shaping of an organism</term>, as well as in that of instinct, we must recognize a **clairvoyance of the unconscious** <term>German "Hellsehen des Unbewussten"; the idea that the unconscious mind "sees" and prepares for a future need it has not yet experienced</term>. This is because all organs are developed in fetal life earlier than they come into use, and often even significantly earlier (e.g., the reproductive organs). The child has lungs before it breathes, eyes before it sees, and yet it can in no way have knowledge of its future states except through clairvoyance while it is still forming these organs;

Just as instinct teaches squirrels and other animals to collect and store food more abundantly when a cold winter is approaching, so too do dogs, horses, and wild game grow a thicker winter coat in such years; but if one moves horses to hot climates, after a few years they no longer grow any winter hair at all. Predators, which through their digestion are instinctively dependent on a diet of meat, have also provided themselves with the necessary strength, speed, weapons, and keen sight or smell. 

Just as instinct teaches many birds to hide their nests through similarity of color to the surroundings, so **formative activity** has granted protection to countless beings through similarity to their habitat (especially parasites). Could it really be a different principle that inspires the urge to act and simultaneously provides the means to carry it out?

This, then, is the answer to all objections that might have been raised in the course of this investigation regarding the well-known evidence of functional **mechanisms**: 1) the concept of a mechanism does not exhaust the facts; rather, the outputs of a mechanism, where one exists, always leave a remainder for the <term>psychic activity</term> <note>original: *seelischen Wirken*; the active influence of the soul or unconscious mind on physical matter.</note> to perform immediately; and 2) the <term>purposefulness</term> <note>original: *Zweckmässigkeit*; the teleological idea that biological structures are designed for a specific goal or function.</note> of the mechanism implies the **purposefulness of its origin**, and this origin is always left to the soul.

If we continue backward in the chain of material causes, considering that every organic process has two causes—one psychic and one material—we arrive, with total strictness and regardless of our starting point, at the newly fertilized egg as the final material cause. Where the development of the egg occurs entirely or partially within the maternal organism, the material influences of the mother certainly play a role; however, in the case of the eggs of fish and amphibians fertilized outside the female body, this is not even the case. In this backward progression, it should be noted that the psychic causes generally become more significant relative to the material ones the younger the individual is (as we have already seen in the strength of the <term>natural healing power</term> <note>original: *Naturheilkraft*; the "vis medicatrix naturae," or the body's innate ability to heal itself.</note>). In older age, the organism mostly lives off the achievements of better times; before puberty, however, it continually produces partly growing and partly new feats, and in the life of the <term>embryo</term>, the importance of psychic influences increases all the more the younger the periods in which we observe it.

The newly fertilized egg is a cell (it consists only of the yolk), the wall of which represents the <term>yolk membrane</term> <note>original: *Dotterhaut*; the vitelline membrane surrounding the egg cell.</note>, the content of which is the yolk, and the nucleus of which is the <term>germinal vesicle</term> <note>original: *Keimbläschen*; an early biological term for the nucleus of the oocyte.</note>. In higher animals, the germinal disc within the germinal vesicle (which in humans is about 1/200 of a <term>line</term> <note>A "line" was a historical unit of measurement; 1/200 of a line is approximately 0.01 millimeters.</note> in size) is the part from which the embryo alone develops, albeit with the help of the yolk. Every part of the egg shows within itself a thoroughly uniform structure (partly granular with embedded fat droplets, partly membranous and...

# I.

## Instinct in the Human Spirit.

Just as it is impossible to strictly separate **body and soul** <note>original: *Leib und Seele*; *Leib* refers specifically to the living, physical body, while *Seele* is the animating soul or psyche.</note> in our observations, it is equally impossible to separate those **instincts** that relate to bodily needs from those relating to mental needs. Thus, in the previous section, we have already mentioned various instincts of the **human spirit**, such as: the capricious **appetites** of the sick or the pregnant, and the **healing instincts** of children or **somnambulist persons** <note>In the 19th century, "somnambulism" often referred to a trance-like state associated with mesmerism or "animal magnetism," where individuals were thought to possess heightened intuitive or healing powers.</note>; several others connect directly to the bodily instincts, for example: the fear of a yet-unknown fall in young animals and children, who, for instance, are calm when carried up the stairs but restless when carried down; the greater caution and deliberateness in the movements of pregnant horses and women; the drive of mothers to place the **newborn** at the breast; the child’s drive to suckle; the peculiar talent of children for distinguishing true friendliness from that which is feigned; the instinctive shyness toward certain unknown persons, which occurs specifically in pure, inexperienced girls; the good and bad premonitions which—particularly in the female sex—possess great motivational power for the commission or omission of actions, and so on. — In this chapter, we wish to consider those human instincts that align even more closely with physicality, and which, for that reason, are usually granted the name "instinct." Meanwhile, the hollow conceit of "human dignity" recoils at allowing this word for any expressions of the **Unconscious** <note>original: *Unbewusstes*; a central concept for the author, referring to the mental processes that occur without conscious awareness but guide biological and psychological life.</note> that are further removed from physicality, because the term seems to carry a certain animalistic quality.

First, we must consider several **repulsive instincts** <note>In this context, "repulsive" (*repulsive Instincte*) refers to defensive or "pushing away" drives—the instinctive avoidance of harmful things—rather than "repulsive" in the sense of being disgusting.</note>

It is not the fear of the Last Judgment or other metaphysical hypotheses, nor **Hamlet's** doubt regarding "what dreams may come," nor **Egmont's** "friendly habit of existence and activity" <note>A reference to Goethe’s play *Egmont*, where the hero speaks of his natural, cheerful attachment to life.</note> that would stay the hand of the suicide; rather, **instinct** does it with its mysterious shudder, with its racing heartbeat that drives all the blood raging through the veins.

Just as compassion is the primary instinct for the **production** of charitable actions—those whose effects extend beyond the sphere of egoism—so the instinct of gratitude appears as a **multiplier** of these actions. Even if gratitude occasionally leads to the injury of a third party <note>For example, showing favoritism to a benefactor at the expense of someone more deserving.</note>, these are rare cases; the overall utility of this instinct cannot be overlooked, even if it finds its correction—or even its replacement—in a fully developed moral system <term>Sittenlehre: The formal study of morals and customs; ethics.</term>. Just as the impulse for retribution becomes a **multiplier** of morally beautiful action in relation to benefits received, so it becomes the first founder of a sense of justice as the instinct for revenge in relation to injuries. For as long as the community <term>Gemeinwesen: The collective society or "commonwealth."</term> has not taken it upon itself to satisfy the individual's desire for vengeance, revenge through self-help is rightly regarded as something sacred—a primitive institution of law. It is revenge that must gradually form, heighten, and clarify the sense of justice until the conception of law gains a firm footing in national custom; only then can the transfer of retribution to the community take place. By this, I by no means intend to claim that compassion and the impulse for retribution are the factors from which moral and legal theory must be theoretically derived and justified—on the contrary, I would not concede that. My only claim is that, in practice, they are indeed the roots from which those feelings and actions sprout, from which humans first obtain the concepts of moral beauty and law through abstraction.

From these first two laws, the following can be concluded: the instinct of motherly love generally gains greater significance and scope the higher the stages of the animal kingdom we ascend—though these stages are intended psychologically rather than zoologically. However much the **method** of this instruction is a conscious product of these animals' minds, the drive to instruct the young at all is fundamentally **instinct**.

I am not speaking here of love, nor of the sexual drive in general; rather, where the former is entirely absent and the latter would by no means provide a sufficient motive, the drive to establish a household sets in during a man's more mature years. Even if the poor fellow clearly sees that he must go hungry, while as a bachelor he would have a good livelihood, he marries anyway. It is the same drive that commands the four- to five-year-old young stallion to leave his parents' family with some of his sisters to form his own family, and which compels birds to build nests. They know as little as that "poor fellow" does that the toil and deprivation they impose upon themselves out of instinct have no other purpose than to make the preservation of the species <term>Erhaltung der Gattung</term> possible.

Thus, among many animals (chickens, seals, moles, certain monkeys), the males fight for possession of the females who appear particularly desirable; among many colorful animals, these particularly desirable ones are those with the most beautiful colors; among different races <note>In 19th-century biological contexts, "race" (*Race*) was frequently used to describe what we would now call breeds or sub-species.</note> or varieties within a genus, they are individuals of the same race—for example, among humans and dogs. Mutts often make the greatest sacrifices to get together with a female of their own race with whom they have fallen in love. They not only run many miles, but I also know of a case where a dog, despite his wooden clog <note>original: *Kreuzknüppel*. A heavy piece of wood or "clog" fastened to an animal’s neck or leg to hinder its movement and prevent it from running away.</note>, visited his beloved every night over a mile away, and arrived back every morning exhausted and chafed; since the clog did not help, he was put on a chain; here, however, he became so unruly that he was let completely free again, because it was feared he would go mad <note>original: *toll*. This could refer to rabies or simply a state of frantic insanity caused by distress.</note>. At the same time, there were plenty of female dogs in his own yard. Noble stallions, too, are said to usually disdain mating with common, worn-out mares.

Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), the German philosopher whose "Metaphysics of Sexual Love" heavily influenced the author's views on instinct and the "Will."</note> remarks very correctly that from the instinct of sexual love which we experience in ourselves, we may draw conclusions about animal instincts, and assume that in them, too, consciousness is deceived by the expectation of a special pleasure. This delusion, however, arises only from the drive, is proportional to the strength of the drive, and is nothing other than the drive itself in connection with the application of conscious experience: that pleasure in the satisfaction of a drive is generally proportional to the strength of that drive. This is a premise that is simply not confirmed in the case of those drives whose primary weight and significance fall into the **Unconscious** (see Chapter C. III.) and therefore becomes a deceptive delusion. This remark is therefore to be restricted to those animals whose consciousness is capable of such generalizations; in the case of lower animals, it simply remains a compelling drive, without reaching the expectation of pleasure. — Moreover, how useful that delusion is even for the individuals of the higher animal species can be seen from the fact that precisely

One might perhaps wish to object that, according to the theory of polar completion <note>The idea that individuals seek a partner who "completes" their own biological or spiritual imbalances (e.g., a very tall person being attracted to a shorter person to maintain a medium height in the next generation).</note>, there could be no such thing as unrequited love; however, this is clearly a hasty and false objection. Added to this in such a case is that not only do the children benefit from this polar correspondence, but in **another** respect than the passion of love imagines, so do the **parents**; because for the **highest friendship**, the **polar correspondence** of souls is also the most favorable condition.

# III.

## The Unconscious in Feeling.

---

If I have a toothache and a pain in my finger, these are clearly two different things, for one is in the tooth and the other is in the finger. If I did not have the ability to **spatially project** <term>spatial projection: The psychological process by which the mind assigns a physical sensation to a specific location in space or on the body.</term> my perceptions, I would not perceive two distinct pains, but rather one mixed sensation composed of both. This is similar to how, when two pure tones (without overtones) are played an octave apart, one hears absolutely only one tone—the lower one—but with a changed **timbre** <note>original: *Klangfarbe*. Literally "sound-color," referring to the quality or character of a musical sound.</note>. The difference in the *location* of the perception thus gives the soul the ability to break down the "consonance of pain" into its elements according to the different locations perceived. It allows the soul to link one part of the pain with one spatial representation and the other part with another, thereby establishing the fact that there are two separate pains.

Now, things can be spatially distinct and yet otherwise identical, such as two congruent triangles. This certainly cannot be said of toothache and finger pain; first, they can differ by *degree*—that is, by **intensive quantity** <note>A philosophical term referring to the strength or magnitude of a sensation (like heat or pain) that can be felt in varying degrees but cannot be measured by physical extension.</note>—and second, they can differ by *quality*. Even at the same level of intensity, a pain can be continuous or intermittent, burning, chilling, pressing, throbbing, stinging, biting, cutting, drawing, twitching, or tickling. It can show an infinite number of variations that simply cannot be described.

Up until now, we have understood "pain" as a single whole. However, the question arises whether we must forbid this from a philosophical standpoint. Instead, within this given "whole," we should distinguish between the **sensory perception** and the **pain**—or **unpleasure** <term>unpleasure: Translated from the German *Unlust*, this refers to the psychological state of dissatisfaction or suffering. It is used here to distinguish the "bad feeling" from the neutral physical sensation of being touched.</term>—in the narrower sense. For we often experience a perception that produces neither pleasure nor pain; for example, if I press my finger lightly or brush my skin. While this perception—

<summary>The author examines how we differentiate physical sensations, arguing that the mind uses spatial location and qualitative variety (like throbbing or stinging) to distinguish between pains. He begins to argue that "pain" is a composite experience, separating the neutral physical sensation from the psychological state of "unpleasure."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "consonance of pain." The word fragment "mung" completes the term "intermittence" (Intermittierung) from the previous page, referring to sensations that pulse or pause.</meta>

[intermittence] remains qualitatively unchanged, and only increases or decreases in its degree, pleasure or displeasure can be added; but should the perception <term>perception (Wahrnehmung): In this context, the raw sensory data or the mental awareness of a stimulus, distinct from the emotional reaction to it.</term> then suddenly be included within the pain or the pleasure? We must therefore separate the two, and we soon recognize that they are so little "at one" that they actually stand in a causal relationship; for the perception (or a part of it) is the cause of the pain, since the pain appears and disappears with it and never appears without it, whereas the perception can, under special circumstances, exist without the pain.

Once this separation is made, the question naturally arises: do the mentioned differences really reside in the pleasure and pain themselves, or merely in the causing and accompanying circumstances—namely, in the perception? It is clear that pain allows for intensive quantitative differences <note>Referring to the strength or "loudness" of the pain.</note>, but does it also allow for qualitative ones? Most differences that we describe with words boil down to different forms of **intermittence** <note>The pattern of stopping and starting or pulsing.</note>, such as throbbing, pulling, twitching, stinging, cutting, biting, or even tickling. Here, of course, the degree of pain changes continuously with the degree of perception according to certain more or less regular types, but no originally qualitative difference in the pain itself is to be found. One might much more readily suspect this in the case of the **pleasure** <note>original: *Lust*</note> or **displeasure** <note>original: *Unlust*</note> evoked by various smells and tastes. However, even here, through sharp self-observation, one will be convinced that the qualitative diversity of pleasure and displeasure is entirely apparent; this deception arises because no one has previously attempted the separation of pleasure and displeasure from perception. Instead, one has been accustomed to grasping both together with the perception as a single whole, so that the differences in perception now present themselves as differences in this unified whole. The reason we have never made this separation is that, from the infinitely manifold composition of **mental states** <note>original: *Seelenzuständen*</note>, we only learn to isolate those groups as independent parts which bring a real benefit to our practical needs.

Thus, for example, in a **chord** <note>original: *Accord*</note> played by a full orchestra, one does not pick out all the tones of a certain pitch, regardless of which instruments they come from (including their **overtones** <note>original: *Obertöne*. The higher frequencies that give an instrument its specific character.</note>), but rather one groups together those from a single instrument...

the various overtones produced by the instrument merge with the fundamental tone of the instrument into its timbre <term>timbre (Klangfarbe): The specific quality of a sound that allows us to distinguish a trumpet from a violin, even when they play the same note.</term>, and the tone clusters thus formed, which represent the tones produced by each individual instrument, are only then grouped together as a chord. This is simply because knowing the overtones offers no practical interest, whereas knowing the timbres of the instruments does. And this practical way of grouping tone clusters is so ingrained in us that doing so based on mere pitches—though it must obviously be much easier—is quite impossible for us; so impossible, in fact, that it was only a few years ago that Helmholtz <note>Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894) was a German physicist and physician who revolutionized our understanding of acoustics by proving that timbre is created by the combination of a fundamental tone and its overtones.</note> strictly proved the origin of timbres through the combination of overtones. This will be achieved more easily the simpler the examples one starts with—for instance, whether the pleasure of hearing the sound of a bell is different when the tone is *c* and when it is *d*. Once one has understood the matter in such simple examples, it will also become clear as one gradually ascends to examples containing greater differences in perception. One can also see a confirmation of the proposition in reverse, in the fact that one is able to **weigh up** different sensory enjoyments or pains against each other (e.g., whether someone, for the thaler <note>A silver coin used throughout Europe for centuries; the ancestor of the word "dollar."</note> they have to spend, would rather drink a bottle of wine, or eat cake and ice cream, or beefsteak with beer, or whether they would grant themselves the satisfaction of some other sensory need; or whether one endures a toothache for days on end or would rather have the tooth pulled). This mutual **weighing up** <note>original: *Abwägen*</note> would not be possible if pleasure and displeasure in all these things were not merely quantitatively different and qualitatively the same; for only like can be measured with like.

Whether my friend A or my friend B dies may change the degree, but not the kind of my pain; just as little as whether my wife or a child dies, even though my love for both was of a completely different kind, and thus the mental images and thoughts <term>mental images (Vorstellungen): In 19th-century psychology, this term refers to the conscious representations, ideas, or "pictures" we form in our minds about objects or losses.</term> which I form regarding the nature of the loss are completely different. That which is pain, and nothing but pain, differs everywhere only by degree. The same applies to the pleasure I feel when someone else finally yields to my stubborn will after long resistance, or when I win the lottery, or receive a higher position. That pleasure and displeasure are everywhere the same is also evident here from the fact that one measures one against the other; upon this weighing of future pleasure and displeasure, every rational practical reflection and every decision made by a human being is based—for one can only **measure like with like**, not hay with straw, or pecks with <note>The "Metze" (peck) was a historical dry unit of measure for grain. ...pounds. This reason, which is also hinted at in the unity of the name itself, is what determines us to consider sensory and mental pleasure as the same. We therefore hold as a result that pleasure and displeasure in all feelings are only *one*, or that they differ not in quality, but only in degree. That pleasure and displeasure cancel each other out—behaving like positive and negative values—and that the zero point between them is the indifference of feeling, is clear; it is equally clear that it is immaterial which of the two one wishes to assume as positive, just as immaterial as the question of whether one takes the right or the left side of the **abscissa axis** <term>abscissa axis: The horizontal (x) axis in a coordinate system. In contrast, it has been recognized by most significant thinkers of all time that pleasure and displeasure stand in the closest connection with the innermost life of man, with his interests and inclinations, his actions and strivings—in a word, with the realm of the **Will**. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding the psychological nature of pleasure and unpleasure. All opinions on this matter can be reduced to two fundamental views: they either understand pleasure as the satisfaction and unpleasure as the non-satisfaction of desire, or, conversely, they see desire as the representation of future pleasure and aversion (negative desire) as the representation of future unpleasure. In the first case, the Will is understood as the primary element; in the latter, Feeling is seen as the primary element. Which of these two is correct is not difficult to see. Firstly, in the case of instinct, the drive <note>German: *Trieb*</note> actually exists before any representation <term>representation: The mental image or idea of something (German: *Vorstellung*). The author argues we often act on impulse before we even have a mental picture of what pleasure the action might bring.</term> of pleasure; its actual goal here is something other than the individual pleasure of satisfaction. Secondly, while the explanation of pleasure as the satisfaction of the Will explains everything about pleasure sufficiently, the reverse—explaining everything about the Will as the representation of pleasure—does not work. In that case, the actual driving force, the Will as acting causality, remains completely incomprehensible. Precisely because the Will is the externalization <note>The outward movement of energy or action.</note>, while pleasure and unpleasure are the return from this externalization to oneself (and thus the conclusion of this process), the Will must be the primary moment, and pleasure the secondary one.

If we let this view stand for the time being, we obtain an unexpected confirmation of the essential equality of pleasure and unpleasure in all feelings. We have, in fact, seen earlier that the Will is also always one and the same, and differs firstly only in its degree of strength and secondly in its object—which is no longer Will, but representation. Now, if pleasure is the satisfaction and unpleasure the non-satisfaction of the Will, it is clear that these too must always be one and the same, and can only differ according to their degree. The apparent qualitative differences they contain are provided by accompanying representations—partly by those that make up the object of the Will, and partly by those that bring about the satisfaction of the Will. From this, there results for all states of the mind <note>German: *Gemüth*</note>, regardless of their variety, such a great simplicity that, according to the old saying: "simplicity is the seal of truth" <note>original: "*simplex sigillum veri*"</note>, this must retrospectively support the propositions from which it arises, just as these support and make each other probable through the power of analogy.

In such doubtful cases, we frequently believe we want what appears good and praiseworthy to us; for example, that a sick relative from whom we are to inherit should not die, or that in a <term>collision</term> <note>A conflict or clash of interests.</note> between the common good and our individual well-being, the former should be prioritized; or that a previously made commitment should remain in force; or that our rational conviction, rather than our inclination and passion, should be satisfied. 

This belief can be so firm that afterwards, when the outcome goes against our supposed will and yet we are overcome not by sorrow but by a sense of exuberant joy, we are utterly beside ourselves with astonishment at our own reaction. In this joy, we suddenly become aware of our delusion and learn that we unconsciously desired the opposite of what we had imagined ourselves to want. Since, in this case, we can only infer our actual will from our pleasure or unpleasure, this pleasure, when it occurs, clearly consists in the satisfaction of an unconscious will. 

This becomes even more evident if we consider how—starting from the most extreme astonishment that such a will could have existed unconsciously in one’s own soul—there is a gradual transition through slight suspicion, doubt, and the hunch that one might actually want "that" and not what one imagines, until finally reaching open self-deception, where one knows perfectly well what they want but tries with more or less success to persuade themselves and others that they want the opposite. # IV.

## The Unconscious in Character and Morality.

---

No manifestation of the will occurs without a cause of arousal, a motive. The will in itself is a potential state of being, a latent force, and its transition into actual being—into the **manifestation of force** <term>manifestation of force: from the German 'Kraftäusserung', referring to the outward expression or exercise of an internal energy or capacity</term>—requires a motive as its sufficient ground, which always takes the form of a **mental representation** <term>mental representation: from the German 'Vorstellung', the internal image, idea, or concept we have of an object or goal that directs our actions</term>. I take these principles of psychology for granted. Willing itself differs only in intensity; all other apparent differences in willing lie in its objects—that is, in the representations of what is being willed—and these objects are, in turn, conditioned by motives. According to the various main classes of the most common **objects of willing** among humans, willing itself is categorized into different primary directions, such as sensory pleasure-seeking, greed and avarice, vanity, ambition and the quest for fame, the impulse for love, the artistic drive, the thirst for knowledge and the urge for research, and so on.

If these objects were dependent **alone** on motives, then psychology would be very simple, and the psychological mechanism would be identical in all individuals. Experience shows, however, that one and the same motive—quite apart from accidental differences in mood—affects different individuals differently. The opinion of others leaves one person indifferent, while to another it means everything; the poet’s laurel crown seems contemptible to one, while another sacrifices his life's happiness for it; likewise with a beautiful woman. One person sacrifices his fortune to save his honor, while another sells his honor for a sum of money; good teachings and noble examples spur one person to emulation, while they leave another untouched; rational deliberation

---

How a specific individual will behave toward this or that motive cannot be known until one has experienced it; but if one knows how a person reacts to all possible motives, then one knows all of their peculiarities, and thus one knows their **character**. Character is therefore the **mode of reaction** <term>mode of reaction: from the German 'Reactionsmodus', the specific way an individual's will consistently responds to external stimuli or internal ideas</term> to every particular class of motives, or what amounts to the same thing, the sum total of the susceptibilities to arousal for every particular class of **desires** <term>desires: from 'Begehrungen', which refers to the various drives, cravings, or impulses that pull a person toward an object or goal</term>. Since there is no motive that belongs exclusively to one of those classes, a greater number of desires are always, or at least as a rule, affected simultaneously, and the **resultant** <note>In physics, a 'resultant' is a single force that represents the combined effect of multiple forces; the author uses this to describe how competing desires resolve into a single action.</note> of these simultaneously excited desires is the **actual will**, which proceeds irresistibly and immediately to action, provided this is not prevented by physical causes.

If we now ask what kind of process this reaction of the will to the motive is, and this interplay of desires into a single resultant, we must admit that although we recognize its existence through indubitable inferences from facts that fall within consciousness, we can say nothing about its nature and manner because our consciousness gives us no report of it. In each individual case, we know only the starting link—the motive—and the ending link—the **actual will**; but we can never experience what the **potential will**, the reacting element, is, nor can we ever gain an insight into the essence of the reaction through which the potential state passes into the actual state. This is a reaction that bears entirely the character of a **reflex action** or a reflexive instinct, as we have already seen above in the special case of **compassion** <note>The author likely refers to a previous chapter where he argues that pity or compassion is an immediate, unconscious response to the suffering of others.</note>. We do have a partial consciousness of the struggle of different desires against one another, but only insofar as we have experienced the individual desires separately as final resultants in earlier, simpler cases, and apply our previous experiences to the present. However, everyone will have already experienced within themselves how incomplete these experiences are, and how imperfectly they are used to understand a present **mental process** <term>mental process: from 'Seelenvorgang', literally a 'soul-process' or psychological event</term>.

How often does **consciousness** believe it has most carefully weighed the strength of all the **desires** involved in a case and left none unconsidered; yet, when it comes to action, it sees to its greatest surprise that its cleverly calculated result does not match at all, but instead a completely different **resultant** <note>original: "Resultante". In the 19th century, philosophers often used physics metaphors; here, the "resultant" is the single final force produced when multiple competing desires pull in different directions.</note> emerges as the sovereign **will**. One may recall the indications regarding the unconscious will given in the previous chapter (p. 195). It thus appears that there is in **fact** only one certain indicator for the actual, true, and final **will**, and that is the **deed** (regardless of whether it succeeds or is stifled in its first attempt by external circumstances). Every other assumption by **consciousness** regarding what one actually wants remains an uncertain, often deceptive presumption, which is by no means based on an immediate knowledge of the **will** by **consciousness**, but rather on analogies of experience and artificial combinations thereof. 

Like chaff before the wind, the firmest **resolution**, the most certain **intention**, often scatters at the **deed**, where the true **will** first emerges from the night of the **unconscious**, while the **will** of the **intention** was only a one-sided **desire**, or perhaps even merely imagined by consciousness and not present at all. But if the **deed** never approaches a person—for example, because they always keep the impossibility of its execution in mind—then they also never gain **certainty** about what they actually want in the depths of their heart. The so-called conscious **choice of will** <term>choice of will: from 'Willenswahl', referring to the process of deliberation before a decision</term> and its **fluctuation** is by no means a conscious **fluctuation** of the **will**, but a **fluctuation** of **cognition** <term>cognition: from 'Erkenntniss', meaning the intellectual process of gathering and processing information</term> regarding the correct **understanding** of **motives** and how circumstances now and in the future will shape and relate themselves to the **will**. 

Once **cognition** is clear, however, so too is the **will**. For example: the **fluctuation** of my **choice** whether I should marry the clever and ugly sister, or the stupid and beautiful one, is not a **fluctuation** of my **will**, which for the time being does not emerge at all, but of my **intellect** <term>intellect: from 'Verstand', the faculty of reasoning and calculating outcomes</term> regarding the magnitude of **pleasure** <note>original: "Lust". In this context, it refers to the psychological satisfaction or happiness expected from a choice.</note> to be expected in each case; only after the intellect has chosen is the **motive** created for the **will**, namely the representation of the greater **pleasure** to be expected.

It is therefore to be maintained that the workshop of the will lies in the unconscious, and that one [perceives] only the finished result, and indeed—

This refers to the internal moral criteria or "yardstick" used to judge one's own behavior.</note>. Thus, it happens that we call one and the same action "moral" or "immoral" in one being, but not in another.

For example, we would describe the strict **sense of property** <note>original: "Eigenthumssinn."</note> found in some animals within their species and close-knit communities—such as wild horses within their herd regarding grazing spots and stored fodder—not as a "moral" trait, but merely as a "good" quality. Similarly, we cannot call it "immoral" when tribal peoples <note>The author uses "wilde Völkerschaften" (wild peoples), reflecting 19th-century anthropological views that categorized cultures by "stages" of development.</note> offer even their wives to a guest; on the contrary, this could be called **moral** as part of the duty of **hospitality**, because their consciousness is developed enough to understand that duty, but not yet developed enough to understand **modesty** <note>original: "Sittsamkeit." This term implies both sexual propriety and social decorum.</note> in sexual relations. 

In a small child, we might call certain outbursts of malice merely "bad" at most, whereas the same character traits in a person of mature age would be condemned as "immoral." **Blood revenge** <note>original: "Blutrache," or the practice of a family seeking lethal retribution for a slain relative.</note> would be immoral among us, but in cultures of "lesser cultivation," it is a moral institution; meanwhile, among completely "primitive" peoples, it is a mere act of passion that can be called neither moral nor immoral.

These examples should suffice to prove that "moral" and "immoral" are not properties of beings or their actions **in themselves** <note>original: "an sich." A philosophical term meaning the essential nature of a thing independent of how it is perceived.</note>. Rather, they are **judgments** passed upon them from a standpoint created only through **consciousness**. They are relationships between those beings and their actions on one side, and this standpoint of a higher level of consciousness on the other. Therefore, nature—insofar as it is **unconscious**—does not know the difference between moral and immoral. 

Indeed, **nature** in itself is not even "good" or "evil," but remains eternally nothing more than **natural**—that is, in accordance with itself. For the **universal will of nature** <note>original: "allgemeine Naturwille." A concept suggesting a single, underlying drive that directs all of existence.</note> has nothing outside of itself, because it encompasses everything and is everything itself; thus, nothing can be "good" or "evil" for it. These terms can only apply to an **individual will**, for the concepts of "good" and "evil" necessarily presuppose a relationship between a specific will and an external object.

<summary>This page argues that morality is not an inherent property of nature or actions, but a subjective judgment that emerges only as consciousness develops. It posits that the universal "will of nature" exists beyond human categories of good and evil.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the author's initial thoughts on how morality requires a certain level of consciousness. In all this, however, the value of this critical standpoint created by **consciousness** should by no means be diminished; only the error should be removed that the possibility of these concepts <note>Referring to "moral" and "immoral."</note> exists outside of this specific standpoint, as they only arise in relation to it. To be sure, if one assumes a consciousness outside of and prior to nature (in a personal God), then one can also apply the **standard** <note>original: "Maassstab." As noted previously, this refers to the internal criteria or "yardstick" used to judge behavior.</note> of those concepts to the world from the standpoint of that consciousness. However, if one denies—as we must do for reasons to be developed later—a consciousness outside the connection between **mind and matter**, then the possibility of applying the standard of those concepts to the entire unconscious world also disappears; a task upon which much useless work has already been wasted. 

All this, however, does not diminish the value of those concepts in any way. For just as consciousness, despite all its one-sidedness and limitation, stands in importance above the **unconscious** for this world, so in the end does the **moral** <term>the moral: "das Sittliche," referring to ethical behavior and social norms</term> stand higher than the **natural**; indeed, since consciousness is ultimately only an unconscious product of nature, the moral is not an opposite of the natural, but only a higher stage of it, to which the natural has raised itself by its own power and through the mediation of consciousness.

With these brief suggestions, I must content myself here, since an **ethics** carried out in this sense would constitute a work of its own. I also believed I had to forgo describing why and how the standpoint of judgment using the predicates **moral** and **immoral** must emerge from a certain height of consciousness, and what the content of those concepts might be. I felt all the more permitted to do this because the general understanding of those concepts as they occur in **civil life** <note>original: "bürgerlichen Leben." This refers to the conventional morality and social standards of everyday society.</note> seems sufficient for the purposes of our current investigation.

# V.
## The Unconscious in Aesthetic Judgment and Artistic Production.

---

In the perception of the beautiful, two extreme views have always stood opposed to one another, taking up varying amounts of space in different attempts at reconciliation. Some base their argument on the fact that the human soul, in art, goes beyond the beauty provided by nature; they consider this impossible unless the soul possesses an inherent **Idea of the Beautiful**. When grasped in a specific direction, this idea is called the **Ideal**, and it is the comparison of this ideal with existing nature that first determines what is beautiful and what is not. Thus, for this group, aesthetic judgment is an **a priori synthetic** <note>original: "apriorisch synthetisches." In Kantian philosophy, this refers to a judgment that adds new information to a concept (synthetic) and is known independently of sensory experience (a priori).</note> judgment. Others demonstrate that in those artistic creations which come closest to the alleged ideals, no elements are contained that nature does not also offer. They argue that the "idealizing" activity of the artist consists only in weeding out the ugly and collecting and uniting those beautiful elements which nature presents separately. These thinkers believe that aesthetic science, in its progress, has increasingly demonstrated the psychological process by which aesthetic judgment emerges from given psychological and physiological conditions, so that a complete illumination of this field and a purging of all "miraculous" a priori concepts is in prospect.

I believe that both sides are partly right and partly wrong. The **empiricists** <term>empiricists: those who believe that all knowledge is derived from sensory experience and observation</term> are right that every aesthetic judgment must be capable of being grounded in other psychological and physiological conditions, and for that reason, they are the ones who are actually creating a scientific aesthetics. Meanwhile, the **idealists** <term>idealists: here, philosophers who believe that the mind or "ideas" are the primary reality and that we have innate concepts of perfection</term>

<note>original vocabulary list: Unconscious, aesthetic judgment, artistic production, Ideal, a priori synthetic judgment, empiricists, idealists, aesthetics</note>

The author suggests a middle path, acknowledging the scientific value of the empiricists while preparing to defend the role of the unconscious.</summary>

<meta>The text continues the critique of the empiricist view of aesthetics begun on the previous page. The author argues that by reducing aesthetic judgment to purely psychological or physiological laws, empiricists fail to account for how beauty actually emerges within the individual’s conscious experience.</meta>

...cut themselves off from the possibility of this science with their own hypothesis. But even if we assume that the empiricists had achieved their goal and completely analyzed aesthetic judgment, they would have only proven its objective connection to other fields—demonstrating, as it were, its "citizenship" in the mind as a natural being. Yet, they would have left the subjective emergence of that judgment within individual consciousness completely untouched. Or, they would have asserted something fundamentally untrue by silently assuming that the objective connection and the process of emergence in the subjective consciousness are one and the same—a claim contradicted by any unbiased self-observation and the testimony of the sense of beauty in both the simplest and most refined individuals.

The idealists, on the other hand, will remain correct in asserting that this process lies beyond consciousness—existing prior to the conscious aesthetic judgment—and is therefore something **a priori** <note>original: "Apriorisches." In philosophy, this refers to knowledge or structures that exist in the mind independent of, and prior to, sensory experience.</note> for that judgment. However, they must also be proven wrong when they destroy the *process* within this *a priori* by replacing it with a "ready-made" ideal—one that appears from heaven knows where, whose existence consciousness knows nothing of, whose objective connection to other mental spheres remains eternally incomprehensible, and whose rigid nature ultimately proves inadequate when faced with the infinite variety of individual cases. 

If one were to avoid this latter criticism by assuming the ideal is not fixed but fluid, one would simply be positing infinitely many miracles instead of just one—though once you have allowed for *one* miracle, a few more hardly matter. 

To take an example, the idealists would have to judge tone, harmony, and **timbre** <term>timbre: the "color" or quality of a musical sound—for example, the difference between a trumpet and a violin playing the same note</term> based on an "ideal tone," "ideal harmony," and "ideal timbre," determining the value of a sound by how closely it approaches these perfections. Meanwhile, **Helmholtz** (in his work ***On the Sensations of Tone*** <note>original: "Ueber Tonempfindungen." A foundational 1863 text by Hermann von Helmholtz that merged the physics of sound with the physiology of the ear.</note>) demonstrates that in all three cases, **pleasure** is to be understood as the negation of a **displeasure** <note>original: "Lust" and "Unlust." These terms are central to 19th-century German psychology, describing the basic spectrum of positive and negative sensory experience.</note>. This displeasure is caused by disturbances in the ear—similar to the flickering of a light—produced by noise, dissonance, or an "ugly" timbre. 

This **displeasure** is no longer strictly aesthetic; it is just as much a slight physical **pain** as a stomach ache, a toothache, or the **pain** felt when a slate pencil screeches across a chalkboard. Thus, **aesthetic pleasure** in the sensory part of the

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how aesthetic judgments are formed, moving from the critique of empiricism and idealism to a psychological analysis of how sensations of pleasure and beauty arise from unconscious processes, drawing on the philosophy of John Locke.</meta>

Music has been proven in its objective connection to physical pain, but the way aesthetic judgment arises—the statement "this tone, this harmony, this timbre is beautiful"—is by no means characterized by me becoming conscious, while listening, of the following: "I am now feeling no pain through disturbances, and yet I feel a gentle stimulation of the organ's function, therefore I feel pleasure." Nothing of this or similar processes is found in consciousness; rather, the pleasure is **intrinsically** <note>original: "eo ipso." A Latin phrase meaning "by that very fact" or "thereby."</note> present in consciousness along with the listening. It stands there as if by magic, without the most intense attention being able to find a single hint in the subjective process regarding the manner of its origin. This by no means excludes the possibility that the objectively recognized connection actually takes place in the **unconscious** <note>The author suggests that while we don't "think" about the mechanics of why music sounds good, our nervous system and "unconscious" mind are doing the work behind the scenes.</note> as a process; in my view, this is even the only probable explanation. However, the result of this process is the only thing that enters consciousness—firstly, **momentarily** after the complete perception of the sensory observation (so that here, once again, the instantaneity of the process in the unconscious, its compression into a timeless moment, is confirmed), and secondly, not as an aesthetic judgment, but as a **sensation of pleasure or displeasure**.

This latter point must be considered more closely and will provide the best clarification of any remaining ambiguity. As **Locke** <note>John Locke (1632–1704) was an influential English philosopher who argued that qualities like color, taste, and sound are not "in" the objects themselves, but are produced in our minds by the objects.</note> already demonstrated, the words that designate the sensory qualities of bodies, such as "*sweet, red, soft*," have a double meaning, which common sense identifies without harm to practical life. Firstly, they designate the **state of the soul** during perception and sensation, and secondly, that quality of external objects which is supposed to be the cause of this state of the soul. Every sensation in itself is an individual occurrence; but by abstracting the common elements from various series of similar sensations, the concepts of "*sweet, red, soft*" are gained. By then placing the objective causes of these abstracted sensations into things as characteristic components—things already known through other influences—judgments arise such as: "sugar is sweet, the rose is red, fur is soft." — The same development underlies aesthetic judgment. The soul finds within itself a multitude of sensations which, though linked with individual peculiarities, yet share so much...

Conscious combination can be forced over time through the effort of the conscious will, through diligence, perseverance, and the resulting practice. The <term>conception</term> of the genius, however, is a passive reception without will; it does not come to him during the most strenuous searching, but quite unexpectedly—as if fallen from heaven—while traveling, at the theater, in conversation, wherever he least expects it, and always suddenly and momentarily. 

Conscious combination works laboriously from the smallest details upward, gradually building the whole while agonizing with doubt and racking one's brain, frequently discarding and resuming individual parts. The conception of genius receives the whole "as a single cast" <note>original: "aus Einem Guss"; a metaphor for a statue cast in a single mold rather than assembled from pieces</note> as an effortless gift from the gods. It is precisely the details that the genius still lacks—and must lack—because in larger compositions (group portraits, poetic works), the human spirit is too narrow to survey more than the most general total impression at a single glance. Combination creates the unity of the whole through laborious adjustment and experimentation with details, and therefore, despite all the work, never properly achieves it; instead, the "conglomerate" of many individual parts always remains visible in the finished product. > "...just as the artist is driven to production involuntarily and even with internal resistance (hence the sayings among the ancients: *to suffer God* <note>original: "pati Deum"; a phrase indicating that the artist is a passive vessel for divine influence</note> etc., and hence the general idea of inspiration through a foreign breath), so too does the objective element of his production come to him, as it were, without his assistance—that is, purely objectively. [On page 454 he says: 'Only that which arises unconsciously is objective; therefore, the truly objective in that intuition must not be capable of being added through consciousness.'] Just as the man of destiny does not perform what he wants or intends, but what he must perform through an incomprehensible fate under whose influence he stands, so the artist, however intentional he may be, seems to stand under the influence of a power regarding the truly objective aspect of his production. This power sets him apart from all other men and compels him to express or represent things which he himself does not fully see through, and whose meaning is infinite."

# VI.
## The Unconscious in the Origin of Language.

---

> “Since not only no philosophical consciousness, but no human consciousness at all, can be conceived of without language, the foundation of language could not have been laid with conscious awareness; and yet, the deeper we penetrate into it, the more clearly we discover that its depth far exceeds that of even the most consciously designed creation. — It is with language as it is with organic beings; we believe we see them arise blindly, yet we cannot deny the unfathomable intentionality of their formation down to the smallest detail.”

In these words by Schelling <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), a major German philosopher who argued that nature and spirit are part of a single organic whole.</note> (Works, Section II, Vol. 1, p. 52), the content of this chapter is outlined.

Let us first consider the philosophical value of grammatical forms and the formation of concepts. In every more highly developed language, we find the distinction between **subject** and **predicate**, between **subject** and **object**, between **noun** <note>original: "Substantivum"</note>, **verb** <note>original: "Verbum"</note>, and **adjective**, as well as the same conditions in sentence structure; in less developed languages, these basic forms are at least distinguished by their position in the sentence. Anyone familiar with the history of philosophy will know how much it owes to these linguistic forms alone. The concept of **judgment** is clearly abstracted from the grammatical sentence by stripping away the specific word forms; in the same way, the categories of **substance** and **accident** <term>Accident (Accidenz): In traditional philosophy, a property or quality that a thing possesses (like the color of a chair) which is not essential to its core nature (the "substance").</term> were extracted from subject and predicate. To find a corresponding conceptual opposition between noun and verb remains an unsolved, yet perhaps very fruitful, philosophical problem to this day; here, conscious speculation still lags far behind the unconscious creation of the genius of the

mankind. That the philosophical concepts of the **subject** and **object**—which, strictly speaking, were absent from ancient consciousness and today absolutely dominate speculation—developed from grammatical concepts in which they lay enveloped and unconsciously prefigured, is certainly not improbable, as their very names suggest. A corresponding philosophical yield from the other parts of the sentence, such as the so-called indirect object <note>original: "entfernteren Objects"</note> or the third person, is, in my conviction, still to be expected. By bringing this metaphysical thought—for which the word-form serves as a garment—to consciousness, no new relationships are **created**. Rather, those relationships that previously existed only through great detours in consciousness, or existed unified only in intuition or instinct, are brought into a unified form within the mind. Only then can they serve as a secure foundation for further speculation, much like how in mathematics the circular, elliptical, and Abelian functions <note>Named after Niels Henrik Abel, these are complex mathematical functions that helped unify and simplify various mathematical series.</note> suddenly enclose certain long-known series into a unified form, thereby first granting the possibility of their general use.

As the human spirit for the first time in world history pauses before itself and begins to philosophize, it finds before it a language equipped with a full richness of forms and concepts, and "a large part, perhaps the largest part, of the work of his reason consists in the analysis of concepts which he already finds within himself," as Kant <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), whose "Critique of Pure Reason" argues that we process the world through innate categories of understanding.</note> says. ## VII.

### The Unconscious in Thought.

---

In the second to last chapter, we saw that every instance of a memory appearing for a specific purpose requires the assistance of the Unconscious if the correct **idea** <note>German: "Vorstellung." This refers to the mental images or representations we have of things.</note> is to come to mind. This is because consciousness does not encompass dormant memories and therefore cannot choose among them. When an unsuitable idea appears, consciousness immediately recognizes it as inappropriate and rejects it; however, all memories that have not yet appeared, but are intended to appear, lie outside its field of vision—and thus outside its power of choice. Only the Unconscious can perform this purposeful selection. 

One might perhaps suggest that memories appear in a completely random fashion relative to our interests, and that consciousness simply keeps rejecting the wrong ones until the right one finally shows up. In the realm of **abstract thinking**, cases certainly occur where one rejects five or even more ideas before the right one comes to mind. In such instances, however—much like guessing riddles or solving problems through trial and error—the issue is that consciousness itself does not quite know what it wants. That is, it knows the conditions of suitability only in the form of abstract verbal or numerical formulas, but not through immediate **intuition** <term>intuition|Anschauung; in German philosophy, this refers to the direct, "vivid" mental seeing of something, as opposed to thinking about it through abstract words or logic</term>. 

Consequently, in every individual case, consciousness must first plug the concrete value into these formulas and see if the result is correct. From this, it is also evident that the reaction of an interest upon the Unconscious—which is itself so unclear that it can only become clear about itself by applying it to a concrete case—must be more imperfect than in those instances where the interest is expressed in an immediately concrete and intuitive [manner...]

In thinking, everything depends on the right **idea** <note>German: *Vorstellung*. In this philosophical context, it refers to a mental representation, image, or "presentation" in the mind.</note> occurring to one at the right moment. Let us examine this proposition more closely. In a narrower sense, thinking is understood as the dividing, uniting, and relating of ideas. Dividing can consist of spatial or temporal cutting, or in the **abstractive dividing** of ideas. Every idea can be divided in infinitely many ways; therefore, it is essential how the "cut" is made between the part one wishes to keep and the part one wishes to discard. However, how much and what part of an idea one wants to keep depends on the purpose for which it is needed. The primary purpose of abstractive dividing is the grouping of many individual sensory perceptions into a single, common **concept** <note>German: *Begriff*.</note>; this can only contain what is identical in all of them. The cuts must therefore be made so that from all the individual ideas, only the identical part remains, and the dissimilar, individual remnants are discarded. 

In other words, when one has many individual instances, the idea of the part common to all must occur to one. This is just as surely an *occurrence* <note>German: *Einfallen*. This describes an idea "falling into" the mind—a sudden flash of insight that cannot be produced by sheer willpower.</note> that cannot be forced, just as in the earlier examples; for millions of people stare at the same individual ideas, and finally, one brilliant mind grasps the concept. How much richer in concepts is the educated person than the uneducated! And the sole reason for this is the *interest in the concept*, which is instilled in him through education and teaching; for one cannot directly teach anyone a concept. One can certainly assist him in the process of abstraction by providing many individual sensory examples and excluding other concepts already known to him and so forth, but in the end, he must find it himself. Since this condition can never be fulfilled in reality <note>Latin: *realiter*</note>, the process can only be that the soul conceptually isolates the identical portion of both ideas. If it then recognizes that the individual remnants consist only of the place and time of the ideas and no longer affect their content, it calls them "equal," and has thus gained the concept of equality. Another example is causality <term>Causality: the principle that every event has a cause; the relationship between cause and effect</term>. It is certainly possible to develop this concept logically, specifically from the calculus of probability, which operates on the simple assumption of absolute chance—that is, the absence of causality. If, for instance, an event has occurred *n* times under specific circumstances, the probability that it will occur again under those same circumstances the next time is $\frac{n+1}{n+2}$ <note>This is a reference to Laplace’s Rule of Succession, a mathematical formula used to estimate the probability of a future event based on past occurrences.</note>; now, if we declare the occurrence of the event to be "necessary" when its probability reaches $1$, we can then develop the **probability** of whether the occurrence of the event is necessary or not. However, as Kant <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), a central figure in modern philosophy who argued that causality is a category of the mind we use to organize experience, rather than something we observe directly in the world.</note> already demonstrated, there is no meaning in causality other than the **necessity** of an occurrence under the relevant circumstances; the concept of "generation" <note>Original: *Erzeugung*. In this context, it refers to the idea that a cause "produces" or "gives birth" to an effect.</note> is a concept arbitrarily inserted, and ultimately only an **unsuitably** used metaphor.

Thus, we can demonstrate the probability that this or that phenomenon is caused by these or those circumstances, and indeed, our knowledge goes no further. Certainly, no one believes that this is the way children and animals arrive at the concept of causality. And yet, there is no other way to move beyond the concept of a mere sequence of events to that of a necessary consequence or effect. Consequently, this process must also take place in the Unconscious, and the concept of causality must enter consciousness as its finished result.

The same proof can be applied to other relational concepts; they can all be developed logically and discursively <term>Discursive: reasoning that moves step-by-step from premises to a conclusion, rather than arriving at knowledge through direct intuition</term>. However, these developments are all so subtle and, in part, so complicated that it is entirely impossible for them to be carried out in the consciousness of beings who are forming these concepts for the first time; therefore, they appear before consciousness as something already finished. Now, anyone who recognizes the impossibility of obtaining these concepts from the outside and the necessity of forming them **ourselves** asserts their apriority <term>Apriority: the quality of being *a priori*, or knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than from observation or experience</term>; whereas those who rely on the fact that such formation-

It can also be a **uniting of mental images through relational forms**, where one seeks the ground for a consequence, the content for a form, the like for the like, one alternative for another, or the universal for the particular, and vice versa. In all cases, one has one mental image and seeks another that fulfills the given relationship. Either one possesses the sought-after image within oneself as a slumbering memory, or one does not. However, for every particular, there are very many universals contained within it; therefore, every subject can rightly accept many predicates. Which one happens to fit depends solely on the goal of the train of thought. Thus, in judging, it again depends on the right mental image occurring to the person—the same is true whether one seeks the predicate for a subject or the subject for a predicate, for a universal likewise encompasses many particulars.
