<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the mind joins mental images and concepts. The previous page explored how the "uniting of mental images" occurs through various relational forms, such as seeking a universal for a particular instance.</meta>

can be proven by contradiction. Now, it very quickly becomes apparent that the **syllogism** <term>Syllogism: a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal).</term> offers nothing new at all, as has been demonstrated by **John Stuart Mill** <note>John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was an English philosopher who argued that the syllogism is a summary of previous knowledge rather than a tool for discovering new truths.</note> and others. This is because the general **major premise** <term>Major premise (Obersatz): the broad rule or general statement in a syllogism.</term> already implicitly contains the specific case within itself, which is merely made explicit in the **conclusion** <term>Conclusion (Schlusssatz): the final logical result derived from the premises.</term>. Since everyone can only be convinced of the major premise as a universal truth if they are convinced of all its specific cases, they must also already be convinced of the conclusion; otherwise, they are not actually convinced of the major premise. Furthermore, if the major premise carries no certain validity but only a probable one, then the conclusion must also carry the same coefficient of probability as the major premise.

This demonstrates that the syllogism does not increase knowledge in any way once the premises are given. This aligns perfectly with the fact that no rational person dwells on a syllogism; instead, by thinking of the premises, they have **by that very fact** <note>original: "*eo ipso*"</note> already thought of the conclusion as well. Thus, the syllogism as a distinct stage of thinking never actually enters consciousness. Consequently, the syllogism can have no direct, but only an indirect significance for knowledge.

In truth, in all specific cases (where the **minor premise** <term>Minor premise (Untersatz): the specific instance or fact that is applied to the major premise.</term> is given), the goal is to find the appropriate major premise. Once this is found, the conclusion is immediately present in consciousness; indeed, the major premise itself often remains an unconscious link in the process. Naturally, the same minor premise can be related to many major premises, just as a subject can be related to many predicates. However, just as for the specific purpose of a judgment only one predicate provides the definition of the subject that serves to continue the train of thought toward a intended goal, only one specific major premise can help generate the conclusion that can advance this train of thought. The task, therefore, is to call into consciousness, from among those general propositions stored in memory with which the given case can be linked as a minor premise, exactly the one that is needed. That is to say, our general assertion is confirmed here as well. For example, if I want to prove that in an **isosceles triangle** <term>Isosceles triangle: a triangle with at least two equal sides.</term> the angles at the base are equal to one another, I only need to remember the general rule that in every triangle, equal angles lie opposite equal sides. As soon as this has previously become clear to me and I [recall] it...

Of course, one usually has only a vague idea of this numerical value of the probability coefficient, which consequently contains a great deal of inaccuracy, so that, for example, a somewhat high probability is always confused with certainty. Nonetheless, by proposing a bet, upper and lower limits can very soon be found, through which the magnitude of the probability is at least determined to a certain degree; and with sharp minds, these limits can be moved quite close to one another through continued bargaining over the conditions of the bet.

Despite all this, we cannot doubt that the same logical links are present in the intuition of the Unconscious—only they are compressed into a single point in time, whereas in conscious logic they follow one after another. That only the final link falls into consciousness is because only this link is of interest; however, one can recognize that all others are present in the Unconscious if one intentionally repeats the intuition in such a way that first the penultimate, then the link before that, and so on, falls into consciousness. The relationship between the two types is thus to be thought of as follows: the intuitive spirit leaps across the space to be traversed in one bound; the discursive spirit takes several steps. # VIII.

## The Unconscious in the Origin of Sensory Perception.

---

Kant <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) was a landmark German philosopher who argued that the human mind actively shapes our perception of reality.</note> claimed in his *transcendental Aesthetics* <term>Transcendental Aesthetic: The section of Kant’s "Critique of Pure Reason" that examines how our senses perceive objects through the fundamental frameworks of space and time.</term> that space is not passively received by the soul <note>original: "Seele"; often used interchangeably with "mind" in 19th-century psychology and philosophy.</note> from some external source, but is instead actively produced by the soul itself. With this proposition, he brought about a total revolution in philosophy. Why, then, has this correct statement always been so completely resisted, with few exceptions, by both common sense and the scientific way of thinking?

1) Because Kant, and after him Fichte <note>Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814), a successor to Kant who emphasized the "I" or the self as the starting point of philosophy.</note> and Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a philosopher who viewed the world as "representation" created by the mind, though driven by a blind "Will."</note>, drew false and one-sidedly idealistic consequences from this correct statement—conclusions that clash with the instinct of healthy reason;
2) because Kant provided false proofs for his correct assertion, which in reality proved nothing at all;
3) because Kant—without fully accounting for it himself—speaks of an **unconscious** process in the soul, whereas the previous way of thinking only recognizes and considers conscious processes of the soul to be possible. Consciousness, however, denies that it actively generates space and time; it quite rightly asserts that they are simply "given" through sensory perception as an accomplished fact <note>original French: *fait accompli*</note>;
4) because Kant placed time on the same level as space, even though this principle does not apply to time.

We must examine these four points in order, as the unconscious generation of space is the foundation for the origin of sensory perception. It is with sensory perception that consciousness first begins, and it is, in turn, the foundation of all conscious thinking.

The author argues that while Kant was right, his theory was rejected because he misidentified the process as conscious rather than unconscious and incorrectly applied the same logic to the concept of time.</summary>
<keywords>Immanuel Kant, transcendental aesthetics, sensory perception, space and time, the unconscious, German Idealism, cognition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of Immanuel Kant’s philosophy, moving from the assertion that the mind produces space and time to a debate over whether these concepts also exist in the objective world (Being) or only within the subject (Thought).</meta>

*Regarding point 1.* Let us first assume it is proven that space and time can enter into thought in no other way than by the mind actively producing them from within itself. Even so, it does not follow in any way that space and time can only have real existence within thought, and not also outside of thought within Being <note>original: "Sein"; in this context, it refers to objective reality or existence independent of the human mind.</note>. The hastiness of this conclusion—which Kant actually makes, and by which he arrives at the denial of the **transcendental reality** <term>Transcendental Reality: The idea that things like space and time exist as real features of the world itself, not just as filters in our minds.</term> of space and the one-sided idealism of his system—has already been pointed out by Schelling <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), a philosopher who argued that Nature and Mind are two sides of the same absolute reality. The work cited is "Representation of the Process of Nature."</note> (Representation of the Process of Nature, Works I. 10, 314–321); we must now briefly consider the reasons that make it probable that space and time are truly just as much forms of Being as they are of Thought.

a) We must first clarify the reasons for the real existence of a "Not-I" <note>original: "Nichtich"; a term used in German Idealism to refer to everything that is external to the self or the "I".</note> lying beyond the "I," or an external world. Logically, only two hypotheses are possible: either the "I" unconsciously spins the apparent external world out of itself—in which case only the "I" has existence, and every reader would have to deny the existence not only of external things but of all other people—or there exists a "Not-I" independent of the "I," and the representation of the external world within the "I" is the product of both factors. Which of these two hypotheses is the more probable must be decided by which one explains the phenomena of the world of representation more naturally; both are possible.

α) Sensory impressions possess a degree of vividness that mere mental representations, generated by one's own intellectual activity, usually only reach in pathological states. Furthermore, they often bring something new (especially in childhood years), whereas the latter are always composed only of known memories and parts of such memories. This is easily explained by the influence of an external world, but difficult to explain from the "I" alone.

β) For a sensory impression to arise, the feeling of an "opened sense" <note>Referring to the conscious awareness of using a sense organ, like having one's eyes open.</note> is required; conversely, the feeling of an opened sense does not necessarily produce a sensory impression—for example, in darkness or in the absence of odor. This is easily explained by the influence of an external world, but difficult to explain from the "I" alone.

γ) Sensory representations arise according to the law of the sequence of thoughts from the preceding one under in-

<meta>This page continues the argument for the existence of an external world (a "Not-I"). The author is presenting logical proofs that our sensory experiences cannot be produced solely by our own minds, as Kantian idealism might suggest.</meta>

...the effect of mood, and so on. — **Sensory impressions** <term>Sensory impressions: The data we receive through our physical senses, such as sight or touch.</term> mostly occur suddenly and unexpectedly, and always without any connection to our internal chain of thoughts. This phenomenon would only be possible without the influence of an **external world** <term>External world: The objective reality that exists independently of our individual minds.</term> if the law of the sequence of thoughts in the mind applied at some times and not at others; however, even with that assumption, this phenomenon cannot be explained by the **"I"** <note>original: "Ich"; the conscious self or the ego.</note> alone.

δ) Most impressions possess a specific peculiarity: the object to which we attribute them is simultaneously confirmed by another impression from a different sense (for example, one can see, smell, taste, and feel a piece of food at the same time). This is easily explained by the influence of an external world, but is difficult to explain through purely internal mental processes. If one were to assume that related sensory impressions evoke each other—for example, that the visual impression of food brings the smell of the food along with it whenever the sense of smell is "open"—this is refuted by the fact that one can alternately open and close the senses of smell and sight and still receive the respective sensory impression of the food each time.

If one were to make the further assumption that not only the simultaneous impression, but also the *preceding* visual impression of the food could cause the smell and vice versa, this is countered by another circumstance: during the alternating opening and closing of both senses, the visual impression might be present one time but not another (specifically, if the food has been moved away). Thus, under otherwise identical circumstances, the smell would have to evoke the visual impression one time but not the other, which contradicts the law of **"same causes, same effects."** (For further details, see Wiener, "Principles of World Order," Book 3, under "Proof for the Reality of the External World.") <note>Christian Wiener (1826–1896) was a German mathematician and philosopher who sought to bridge the gap between physics and philosophy.</note>

ε) The objects of our sensory impressions act upon one another according to very specific laws; if one wanted to explain these sensory impressions purely from the "I," then these laws would have to be transferable to our internal mental processes. However, they are not. Only in the rarest of cases do the sensory impressions of **cause and effect** follow one another in the mind in the same way that cause and effect occur outside in the world; frequently, by contrast, one perceives the effect at one time, and <note>The text breaks off here; the author is likely about to explain that we often see the result of an action before we understand the cause, or see them in an order that doesn't match our internal logic.</note>

$\zeta$) <note>The sixth point in the author’s list of arguments (using the Greek letter zeta).</note> Every **"I"** <note>original: "Ich"; the conscious self.</note> receives, alongside the representation of its own body, representations of a great number of foreign bodies similar to its own, which are inhabited by **mental faculties** <term>Mental faculties: The powers of the mind, such as reason, memory, and will.</term> similar to its own. This would be an illusionary charade in which there would be no sense or reason at all and where, as the previous points demonstrate, the wildest whim and arbitrariness would have to unite with the strictest **lawfulness** <term>Lawfulness (Gesetzmässigkeit): The quality of following consistent, predictable rules or natural laws.</term> in an incomprehensible way, and the highest wisdom would be spent on a soap bubble, a mad dream. —

One sees from what has been cited that the probability for the existence of a **"Not-I"**—which exists independently of the **"I"** and causally influences it—is as great as possible, and that here again, natural instinct is justified by scientific observation. For our understanding would not be advanced at all if the "Not-I" were always one and the same and consequently always acted in exactly the same way, merely providing a single external impulse. For then it would again be left to the "I" to hang this or that spatial or temporal definition, or category of thought, onto the eternally identical impulse of the "Not-I" like an arbitrary cloak, as if by some strange whim <note>original: "Caprice"</note>. Thus, the "I" would construct the entire **"how"** and **"what"** of the external world itself, while the impulse would only guarantee the fact **"that"** it exists. Here, all the mentioned difficulties would repeat themselves unchanged. 

Consequently, every **individual determination in perception must be understood as an effect of the Not-I**; and since different effects presuppose different causes, we arrive at a system of as many variations within the "Not-I" as there are differences in perception. Now, these variations in the "Not-I" could certainly be of a non-spatial and non-temporal nature, with space and time being forms belonging to thought alone; however, these variations would then have to operate within two other objective forms that run parallel to the subjective forms of space and time. These run so perfectly parallel to the mental laws of space and time that, here again, the assumption of a pre-established harmony is unavoidable; meanwhile, a theory of the identity of laws linked to the identity of forms requires no such forced assumption.

These are based on the displacement, tension, stretching, and participation of adjacent and underlying sensory parts—which vary entirely depending on the softness or hardness of the pressure, the shape of the limb, the nature of the parts lying beneath, and the density of the <term>tactile papillae (Tastwärzchen)</term> <note>These are the small projections on the skin, particularly on the fingertips, that increase the surface area for sensory receptors.</note>. These differences are partly transmitted to the brain through the optic nerve <term>optic nerve (Sehnerv)</term>, and partly felt within the brain itself through the resistance that the will must oppose to the reflexive effort of the eye's rotation in order to prevent it. In contrast to the sensations of smell, taste, and hearing, it is now understandable how **visual and tactile sensations** specifically can stimulate the soul toward **spatial perception**. This is because in these senses, the stimulus transmitted by every individual primitive nerve fiber has its qualitative **definition** <term>definition/specificity (Bestimmtheit)</term> through a well-organized system of accompanying differences. It is quite obvious that this lawful <term>causal connection (Causalverbindung)</term> between a form of vibration and a sensation is, in itself, no more miraculous than any other incomprehensible, lawful causal connection within the realm of matter, such as that between electricity and heat. On the other hand, we will unhesitatingly lean toward the view that here, as there, causal intermediate links exist. These links would reduce the current complexity of these processes to simple laws, whose multifaceted interactions produce the variety of observed phenomena. If, therefore, we cannot bring ourselves to rest on the current result as a final one, but must instead suspect various interconnected links in these processes, then this much is clear: that these links, insofar as they fall within the psychological realm, exclus—

...must necessarily belong to the realm of the unconscious. It is therefore an **unconscious process** that makes acid seem sour to us, sugar sweet, this light red, that one blue, these air vibrations appear as the tone A, and those as middle C <note>The original text uses "c̅", a notation for middle C.</note>. However, with all these qualitative, intensively and extensively quantitative determinations of sensation, we never move beyond the sphere of the subject <note>In 19th-century philosophy, the "subject" refers to the individual mind or the internal experience of the observer, as opposed to the "object" or external reality.</note>. Thus, the spatial surface currently lies purely within the soul <note>The author uses "soul" (Seele) to mean the psyche or the seat of consciousness.</note> and is purely subjective. The soul does not even know the eye as an organ of sight; it does not perceive the visual image either in front of the eye or within the eye, but possesses it only within itself—just as a faint memory-image can only be thought of in the subjective space of the soul, without any relation to external space.

It is similar with the perceptions of the **sense of touch**. Here, too, there is only surface extension corresponding to the body's surface, though much less definite than with sight. Only through the simultaneous occurrence of the same perception at several points, combined with certain feelings of muscular movement, do experiences arise. With their help, the soul can use other processes to fix these tactile perceptions onto the epidermis <note>The "Oberhaut" or outermost layer of the skin.</note>, so that they are now, as it were, fixed in terms of the **third dimension**.

Some physiologists claim that this is immediately the case according to the law of eccentric projection <note>Original: "excentrischen Erscheinung." However, this much is certain: even when the point is reached where internal sensations are so fixed in the third dimension that they objectively coincide with the skin of the body—and, for the eye, with the <term>retina</term> <note>The light-sensitive inner surface of the eye.</note>—it is still not apparent how the step out of the subjective realm is to be made through perception or **conscious thinking**.

For, at best, perception never points beyond the boundaries of one's own body; in my view, it remains purely within the soul, without pointing toward one's own body at all. Consequently, even if causality plays a role in it—which we can never actually determine—one cannot say, as **Schopenhauer** <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a philosopher who famously argued that the human intellect creates the world of experience by applying the law of causality to sensory data.</note> does, that the **a priori** <term>A priori: Knowledge or concepts that exist in the mind independently of and prior to experience.</term> given concept of causality *creates* the external object. Using such phrasing implies the concept is a conscious one, which it decidedly cannot be, as it is formed much, much later—specifically, first from the relationships between already "ready-made" objects.

Having reached the point where we see external objects in our perceptions, we must now address the development of these perceptions—for example, in the case of sight, the perception of distances measured from the eye, simple vision with two eyes, and the perception of the third dimension in solid bodies...

# IX.

## The Unconscious in Mysticism.

---

The word “mystical” is on everyone's lips; everyone knows the names of famous mystics, and everyone knows examples of the mystical. And yet, how few understand the word, the meaning of which is itself mystical, and therefore can only be truly grasped by someone who carries a mystical vein within them, however faint it may be. We shall attempt to come closer to the essence of the matter by observing the various primary phenomena that occur in the mysticism of different times and individuals.

In the majority of mystics, we find a turning away from active life and a withdrawal into quietistic <term>Quietism: A form of religious mysticism that emphasizes interior passivity and the silencing of the will to achieve union with the divine.</term> contemplation—even a striving toward spiritual and physical nihilism <term>Nihilism: Here used in a philosophical or spiritual sense to mean the desire for the dissolution of the self into "nothingness" or the void.</term>; but this cannot express the essence of mysticism, for the world's greatest mystic, Jacob Boehme <note>Jacob Boehme (1575–1624) was a German shoemaker and Christian mystic whose complex cosmological visions influenced later German philosophy and Romanticism.</note>, managed his household properly, worked, and raised his children well. Other mystics plunged so deeply into practical life that they appeared as world reformers; still others practiced theurgy <term>Theurgy: Rituals or "divine work" intended to invoke the presence of gods or supernatural powers.</term> and magic, or practical medicine and scientific travels. Another series of phenomena found in higher degrees of mysticism are physical occurrences, such as convulsions, epilepsy, ecstasies, delusions, and the "fixed ideas" of hysterical women and hypochondriacal men, as well as the visions of ecstatic or spontaneous somnambulists <term>Somnambulist: In the 19th century, this referred not just to sleepwalkers, but to people in "magnetic" trances who were believed to possess heightened spiritual clarity.</term>. All of these bear the character of physical illness so strongly that the essence of mysticism certainly cannot consist of them, even if they are largely brought about intentionally through voluntary fasting, asceticism, and the constant concentration of the imagination on a single point.

<summary>This page introduces the study of mysticism, arguing that while it is often associated with withdrawal from the world or pathological physical symptoms, these outward signs do not constitute its true essence.</summary>
<keywords>mysticism, Jacob Boehme, quietism, theurgy, ecstasy, somnambulism, asceticism, the unconscious</keywords>

--- Page 278 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of mysticism. Having previously noted that mysticism cannot be defined solely by quietism or active reform, the author now examines more extreme psychological manifestations, asceticism, and the "miracles" attributed to mystics, moving toward an analysis of their unique literary style.</meta>

They are the ones who, in the history of mysticism, give rise to those repulsive phenomena that we still pity today in insane asylums, but which in their own time were idolized as prophets and persecuted and killed as martyrs—such unfortunate souls, for example, who believed themselves to be Christ (Esaias Stiefel <note>Esaias Stiefel (1561–1627) was a German sectarian leader who claimed a mystical union with God, eventually identifying himself with Christ, leading to his condemnation by orthodox theologians.</note> around 1600) or even God the Father Himself. Nevertheless, one might say that visions and ecstasies transition by degrees into those purer and higher forms to which history owes so much; this is certainly granted—only one must not mistake these variable elements for the core essence of mysticism.

A third element we encounter is asceticism; it is either a mindless madness or a morbid lust unless it is understood as an ethical system, which is indeed the case among Indian, Neo-Persian, and Christian penitents. In this, too, there is no mysticism in itself, for on the one hand, Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher whose work "The World as Will and Representation" argues that asceticism is a rational method for silencing the painful "will to live."</note> has provided proof that one can be a perfectly clear thinker and yet consider asceticism the only correct system; on the other hand, mysticism is just as compatible with the most unrestrained pursuit of pleasure and debauchery as it is with the strictest asceticism.

A fourth series of phenomena in the history of mysticism is the miracles of prophets, saints, and magicians that span all ages. After moderately strict criticism, the only thing remaining from these legends is reduced to healing effects. These can be understood partly as simple medicine, partly through conscious or unconscious magnetizing <term>Magnetizing: Referring to "animal magnetism" or Mesmerism, a 19th-century theory that an invisible natural force (fluid) possessed by all living beings could be used for healing.</term>, and partly through sympathetic action <term>Sympathetic action: The historical belief that things can affect each other at a distance through a hidden "sympathy" or occult connection, often through the power of the will.</term>. Thus, they can be integrated into the order of natural laws—if one accepts the idea of magical-sympathetic action through mere will as a natural law. As long as one does not do so, the latter remains, of course, mystical in itself; but as soon as one accepts it, it is no more mystical than the operation of any other natural law—none of which we truly understand, yet none of which we call mystical. —

Hitherto we have spoken of how mystics acted and lived; now we must mention the manner in which they spoke and wrote. Here we first encounter a predominantly figurative style of expression, which is sometimes plain and simple, but more often turgid and bombastic, frequently possessing a fantastic extravagance in both content and form. This is due partly to the nations and eras to which the mystics in question belong; partly, one finds

<keywords>Esaias Stiefel, asceticism, Schopenhauer, miracles, animal magnetism, sympathetic action, mystical language, nature of mysticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the defining characteristics of mysticism. Having dismissed visions, ecstasies, and asceticism as the essential core of the mystical experience on the previous page, the author now turns to the literary and philosophical styles often associated with mystical traditions.</meta>

...we find the same phenomenon among poets and other writers, and thus we cannot find the character of the mystical within it. Furthermore, we see in mystical writings, on the one hand, a mass of allegorizing, arbitrarily playful quibbling with words (from the Bible, the Quran, other scriptures, or legends) or formal rituals (of Jewish, Muslim, and Christian worship); on the other hand, we see a fantastically fertile and formalistically parallelizing schematism of an unscientific natural philosophy <note>The author refers to *Naturphilosophie*, a 19th-century movement, particularly in Germany, that sought to understand the natural world through philosophical speculation and organic unity rather than purely empirical experimentation.</note> (Albertus Magnus, Paracelsus, and others in the Middle Ages; Schelling, Oken, Steffens, Hegel in more recent times). In both of these phenomena—which are essentially the same and differ only in their subject matter—we cannot find the character of the mystical; we see in them only the drive inherent to the human spirit to systematize. Misled by ignorance or a disregard for the materials and principles of the natural sciences, this spirit builds playful houses of cards; often, a successor, busy building his own house of cards, does not even take the trouble to blow them down, as they tend to collapse on their own—though not before impressing many another child. One characteristic that people have often believed they could rely on is the incomprehensibility and obscurity of language, because it is common to almost all mystical writings. However, it must not be forgotten, first, that very few mystics have written, and many have not even spoken, or at least provided nothing more than the accounts of the visions they had; and second, that many other writings are incomprehensible and obscure, to which neither their authors nor other people would wish to apply the label "mystical." For lack of clarity in expression can stem from lack of clarity in thought, inadequate mastery of the material, a clumsy writing style, and many other reasons.

Consequently, all the phenomena considered so far are unsuitable for fathoming the essence of mysticism; rather, any of them may become the expression of a mystical background, but is then only a garment accidentally donned by mysticism, and might just as well have nothing at all to do with mysticism at another time. It is now a matter of finding the common core and center of all these phenomena in those cases where we regard them as the garment of a mystical background.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the defining characteristics of mysticism. One would be very mistaken if one regarded religion as this common core; religion, as an unpretentious faith in revelation, is not at all mystical. For if something has been revealed to me through an authority I recognize as fully valid, why should there be anything still "mystical" about it for me, so long as I am simply content with this external revelation? And no religion demands more than that. Furthermore, it is also easy to see that there is a mysticism of irreligious superstition (for example, *black magic*), or a mysticism of self-deification which defies all gods, good and evil alike, or even a mysticism of irreligious philosophy—although experience shows that the latter, at the very least, often likes to form an external alliance with a positive religion (for example, *Neoplatonism* <note>A philosophical system arising in the 3rd century AD, based on the teachings of Plato but heavily influenced by mystical concepts of "the One."</note>).

Despite all this, we do not wish to ignore that religion is the very soil and ground upon which mysticism grows most easily and luxuriantly; however, it is by no means its only nursery. Mysticism is, rather, a climbing plant that grows up every stake it finds and knows how to reconcile itself equally well with the most extreme opposites: pride and humility, lust for power and endurance, egoism and self-denial, abstinence and sensory excess, self-mortification and hedonism, solitude and sociability, contempt for the world and vanity, Quietism <term>Quietism: A form of Christian mysticism that emphasizes internal stillness and the passive withdrawal of the soul from worldly concerns.</term> and the active life, Nihilism and world reformation, piety and godlessness, Enlightenment and superstition, genius and animalistic narrow-mindedness—everything fits equally well with mysticism. — Thus, we have come to see in all such extremes, and in all the phenomena mentioned above that historically present themselves in the lives of mystics, not the *essence* of mysticism, but rather *outgrowths*. These were brought about partly by the spirit of the age and national character, partly by individual pathological predispositions, partly by perverted religious, moral, and practical principles, partly by the contagious example of spiritual wandering, partly by dissatisfaction with the pressure of harsh times (which had nothing alluring to offer those striving for higher things in worldly life and could only deter them), partly by a danger of "over-flying" <note>original: "Ueberfliegens"; the author suggests a spiritual "overshooting" or losing one's grounding while pursuing the ultimate mystical goal.</note> that we will consider later and which lies within the final goal of mysticism itself, and partly through a chain of all sorts of causes resulting from the aforementioned and other circumstances.

<summary>The author argues that mysticism is not synonymous with religion but is a psychological "climbing plant" that can attach itself to any ideology, often resulting in extreme or contradictory behaviors depending on the era and the individual's temperament.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's effort to redefine mysticism by distinguishing its healthy, historical core from "pathological" or "sickly" distortions. I considered this negative analysis essential in order to purify the concepts of the mystical, which for most people are composed only of a **sum of these pathological excesses** of mysticism, and might thereby prevent them from recognizing mysticism in its purer forms. If we now return once again to the core of all those phenomena—to true mysticism—it will first become clear that it must be deeply rooted in the innermost essence of humanity (even if, like artistic talent, it does not develop in everyone, or at least not in everyone equally or in the same directions); for it runs without interruption, with greater or lesser prevalence, through cultural history from the oldest prehistoric times to the present. It has certainly changed its character with the "spirit of the times," but no cultural progress has ever been able to displace it; it has stood just as invincibly against the disbelief of materialism <note>A philosophy that holds that matter is the only reality, often dismissing spiritual or mystical experiences.</note> as against the horrors of the Inquisition. 

But mysticism has also performed invaluable cultural-historical services for the human race. Without the mysticism of Neoplatonism, Johannine Christianity <note>Refers to the Gospel of John and its associated writings, which are often characterized by a more philosophical and mystical focus on "the Word" and "the Light" compared to other parts of the New Testament.</note> would never have arisen; without the mysticism of the Middle Ages, the spirit of Christianity would have perished in Catholic idolatry and scholastic formalism <note>The highly structured, logic-based method of theology and philosophy taught in medieval European universities, which the author views here as dry or overly rigid.</note>; without the mysticism of the persecuted heretical communities since the beginning of the 11th century—which, despite all oppression, always arose anew with increased strength under different names—the blessings of the Reformation would never have chased away the dark shadows of the Middle Ages and opened the gates to the modern era. Without the mysticism in the soul of the German people and in the heroes of modern German poetry and philosophy, we would have been so completely flooded by the shallow quicksand of French materialism <note>A reference to 18th-century Enlightenment thinkers who proposed that humans were essentially biological machines.</note> as early as the last century that we might not have cleared our heads for who knows how long. Just as it is for the human race as a whole, mysticism is of inestimable value for the **individual**, so long as they keep themselves free from pathological excesses and an overgrowing one-sidedness. For we see indeed that all mystics have felt exceedingly happy in the exercise of their mystical talents and have joyfully borne all privations and sacrifices in order to...

> "Faith is a secure premonition of a truth not yet fully revealed, grasped with the will, and is grounded on authority or revelation; whereas inner contemplation <note>original: *contemplatio*</note> is the certain and at the same time manifest knowledge of the invisible."

This is further elaborated in his school (by **Richard** and **Hugh of Saint Victor** <note>The Victorines were a 12th-century community of canons in Paris known for blending mystical theology with rigorous academic study.</note>), by whom inner revelation is described as the deeper mystical knowledge which is granted only to the chosen; as the enlightenment of reason through the Spirit; as a supernatural power of knowledge; and as an inner, immediate vision which is exalted above reason. —

The champion of modern mysticism against the rationalistic excesses of the Enlightenment is **Hamann** <note>Johann Georg Hamann (1730–1788) was a German philosopher known as the "Magus of the North," who argued that faith and language are more fundamental than abstract reason.</note>; he wishes to see the content of external divine revelation recreated vibrantly from the soil of one's own spirit, and to find the solution to all contradictions in faith, which is certain of itself and which emerges for him from feeling and from the immediate revelation of truth. "If holding something to be true <term>Fürwahrhalten; a technical term in German philosophy for the subjective acceptance of a proposition as true</term>, which does not arise from rational grounds, is faith, then conviction based on rational grounds must itself come from faith and receive its power from it alone. — Whoever knows must ultimately appeal to sensory sensation or to spiritual feeling. — Just as there is a sensory intuition through the senses, there is also a rational one through reason. Both are, in their respective fields, the final and unconditionally valid authority. — Reason, as the faculty of feelings, is the incorporeal organ for the perceptions of the supersensible <note>original: *Uebersinnlichen*; referring to that which exists beyond the reach of the five physical senses</note>. Rational intuition, although given in exuberant feelings, is nonetheless truly objective. — Without the positive rational feeling of something higher than the world of the senses, the understanding would never have stepped out of the circle of the conditioned." Fichte and Schelling adopted these views, while Kant, in his categorical imperative <note>Kant’s moral law: "Act only according to that maxim whereby you can, at the same time, will that it should become a universal law."</note>, made use of them only as something hidden behind formal intellectual knowledge. Fichte says in his *Introductory Lectures on the Science of Knowledge* <note>original: *Wissenschaftslehre*; Fichte’s foundational philosophical system</note>: "This doctrine presupposes a completely new inner sensory tool, through which a new world is given, which does not exist at all for the ordinary person. It is not, as it were, the thinking up and creating of something new or not given, but rather the assembling and grasping into a unity of something *given through a sense that is newly to be developed*." This "rational faith" of Jacobi’s receives its most striking name from Schelling: **intellectual intuition**. Schelling presents this as the indispensable organ of all transcendental philosophizing, as the principle of all demonstration, and as the unprovable, self-evident ground of all evidence—in a word, as the absolute act of cognition. It is a type of knowledge that must always remain incomprehensible from the conscious empirical standpoint, because it does not have an "object" in the way that empirical knowledge does; it cannot occur within consciousness at all, but rather falls outside of it (see Schelling I. 1, p. 181–182). — Thus, we have traced this way of a certain content reaching consciousness from the raw, pictorial expression of a personal divine communication all the way to Schelling's intellectual intuition, and in this, we have found that which makes a feeling or a thought "mystical" in its form.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of German Idealism’s relationship with mysticism. It builds upon the previous discussion of Jacobi's "rational intuition" by citing Fichte and Schelling to argue that mystical experiences—though appearing "given" or external—are actually products of the Unconscious rising into conscious awareness.</meta>

To this, Fichte and Schelling give us an answer. Fichte says in the *Facts of Consciousness* <note>original: *Thatsachen des Bewusstseins*; published in 1817, this work explores how consciousness perceives its own processes</note>: “Man has nothing at all but experience, and he arrives at everything he reaches only through experience, through life itself. Even in the Science of Knowledge <term>Wissenschaftslehre; Fichte’s foundational philosophical system which seeks the absolute basis of all human knowledge</term>, as the absolutely highest power above which no consciousness can rise, nothing at all can occur that does not lie within actual consciousness or experience, in the highest sense of the word.” And Schelling confirms (*Works* Vol. II, Part 1, p. 326): “For indeed there are also those who speak of thinking as an opposite of all experience, as if thinking itself were not also experience!” Immediate or mystical knowledge is very well captured here under the concept of experience, because it is found “in actual consciousness” as something given, without the will being able to change it in any way. It makes no difference whether this “given” is provided from within or from without; in both cases, the conscious will has nothing to do with it. Consciousness—to which its own unconscious background is, by definition, unknown—must therefore receive its inspirations just as it would something foreign. This is the origin of the belief in divine or demonic inspiration of intellectual intuition <note>original: *intellectuale Anschauung*; a philosophical term for the direct perception of truths or spiritual realities without the need for sensory evidence</note> in earlier times and among the philosophically uneducated.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the individual's relationship with the Absolute, specifically addressing the impossibility of a perfect conscious union and the historical attempts by mystics to achieve it through the "annihilation" of the self.</meta>

...individual, whose individuality or I-ness <note>original: *Ichheit*; the quality of being an "I" or a distinct self</note> is given through consciousness. For this reason, however, every attempt to make this unity more intimate than it already is remains both absurd and useless. The path historically taken toward this goal is almost always that of the annihilation of consciousness—the striving to let the individual be absorbed into the Absolute. However, this path contains a great error: it assumes that if the goal of annihilating consciousness were achieved, the individual would still exist. The "I" wants to destroy itself and yet remain in existence at the same time in order to enjoy this destruction. Consequently, this goal is only ever partially reached from either side, although the reports of mystics show us that some have taken this path to an admirable height—or rather, depth—of which I wish to cite a few examples. True self-annihilation is, of course, only suicide, but here the contradiction is too obvious for it to have frequently become the result of mysticism.

Michael Molinos <note>a Spanish mystic (1628–1696) and chief representative of religious Quietism</note>, the father of Quietism <term>a movement emphasizing internal stillness and the passive abandonment of the soul to God</term>, says among the sixty-eight propositions of his famous "Spiritual Guide" <note>original: *Guida spirituale*</note> condemned by Pope Innocent XI:

> "Man must annihilate his powers, and the soul annihilates itself by performing no action. And if the soul has reached the point of mystical death, it can—having now returned to its primary cause, to God—will nothing further than what God wills."

The mystics of the early Middle Ages distinguished between a greater or lesser number of stages in various ways: the final stage is always "absorption," the same state we have already found described among the Buddhist Gymnosophists <term>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by the Greeks for ancient Indian ascetics</term>, the Neo-Persian Sufis, and the Hesychasts—also known as Quietists or "Navel-Gazers" on Mount Athos. It is said that in this absorption, a person no longer feels anything of their body, nor anything external at all; indeed, they no longer even perceive their own inner being.

> "To merely think of absorption is already to fall out of absorption."

To die to one's selfhood, to completely annihilate the personality, and to let it be absorbed into the divine essence is explicitly demanded. Indeed, even the essential forms of consciousness—space and time—must vanish, as we [see] from a conversation...

How sublime and pure these conceptions were even in very early times in the esoteric teachings of many peoples is shown to us by the Indians <note>referring to ancient Indian or Vedic philosophers</note>, who essentially possessed the entire history of philosophy implicitly, though in a figurative and undeveloped form—the same history that we find all too abstractly in all too many writers and volumes.

As soon as he himself, or his successors, become incapable of grasping the idea hidden behind the symbols and take the symbols themselves for the truth, they cease to be mystics and become religious. Since they can no longer reproduce the symbols mystically for themselves, and since these symbols are not rationally comprehensible, they must appeal to the authority of the founder for their truth. Because human authority appears too insignificant for such important matters, and perhaps because the founder himself already claimed divine communications, their truth is traced back to divine authority itself. 

This is how the structures that form the dogmatic content of religion arise. The more adequate the symbols are to the mystical idea, the purer and more sublime the religion is, but the more abstract and philosophical the symbols must also be. The more inadequate and sensory they are, the more religion sinks into superstitious idolatry and priestly formalism. 

Therefore, anyone who understands the symbols of religion once again merely as symbols, and wishes to seize the idea dwelling behind them, steps out of religion as such—which demands, and must demand, a literal belief <term>original: *Buchstabenglaube*; literally "belief in the letter," referring to a dogmatic or fundamentalist adherence to scripture</term> in the symbols—and becomes a mystic again. This is the most common path by which mysticism is formed: when brighter minds find the historically given religion insufficient and wish to grasp the deeper ideas that dwell behind its symbols. <meta>This page continues the argument that mysticism, while being the root of both philosophy and religion, is fundamentally distinct from the organized structures that grow from it. It explores why the raw experience of the "supersensible" must eventually take on more rigid forms.</meta>

...how they are, after all, fundamentally different things; one also sees why an established church must always be hostile toward mysticism.

If we now ask why it was that mysticism—which brought humans the first revelations of the **supersensible** <term>original: *Uebersinnliches*; that which exists beyond the reach of the physical senses or the natural world</term>—did not remain as it was, but instead transformed into philosophy and religion, the reason lies in the *formlessness* of the purely mystical result. This result must necessarily strive to take on a form; just as the mystical is not communicable to another in itself, it is equally ungraspable for the consciousness of the thinker themselves. Like everything unconscious, it only becomes a definite content for consciousness once it has entered into the forms of the senses—as light, clarity, a vision, an image, a symbol, or an abstract thought. Before this, it is only an absolutely indeterminate feeling; that is, consciousness experiences nothing but sheer **bliss** or **misery**. 

If the feeling is first defined through images or thoughts of this kind, the content of the mystical result rests for consciousness in this image or thought alone. It is therefore no wonder that when mystical power weakens and new inspirations fail to appear, consciousness clings to these sensory residues—especially when others do so, to whom only those residues can be communicated, and not the feelings linked to them. They cannot receive that "indeterminate something" which tells the productive mystic that his images and thoughts are still an imperfect expression of the supersensible idea. 

However, communication demands even more: the other person wants not just the *what* of the mystical results, but also the *why*. For while the productive mystic gains immediate certainty through the way he arrives at them, where is a third party to find such conviction? **Religion** helps itself here with the surrogate of **faith in authority** <term>original: *Autoritätenglaube*; accepting something as true solely because an authority figure or institution asserts it</term>, which destroys independent judgment. **Philosophy**, on the other hand, attempts to rationally prove what it has received mystically, thereby turning the "private property" of the mystic into the "common property" of thinking humanity. All too often—as could not be otherwise given the difficulty of the subject—these rational proofs have failed. This is because, quite apart from what is actually incorrect in them, they themselves rely on premises whose truth can only be established through mystical conviction; and so it happens

But these thinkers do not get very far and cannot really be called "systems" in the full sense. The complete rational proof for mystical results can only be ready at the conclusion of the history of philosophy; for the latter consists, as has been said, entirely in the search for this proof.

Finally, we must not fail to draw attention to the danger of error that lies within mysticism. This danger is much worse in mysticism than in rational thinking because the latter possesses within itself—and in the cooperation of others—the means of control and the hope of improvement. # X.

## The Unconscious in History.

Nature and history—or the emergence of organisms and the development of the human race—are two parallel problems. In both cases, the question is: *particular randomness* or *universal necessity* of results? *Dead causality* or *living purposefulness* <term>purposefulness</term> <note>German: *Zweckmässigkeit*; the idea that things happen for a reason or toward a goal rather than by blind chance</note>? Is it a *mere interplay of atoms and individuals*, or a *unified plan and guidance of the whole*? For those who have already decided the question regarding nature in favor of *purposefulness*, it will not be difficult to do the same for history. What can be deceptive here is the appearance of the *freedom of individuals*.

First, I believe I can appeal to the fact that modern philosophy has unanimously decided the question of *free will* in this way: there can be no talk of an *empirical freedom* <term>empirical freedom</term> <note>freedom that can be observed or proven through experience</note> of the individual act of will in the sense of *unconditionality*. This is because the individual act, like every other phenomenon of nature, stands under the *law of causality* <note>the principle that everything that happens is the result of a previous cause</note>. It follows with *necessity* from a person's current mental state and the motives acting upon them. Rather, if one can speak at all of a *free will* existing outside the causality of natural law, this can only be *sought in the supersensible realm* <note>original Latin: *mundus noumenon*; the world of things as they are in themselves, independent of our sensory perception</note>, or in *Kant's intelligible character* <note>Immanuel Kant's idea that while our actions in the physical world are determined, our true inner nature remains free</note>. However, freedom cannot reside in the individual act of will itself, because every such act occurs within time; it therefore belongs to the world of appearances and is subject to the law of causality—that is, to *necessity*. This point, and the reasons why we are subject to the illusion of *free will*, can be studied in *Schopenhauer's work: "On the Freedom of the Will."*

<summary>Hartmann argues that history, like nature, is guided by an underlying purpose rather than chance. He asserts that individual "free will" is an illusion in the physical world, as every action is determined by prior causes, though a deeper form of freedom may exist in a realm beyond our senses.</summary>

<keywords>philosophy of history, teleology, determinism, causality, free will, Immanuel Kant, Arthur Schopenhauer, necessity, purposefulness</keywords>

But even assuming the case that we were to grant the validity of empirical free will, if we recognize any sort of planned course of development in history at all, it could only be the result of individual freedom if every person participating in history were fully conscious of the significance and consequences of their next step before they acted.

It is true that since the last century we have been approaching that ideal state where the human race creates its history with consciousness, but we are still far from it, and this consciousness exists only in exceptional minds. No one would seriously claim that the vast majority of the path we have already traveled was navigated in this manner. For the goals of the individual are always selfish; everyone seeks only to promote their own well-being, and if this happens to benefit the whole, it is certainly not through their own merit. The exceptions to this rule are so rare that they do not even factor into the grand scheme of things. The wonder of it, however, is precisely this: that even the spirit that "wills evil, yet creates the good" <note>An allusion to Mephistopheles in Goethe’s *Faust*, who describes himself as "part of that power which eternally wills evil and eternally works good."</note>, and that the results emerging from the combination of many diverse selfish intentions are quite different from what any single individual intended. In the end, these results always turn out for the benefit of the whole, even if the benefits are far-reaching and centuries of regression seem to suggest otherwise. But this contradiction is only an illusion; such periods serve only to break down the strength of an old building to make room for a new and better one, or to allow vegetation to decay so that it may provide the fertilizer for a new and more beautiful growth. Even thousands of years of stagnation in one part of the world should not lead us astray, so long as that specific stage of culture <term>stage of culture</term> <note>German: *Culturstufe*; a specific phase in the social or intellectual development of a society</note> fulfilled its particular unique calling at some point, and provided that the process of development was moving forward somewhere else at the same time.

Just as little should we demand—as is so often unfairly done—that every branch or direction of progress advance simultaneously and without hindrance in the same place. What we see in the emergence of the state in general recurs in an even more wonderful form in the historical development of the **idea of the state** toward ever more perfect forms, which indeed constitutes one of the most important aspects of history. For the establishment of the most perfect state association, encompassing the entire habitable earth, is obviously the goal of political history; only within it, only in secured peace, where all expenditures actually benefit culture <note>The author uses "culture" (*Cultur*) here in the broad sense of human development, education, and civilization.</note> once again, can all the human predispositions of individuals develop unhindered; and this development of all existing predispositions—the realization of all possibilities slumbering in the human race—is, if not the positive task of humanity itself, then at least its immediate prerequisite.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the evolution of human society, moving from the philosophical origins of the state discussed on the previous page to a historical analysis of state forms—specifically the tension between size, governance type, and administration.</meta>

History shows three primary oppositions in the life of states: the **large state** and the **small state**, **republic** and **monarchy**, and **indirect** and **direct administration**. The task at hand is to combine the large state and the republic, as these are the superior forms; the means to achieve this is indirect administration.

The patriarchal tribal chieftainships and kingdoms show us the combination of the small state and monarchy, while the Asian despotisms show that of the large state and monarchy. In the latter, only one person possesses civil liberty; all others are unfree slaves or serfs of the ruler. The Greek cities and regional republics are the first example of the republic; favored by their fractured territory, the Greeks—even in their tiny small states—could only represent the republic as an aristocracy of free citizens ruling over double the number of slaves. The Roman Empire <note>original: *Römisches Weltreich*</note> combines the Greek city-republic with Asian large-state despotism; the Roman citizenry takes the place of the despot, and all conquered lands contain only slaves. Therefore, when the republican strength of the Roman citizens withered, the state likewise fell back into a large-state monarchy.

The Germanic spirit <note>original: *Germanenthum*; referring to the cultural and political influence of Germanic peoples in the Middle Ages.</note> brings a new principle to the idea of the state through the feudal system: that of **indirect administration** or the pyramidal hierarchical structure of rule, whereas antiquity had known only direct administration. The ancients had only free men and slaves, but now a gradation of freedom emerges, from the king down to the serf farmer, as everyone is the lord of their own vassals. I would therefore like to call the state of the Middle Ages the **monarchy pyramid**.

Finally, the modern era speaks the decisive word with the postulate of universal human freedom. It strives for large states that find their natural borders in nationalities; it brings back the Greek city-republic through the self-governance of cities and municipalities; and in the principle of representation by elected delegates, it finds the means to build a **republic pyramid**. The best (though by no means perfect) example of this currently exists in North America <note>Likely referring to the United States as a federal republic.</note>, but one day, following the general spread of culture, it must and will encompass all the countries of the earth.

The constitution—as a hybrid of monarchy and republic—is nothing but a monstrous, blatant lie, and it possesses historical justification only as a transitional formation and a political school for nations.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the evolution of political forms, specifically moving from the internal structure of the state (republics and administration) to the relationship between states and the broader social evolution of humanity.</meta>

In the federation of states <term>Staatenrepublik; a "republic of states" or a confederation of individual republics</term>, which admittedly will only come into existence when the individual states have themselves become republics, the "state of nature" between states will transition into a legal state. Self-protection through war will be replaced by legal protection through the federation, just as the individual's state of nature and self-defense transition into a legal state and legal protection during the initial formation of a state.

Alongside this line of development runs another of subordinate, but nonetheless not to be underestimated, importance: the transition from the national theocracy <note>A system of government in which priests or religious laws rule in the name of God</note> of Judaism to the attempt at a cosmopolitan <note>universal or world-encompassing</note> theocracy by Catholicism. The cosmopolitan preparation provided by the Christian ideas of Catholicism has contributed significantly to the expansion of modern cosmopolitanism.

A second aspect of history, equal in status to the political, is **social development**. It exhibits four main phases. The first is the free **state of nature**, where everyone works only for themselves and their family—for example, as seen among indigenous hunting tribes. From this state, an ascent to greater prosperity, and thereby to higher culture, is impossible. This is because, within the atomistic <note>fragmented or isolated</note> freedom of individuals, there is no motive to bring about a division of labor. Only through a division of labor can the labor-saving be achieved that is necessary for production beyond immediate life necessities—that is, for the increase of national wealth through the accumulation of capital.

The second phase is that of **personal rule**, where the master is the owner of the persons or at least the labor power of his slaves or serfs. Here, the master very quickly finds it in his interest to introduce a division of labor among his slaves, whose work now yields a surplus beyond their and his own immediate needs. This surplus is utilized for the creation of productive assets (capital). In this way, national wealth grows through the accumulation of capital, but of course, it benefits only the masters, not the servants. The Roman Empire and the Middle Ages provide examples of this stage.

The third phase, which is only made possible through the long-term influence of the second, is the **rule of capital**. In this period, what has been the only important factor until now—immobile capital...

<meta>This page concludes the argument from page 298-299, synthesizing the conflicting views of historical necessity—represented by ancient fate and religious providence—with the modern emphasis on individual agency. It introduces the author's concept of the "Unconscious" as the missing link that harmonizes these perspectives.</meta>

...exclusive **self-activity** of individuals in history is not in itself unjustified, but rather that it is one-sided. The Greeks, Romans, and Muslims are quite right with the idea of **ordained fate** <note>original: "εἱμαρμένη" (heimarmene), a Greek term for the lot or destiny assigned to a person.</note> or **destiny** <note>original: "Fatums."</note> insofar as this signifies the absolute necessity of everything that happens along the thread of **causality**, so that every link in the series is determined by the one before it, and thus the entire series is determined and predetermined by the starting link. **Christianity** is right with the idea of **providence** <note>original: "Vorsehung," the belief in God's guiding hand in worldly affairs.</note>, for everything that occurs happens with absolute wisdom and is absolutely purposeful—that is, as a means to a foreseen end—directed by the never-erring **Unconscious**, which is itself absolute logic. In any given moment, only one thing can be logical; therefore, only that one thing can happen, and it must happen as a logical requirement, being as purposeful as it is necessary. Finally, the modern **rationalist-empirical** view is right that history is the exclusive result of the **self-activity** <note>original: "Selbstthätigkeit," referring to the independent, self-directed actions of humans.</note> of individuals who determine themselves according to psychological laws, without the miracle of any intervention by higher powers. However, the followers of the first two views are wrong to deny individual agency, just as the followers of the last view are wrong to deny fate and providence. The truth is only found in the union of all three perspectives. Yet, this very union was self-contradictory as long as one assumed only the conscious activity of the individual soul; only the recognition of the **Unconscious** makes this union possible and, at the same time, makes it self-evident.

# XI.

## **The Unconscious and Consciousness in their Value for Human Life.**

I have emphasized the value of the Unconscious enough up to this point that it might seem as if I intended to be guilty of a partiality toward it over and against consciousness. To reject this reproach, to bring back to mind the value of conscious thinking, and to compare the value of the Conscious and Unconscious and their different positions in relation to life, is the task of this chapter.

Let us first consider the value of the Conscious—that is, of conscious deliberation and the application of acquired conscious knowledge for the human being.

The fundamental question would be this: "Can deliberation and knowledge have a determining influence on action and on character, and in what way?" The affirmative answer, with which common sense would not hesitate, could be cast into doubt by the consideration, firstly, that the specific **will**, from which the action arises, springs from a reaction of the **character** to the **motive**—a process that remains eternally closed to consciousness; and secondly, that **willing** and **representing** <note>original: "Vorstellen." However, the heterogeneity and incommensurability of both find their limit in the fact that a representation forms the *content* of the will, and a representation is its *motive* or ground of excitement; and the eternal unconsciousness of the process generating the will would only then make every knowledge of the interconnectedness of motive and desire completely impossible if either the character...

This is done by voluntarily presenting suitable motives to oneself, thereby awakening one or more new desires or strengthening those already present. 4. **The determination of the will not according to momentary affect, but according to the principle of the greatest possible total happiness of one's own.**

The animal—with the few exceptions of the highest-standing animals trained by humans—is essentially dependent in its determination of the will <term>Willensbestimmung: the internal process by which a person or creature decides on a course of action</term> on the momentary affect <note>original: "Affect" — a strong, immediate emotion or impulse</note>, excited by the senses and instinct; where instinct does not take the future into account, the animal's consciousness also does not easily concern itself with it, and all too often it must suffer under the consequences of its absolute recklessness. ### 5. **Value of Conscious Reason for Morality.**

The vast majority of immoral acts are completely prevented by a clever egoism <term>Egoismus: in this philosophical context, this refers to "enlightened self-interest"—the idea that acting rightly often benefits the individual in the long run</term> that proceeds according to the principle of the greatest possible total happiness for oneself. This is especially true in a state with an organized administration of justice and a society that punishes with its contempt those immoralities that the state cannot punish. That there are not many cases left where the command of morality cannot be justified in an egoistic way is already proven by the fact that so many systems of ethics—openly or covertly—are based on egoism and the principle of the greatest possible total happiness of one's own: for example, the Epicurean <note>The school of Epicurus, which sought "ataraxia" (peace and freedom from fear) and "aponia" (absence of bodily pain)</note>, Stoic <note>The school that taught virtue as the only good and urged living in accordance with reason</note>, and Spinozist <note>Referring to Baruch Spinoza, who argued that our highest good is the knowledge of God/Nature through reason</note> schools. In all such cases, one realizes that the application of reason discussed so far must suffice for morality; and indeed, next to habit through coercion, this reduction to egoism is almost the only successful way to teach and improve morality. Whatever is not achieved through this method will likely hardly be achieved at all.

However, if one sets aside the practical, living impact of moral teaching and considers the theoretical value of ethical systems, there would likely be no doubt that—whatever theoretical foundations of ethics one considers true—they can only be those consisting of principles of conscious reason, if they are to possess any scientific validity and be capable of supporting a system. I do not wish to express myself further here, so as not to stray too far from the topic.

If we now compare the Conscious and the Unconscious with one another, it is immediately apparent that a sphere exists which is everywhere left to the Unconscious alone, because it is eternally inaccessible to consciousness; secondly, we find a sphere which, in certain beings, belongs only to the Unconscious, but in others is also accessible to consciousness. Both the scale of organisms and the course of world history can teach us that all progress consists in the enlargement and deepening of the sphere opened to consciousness—that consciousness, therefore, must in a certain sense be the higher of the two. <margin>[Vertical pencil stroke in margin]</margin> Furthermore, if we consider in humans the sphere belonging to both the Unconscious and the Conscious, it is certain that everything the consciousness is capable of achieving can likewise be achieved by the Unconscious—and indeed always more strikingly, and moreover faster and more conveniently for the individual, since one must exert oneself for conscious achievement, whereas the unconscious comes of itself and without effort. Humans know this convenience of surrendering to the Unconscious, to its feelings and inspirations, quite well; and for this reason, among all lazy minds, the application of conscious reason <term>Vernunftanwendung: the active, disciplined use of logic and critical thinking</term> in each and every thing is so decried. That the Unconscious really [does] all...

After this comparison, there will be no doubt in recognizing consciousness as the more important element for us, thereby confirming our previous conclusion drawn from the organic hierarchy and the progress of history. Everywhere where consciousness is capable of replacing the unconscious, it *should* replace it, precisely because it is the higher element for the individual. All objections against this—such as the idea that the constant application of conscious reason makes one pedantic, costs too much time, etc.—are false. Pedantry only arises from the *imperfect* use of reason, specifically when one fails to account for the differences of the *particular* <note>original: "Besonderen"; referring to specific, individual cases as opposed to general rules</note> while applying a general rule. Therefore, the Unconscious is indispensable to him, and woe to the age that violently suppresses it because, in a one-sided overestimation of the conscious-rational, it wishes to allow only the latter to count; it then falls irretrievably into a watery, shallow **Rationalism**, which boastfully overestimates itself in childishly senile precociousness <note>original: "kindisch greisenhafter Altklugheit"; a stinging critique of an era that thinks it is wise but has actually lost its creative vitality</note>, without being able to do anything positive for its children—like the era of the **Wolff-Mendelssohn-Nicolai**-style "Enlightenment-mongering" <note>Christian Wolff, Moses Mendelssohn, and Friedrich Nicolai were prominent 18th-century thinkers. # I.

# The Differences between Conscious and Unconscious Mental Activity and the Unity of Will and Representation in the Unconscious.

---

1. The *Unconscious* does not fall ill, but conscious mental activity can fall ill when its material organs suffer disturbances, whether through physical causes or through violent shocks which result from strong emotions <note>original: "Gemüthsbewegungen." In 19th-century psychology, this term refers to intense passions or emotional states that affect both the soul and the physical body.</note>. This point, as far as we can go into it here, has already been touched upon in the chapter on the healing power of nature (pp. 118–122).

2. The *Unconscious does not grow weary*, but every conscious mental activity tires because its material organs occasionally become unfit for use as a result of a faster consumption of matter than nutrition [metabolism] can replace in the same amount of time. To be sure, fatigue can be removed by a change of the specifically taxed sense, or of the object of thought or sensory perception, because different organs and parts of the brain—or at least the same organs in a different kind of activity—are then put to work. However, the general fatigue of the central organ of consciousness <note>A reference to the brain as the physical seat of conscious thought.</note> cannot be prevented even when the objects of focus are changed; it occurs all the more rapidly with each new object the longer the attention has already been active with other objects, until finally complete exhaustion follows, which can only be compensated for by new oxygen intake during sleep. The closer we approach the realm of the Unconscious, the less fatigue is to be noticed—for example, in the realm of feelings—and the less clarity they possess for consciousness, the more...

...more does their true essence belong to the Unconscious. While a thought can hardly be held in consciousness for more than two seconds without interruption, and thinking grows weary within a few hours, one and the same feeling—though varying in intensity—often persists uninterrupted for days and nights, or even months. When it finally dulls, the receptivity for other feelings does not appear impaired, in contrast to thinking; these new feelings do not tire any sooner than they would have otherwise. This latter assertion only requires limitation insofar as the law of mood must also be taken into account. — Before falling asleep, when the intellect grows weary, the feelings that burden us emerge all the more powerfully because they are not hindered by thoughts—so strongly that they frequently prevent sleep. Even in dreams, vivid feelings are much more frequent than clear thoughts, and very many dream images evidently owe their origin to existing feelings. Furthermore, consider the restless night before an important event, the mother’s awakening at the child's faintest cry while remaining insensitive to other louder noises, or waking up at a specific hour if one has a firm will to do so, and the like. All this proves the tireless persistence of feelings, interest, and will in the Unconscious—or perhaps with only a very faint impression <term>affection: In this context, the term refers to the way the mind is "affected" or touched by a stimulus, a core concept in 19th-century psychology.</term> on consciousness—while the weary intellect rests or, at most, idly watches the deceptive play of dreams. Christian ascetics who lived on top of pillars (columns) for years as a form of devotion.</note> or the Indian penitents and their convoluted positions.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Unconscious, specifically contrasting the way human consciousness processes information through sensory filters versus how the Unconscious operates.
