...then we directly take up sensory impressions and their transformations and combinations from memory, or we think in abstractions. These abstractions, however, are also merely abstracted from sensory impressions; and no matter how much one might discard during the process of abstraction—so long as one retains anything at all—it can only be something that was already contained within the whole from which one first abstracted. That is to say: for us, even abstractions are only remnants of sensory impressions and therefore possess the **form of sensibility**. <note>The "form of sensibility" (Form der Sinnlichkeit) is a reference to Immanuel Kant’s philosophy, suggesting that humans can only perceive the world through the filters of space, time, and the five senses.</note> — It is already sufficiently known from natural science that the sensory impressions we receive from things have no similarity to the things themselves. Since the *Unconscious* obviously cannot participate in *sensory perception*—because every *sensory perception* absolutely *presupposes consciousness*, and where consciousness is absent, perception is lacking—the unconscious representation can likewise never have the *form of sensibility*. But since *consciousness* absolutely cannot represent anything at all except in the form of sensibility, it follows that *consciousness* can nevermore form a direct representation of the manner in which the unconscious representation is represented; it can only know negatively that the former is in no way represented in a manner of which consciousness can form a representation. At most, one can express the very probable conjecture that in the unconscious representation, things are represented as they are in themselves, <note>original: "wie sie an sich sind". This refers to the "thing-in-itself," the reality of an object independent of how our senses perceive it.</note> since it is not apparent why things should appear differently to the Unconscious than they actually are; however, this explanation gives us absolutely no positive grasp of the representation, and we are made no wiser regarding the manner of unconscious representing.

4. *The Unconscious does not waver or doubt*,
it needs no time for reflection, but rather grasps the result instantaneously in the same moment where it thinks the entire logical process that produces the result—all at once and not sequentially, but *within* one another. This is the same as if it does not "think" the process at all, but instead looks directly at the result in *intellectual intuition* <term>intellectual intuition: A type of direct, non-sensory knowledge where the mind perceives a truth or reality immediately, without needing to reason it out step-by-step.</term> with the infinite power of the Logical. We have already mentioned this point often and found it so thoroughly confirmed everywhere that we could use it outright as an infallible criterion to determine, in particular cases...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Unconscious, specifically focusing on how it differs from conscious thought regarding the concepts of space and time. ...to decide whether we were dealing with an influence of the Unconscious or with a conscious performance. Therefore, the conviction of this proposition must be gained essentially from the sum of our previous considerations. — Here, I only wish to add the following: Idealist philosophy <note>German: *Ideal-Philosophie*. This refers to the school of thought, led by thinkers like Kant and Hegel, which argues that reality is mentally constructed or otherwise immaterial.</note> demands an intelligible world <note>A realm of reality that can only be understood by the intellect, not through physical senses.</note> without space and time, which stands in contrast to the world of appearance <note>German: *Erscheinungswelt*; the physical world as we perceive it through our senses.</note> with its forms valid for conscious thinking and being: space and time.

How space is first established in and with nature, we shall see later; here, the concern is with time. If we may now assume that the Unconscious condenses every thought process and its results into a **mo-ment**, that is, into zero-time, then the thinking of the Unconscious is timeless—even though it is still "in" time, because the moment in which the thinking occurs still holds its temporal place in the remaining series of temporal phenomena. 

But if we consider that this moment in which the thinking occurs is only recognized by the manifestation <note>German: *In-Erscheinung-Treten*</note> of its result, and that the thinking of the Unconscious in each particular case only gains existence for a specific intervention in the world of appearance (for it requires no prior deliberation or resolutions), then the conclusion is obvious: the thinking of the Unconscious is only "in time" insofar as the manifestation of this thinking is in time. Apart from the world of appearance and the intervention therein, the thinking of the Unconscious would in fact be not only timeless, but also non-temporal—that is, outside of all time. 

Then one could no longer speak of the representational activity <note>German: *Vorstellungs-Thätigkeit*; the mind's ability to form mental images or concepts.</note> of the Unconscious in the proper sense. Instead, the world of possible representations would lie enclosed as an ideal existence in the womb of the Unconscious. Activity—which by its very definition is something temporal, or at least something that establishes time—would only begin in the moment that one or another representation from this resting, ideal world of all possible representations enters into real appearance. This occurs, as we shall see later at the end of this chapter (pages 330–331), when it is grasped by the Will as its content. Thus, we would have understood the realm of the Unconscious as Kant's "intelligible world." <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) distinguished between the world we experience through our senses (sensible) and the world of things-as-they-are (intelligible).</note> — This is in full agreement with the fact that **duration of time** enters into conscious thought only through the material organ of consciousness...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Unconscious, specifically transitioning from the concept of time in thought processes to the infallibility of the Unconscious. 5. *The Unconscious does not err.* The justification for this proposition must limit itself to the proof that what one might take for errors of the Unconscious upon superficial observation cannot be regarded as such upon closer consideration. Thus, for example, the alleged errors of instinct can be traced back to the following four cases:

a) Where no specific instinct exists at all, but merely an organization <note>In this context, "organization" refers to the physical structure or biological makeup of a living being.</note> which, through the particular strength of certain muscles, directs the general drive for movement primarily toward these muscles. For instance, the purposeless butting of young cattle that do not yet have horns, or when the secretary bird <note>German: *Schlangengeier*, literally "snake-vulture."</note> stomps all its food with its strong legs before eating, even though this only serves a purpose with live snakes. In these cases, the physical organization exists to make a specific instinct redundant and to replace it—one that would be purposeful in certain cases; however, the organization drives the same movements that are purposeful in certain cases even in other cases where they are superfluous and useless. But since the Unconscious, through the machinery of the physical organization, performs the work once and for all that it would otherwise have to do in every individual case, one would have to recognize this arrangement as purposeful due to the conservation of effort <note>German: *Kraftersparniss*; the idea that the Unconscious "saves energy" by automating behaviors through physical anatomy rather than active "thought."</note> of the Unconscious—even if in certain cases this organization were not only superfluous but actually counterproductive and harmful, provided that the number of cases where it is purposeful greatly outweighed the others. However, I am not aware of even one example of this.

b) Where instinct is killed off by habits contrary to nature—a case that frequently occurs with humans and their domestic animals—when, for example, the latter eat poisonous herbs and plants in the pasture which they would avoid in a state of nature, or when humans artificially habituate some animals to a diet that contradicts their nature.

c) Where instinct does not function for accidental reasons, so that the inspiration of the Unconscious is entirely absent, or occurs to such a weak degree that other opposing drives [overcome it]...

--- Page 327 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from page 323 regarding the infallibility of the Unconscious. Having previously established that the Unconscious does not experience the passage of time in the same way as the conscious brain, the author is now systematically addressing four categories of "apparent errors" of instinct to prove they are not errors of the Unconscious itself.</meta>

...overcome, for example, when an animal does not fear its natural enemy and thereby falls victim to it—an enemy that other animals of its species usually flee instinctively—or when maternal love in a sow is so weak that the hunger drive leads her to devour her young.

d) Where <term>instinct</term> <note>German: *Instinct*; defined by the author as an unconscious purpose acting through a conscious mental image.</note> indeed functions correctly based on the conscious representation <note>German: *Vorstellung*; a key philosophical term for a mental image or idea of an object.</note> it is meant to act upon, but this conscious representation itself contains an error. If, for example, a hen broods on an oval-shaped piece of chalk placed beneath her, or a spider carefully tends to a small ball of cotton swapped for its egg sac, the conscious representation in both cases errs due to faulty sensory perception, which mistakes the chalk for an egg or the cotton ball for an egg sac. The instinct itself, however, does not err, as it responds perfectly to that mental image. It would be unfair to demand that the clairvoyance <note>original: "Hellsehen"; in this context, it refers to the Unconscious mind's capacity to possess "knowledge" of a goal without sensory information.</note> of instinct should intervene here to correct the error of the conscious representation. This is because the clairvoyance of instinct only ever concerns those points that conscious perception is fundamentally unable to reach, not those for which the mechanism of sensory cognition is sufficient in all ordinary cases. But even if one were to make this demand, one still could not say that the <term>Unconscious</term> <note>original: "Unbewusste"; the core concept of the book, referring to the absolute biological and psychological ground of existence.</note> erred, but only that it did not intervene with its clairvoyance where it might have.

An objection could still be raised here: namely, that the Unconscious only wills the final results, yet it must think through the entire **thought process** that leads to these results. However, anyone who has carefully read Section 4 of this chapter will have already found the answer to this objection there. Unconscious thinking simply grasps all links of a process—**ground and consequence**, **cause and effect**, **means and end**, and so on—together into a single moment. It does not think them before, alongside, or outside the result, but rather *within* the result itself; it does not think them in any other way than *through* the result. Therefore, this thinking cannot be asserted as a separate act of thought outside the result; rather, it is implicitly contained within the thinking of the result without ever being made explicit. Consequently, only the result is "thought" in our usual sense of the word, and the proposition remains valid: only that which is willed can be thought unconsciously. — Moreover, even within the common category of unconscious thought regarding means and ends, one can say that the end <note>The "Zweck" or goal</note> implicitly thought of within the representation of the willed means is also implicitly willed along with it.

After all this, the sole **activity** of the Unconscious consists in Willing. The unconscious representation that fulfills the Will is, even for this activity, only the non-temporal content—drawn, as it were, into temporality only by association. Willing and being active are therefore identical or interchangeable concepts. It is only through them that time is established; only through them is the representation thrown from being **in potentiality** <note>original Latin: *potentia*</note> into being **in actuality** <note>original Latin: *actu*</note>—from being in the essence into being in appearance, and thus into time itself. It is quite different with conscious representation, which is a product of various factors, one of which—**brain vibrations** <note>The author uses "Hirnschwingungen" (brain vibrations) to refer to the physical, neural processes that 19th-century scientists believed created conscious thought</note>—is from the very beginning tied to duration.

# II.

## The Brain and <term>Ganglia</term> <note>Clusters of nerve cells that function as local control centers in the nervous system, often described as "mini-brains" in 19th-century physiology.</note> as the Condition of Animal Consciousness.

---

Almost all naturalists, physiologists, and physicians are materialists; and the more the knowledge and mindset of the natural sciences and physiology spreads among the educated public, the more the materialistic worldview <note>original: "Weltanschauung"</note> gains ground. What is the reason for this? It lies in the simplicity and striking evidence of the facts upon which the materialistic conception of the animal and human soul—the only spirit <note>The author uses "spirit" (Geist) here to refer to the measurable phenomena of the mind.</note> known to us—is based. Only those who do not know these facts, such as the unscientific masses, or the scholarly world lacking scientific and physiological knowledge, or those who approach these facts with the preconceived opinions of religious or philosophical systems—only they can escape their influence. However, they must absolutely convince every unbiased, thinking person, because they simply need to be taken as they are; they express their meaning with such naive clarity on their own that one does not even need to seek it out. And it is this naive clarity and immediacy of the result, this drastic evidence which can only be denied by force, that secures for the materialistic conception of the mind such a great preponderance over the difficult and subtle deductions and proofs of probability, and against the arbitrary assumptions and often skewed consequences of <term>spiritualist psychology</term> <note>A school of thought arguing that the soul is a non-physical substance entirely separate from the body.</note>. It is what makes all clear minds, who are averse to mystical-philosophical speculations, swear by the banner of materialism, which is as simple as the nature that teaches it, and clear and accurate in all its correct conse- <note>The text breaks here; the intended word is "consequences" (Consequenzen).</note>

As long as one knows or wishes to know no other mental activity than conscious activity, then this sentence says: "all mental activity can only come about through the function of the brain." The conclusion is obvious: "either all mental activity is a mere function of the brain, or it is a product of brain function and another element, which on its own cannot manifest but is purely potential, and only reaches expression in and through normal brain function, which then presents itself as mental activity." The matter appears quite differently as soon as one recognizes unconscious mental activity as its original and primary form, without whose assistance conscious mental activity would be paralyzed at every step. Thus, since all phenomena prove its independence from brain functions, it remains as something autonomous, and only the form of consciousness appears conditioned by matter.

The same relationship generally exists between the unrefined and the educated classes of the present day, as the experiences of hatters <note>Hat makers kept records of head sizes, which 19th-century scholars used as data for "social craniometry"—the study of skull size in relation to social class.</note> prove, among other things. What we know about the influence of quality is little, but it is something. For example, the child's brain is pulpier, richer in water, and lower in fat than that of an adult; the differences between gray and white matter and the microscopic peculiarities only develop gradually. The so-called fibrous structure of the brain, which is very distinct in adults, cannot be recognized in the child’s brain; the more distinct this fibrous structure becomes, the more clearly mental activity emerges. The fetal brain has very little fat (and thus phosphorus), and the fat content increases until birth and, in the newborn, quite rapidly with advancing age. Among animals, too, the brain has, on average, more fat the higher they stand [in the evolutionary hierarchy], and the smaller the brain is in proportion to the animal's intelligence—for example, in the horse. This fat seems to be very important, for in animals that are starved, the brain does not lose a portion of its fat content like other organs do. — Given the same volume, the size of the brain's surface area depends on the number, depth, and shape of the brain convolutions—a highly important factor that can compensate for a lower weight. On average, the convolutions and furrows are also more numerous, deeper, and more intricate the higher an animal species or human race stands.

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that the brain acts as a physical organ of thought, similar to how muscles act as organs of movement. It transitions from discussing brain quality to comparing human brains with large animals and examining the metabolic effects of thinking.</meta>

animals, the largest of the present age, might seem to be an exception, as they exceed the human brain in mass; nevertheless, even this apparent deviation is based only on a predominance of those parts of the brain which serve the body's nervous system as the central organ for voluntary movement and sensation. These parts must present a larger volume, partly because of the greater quantity and thickness of the nerve fibers converging in them, and partly because of the greater development of mechanical force necessary to move a larger mass. In contrast, in no animal do the frontal parts of the brain, which primarily govern the functions of thought <term>Denkfunctionen: The specific intellectual operations of the mind, localized by 19th-century scientists to the frontal lobes.</term>, achieve the same level of development—even in terms of raw quantity—as they do in humans.

6) Conscious thinking strengthens the brain, just as every activity strengthens its organ, and the exertion of thought is always accompanied by the consumption of matter <note>Original: "Stoffverbrauch." This refers to the 19th-century understanding of metabolism, where physical or mental effort "burns" or uses up the physical substance of the organ.</note>. Just as every muscle becomes stronger and increases in mass when it is preferentially exercised (for example, the calves of dancers), the brain also becomes more capable of thinking through mental exercise and increases in both quality and quantity.

Albers in Bonn <note>Johann Friedrich Hermann Albers (1805–1867), a German pathologist and professor.</note> reports that he dissected the brains of several people who had performed a great deal of mental work for many years; in all of them, he found the brain substance to be very firm, and the gray matter and the brain convolutions <note>The folds and ridges on the brain's surface (gyri).</note> to be remarkably developed. This increase in mass is proven partly by the difference between the educated and lower classes, and partly by the growth resulting from the progress of civilization in Europe; both factors, admittedly, only accumulate through the help of inheritance <note>Vererbung: The author is suggesting that the "gains" in brain development from one generation's education are passed down biologically to the next.</note> to the point where they can be observed. 

The fact that all thinking is connected to the consumption of matter in the brain is evident from the simple phenomenon of mental fatigue, which would be completely incomprehensible otherwise. Mental labor increases the appetite to replace the consumed matter just as much as physical labor does. Furthermore, according to Davy's <note>The OCR reads "Dary," but this almost certainly refers to Dr. John Davy, who conducted famous 19th-century studies on "animal heat" and metabolism.</note> measurements, it even increases animal heat <note>A historical term for body temperature produced by metabolic processes.</note>. This is indicated by accelerated breathing, which occurs to "de-carbonize" the blood that is more rapidly carbonized by the faster metabolism. Furthermore, it is well known that the sedentary trades involving no physical exertion—such as tailoring, shoemaking, and light factory work—are those that produce the most brooders <note>People who dwell gloomily or obsessively on certain thoughts.</note> and those with warped religious and political views, whereas physically exhausting trades leave the brain with no strength left for thinking.

7) Every disturbance of the integrity of the brain produces a disturbance of conscious **mental activity**, unless the function of one hemisphere is replaced by the corresponding part of the other hemisphere. Nonetheless, this substitution in the brain is the rarer case. It occurs only if, firstly, the diseased or damaged area does not impair the functions of the rest of the brain—which usually happens in one way or another, for example, through the transmission of pressure—and secondly, if the damage is of such a nature that it completely cancels out the functions of the affected part, rather than letting them persist in an abnormal state. What we have demonstrated in this chapter regarding human consciousness—as the highest known to us, and the one where one might most likely suspect an independence from the body—naturally applies as well to the <term>ganglia</term> <note>Clusters of nerve cells that function as a localized brain or control center in simpler organisms.</note> of lower animals, which replace the brain found in vertebrates. It applies equally to the specific consciousness of every independent ganglion node in humans, as well as in higher and lower animals. Finally, it also applies to the substances that replace the central nervous system in the lowest animals; and should consciousness also be discovered in plants or inorganic matter, it would apply to that as well.

To conclude this chapter, a passage from <term>Schelling</term> <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854), a central figure in German Idealism who sought to bridge the gap between nature and spirit.</note> (Works I. 3, 497) may find its place, which contains the essence of this chapter in a few words, even if the claim in Schelling's mouth takes on a slightly different meaning due to the background of <term>transcendental idealism</term> <note>The philosophical view that our experience of things is determined by the way our mind works, rather than how things are in themselves.</note>:

> “It is not the idea itself, but rather the *consciousness* of it that is conditioned by the <term>affection</term> <note>original: "Affection"; here meaning the physical impact or stimulation of a bodily organ.</note> of the organism; and if <term>empiricism</term> <note>The theory that all knowledge originates from sensory experience.</note> restricts its claim to the latter, then there is nothing to be said against it.”

### III.
# The Origin of Consciousness.

---

Consciousness is not a resting state, but a process, a continuous <term>becoming-conscious</term> <note>original: "Bewusstwerden." The author emphasizes that consciousness is an ongoing activity rather than a static thing.</note>. It goes without saying that this mental process, to which consciousness owes its origin, cannot be directly grasped by the observer’s consciousness; for that which first generates consciousness must naturally lie "behind" consciousness and be inaccessible to conscious self-observation. We can, therefore, only hope to reach our goal by an indirect path. The first condition is that we define the concept of consciousness more precisely than has been necessary until now. — First, it must be distinguished from self-consciousness. My self-consciousness is the consciousness of myself—that is, the consciousness of the <term>subject</term> <note>In philosophy, the "subject" is the "I" or the observer who experiences and acts.</note> of my mental activity. By the "subject of my mental activity," however, I mean 그 portion of the complete cause of my mental activity which is not external; in other words, its internal cause. Self-consciousness is thus only a special case of applying consciousness to a specific <term>object</term> <note>The "object" is whatever the mind is focused on—be it a physical thing, a feeling, or a thought.</note>, namely to the supposed internal cause of mental activity, which is designated by the name "subject." Consciousness as such is therefore, by its very definition, free from a conscious relationship to the subject, as it is directed in and of itself only toward the **object**; it only becomes self-consciousness when the representation of the subject happens to become its object. It follows from this that while no self-consciousness can be conceived without consciousness, consciousness can indeed be conceived without self-consciousness. Only for conscious <term>reflection</term> <note>The act of the mind turning back to look at its own operations.</note>—as it occurs in the mind of the philosopher who stands outside the process in thought and observes it objectively—but not for the subject of the process itself <note>The text ends mid-sentence here.</note>

<note>Vocabulary used in this section: Consciousness, Self-consciousness, Process, Mental activity, Subject, Object, Reflection.</note>

<summary>The author argues that consciousness is a dynamic process rather than a state, and distinguishes basic consciousness (focusing on objects) from self-consciousness (focusing on the "I"). He posits that because consciousness is a product of a process, the underlying cause of that process remains hidden from our direct self-observation.</summary>

Experience corresponds to this completely, in that nothing speaks more emphatically to **consciousness** than **pain**—even **pain** conceived in isolation from the more specific determinations belonging to mental representation <note>Hartmann is arguing that "pain" is the purest form of consciousness because it represents a direct clash between our will and a reality we cannot control.</note>.

The feeling of **pleasure**, or the satisfaction of the **Will**, cannot in and of itself become conscious. This is because, as the Will realizes its content and thereby brings about its own satisfaction, nothing occurs that would come into opposition with the Will. Since every external compulsion is lacking and the Will only gives way to its own consequences, no **consciousness** can arise. The matter presents itself differently where a consciousness has already been established, which collects and compares observations and experiences. This consciousness soon learns from many instances of non-satisfaction to recognize the resistances that oppose every will in the external world, as well as the external conditions necessary if the realization of the **Will** is to succeed. As soon as it must acknowledge these external conditions for success—and thus recognize satisfaction as something partially or entirely conditioned from the outside—consciousness of pleasure also occurs. All of this is confirmed by experience in the best possible way.

First, one observes in infants that they give very emphatic expressions of **pain** for months before the slightest trace of pleasure can be read in their expressions and gestures. This is also very clearly confirmed in spoiled children, whose will is always done and who do not know at all what it is like for their will to go unsatisfied. These children, in fact, have almost no enjoyment from the satisfaction of their will, because these satisfactions remain for the most part unconscious. They derive almost their only enjoyment from sensory satisfactions (sweets <note>original: *Genäsch*; referring to the habit of nibbling on delicacies or treats.</note>), because here the care of those around them cannot spare them the unpleasant comparisons. Any judge of character <note>original: *Menschenkenner*; someone with a deep intuitive understanding of human nature.</note> will likely admit how much our assertion holds true for adults as well; for every kind of satisfaction that occurs without interruption by non-satisfaction—

Now, as far as the will itself is concerned, we have hitherto called it *conscious* if it has a *conscious* representation as its content, and *unconscious* if it has an *unconscious* one. However, it is easy to see that this is only an improper expression, since it refers only to the content of the will; the will itself, however, can never become *conscious*, because it can never be in *contradiction* with itself. Multiple *desires* may well be in *contradiction* with one another, but the *willing* of each moment is, after all, only the resultant of all simultaneous desires; consequently, it can always only be in accordance with itself. Finally, however, I have one last striking reason to offer for the unconsciousness of all will, which decides the question quite directly. Every person knows **precisely only to the extent** what they want as they possess the **knowledge of their own character** and the psychological **laws**—of the connection between motive and desire, between feeling and desire, and the strength of the various desires—and from these can calculate in advance the **result** of their struggle or their "resultant," the will. ...rect way, it would be completely indifferent whether the representation <note>In German philosophy, "representation" (*Vorstellung*) refers to the mental image, idea, or concept that the mind forms of an object or a goal.</note> which forms the content of the will is conscious or unconscious; at most, it might seem important for the becoming-conscious of pleasure. Specifically, if out of *n* cases these accompanying feelings and perceptions have resulted *m* times in displeasure <note>The German terms *Lust* and *Unlust* refer to the basic spectrum of "pleasure" and "unpleasure" (or pain/distress).</note>, and *n*—*m* times in none, then one instinctively concludes that these feelings and perceptions are the mark of an unconscious will which was not satisfied *m* times (that is, it produced displeasure), from which it directly follows that it must have been satisfied *n*—*m* times. The insight just gained regarding the unconsciousness of the will in itself throws interesting light on recurring efforts in the history of philosophy to dissolve the Will into "Representation." I mention only the most prominent: Spinoza, and in more recent times Herbart and his school, who made the most detailed attempt in this regard. This endeavor—which also appears to a lesser degree in Hegel—would be purely inexplicable in such great thinkers if the Will (which is entirely heterogeneous to Representation in its essence) were something directly given in consciousness. However, because one never finds the Will itself in consciousness, but always only the ***representation* of the will**, these efforts become not only explicable, but something justified and required for those who take an **exclusively conscious standpoint**, since the Will has its actual existence only in the realm of the Unconscious. Therefore, it is also characteristic that precisely the most dilettantish of all renowned philosophers, Schopenhauer, setting himself above this requirement of rigorous thinking, claims to find the Will as the core of one's own being directly in consciousness.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Will and consciousness, specifically critiquing Schopenhauer's view that the Will is directly perceptible. It builds on the previous discussion regarding the indirect calculation of unconscious desires by moving into a technical definition of consciousness as a binary state (on or off) rather than a matter of degree.</meta>

Just as the philosophizing of common sense <note>Common sense philosophy refers to the "naive" view that the world is exactly as we perceive it through our senses.</note> believes it can grasp things directly in outer perception, Schopenhauer dogmatically believed he could grasp the Will directly in inner perception. Critique destroys both the one and the other dogmatic illusion of instinct, but science restores knowledge to us as a conscious, indirect possession, replacing the blind, immediate belief of instinct it has destroyed.

Our principle must now prove itself in one final test. Namely, if our assumption is correct—that consciousness is a phenomenon whose essence consists in the opposition of the Will against something that does not originate from it and yet is perceptibly present—it follows that only those elements of representation <note>In German philosophy, "representation" (*Vorstellung*) refers to the mental image, idea, or concept that the mind forms of an object.</note> or feeling can become conscious which encounter a Will in opposition to them. That is, they encounter a Will which "not-wills" or negates them. From this, it follows that consciousness can no more have gradations or degrees than "the Not" or negation can. We are dealing here with a pure alternative: "becoming-conscious or remaining-unconscious." If the Will behaves affirmatively, the latter occurs; if it behaves negatively, the former occurs. There is no "stronger" or "weaker" of negation, for negation is a positive concept <note>In this logical context, "positive" means it is a definite, distinct state or category, rather than a "comparative" quality that can be measured on a scale.</note>, not a comparative one. There is indeed partial and complete negation, but this is not a difference in the act of negating, but in the object being negated. Therefore, it cannot justify a difference in the degree of negation itself. In our case, a partial negation would result in one part becoming conscious and the other remaining unconscious, but in no case could a difference in the degree of consciousness *as such* arise from it.

Therefore, that *which* becomes conscious—the object or the content of consciousness—can show a "more" or "less," but consciousness itself can only be or not be; it can never be "more" or "less." To be sure, the Will, which establishes the becoming-conscious of the object through its negation of it, can also show differences of degree, being stronger or weaker; but the strength of this Will has no influence at all on the alternative of "becoming-conscious or not." Only whether its *content* behaves affirmatively or negatively toward the object of consciousness—only that decides the alternative. For this reason, one cannot speak of the strength of the opposing-

Attention, therefore, consists of material nerve vibrations; as these run from the center toward the periphery, it is impossible for them not to be reflected back from the periphery to the center, even without having encountered a perception. One cannot claim with certainty that it increases the amplitude of the vibrations, because the intensity of a sensation (e.g., the volume of a sound) does not appear to be increased by raising the level of attention; yet this too may, as I consider highly probable, be merely an appearance, since the increase in intensity is already unconsciously discounted. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of attention, specifically shifting from how attention sharpens our mental images to the philosophical distinction between attention, consciousness, and self-consciousness. ...distraction forms a contrast. Instead of infinitely many weak perceptions, consciousness now finds a single energetic <term>representation<note>Original: *Vorstellung*. One can see that the content has changed essentially—so much so that this change is entirely sufficient to explain the altered state of mind. There is nothing present here that would indicate a gradual change in consciousness itself. On the other hand, it is obvious how easily a poor distinction between attention and consciousness can lead to the opinion that consciousness has degrees, just as attention does; indeed, one will very frequently find that "consciousness" is said when "attention" is actually meant. Attention can have degrees because it consists of <term>nerve vibrations<note>The author is using a common 19th-century physiological theory that mental activity corresponds to literal physical oscillations or "vibrations" in the nervous system.</note></term>, and in all nerve vibrations, the size of the oscillation amplitude determines the strength of the sensation. Consciousness, however, can have no degrees because it is an immaterial reaction that either occurs or does not; but when it does occur, it always happens in the same way.

The difference between consciousness and self-consciousness was already suggested at the beginning of this chapter. Self-consciousness, of course, cannot be conceived of without consciousness, but consciousness can certainly be thought of without self-consciousness. To what extent a complete absence of self-consciousness can be proven in reality remains to be seen, since self-consciousness is initially born instinctively as a so-called "dim sense of self." What is certain is that a very clear consciousness often occurs alongside a vanishingly small minimum of self-consciousness; indeed, the clearer the <term>objective consciousness<note>Original: *gegenständliche Bewusstsein*. This refers to consciousness that is focused outward on objects or ideas, rather than inward on the self.</note></term> becomes in an individual, the more their self-consciousness disappears. No one is able to truly enjoy a work of art unless they truly forget themselves. Likewise, self-consciousness almost entirely ceases when one is immersed in scientific reading; and when one is producing work and is sunk in deep reflection, one is so absent not only from their surroundings but also from oneself, that one has no memory of one's most important interests—indeed, even to the point that, if suddenly called upon, one must first remember one's own name. And yet, in these moments, consciousness is at its clearest, precisely because it is entirely immersed in the object of focus.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the unity of consciousness. ...<term>discursive|Proceeding by logic or reasoning rather than immediate intuition</term> moments, when broken down, has the following meaning: alongside the **primary representation** <note>original: "Hauptvorstellung"</note>, I have a much weaker **secondary representation** <note>original: "Nebenvorstellung"</note> stimulated by the first, which I recognize as being in a **causal connection** with an earlier, identical representation. The place and time of this earlier representation can likewise be fixed by the accompanying circumstances emerging in the **memory**.

It is, therefore, nothing other than the **comparison** of a present and a past representation in which the **unity of consciousness** between moments separated by time consists; the possibility of this comparison is achieved by the fact that, of two present representations, one represents the present and the other represents the past. The latter is made possible because I recognize the present representation as being in a causal connection with a past representation identical to it. Now, because one of the two representations represents the past, consciousness—in the unified act of comparison—merges the representatives of present and past consciousness into one, and thereby becomes aware of the unity of consciousness for those past and present representations. If I have two conscious representations, there exists a consciousness of the one and a consciousness of the other, and I would never have the right to claim a unity of these two consciousnesses if I could not prove it. However, by now grouping both representations together in comparison, I suspend both individual consciousnesses within a third "consciousness of comparison," and have thus brought their unity into **immediate intuition** <note>original: "Anschauung"; the direct, non-rational perception of something</note>. Comparison is therefore the moment that makes the thought of a unity of consciousness possible in the first place, and the possibility of the unity of consciousness ends wherever the possibility of comparison ends.

Just as we have seen comparison judge the unity of consciousness of a past and a present representation—that is, representations separated in time—it also judges representations separated in space, meaning those excited by different material parts. <meta>This page continues the technical explanation of the "unity of consciousness." ...brain-consciousness. The reason is simply that in a healthy waking state, every **representation** <note>In this context, a "representation" (Vorstellung) refers to a mental image, thought, or perception</note> emerging anywhere in the brain can be compared with every other representation emerging elsewhere. In contrast, the representations of the spinal cord and the **ganglia** <note>Clusters of nerve cells found throughout the body</note>—which must necessarily exist, for example, during reflex movements, injuries to the internal organs, and the like—generally possess no unity of consciousness with the brain’s representations. The cause of these phenomena is obvious. In the brain, besides the specific <term>commissures|Bundles of nerve fibers that connect the two hemispheres of the brain</term>, countless nerve fibers pass through the entire mass and establish a manifold, intimate connection between every tiny part and the next. The spinal cord already has a much more imperfect connection with the brain; the sympathetic nervous system is linked to the brain only through the single **vagus nerve** <note>original: "nervus vagus"</note>; in conjoined individuals, only more or less accidental fusions of subordinate nerve strands can occur; and in separate individuals, any connection is entirely absent. The more perfect the conduction between the functioning regions of the central nervous system, the less excitation is required in them to propagate the excitation from one to the other without it being weakened or clouded. The more imperfect and longer the pathways of conduction, the greater the **conduction resistance**, the stronger the excitations must be if they are to be propagated to the other central location, and the more unclear and blurred they arrive there. <meta>This page continues the physiological argument regarding the unity of consciousness. ...this view of nerve processes, according to which every thought at one point in the brain is simultaneously telegraphed to all other points of the same, can have nothing surprising about it; it is impossible to interpret the anatomical construction of the brain with its countless fiber connections in any other way. **It is therefore indeed this conductivity that conditions the unity of consciousness**, and with which this unity is proportional. We therefore state as a principle: **Separate material parts produce separate consciousness**, a proposition that commends itself *from first principles* <note>original: "a priori"</note> just as much as separate individuals confirm it empirically. As long as the Australian ant <note>This likely refers to the "bulldog ant," a common example in 19th-century biology; researchers observed that if the ant were cut in half, the head and tail would fight each other, demonstrating that the physical connection is required for a unified "will."</note> is **one** animal, its forebody and hindbody act with a unified consciousness; as soon as it has been cut in two, the unity of consciousness is abolished, and both parts turn against each other in combat. — We further assume: the comparison of two <term>representations|Vorstellungen; the mental images, thoughts, or perceptions present in the mind</term> produced in different locations is only possible because the vibrations of one location are conducted, undiminished and unclouded, to the other; only through the comparison of both representations is the **resolution** <note>original: "Aufhebung." In this context, it refers to the way the mind synthesizes two different thoughts into one higher understanding.</note> of their two consciousnesses into the unified consciousness of the act of comparison possible—but with it, we may add, it is also *by that very fact* <note>original: "eo ipse"</note> granted. The Siamese twins <note>A reference to Chang and Eng Bunker (1811–1874), the famous conjoined twins who were a subject of great scientific interest during this period.</note> refused to play board games with one another, remarking that this would be the same as if the right hand were to play against the left; — however, if one were to imagine the connection of the brains of two people were possible through a bridge just as conductive as the one between the two hemispheres of the same brain, then a common and unified consciousness encompassing the thoughts of both brains would immediately embrace the previously separate consciousnesses of both persons. Each would no longer be able to distinguish their thoughts from those of the other; that is, they would no longer know themselves as two "I's," but only as **one** "I," just as my two brain hemispheres know themselves only as **one** "I."

# IV.

## The Unconscious and Consciousness in the Plant Kingdom.

---

The question regarding the possession of a soul <note>original: "Beseelung"</note> in the plant kingdom is ancient; outside of Judaism and Christianity, it has been answered in the affirmative almost everywhere. Our era, which grew up with the views of these latter two and has far from bridged the chasm between spirit and sensuality torn open by Christianity, has only with difficulty reinstated animals into the right of brotherhood with man; it is no wonder that it has not yet been able to rise to the recognition of the plant soul, since its physiology is accustomed to viewing organic functions and reflex actions even in animals merely as material mechanisms. The question has been treated best by Fechner <note>Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801–1887), a pioneer in experimental psychology and psychophysics</note> in the work *Nanna, or On the Soul-Life of Plants* <note>original: "Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen"</note>, Leipzig 1848, even if some flights of fancy are included; see furthermore Schopenhauer, *On the Will in Nature* <note>original: "Ueber den Willen in der Natur"</note>, chapter on "Plant Physiology," and Autenrieth, *Views on Nature and the Life of the Soul*. It remains for me here partly only to give a brief excerpt, but partly also to emphasize the considerably greater clarity spread over this entire question by the distinction between unconscious and conscious <term>mental activity|Seelenthätigkeit; literally "soul-activity," referring to any process of the mind or psyche</term>. I am convinced that many a person who had to maintain a negative stance toward the previous methods of treatment will become reconciled with the idea of a plant soul by means of the separate consideration of the unconscious and consciousness.

1. **The unconscious mental activity of the plant.** The plant possesses an organic formative activity, a <term>natural healing power|Naturheilkraft; the inherent ability of an organism to repair itself</term>, reflex movements, instinct, and a drive for beauty just like the animal; and if in the animal these phenomena are recognized as the unconscious effects of a soul...

If the unconscious mental achievements of the plant do not rise to the level of the intellectual processes of the animal, but instead remain entirely immersed in physicality, should its soul therefore be any less a soul? This is especially true if what the plant achieves in its own domain is just as perfect as what the animal achieves in its own—indeed, it stands even higher. This is because the plant builds up stubborn inorganic substances into higher and higher organic stages, while the animal, on the whole, only directs and monitors the natural breaking down <note>The author refers to the metabolic process where animals consume plants and break down complex organic matter back into simpler forms</note> of these substances. Let us consider the individual moments one after another.

    a) **The organic formative activity**; this works just as in the animal according to a typical <term>species-idea|Gattungsidee; a 19th-century biological concept suggesting an archetypal plan or "blue-print" that guides the growth of a species</term>. While this "idea" allows for a great deal of leeway regarding the number of branches, leaves, and so on, it is nonetheless completely determined by the laws governing leaf arrangement, blossoms, and internal structure. To be sure, one can divide plants just as one can divide lower animals, so that each part still possesses the ability to complete the type again from within itself; but as with animals, this division in plants is by no means unlimited if a restoration is to remain possible. In the plant, too, all parts exist in a state of reciprocal interaction. Every part closer to the earth processes the substances exactly as the next most distant part must receive them for further processing; an oak root would never nourish a beech, nor a tulip bulb a hyacinth. A harmonious cooperation of all parts takes place in the plant as well, and only this can lead to the goal of manifesting the species-type through all the developmental stages that follow one another over time.

    If, in winter, one guides a branch of a tree standing outdoors into a greenhouse, that branch develops its leaves and flowers while the rest of the tree remains dormant <note>original: "erstarrt", meaning stiffened or frozen in a winter state</note>. The roots suck up the water used by the tree for this purpose, as observation proves; therefore, these roots have been stimulated to increased absorption by the increased life-activity of a single branch (De Candolle <note>Augustin Pyramus de Candolle (1778–1841), a Swiss botanist who established important principles of plant physiology</note>, *Plant Physiology*, I. 76). ...[transmission between] individual parts is mediated by conduction, and to what extent it is an immediate clairvoyant <note>original: "hellsehendes"; here referring to an instinctive, immediate psychic connection similar to what we might now call a "hive mind" or collective instinct</note> process, such as that of individuals in a colony of bees or ants. Reproduction occurs in the animal and plant kingdoms according to the exact same principles: through cell division <term>cell division|Zellentheilung</term>, spore or bud formation, and sexual generation. The similarity in both realms is so striking, particularly in the first stages of generation, that the very same reasons compel us to assume an unconscious-psychic <term>unconscious-psychic|unbewusstpsychisch; a 19th-century philosophical concept suggesting that biological growth is guided by a mind-like force that operates without conscious awareness</term> influence in the origin of the plant as in the origin of the animal.

Admittedly, the embryonic states soon diverge thereafter, which is only to be expected given the difference in the types to be produced; but in both, the progressive development is a constant struggle of the organizing soul against the tendency toward decomposition, regression, and the destruction of form inherent in material elements. Only through the constant prevention of these processes of regression and the incessant creation of conditions that drive further development is the mastery of formless, inorganic matter into formed, organic matter possible—as is the realization of a new, higher stage of the species-type <term>species-type|Gattungstypus</term> at every moment. Every individual cell is active in this process, for the living part of every plant, just like every animal, consists of the sum of living cells; the only difference is that in animals, on average, the changes in form and the merging of cells are somewhat more extensive, and the intercellular substance <term>intercellular substance|Intercellularsubstanz</term> secreted and nourished by the cells is more abundant. The cell is the chemical laboratory for the preparation of various organic compounds; the division and merging of cells are the sole means for producing the external form. In this, a division of labor <term>division of labor|Arbeitstheilung</term> just as strict as that in the animal is carried out: one type of cell is to form this substance, another that. Just as cells in the animal develop into bones, muscles, tendons, nerves, connective tissue, and epithelial cells, so in the plant they develop into pith cells, wood cells, bast <note>The fibrous inner bark of a plant</note> cells, sap cells, starch-flour cells, and so on. Each cell takes up through resorption <term>resorption|Resorption; the selective intake of nutrients</term> by its walls only those substances that it can use; if it has taken up others, it passes them along unused. A circulation of sap <term>sap circulation|Saftkreislauf</term> occurs in every individual cell, and in the entire plant as well. To be sure, no open vessels are present; rather, the flow of sap is [maintained] through endosmosis <term>endosmosis|Endosmose; the inward flow of fluid through a biological membrane</term> and exosmosis <term>exosmosis|Exosmose; the outward flow of fluid through a biological membrane</term>...

The most wonderful things in plants are those mechanisms that serve sexual reproduction. In upright flowers, the stamens <note>the male, pollen-producing parts</note> are generally longer than the pistil <note>the female, seed-bearing part</note>; in hanging flowers, the opposite is true. Where the pollen grains cannot simply fall onto the stigma <note>the receptive tip of the pistil</note>, and the wind is not sufficient to carry them there, insects must take over the mediation. This is the reason for the alluring bright colors of the blossoms; the reason for their far-reaching scent, which always develops most strongly at the time of day when the insects most suitable for that particular flower are swarming; and the reason for the sweet nectar at the base of the flower, which forces the snacking animal to crawl deep enough inside so that it wipes off the pollen grains with its usually bristly body. These grains then remain stuck to the stigma, whether in the same flower or another. Among the milkweeds <note>original: "Asklepiadeen"</note> and orchids, the pollen sticks to the insects by a birdlime-like substance. The birthwort <note>original: "Aristolochia clematitis"</note> has a bulbous flower with a narrow entrance which, by means of downward-pointing hairs, prevents the small gnats that have crawled in from exiting. These swarm around in their prison until they have brushed off the pollen dust with their feathered antennae and deposited it onto the stigma. Immediately after fertilization, the hairs begin to wither and fall away, releasing the flies from their dungeon. — If the pollen grains get wet, they expand and burst; fertilization is then impossible. In this way, rainy weather during the blooming of fruit and grain is very detrimental to them. The precautions taken by blossoms to avoid moisture are very diverse. Protection [is provided by] the banner <note>original: "vexillum," the large upper petal of certain flowers</note>; in the case of the mint family <note>original: "Labiaten"</note>, this is the upper lip of the corolla <term>corolla|the collective term for the petals of a flower</term>; in the *Calyptranthes* species, it is the lid-shaped calyx <term>calyx|the outer protective covering of a flower bud</term>. Many plants close their corolla when it is about to rain (this is already an instinct), many also at night against the dew; others bend their flower stalks over at night so that the open side of the petals is turned downward. ***Impatiens noli me tangere*** <note>the common touch-me-not or yellow jewelweed</note> even hides its flowers under its leaves at night. In most aquatic plants, dry fertilization is made possible by the fact that they do not bloom until their stems have reached the surface of the water. Sea-grass <note>likely *Zostera*</note>, which is anchored to the bottom of the sea, blooms within leaf folds; while these are open at the sides, they prevent water from entering by secreting gases. The **water crowfoot** (***Ranunculus aquaticus***), whose blossoms are submerged during high water levels, protects itself by releasing its pollen from the anthers while the flower is still a closed bud that holds air inside. The water chestnut, ***Trapa natans***, lives on the bottom of the water until flowering time, when the leaf stalks—arranged next to each other in a sort of leaf-rosette—swell into cellular, air-filled bladders and lift the entire plant to the surface of the water. In this way, flowering and fertilization take place in the air; once this is over, the bladders fill with water, and the plant sinks back to the bottom, where it then brings its seeds to maturity. Even more complicated is the mechanism of the ***Utricula***-species <note>the bladderwort, now classified as *Utricularia*</note> for the same purpose. Their heavily branched roots are covered with a multitude of small, rounded bladders <note>original: "utriculi"</note> which possess a kind of movable lid and are filled with a mucus that is heavier than water. Through this ballast, the plant is held back at the bottom of the water until, at flowering time, the mucus is displaced by secreted gases. Now it rises slowly to the surface, carries out flowering and fertilization, and is then pulled down again as the root once more secretes mucus, which in turn displaces the air from the bladders. b) **Natural Healing Power.** Animals possess each organ only as often as the entire organism requires for its existence; hence the endeavor to replace a lost organ in the same manner. The "Idea of the Plant" demands a numerically unlimited repetition of the same organs, which is why a partial loss is usually not dangerous to the survival of the whole. Therefore, there is no reason here to replace the lost parts in the same location and in the same way, as the plant finds it much easier to provide a replacement in other locations through the buds already present. Nevertheless, there are opportunities enough to see that natural healing power <term>natural healing power|Naturheilkraft; the innate ability of an organism to restore itself to health or repair damage</term> is also present in the plant; one only needs to rob a plant of a certain class of organs necessary for its survival—for example, all the roots—and it will immediately drive out new roots, or die if it no longer has the strength to do so. The scarring process <term>scarring process|Vernarbungsprocess</term> of wounds or severed surfaces is also completely analogous to that in animals.

Finally, in the plant as in the animal, life as a whole is an infinite sum of infinitely many acts of natural healing power, since at every moment the destructive physical and chemical influences must be paralyzed and overcome.

c) **Reflex Movements.** Physiologists distinguish between reflex movement and the "simple stimulus phenomenon of contractile tissue"; this is correct if one asks for the location where the reflection of the stimulus into movement takes place—namely, whether the center of reaction <term>center of reaction|Reactionsheerd; the focal point where a physiological response is triggered</term> lies at the stimulated site itself or at another; but it is wrong to want to find a difference in principle here. The essence of the reflex in both cases is the conversion of an acting stimulus into reactive movement;

an absolute restriction to the irritated point never occurs; whether the conduction leads a little further or not cannot establish a difference in principle. That which characterizes a reactive movement as a reflex action is only the insufficiency of generally valid laws of nature to produce it; only where we can content ourselves with such laws (e.g., in elasticity or chemical reactions), only there can one deny the reflex action, the inner essence of which is an unconscious-psychic, an instinctive reaction. Whether a reflex is mediated through nerves and muscles, or through other mechanisms that replace them, can just as little justify a fundamental difference in principle.

If one shakes the water in which a polyp <note>original: "Polyp"; likely referring to a Hydra or similar simple aquatic organism used in early biology to study basic life functions</note> lives, it contracts into a ball; everyone would call this a reflex action, regardless of whether nerves and muscles may or may not be found in the future within the uniformly slimy mass of the polyp; and when the *Mimosa pudica* <note>original: "Mimosa pudica"; often called the "sensitive plant," it is famous for folding its leaves when touched or shaken</note>, shaken by the footstep of a passerby, folds its leaves together, should this not also be a reflex action? If the irritated penis reaches erection through a change in blood circulation, this is recognized as a reflex movement; why then should the altered circulation of sap <term>circulation of sap|Saftcirculation; the movement of vital fluids within a plant, which early physiologists compared to the blood of animals</term> in plants not be an equally valid means for reflex movements? After all, the plant does not require the sustained, rapid movements for which an animal needs its muscles; therefore, muscles would be a useless luxury for it. In animals, a sign of a reflex is that roughly the same reaction occurs whether one applies a mechanical, chemical, thermal, galvanic, or electrical stimulus; this is also the case with plants, whereas inanimate ("dead") mechanisms usually respond only to one very specific type of stimulus. Strong electric shocks destroy both animal and plant irritability <term>irritability|Reizbarkeit; a fundamental concept in 18th and 19th-century physiology describing the inherent power of living tissues to respond to stimuli</term>. If one sticks a needle connected to the positive pole of a galvanic battery through the stem of a Barberry flower <note>original: "Berberis-Blume"</note> and connects the wire of the negative pole to a petal using a gently applied piece of damp paper, the stamen <note>original: "Staubfaden"</note> belonging to that leaf snaps over to the pistil <note>original: "Pistill"</note> at the moment the circuit is closed. If the poles are reversed, the current is less effective, just as animal preparations react more strongly when the negative pole is connected to the peripheral end. <meta>This page continues the argument that plants exhibit reflex actions and irritability similar to animals. The previous page established that the lack of a nervous system does not preclude "reflexes," defining them as unconscious-psychic reactions to stimuli.</meta>

...just as with frog legs, no movement occurs. An irritated animal part returns slowly to its position once the stimulus is removed; thus an irritated oyster or polyp <note>original: "Polyp"; likely referring to a Hydra or similar simple aquatic organism used in early biology to study basic life functions</note> contracts quickly but opens slowly. A repetition of the stimulus dulls the irritability; rest restores it. Irritability further manifests differently according to the state of health, age, sexual relations, season, weather, and other external circumstances. All of this is exactly the same in plants as in animals.

I have already mentioned the reflex movements of the *Dionaea muscipula* <note>original: "*Dionaea muscipula*"; the Venus flytrap</note> above; if an insect lands on one of its leaves, it is first held fast by the hairs folding over, and only gradually does the entire leaf roll shut. Here we have, upon a simple stimulus at one point, a participation of many points of the leaf—partly simultaneous, partly following one another purposefully—exactly as we are accustomed to seeing in animals, except that instead of the monarchic command of a nerve center, a "republican" participation of all points takes place in harmonic agreement. Already more centralized and therefore more animal-like is the phenomenon in all leaves, stamens <term>stamens|Staubgefässen; the pollen-producing reproductive organs of a flower</term>, etc., where the center of reaction <term>center of reaction|Reactionsheerd; the specific point or "hearth" where a physiological response is triggered</term> is to be found in the joints with which these parts are attached.

In many blossoms, the mature stamens gradually lean toward the pistil <term>pistil|Stempel; the female reproductive part of a flower</term> of their own accord; in some, a joint is formed which, upon the stimulus of some insect, snaps the filament <term>filament|Staubfaden; the slender stalk that supports the stamen's anther</term> over toward the stigma <term>stigma|Narbe; the receptive tip of the pistil where pollen germinates</term>. In others, even the bent pistil is irritable and stretches out upon a stimulus striking it, whereby it brushes pollen grains off the anthers <term>anthers|Staubbeuteln; the pollen-containing sacs of the stamen</term>. *Mimosa pudica* <note>original: "*Mimosa pudica*"; the "sensitive plant," known for folding its leaves when touched</note> has doubly pinnate <term>pinnate|gefiederte; a leaf arrangement where leaflets are pairs along a central axis, like a feather</term> leaves, and the leaflets, leaf ribs, main petiole <term>petiole|Blattstiel; the stalk that joins a leaf to a stem</term>, and even the branch itself each have their own particular movement. If one carefully applies some strong acid to a leaflet while avoiding any shaking, all nearby leaves close one after another; according to Dutrochet <note>Henri Dutrochet (1776–1847), a French physiologist who was among the first to investigate the mechanisms of plant movement and osmosis</note>, this speed of propagation <term>speed of propagation|Fortpflanzungsgeschwindigkeit; the rate at which a stimulus travels through biological tissue</term> amounts to eight to fifteen millimeters per second in the petioles, and at most two to three millimeters in the pistil. Here, the conductivity <term>conductivity|Leitungsfähigkeit; the ability of tissue to transmit a signal or stimulus</term> is visible before our eyes. The same is achieved if one gently burns a leaflet; the leaves fold together far beyond where the effect of the heat reaches.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the physiological responses of plants are fundamentally similar to the reflex actions seen in animals, further extending this logic to the concept of instinct. It is impossible to overlook the profound analogy between the reflex actions of animals and plants; the differences extend only as far as the overall arrangement of the organisms and the specific purposes of each reaction differ. Once one has recognized reflex actions in animals as acts that are ultimately of a psychic nature <note>The author uses "psychic" in the 19th-century philosophical sense, referring to an underlying mental or vital force that guides life, rather than conscious thought.</note>, one cannot help but attribute this unconscious-psychic element to plants as well, just as one must grant it to every animal part that is still capable of reflex movements on its own.

d) **Instinct.** Already in the animal kingdom, we have seen the inseparability of instinct, reflex movement, and organic formation; in the plant kingdom, they can be separated even less. On the one hand, due to the plant’s limited means of movement, organic formation must achieve much through purposeful mechanisms—things that animals accomplish through instinctive movement (consider fertilization and the dispersal of seeds). On the other hand, the consciousness of plants sits so low that the difference between the stimulus of a reflex movement and the motive of an instinctive action shrinks to a minimum. Nevertheless, we will still find abundant traces which confront us unmistakably as the same phenomenon that we call instinct in the animal kingdom. A polyp <note>original: "Polyp"; likely a Hydra or similar simple aquatic organism</note> instinctively moves from the shaded half of its container to the one illuminated by the sun; and if the sunflower almost wrenches its neck to turn its face toward the sun, should that not also be called instinct? Dutrochet <note>Henri Dutrochet (1776–1847), a French biologist who was a pioneer in the study of cell biology and plant physiology.</note> recounts in his researches <note>original: "s. rech."; referring to *Recherches anatomiques et physiologischen sur la structure intime des animaux et des végétaux* (1824)</note> p. 131: “I saw that when the upper surface of a leaf on a plant standing in the open air is covered with a small board, this leaf tries to escape this screen by means which are not always the same, but are always of the kind that must lead most easily and quickly to the goal; thus it happened sometimes through a lateral bending of the leaf stalk, sometimes by a bending of the same leaf stalk toward the stem.”

Knight <note>Thomas Andrew Knight (1759–1838), a British horticulturalist who studied plant physiology and gravity.</note> saw a grapevine leaf whose underside was illuminated by sunlight; although he had blocked every path for it to return to its natural position, it made almost every possible attempt to turn the correct side toward the light—the side with which it must primarily breathe. (Treviranus, *Contributions* <note>original: "Beiträge"; likely referring to Gottfried Reinhold Treviranus's "Beiträge zur Pflanzenphysiologie" (1811), a foundational work in plant physiology</note>, 119.)

Dutrochet <note>Henri Dutrochet (1776–1847) was a French physician and botanist who discovered the process of osmosis and studied how plants react to stimuli.</note> covered the terminal leaflet of a three-leaved bean leaf (*Common bean* <note>original: "Phaseolus vulgaris"</note>) with a small board. "When one," says this researcher, "sees how many means are employed here to achieve the same goal, one is almost tempted to believe that a secret intelligence is at work here, choosing the most appropriate means to reach that goal." Thus, a scientist, pressed by the sheer power of facts, expresses a truth that remains incomprehensible to him only because he is unaware of the <term>unconscious activity of the soul|A philosophical concept suggesting that life processes are guided by a mental force that operates without conscious thought</term>. It is easy to see that this is not merely a reflex action to a stimulus, for it is precisely the *absence* of a necessary stimulus that is being avoided.

The phenomena of "plant sleep" <note>Known scientifically as nyctinasty, these are the rhythmic movements of plants, such as folding leaves or closing petals, usually in response to the onset of darkness</note> are fairly well-known; the leaves partly droop or fold, and the flowers lower their heads or close. Some of these phenomena have already been mentioned and find their purpose in protecting the pollen grains from dew. One can easily be convinced, however, that the drooping of the flower stalks is not based on mere limpness; rather, they are tense and elastic in their bent state. *Malva peruviana* <note>A species of Mallow</note> forms a kind of funnel in its sleeping state by raising its leaves around the stem or the tips of the branches, under which the young flowers or leaves are protected; the *Touch-me-not* <note>original: "Impatiens noli me tangere"</note> forms a vault for the young shoots from its lowered uppermost leaves, and some others enclose the flowers by folding the leaflets of their compound leaves together. The times for sleep and waking are as varied for plants as they are for animals. Some of our plants follow the sun; others keep precise, specific times.

Finally, the stem can no longer support its own weight; it falls to the ground and continues to creep straight ahead. **2. Consciousness in the Plant.** The preceding result was easy to foresee and required no particular acumen; however, the question of whether a consciousness dwells within the plant is more difficult. — The dispute over the plant-like or animal-like nature of certain creatures is as old as natural science itself, and it can be decided no better today than in Aristotle's <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) classified living things in a hierarchy where plants possessed only a "vegetative soul"</note> time, because as an alternative choice, it cannot be decided at all. As organic beings, plants and animals have certain properties in common; they are distinguished by other properties according to their different roles in the economy of nature <note>original: "Haushalt der Natur"; a common 19th-century term for what we now call ecology</note>. But when the entirety of life's phenomena are reduced to such a simple form that those distinguishing characteristics more or less disappear, and essentially only those shared by both kingdoms remain, then the differences between animal and plant must also vanish. It is foolish to maintain a dispute which, by its very nature, must remain without result. Microscopic observation has progressed so far that, if there were certain criteria for a plant-like or animal-like nature, they could surely not escape the researcher, and the dispute would have long been settled; the fact that there are, indeed, no criteria mutually recognized by the contending parties proves precisely that they are not even clear about what they are arguing over. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the plant and animal kingdoms. Having previously argued that plants possess an unconscious will, the author now addresses the evolutionary and geological shared origins of both kingdoms, moving toward a definition of their fundamental difference: production versus consumption.</meta>

...it would follow only that the domain of shared characteristics between the two kingdoms has been drawn too narrowly until now; that there are far fewer differences between animal and plant than previously believed; and that these differences only become so striking <note>original: "eclatant"</note> in their more advanced forms that no one can fail to recognize them. — This perspective is also the only one that can be supported by geology. While the current creation of the Earth is sustained by the balance between the products of the animal and plant kingdoms, the first foundation of organic nature could evidently only be laid with such beings that contained this balance within themselves, and thus still stood at the **point of indifference** <term>indifference point: a philosophical and scientific term of the era referring to a neutral state where the specific traits of two categories—like "animal" and "plant"—have not yet branched off or specialized</term> between animal and plant. 

Only from this humble beginning could development proceed in different directions, as sea animals emerged which lived off these **indifferent plant-infusoria** <term>infusoria: a historical term for microscopic organisms found in water; here, the author refers to organisms that seem to be both plant and animal at once</term> (polyps, etc.), and as their counterweight, the first stages of more distinct plant formations became possible. The more both kingdoms became populated, the more nutrients became available for higher animal classes, and the more higher plant classes could in turn exist upon the products of life and death from these animals. Thus, development in both kingdoms always kept pace with one another, as geology teaches us, while within each kingdom, the lower stages generally always precede the higher ones. 

From this, one should also draw the conclusion that the plant kingdom and animal kingdom as a whole are not subordinate but **coordinate** domains of creation. If the animal kingdom, relying on its higher development of consciousness, presumes to elevate itself above the plant kingdom, it can only do so because the latter is just as superior in organic terms: for the plant forms the very substances to whose effortless consumption the animal owes its higher consciousness. 

This **building** and **consuming** is the actual and essential difference between both kingdoms; where the former predominates, the character is primarily plant-like; where the latter prevails, it is animal-like; where both stand in balance, there is the point of indifference between animal and plant. All other differences commonly cited are entirely of a secondary and derived nature, just as I have outlined such a derivation for the animal kingdom in Chapter A. VIII. pages 140–143 in the general plan.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the blurred boundaries between the plant and animal kingdoms. However, it is by no means my intention to claim that the plant **merely** produces and the animal **merely** consumes; for in every animal we also see processes, partly of the higher formation of ingested substances (for example, the formation of brain fats <note>original: "Gehirnfette"; referring to the complex lipids or fatty acids essential for neural tissue</note>), and partly of their transformation without regression.
