Consequently, on both sides, it can only be a question of "more or less"; every animal is in part of a plant-like nature, and every plant is in part of an animal-like nature. Where one side clearly dominates the other, the whole is rightly named after that side; but where both sides are fairly balanced, naming it after one side becomes difficult, or even inadmissible. We should no longer find it marvelous if one and the same being shows a predominantly plant-like nature during one part of its life and a predominantly animal-like quality during another; this is no greater a metamorphosis <term>metamorphosis: a biological process of transformation, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly</term> at those stages near the point of indifference <term>point of indifference: a concept from 19th-century natural philosophy referring to a neutral state where the specific traits of two categories—like "animal" and "plant"—have not yet branched off or specialized</term> than that of insects, frogs, or fish. No less can similarities be found with oak and acanthus branches, with fungi, mosses, and lichens” (Dana in Schleiden's and Froriep's Notices, June 1847, No. 48). — Chemical substances certainly cannot establish a distinction; the similarity of plant and animal protein substances is well known; fungi in particular are rich in animal-like compounds; cellulose <note>original: "Holzfaserstoff"; literally "wood fiber material," now known as cellulose, which was surprisingly discovered in some marine animals</note> is found in the mantle of ascidians <note>sea squirts</note> and other salp-like tunicates; chlorophyll <note>leaf green</note> has been detected in turbellarians <note>a type of flatworm</note> and in infusoria <note>a historical term for various microscopic aquatic organisms</note>.

Often, different species of a single genus belong partly to the plant kingdom and partly to the animal kingdom; for example, the *Alcyonium* species <note>a genus of soft corals often called "dead man's fingers"</note> are all of such a fundamentally similar nature that Linnaeus <note>the father of modern taxonomy</note> was certainly not wrong to group them into one genus. Nevertheless, some of them are the very definition of "ambiguous animals" <note>original: "Animalia ambigua" (Latin)</note> (according to Pallas), which therefore rank very well among the amorphozoans <note>an obsolete term for "formless animals" like sponges</note>, such as *Alcyonium cidaris*, *cydonium*, and *ficiforme*. Others are generally reckoned to the plant world, specifically several species in the related and species-rich genus *Peziza* <note>a genus of cup fungi</note>. In yet others, not only the animal nature but even the polyp nature is so decisively proven that they have been separated from the sponges <note>original: "Spongozoen"</note> and included among the polyp-bearing animals <note>original: "Polyparien"</note>, while simultaneously being assigned a second genus name; thus *Lobularia digitata*, *palmata*, and *arborea*—from the Alcyonians of the zoo-corals—are synonymous with *Alcyonium lobatum*, *palmatum*, and *arboreum*. The prehistoric species *Manon peziza* is composed of both an animal and a plant name. Here we only find a repetition of phenomena from other areas of the animal kingdom, where, for example, some rotifers <note>microscopic "wheel animals"</note> are counted among the worms and others among the infusoria, or one species of *Cercaria* <note>a larval stage of parasitic flukes</note> is counted among the worms while other species of the same genus are reckoned to be spermatozoa.

The small vesicles of which the red-coloring matter of snow consists (*Protococcus nivalis* <note>the "red snow" alga</note>), were regarded as algae by Agardh, De Candolle, Hooker, Unger, Martins, Harvey, and Ehrenberg...

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of plant consciousness and the role of the Unconscious in biological life (from the previous page) to a metaphysical investigation into the fundamental nature of the physical world. ## V.

### Matter as Will and Representation.

---

Natural science deals with three interlocking subjects: *laws*, *forces*, and *matter*. This separation is entirely to be approved, for it clearly groups different sets of phenomena under unified perspectives and simplifies our mode of expression. The question now is whether these three are truly of different natures, or whether they are actually only *one*, which, viewed merely from different perspectives, appears in three different ways. In the case of *laws*, this may be admitted without hesitation, for it is obvious that they are not existences hovering in the air, but mere abstractions of forces and matter; it is only because this *force* and this *matter* *are* what they are that they act in this manner, and as often as we encounter such a force, it must act in just such a way. This constancy of *acting-so* is what we call *law*. This relationship is also generally recognized, and indeed we hear the *materialists* <note>Materialism is the philosophical view that everything in the universe, including thoughts and consciousness, is the result of material interactions.</note> always naming only *force* and *matter* as their principles, which naturally include the *laws*. In Chapter C. II., we defended *materialism* insofar as it asserts organized matter as the *essential condition* <note>original: "conditio sine qua non"</note> of conscious mental activity; throughout the preceding investigations, we have demonstrated an *unconscious psychic principle* <note>The "unconscious psychic principle" is Hartmann's core idea: a hidden, purposeful mental force that operates beneath the level of conscious awareness to organize life and the universe.</note> as standing above matter, and thereby already shown the one-sidedness of that *materialism* which recognizes no principles other than *material* ones; we have now reached the point where we occupy ourselves with that—

<summary>Hartmann begins a metaphysical analysis of the components of natural science—laws, forces, and matter—suggesting they may be different manifestations of a single underlying principle. He critiques pure materialism for ignoring the "unconscious psychic principle" that he argues governs these material elements.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of biological life to a metaphysical investigation of the physical world. Having established the "Unconscious" as a factor in organic life, Hartmann now turns to the fundamental building blocks of reality—Force and Matter—to show that even the inorganic world is governed by the same underlying principles.</meta>

...[we] must [engage with] <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the thought that we must address the claims of materialist philosophy.</note> what one-sided *Materialism* posits as the exclusive *principles* of all existence—that is, as philosophical *original principles*—namely *Force* and *Matter*. I would consider it useless to attempt a dialectical discussion of these concepts here; one could never be certain of treating exactly those concepts intended by *Materialism*, nor would a *Materialist* ever be moved to change their view by such means. I believe the only appropriate path is the *deepening* of the scientific *investigation* of *matter*. Although the future may bring invaluable insights in this direction that we cannot yet imagine, I believe that the fundamental features of the only possible way of conceiving matter have been so firmly established by the recent successes of *physics* and *chemistry* that no time will ever be able to shake them; furthermore, I believe they offer sufficient starting points to penetrate into the furthest depths of this mystery. If this has not yet happened, or at least has not happened from the side of *natural science*, it is simply because science, at its core, only has an interest in *hypotheses* insofar as they provide guidance for new *experiments* or are indispensable for the application of *mathematical calculation* <note>original: "Calculs"</note>; beyond that, science sees no *practical* value, and it is therefore indifferent to such things. We must therefore first *recapitulate* what science knows about the *constitution* of *matter* and its inherent *forces*, and then see if these results are capable of being *deepened* in a simple and natural way.

If one imagines a chemically homogeneous body—for example, carbonate of lime <note>Modern calcium carbonate (limestone or chalk).</note>—being continuously divided, one eventually reaches parts of a certain size that can no longer be divided if they are to remain carbonate of lime; if one succeeds in splitting them, the resulting pieces are one part carbonic acid <note>In 19th-century chemistry, "carbonic acid" often referred to carbon dioxide (CO2) when separated from a base.</note> and one part lime. ...distributed within every body between the molecules, as well as between celestial bodies, and which is recognized by the resistance against **Encke's Comet** <note>Johann Franz Encke observed that his namesake comet’s orbital period was shortening, leading 19th-century scientists to believe space was filled with a "resisting medium" called the luminiferous aether.</note> and its ability to radiate heat. Bodies and body-atoms attract one another, specifically in an **inverse square ratio** <term>Inverse square law: A principle where a physical force (like gravity) weakens rapidly as distance increases; if you double the distance, the force becomes four times weaker.</term> of the distance; that is, the total force of a body-atom in all directions of space remains constant at any distance.

**Ether** and **ether-atoms** <note>In the 1800s, "ether" was the hypothetical substance thought to carry light and heat through the vacuum of space, much like air carries sound.</note> repel one another, specifically in an inverse ratio of a higher power than the second power of distance—at least the third; that is, the total force of an ether-atom in all directions of space grows at least in inverse proportion to the distance.

All body-atoms would rush together into a single point if the surrounding ether-atoms did not form, as it were, envelopes around every molecule to prevent them from touching. Two ether-atoms can never collide because their repulsion becomes infinitely large at infinitely small distances. Conversely, two body-atoms could never be separated again if they were to touch, because their attraction would then be infinitely great. Therefore, the molecules must be kept apart by ether-atoms even within chemical compounds, because they can be separated again by ether vibrations (heat, **galvanism** <term>Galvanism: An early term for electricity produced by chemical action, named after Luigi Galvani.</term>).

Body-atoms and ether-atoms repel one another. Previously, it was assumed that they attracted each other; up to a certain point, the phenomena are explained equally well by either assumption. However, because one had to decide on one of them for the sake of mathematical calculation, attraction was chosen by chance. **Wiener** <note>Christian Wiener (1826–1896) was a German physicist and mathematician who provided some of the first mathematical explanations for molecular movement.</note> has shown (see **Poggendorff's Annals**, Vol. 118, p. 79, and Wiener, "The Fundamental Principles of the World Order," <note>original: "Die Grundzüge der Weltordnung"</note> Book I), that the explanation of the **liquid state of matter** <note>original: "flüssigen Aggregatzustandes"</note> requires the assumption of repulsion, and that this generally agrees better with our other physical views. The atomic theory, as developed so far, explains in a surprising way the laws of heat and the various **states of matter** <term>states of matter: traditionally solid, liquid, or gas, referred to here by the German term "Aggregatzustände"</term> brought about by changes in heat (see Wiener, "Principles of World Order," first book) <note>Christian Wiener (1826–1896) was a German mathematician and physicist; his 1863 work "Grundzüge der Weltordnung" attempted to explain the universe through atomic mechanics.</note>. — One material force remains to be mentioned: **inertia** <note>original: "Beharrungsvermögen" - the property of matter by which it continues in its existing state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line, unless changed by an external force.</note>. If one imagines a single atom alone in space, the concept of rest or motion cannot yet be applied to it at all, because it has no specific location in space and thus cannot change that location. Consequently, there is no **absolute rest** or **absolute motion**, but only relative. From this it follows that one has no more right to say "A moves toward B" than "B moves toward A," or "the ball moves toward the disk" than "the disk moves toward the ball." Thus, the resistance offered by the disk to the ball is not so much the resistance of a resting disk as it is that of a moving disk—or rather, its **kinetic energy** <term>kinetic energy: referred to in the original as "lebendige Kraft" (vis viva), a historical term for energy in motion</term>. If we imagine two body-atoms A and B, both would still move toward one another even if only A possessed an attractive force; for while A attracts atom B, due to the **relativity of motion**, it necessarily draws **itself toward B** just as much as it draws B toward itself. The same applies to the repulsion of ether-atoms. This latter assumption has nothing against it and would therefore deserve preference as the simpler one; for *principles should not be multiplied beyond necessity* <note>original Latin: "principia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem" — a philosophical rule, often called Occam's Razor, which states that one should not make more assumptions than the minimum needed to explain something.</note>. Natural science explains **mass** as **the product of volume and density**, and this does indeed lead to the way in which any unbiased perception grasps the concept of mass—provided, that is, that one avoids a circular argument when explaining density and does not use the concept of **mass** again. In that case, density is only to be understood as the arrangement of equivalent particles; if the product of volume and density remains unchanged, it is clear that this is only possible if the **number of equivalent particles** remains unchanged. We can therefore define **mass** simply as the **number** of equivalent particles, provided that we continue the division in all things being compared until we have **reached equivalent particles everywhere**.

One sees immediately that only **atoms** satisfy this requirement; but they truly do so, for even the **ether-atoms and body-atoms** are to be considered equivalent, since every **ether-atom** repels every **body-atom** exactly as it does every other **ether-atom** and vice versa; therefore, the **reciprocity of their forces**—that is, their **inertia** <note>The original term is "Beharrungsvermögen," which literally means the "ability to persist." In a 19th-century scientific context, this refers to inertia—the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion.</note>—**is equal**. We must therefore now define the mass of a thing as the **number of its atoms**, and have thus presented the only possible, strictly scientific expression for what everyone thinks of, more or less clearly, when using the word mass.

From this, however, it follows directly that it no longer makes sense to speak of the **mass of an atom**, for one could only imagine it divided once again into equivalent parts, and one would get no further than one already is. One can certainly speak of the mass of a molecule, for it consists precisely of atoms; one can also say by way of comparison that a body-molecule has a much greater mass than an ether-atom; but the masses of two atoms can no longer be compared, for each of them is the **unit of mass**. Furthermore, it would be conceivable that *n* body-atoms had united into one without any intervening ether-atoms, so that they could never separate again; then an ether-atom would repel **each** of these united atoms with single force—thus the complex with *n*-fold force—and the complex would indeed have the...

Even more *courage* is required to break ruthlessly, in *all* its *consequences*, with that which has once been overcome. But even when one has achieved all this, it still requires an almost superhuman energy of the intellect and character not to be ambushed once again—or at least secretly influenced—by that which was believed to have been settled. For no task is more difficult than to win for oneself a full, negative freedom of thought. Precisely because the prejudices arising from sensory perception are not conscious conclusions of the intellect, but rather instinctive, practically sufficient inspirations, they are so difficult to destroy and eliminate through conscious thought. One may tell oneself a thousand times that the moon at the horizon has the same angular size—and thus the same apparent size—as it does high in the sky; that it is an error of the intellect to consider it looking smaller high in the heavens than down at the edge; the same error that makes the celestial vault appear to us not as a hemisphere, but as a flattened segment of a sphere. All of this cannot bring one to see the moon as being the same size in both cases, precisely because the instinctive assumption maintains itself despite better conscious knowledge <note>This refers to the "Moon Illusion," a famous optical illusion where the moon appears larger near the horizon than overhead, which was a frequent topic in 19th-century psychology and optics.</note>.

Such an *instinctive prejudice* originating from sensory perception is also the concept of *matter* <note>original: "Stoff." In this context, it refers to physical substance or "stuff."</note>. No natural scientist has anything to do with matter in his science, except insofar as he decomposes it into *forces*, whereby the *apparent effects of matter* turn out to be *effects of force*; that is, matter is more and more *dissolved into force*. Nevertheless, even today, one will find few natural scientists who would admit the ultimate consequence of their own science: that *matter* is nothing but a system of forces. The reason for this lies purely in sensory prejudice. One forgets that we perceive matter just as little directly as we do atoms; rather, we only perceive its pressure, impact, vibrations, and so on; so that therefore

Obviously, that the force and substance of each atom must separate, for the substance is induced by the external force to change its position, but the force is not. The manner of this action is completely incomprehensible, for if substance becomes actively effective, it essentially becomes force once again. Instead of force A pulling force B toward it, as would be natural, it moves the substance of B, and only then does the substance of B move the force of B.

Atomistic dynamism satisfies all requirements by uniting the positive principles of both sides within itself.

If we briefly recapitulate these principles once more, they are as follows: There are equal amounts of positive and negative—that is, attractive and repulsive—forces. The directions of the effect of each force intersect at a mathematical point, which we call the "seat" of the force. This seat of force is mobile. Every force acts upon every other in the same way, regardless of which sign (positive or negative) it possesses. The positive force is called a **Body-Atom**; the negative force is called an **Ether-Atom** <note>In 19th-century science, "ether" was thought to be an invisible, weightless substance that filled all space and transmitted light and heat.</note>. At a certain finite distance, the repulsion of an ether-atom and the attraction of a body-atom are equal to one another; however, because the law of their change varies with distance, repulsion predominates between ether-atoms and body-atoms at smaller distances, while attraction predominates at greater distances. 

Body-atoms, with ether-atoms positioned between them to keep them apart, combine to form the molecules of the chemical elements; these, in the same manner, form the molecules of chemically compound bodies, and these in turn form the material bodies themselves. Matter is thus a system of atomistic forces in a certain state of equilibrium. From these atomic forces, in the most diverse combinations and reactions, arise all so-called "forces of matter," such as gravitation, gravity, expansion, elasticity, crystallization, electricity, <term>galvanism</term><note>An early term for electricity produced by chemical action, named after Luigi Galvani.</note>, magnetism, chemical affinity, heat, light, and so on; nowhere,

<meta>Continuing from page 421, the author concludes the discussion on "atomistic dynamism," where matter is reduced to mathematical points of force. This page transitions into a deeper metaphysical analysis of what "force" actually is, moving from a physical description to a philosophical examination of "striving."</meta>

<page-num>422</page-num>

...as long as we remain within the inorganic realm, we do not need to call upon any forces other than atomic forces.

We have thus seen that of the two materialistic principles, force and matter, the latter has subtly dissolved and merged into the former; we now know exactly what we are to understand by "force," namely an attractive or repulsive point-of-force acting either positively or negatively. The concept of force is now so precisely defined that we can approach it directly, without fear of having understood the concept differently than natural science and <term>materialism</term><note>The philosophical view that everything in the universe, including consciousness, is the result of material interactions. Here, the author is showing how even materialism eventually relies on "immaterial" forces.</note> intend it. Let us see what this concept reveals itself to be.

The attractive atomic force strives to bring every other atom closer to itself; the result of this striving is the execution or realization of that approach. In force, we must therefore distinguish between the **striving itself** as a pure act <note>original Latin: "actus"</note>, and **that which is striven for** as the goal, content, or object of the striving. Striving precedes execution; insofar as the execution is already established, the **striving is realized**, and thus it **no longer** exists; only the **striving yet to be realized**, and thus **not yet realized**, exists. Consequently, the resulting movement **cannot** be contained as a **reality** within the striving, since both exist at separate times.

If, however, it were **not at all** contained within the striving, then the striving would have no reason to produce attraction rather than something else—such as repulsion—nor why it should change with distance according to one law and not another; it would then be an **empty, purely formal striving without a specific goal or content**; it would therefore have to remain aimless, contentless, and consequently resultless, which contradicts experience. Experience shows, rather, that an atom does not attract one moment and repel the next by chance, but remains entirely consistent and always identical to itself in the goal of its striving. Nothing remains, therefore, but to conclude that the striving of the attractive force contains within itself the **approach** and the **law of change based on distance**, and yet does not contain them **as a reality**.

## VI.

### The Concept of Individuality.

---

Individual means an indivisible thing (just as "atom" does), yet everyone knows that individuals can be cut and divided. One should therefore think of an "individual" only as something which, by its nature, must not be divided if it is to remain what it is; this is, however, the concept of Unity, in Greek *Monas* <note>original: "Monas." In philosophy, a monad refers to an elementary individual being that reflects the order of the world.</note> (not to be confused with the numerical concept of One, in Greek *hen* <note>original: "ἕν"</note>). According to this, the concepts of Unity or Monad and Individual would coincide, yet one very soon sees that Unity is a broader concept than Individual; that is, every individual is a unity, but not every unity is an individual. Thus, for example, every coherent shape is a unity by virtue of the continuity of space; I cannot divide it without destroying it, yet I would not call a purely accidental spatial unity, such as a clod of earth, an individual. Furthermore, every movement or every process has a unity by virtue of the continuity of time—for example, a musical tone—yet this unity is also not an individual. (Compare von Kirchmann, *Philosophy of Knowledge*, Vol. I, pp. 131–141, 285–307 <note>Julius von Kirchmann (1802–1884) was a philosopher and jurist who argued for a "philosophy of reality" based on perception rather than abstract idealism.</note>.) The unity of "being-within-one-another" or mutual penetration, as occurs, for example, with mixtures of colors, tastes, or smells, and with different properties in the same thing, reduces partly to being **in the same place**, partly to the temporal **simultaneity** of the different properties, and partly to the causal unity that follows; it cannot, therefore, be regarded as a special kind of unity. The causal relational unity is the strongest that exists; we have three types of it to

If, secondly, the unity of purpose consists in a building to be constructed, one would not call the total number of workers who share this purpose an individual; if thirdly, a country lives off the natural products of its colonies, and the colonies exist only through the import of manufactured products from the motherland, then a perfect interaction is present, and yet no one will call the sum of the colonies and the motherland an individual.

Every one of these unities thus proves to be insufficient to fix the concept of the individual. That the five types of unity discussed above are indeed all possible and the only possible ones is not difficult to see, for they exhaust the three subjective-objective forms: Space, Time, and Causality.

Thus, we have gained a sufficient definition of the individual; the individual is a thing which combines all five possible types of unity within itself: 1) **spatial unity** (of form), 2) **temporal unity** (continuity of action), 3) unity of the (inner) **cause**, 4) unity of **purpose**, 5) unity of the **interaction** <note>original: "Wechselwirkung." The mutual influence of parts upon one another within a system.</note> of the parts with one another (provided any parts are present; otherwise, of course, the last one falls away). — **Where spatial unity is lacking**, as with a swarm of bees, one does not speak of an individual, despite the fact that all other unities are present in the most striking manner. It is of decisive importance for the concept of the individual that none of these unities is something absolutely rigid or closed off from the outside; rather, each can contain within itself lower unities of the same kind and can be collectively **encompassed** with several of its peers by a higher unity. It is an entirely futile effort to seek a final boundary for any kind of unity; higher unities are always conceivable which include them, just as everything is ultimately preserved within the unity of the world, and this world-unity in turn can be surpassed by a metaphysical unity of various, unrecognizable, coordinated worlds. This illusion, appearing to a superficial observer, arises from the fact that the individual only comes into being through the combination of **all** the aforementioned unities. If multiple individuals are to be contained within an individual of a higher order, then a coincidence of **all** these kinds of unities is required both in the individuals of the lower order and in those of the higher order. If, on the other hand, any kind of unity is missing in the former or the latter, the subordination of the remaining unities to the higher ones continues to exist, but there is no longer a state of multiple individuals being encompassed by a higher one. Even <term>Locke</term> <note>John Locke (1632–1704), an influential English philosopher. He famously argued that "personhood" is not about having the same body, but about the continuity of consciousness—the ability to look back and recognize oneself in past thoughts and actions.</note> expressed that the identity of the person rests exclusively on the identity of consciousness, and this truth has been readily recognized by all later philosophers. The indivisible unity in which the individual has its existence is therefore here the **unity of consciousness**, which we examined in Chapter C. III. For it is only through the fact that the consciousnesses of two ideas—which are separated in the brain by time or space—are lifted into the common consciousness of comparison (that is, they find their higher unity within it), that it becomes possible for the subject, or the <term>instinctively supposed cause</term> <note>original: "instinctiv supponirte Ursache." The author suggests that our minds naturally "assume" there is a single driver (the Self) behind our various thoughts, even if we cannot physically see that cause.</note> of one idea and the other, to be recognized as one and the same. Thus, both are related to a common internal cause (the **"I"**). 

The conscious-mental individual extends only as far as the unity of consciousness reaches, and as far as the unity of **soul processes** <note>original: "Seelenvorgänge." A term used in 19th-century German psychology to describe any internal mental activity, such as thinking, feeling, or perceiving.</note> reaches through a causal relationship to a common subject. Now we know that conscious mental processes take place in the lower nerve centers of humans and animals, which are connected into an intimate unity within each center by virtue of the quality of the conduction; we must therefore necessarily recognize these unities as mental individuals. One should not object that these other centers are mentally too low to achieve self-consciousness or to arrive at an "I"; this "I" is simply instinctively supposed. That is, it does not need to appear as self-consciousness at all; action is nevertheless taken as if self-consciousness were present and as if all actions related to the "I." We see this even in the lowest animals and plants, and call it

Likewise, the contracting muscle fibers or the secreting membranes that change upon nerve stimulation certainly have a certain sensation of these processes, since they are capable of propagating the nerve vibrations that stimulate them beyond the boundaries of the nerve fibers to neighboring parts. This much is certain: that animal cells live, grow, and multiply just as independently, and provide their specific contribution to the maintenance of the whole, as plant cells do; why should they not have just as independent a sensation, if they lead just as independent a life?

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the individuality of cells, following the description of pus cells (white blood cells) and their independent, amoeba-like movements. If we go further into details, we find that in the cell, all requirements to be placed upon the individual are fulfilled.

> “All life is bound to the cell, and the cell is not merely the vessel of life, but is itself the living part” (Virchow, *Four Speeches*, p. 54). <note>Rudolf Virchow (1821–1902) was a pioneering German physician and pathologist. His work "Vier Reden über Leben und Kranksein" (Four Speeches on Life and Disease), published in 1862, is a foundational text of modern medicine.</note>

> “What is the organism? A society of living cells, a small state, well-ordered with all the accoutrements of higher and lower officials, of servants and masters, great and small” (p. 55).

> “Life is the activity of the cell; its uniqueness is the uniqueness of the cell” (p. 10).

> “The nature of the activity, the specific function of organic matter, appears peculiar to us, yet it occurs no differently than the activity and function known to physics in inanimate nature. The entire peculiarity is limited to the fact that the greatest variety of **chemical combinations** <note>original: "Stoffcombinationen"</note> is crowded into the smallest space, that each cell represents within itself a hearth of the most intimate interactions, of the most diverse chemical combinations intermingled, and that therefore results are achieved which occur nowhere else in nature, since nowhere else is a similar intimacy of interaction known” (p. 11).

> “If one is unwilling to decide to distinguish between **collective individuals** <term>Sammelindividuen: complex organisms made of many parts, like a human or a tree</term> and **single individuals** <term>Einzelindividuen: the fundamental unit of life, the cell</term>, then the concept of the individual in the organic branches of natural science must either be abandoned or strictly tied to the cell. Consistent logic must lead both the systematic **materialists** <note>Thinkers who believe that only physical matter and its movements exist.</note> and the **spiritualists** <note>Thinkers who believe in a non-physical soul or life force.</note> to the former result; to the latter, it seems to me, an unbiased, realistic view of nature leads, insofar as only in this way is the unified concept of life preserved throughout the entire field of plant and animal organisms” (pp. 73–74).

This is Virchow’s final conclusion; one sees that he touches upon the truth without having the courage to grasp it firmly. What concerns us here is his well-founded conception of the cell, which he further developed following the precedents of **Schleiden** <note>Matthias Jakob Schleiden (1804–1881), a botanist who helped establish that all plant parts are made of cells.</note> and **Schwann** <note>Theodor Schwann (1810–1882), who expanded cell theory to animals, proving that all living things are composed of cells.</note>, thereby raising animal physiology and pathology, so to speak, to a new level—

> “In Zurich, at the Tiefenhof, stands an old lime tree; every year, when it unfolds its leafy finery, it forms—according to the estimate of Nägeli <note>Karl Wilhelm von Nägeli (1817–1891), a Swiss botanist who discovered what we now call chromosomes.</note>—roughly ten trillion <note>original: "Billionen." Specifically, we distinguish within every cell: the cell wall, the cell contents, the nucleus <note>original: *nucleus*</note>, and in most cases, the nucleolus <note>original: *nucleolus* or "little nucleus"</note>. These parts are to be regarded with certainty as the organs of the cell, which have their own particular functions. The cell wall directs the intake and output according to quantity and quality; the nucleolus <note>original: *nucleolus*</note> handles the reproduction or multiplication of the cells (cells without a nucleolus are sterile); the nucleus <note>original: *nucleus*</note> secures the continued existence of the cell and likely directs the chemical transformations and productions in the cell’s interior. If the relative independence of these organs is to be regarded as established, then one can hardly deny that they too are organic individuals; for undoubtedly, within every such sphere, an organic interaction of parts takes place for the sake of the function to be performed. —

This is Leibniz’s identity of soul and body (thought and extension). This inalienable body is, however, something purely **metaphysical** and not physical; at most, in the case of atoms, one can allow Leibniz’s view to hold true in a physical sense. When several monads come together, they form either an inorganic aggregate or an organism. The higher monads are perceived unclearly and imperfectly by the lower ones, whereas the lower ones are perceived clearly and perfectly by the higher ones. "And one creature is more perfect than another in that one finds in it what serves to provide the reason *a priori* <term>a priori: knowledge that comes from theoretical deduction rather than from observation or experience</term> for what happens in the other, and it is by this that one says it acts upon the other. Leibniz adopted the relationship between the soul and the complex, ever-changing body from Aristotle; it is the relationship of **activity** <note>original Greek: ἐνέργεια (*energeia*)</note> and **matter** <note>original Greek: ὕλη (*hyle*)</note>—of the self-actualizing form and idea and the material in which the idea manifests. In contrast, Leibniz adopted the relationship of the soul and the inalienable, peculiar body from Spinoza, according to whom the One Substance appears everywhere with the two inseparable **attributes: thought and extension**. Remarkably, both relationships coincide in the lowest level—the **atom-monads**—and they do so through a simple trick of nature: relating all directions of effect of such a monad to a single point. Unfortunately, Leibniz did not sufficiently distinguish between these two meanings of "body" or "flesh," which gives rise to confusion, and he has therefore been frequently misunderstood.

The essential point for us in Leibniz’s doctrine is the aggregation of many monads or individuals into a complex, which is subordinated as a "body" to a monad or individual of a higher order, the "soul." Had the results of today's physics, anatomy, physiology, and pathology been available to Leibniz, he would not have failed to further develop his theory with regard to atoms, cells, and organisms; as it was, however, it remained only a brilliant flash of insight that lacked the necessary empirical support. What we, on the other hand, *cannot* accept is the artificial and insufficient hypothesis of pre-established harmony, which became necessary only through the unmotivated denial of the **physical influence** <note>original: *influxus physicus*. The idea that substances can actually affect each other physically.</note> of monads upon one another. Monads are similar beings acting in space; what should they act upon spatially, if not each other? <page-num>VII.</page-num>

# The All-Unity of the Unconscious.

---

That the Unconscious, as it manifests its activity in an organic and conscious individual, does not lack a strong unity is likely immediately evident. Indeed, we generally only recognize the Unconscious through causality <note>Causality: The principle that everything has a cause; here, the author argues we know the Unconscious exists because we see its effects in our bodies and minds.</note>; it is precisely the cause of all those processes in an organic and conscious individual which suggest a psychic, yet not conscious, cause. Everything that we have found within this Unconscious in terms of differences or parts is limited to the two moments of **Will** and **Representation** <note>Representation: (German: *Vorstellung*) In this context, it refers to the mental image or "idea" that gives direction to the Will.</note>, and yet we have also recognized their inseparable unity within the Unconscious. 

However, even if one wishes to stop at grasping **Will** and **Representation** as different parts of the One Unconscious, their **interaction**—the motivation of the Will by the Representation and the awakening of the Representation by the interest of the Will—is quite unmistakable. What we must still grasp in the organism as a unity through the interaction of parts is, in the Single Cause of these processes, sublimated <note>Sublimated: (German: *aufgehoben*) A philosophical term meaning a component is both cancelled out and preserved at a higher level of complexity.</note> into the unity of purpose, toward which these individual activities of the one and the other part are all set only as common means. The unity of time in the continuity of action is likewise present; the unity of space can, of course, no longer be discussed here, because we are dealing with a non-spatial being; and yet it is just as present in the effects as the unity of time. This much is certain, then: that the unity of the psychically Unconscious in the individual is the strongest one can find. However, this does not yet say that there are unconsciously psychic individuals,

<note>original terms: Unbewusste (Unconscious), Causalität (Causality), Wille (Will), Vorstellung (Representation), Wechselwirkung (Interaction), Continuität (Continuity), Organismus (Organism), Individuum (Individual)</note>

<summary>Hartmann argues that the Unconscious possesses a profound internal unity, functioning as the single cause behind the interaction of Will and Representation within a living organism.</summary>
<keywords>Unconscious, causality, Will, Representation, unity of purpose, organic individuality, psychic cause, monism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Hartmann's investigation into the metaphysical unity of the Unconscious. He is moving from the observation of individual biological and conscious units toward the hypothesis that these are all manifestations of a single, universal "Unconscious" rather than many separate "souls" or "monads."</meta>

<page-num>451</page-num>

for if the unity in the Unconscious were so strong that it encompassed within itself all unconscious-psychic elements—wherever they might act in the world—without parts, then there would be only **One** Unconscious and not **multiple** Unconsciousnesses; then there would also no longer be individuals in the Unconscious, but the whole Unconscious would be a single individual without subordinate, coordinate, or superior individuals. Since matter and consciousness are also only forms of appearance of the Unconscious, then this being would be the all-encompassing individual, which is **All Being**, the absolute individual, or the individual <term>par excellence</term> <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν" (kat' exochēn), meaning pre-eminent or above all others.</note>.

In the case of organisms, we did not even need to raise the question of whether we truly have **multiple** things and not **One** before us, because the spatial distinction of their form answered it in advance. In the case of consciousnesses, we have answered the question—which could hardly be decided by logic alone—according to inner experience, which teaches us that the consciousness of Peter and Paul, or of the brain and the abdominal ganglia <note>Abdominal ganglia: Clusters of nerve cells in the belly. In the 19th century, some theorists believed these clusters possessed their own "lower" or local form of consciousness separate from the brain.</note>, are not **One**, but several different ones. But with the Unconscious, this question approaches us in all its seriousness, since the nature of the Unconscious is non-spatial, and the inner experience of consciousness naturally says nothing at all about the Unconscious. No one knows the unconscious subject <note>Unconscious subject: The underlying "actor" or "entity" that produces unconscious thoughts and biological drives.</note> of their own consciousness directly; everyone knows it only as the inherently unknown psychic cause of their consciousness. What reason could they have for the assertion that this unknown cause of their consciousness is **another**, different from that of their neighbor, who knows their own "in-itself" <note>In-itself: A philosophical term (German: *Ansich*) referring to the true nature of a thing as it exists independently of our perception.</note> just as little? In a word, **immediate** inner or outer experience gives us no starting point for deciding this important alternative, which therefore remains, for the time being, a completely **open question**. To decide it, we will have to look around for analogies and indirect arguments, so long as we wish to remain within the realm of observation <term>from experience</term> <note>original: "a posteriori", referring to knowledge derived from observed facts rather than theoretical deduction.</note>.

It is only because one part of my brain is connected to the other by conducting pathways that the consciousness of both parts is unified; and if one could connect the brains of two people through a conduction equivalent to brain fibers, the two would no longer have **two**, but **one** consciousness. If the bisection of lower animals shows us that the same soul, which previously guided the various parts in the whole animal and produced the various consciousnesses, now continues to function unchanged even after the separation, can we then believe that the physical cutting also sliced the soul and separated it into two parts? For all conscious thinking remains caught in the **conditions of consciousness**, and by its very nature can never rise directly above them; rather, it must wrap itself ever more tightly in the illusory veil of Maya <note>Maya is a concept from Indian philosophy (specifically Vedanta) referring to the "illusion" or "magic" that hides the true nature of reality from our perception.</note> the more it unfolds its **own characteristic nature**. So long as one has not strictly separated and developed the idea of the Unconscious, that objection remains in full force; until then, the idea of **All-Unity** <term>All-Unity: The metaphysical concept that all things in the universe are fundamentally one single being or substance.</term> cannot be rationally understood or accepted, but only conceived of mystically, despite the contradictions of consciousness.

Thus far we have shown, first, that there is no reason—and can be no reason—to speak against the unity of the Unconscious, and second, we have provided various *after-the-fact* <gloss>original: "a posteriori"</gloss> reasons of probability for it. However, we can also settle the question quite directly *from-the-outset* <gloss>original: "a priori"</gloss>.

The Unconscious is non-spatial, for it is the very thing that first establishes space (the <term>representation</term> <note>original: "Vorstellung." In this philosophy, this refers to the mind’s ability to form an internal image or idea of an object.</note> establishes ideal space, while the Will establishes real space). Therefore, the Unconscious is neither large nor small, neither here nor there, neither in the finite nor the infinite, neither in a shape nor at a point, neither somewhere nor nowhere. From this it follows that the Unconscious can have **no differences of a spatial nature** within itself, except insofar as it creates them through its representing and acting. That which acts in an atom on the star Sirius is, therefore, not something different from that which acts in an atom on Earth; rather, it **only acts in a different way**, namely, in a different spatial location. We have therefore two effects, without having the right to assume two different beings behind these effects; for a difference in effects only points to a difference of **representations within the Being**, but a difference between two representations in no way implies that the beings doing the representing are not identical. In short, spatial differences cannot belong to the Unconscious; therefore, **no multiplicity of being can exist through spatial definitions**. This is even clearer with temporal differences, since we are already so accustomed to the identity of the continu-

<meta>This page continues the argument for the unity of the Unconscious. ...or religious systems of the first rank, everywhere we encounter the striving toward **Monism** <note>The philosophical view that all of reality consists of one single substance or principle, rather than a collection of independent parts.</note>, and it is only stars of the second and third rank that find satisfaction in an external dualism or even greater fragmentation. Even in explicitly polytheistic religions, such as the Greek and the various Norse mythologies, one recognizes this striving for Monism both in the oldest versions and in the later interpretations of more profound religious minds; and even in the more philosophical interpretations of Christian Monotheism, the world is merely a manifestation established by God, which only endures as long as it is maintained by God—that is, as long as it is incessantly newly established. 

It is not all systems striving for Monism that have succeeded in actually achieving it, yet one senses the unmistakable need for a unified worldview <term>Weltanschauung: a comprehensive philosophy or conception of the universe and humanity's place within it</term>, and only the shallower religious and philosophical systems have contented themselves with an external dualism (for example, Ormuzd and Ahriman <note>The opposing spirits of good and evil in ancient Persian Zoroastrianism.</note>, God and World, the Orderer of the World and matter given as chaos, force and matter, etc.) or even a plurality.

Since the advent of Christianity, this **One Being** has been called God, and the view which asserts that this One Being is the All or the Whole has accordingly been titled **Pantheism** (in the broadest sense of the word). Understood correctly, one can certainly accept the word; however, because of the misunderstandings to which it is exposed, I prefer the word **Monism**, which, according to our explanation of Pantheism, is synonymous with it. 

To be sure, orthodox Catholicism and shallowly rationalistic Protestantism—both of which believed they were exalting God by diminishing him through anthropomorphism <gloss>original: "anthropathisirend," or attributing human emotions and limitations to the divine</gloss>—have always branded as heretics and burned those deeper spirits in the Christian Church who recognized and expressed the need for this Monism (for example, **Giordano Bruno** <note>Giordano Bruno (1548–1600) was an Italian philosopher executed by the Inquisition for his pantheistic views and his claim that the universe is infinite.</note>). This is one of those traits where the involuntary striving of great spirits toward Monism cannot be denied. That **Kant** was nevertheless so hesitant in such conclusions is due to the fact that he formed the beginning of the modern epoch of philosophy—an epoch in which the work formerly concentrated on one or two geniuses had to be distributed across the shoulders of many, because this work became more difficult the more often the old problems reappeared in new and more pointed forms, and the more the scope of knowledge and experience expanded.

What **Kant** proposed as a hesitant conjecture—that the **thing-in-itself** and the **active subject** might be one and the same being—**Schopenhauer** expressed as a categorical assertion by recognizing the positive character of this being as the **Will**. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion of German Idealism. <page-num>458</page-num>

...behaves exactly as if it were connected with representation <note>original: *Vorstellung*; in German philosophy, this refers to the way our minds create a mental image or idea of the world.</note>, even though Schopenhauer does not admit this.

**Fichte** misunderstood the truth of that Kantian suggestion; he denies the appearance of the "thing" any essence independent of the knowing subject, and turns it into an appearance entirely posited <note>In this context, "posited" (*gesetzt*) means "created" or "established" by the mind's own activity.</note> by the representing subject. Thus, the "thing-in-itself" loses its essence directly to the **I**. For Fichte, only what exists in the form of an **I** has true essence, and "dead nature," insofar as it does not enter into this form, remains a purely subjective appearance—that is, an appearance merely established by the subject.

But Fichte, too, must in his own way strive toward **Monism**; the **I** casts off the accidental character of this or that limited empirical **I** by rising to the **Absolute I**. The **Absolute I** is the essence which alone constitutes all the various accidental, empirical, limited "I"s; for the essence that develops in the process of the **Absolute I** is the same as that which produces this process in its accidental empirical limitation. Thus, the many "I"s are once again reduced to mere appearances of the One Absolute.

**Schelling**, in his **transcendental idealism**, seeks to deduce the richness of the external world—which in Fichte’s work had shrunk into the barren abstraction of the "**Non-I**"—from the activity of the **I** in the diversity of its determinations. However, by explaining the agreement between the perceptions of various limited "I"s through the unity of the "infinite intelligence" (or **Absolute I**) within the finite intelligences (or limited "I"s), the standpoint of transcendental idealism necessarily leads him to the **Philosophy of Nature**. There, without considering the limited individual **I**, he undertakes the deduction of external world determinations directly from the **Absolute I** or pure **Subject**. Here, among other natural determinations, he naturally encounters the spirit and its products. In both systems, he proceeds from the identity of the **Subject** and the **Object**, though this "**absolute subject-object**" appears at one time more from the subjective side, and at another more from the objective side.

The method used here—of the pure **Subject** step-by-step setting itself as an **Object**, which from every objectification <note>In philosophy, "objectification" (*Objectivation*) is the process by which a mental concept or a "Subject" expresses itself as a physical or external "Object."</note> into its...

> “The method is only the movement of the Concept <note>original: *Begriff*; in Hegelian philosophy, the "Concept" or "Notion" is the underlying creative logic of the universe.</note> itself, but with the meaning that the Concept is **Everything** and its movement is the universal absolute activity.”

Hegel recognized that Schelling’s deduction had either no value at all or a purely logical value as a process in the realm of thought. However, he claimed that his logic, built upon this, was simultaneously Ontology <note>The branch of philosophy that studies the nature of "being" or reality.</note>; that the Concept is **Everything**, that is, the sole substance and sole absolute Subject; and that the "World Process" is the pure dialectical self-movement of the Concept. Schelling, in his final system, asserted the "Negativity"—that is, the purely logical or purely rational nature—of Hegel’s philosophy. He thus denied that it could say **what** something is and how it is, only conceding that it could say: **if** something exists, then it must be so. He explained that in Hegel’s philosophy, and all those preceding it, one could only speak of an **eternal** happening; “but an eternal happening is no happening at all. Therefore, the entire representation of that process and that movement is itself illusory; in truth, nothing has happened. Everything has occurred only in thought, and this entire movement was merely a movement of thinking” (Works I. 10. pp. 124—125).

He declares existence to be the truly **Over-rational** <note>original: *Uebervernünftige*; that which exists beyond the reach of human reason or logical deduction.</note>, which as reality can now and forever exist only in experience, never in reason (Works II. 3. p. 69), and in this regard, he calls nature and experience "foreign to reason" (ibid. p. 70). regard, go beyond the Idea as such toward a Being that exists outside and independent of thought—toward something that precedes all thought (Vol. II, 3. p. 164), toward an **un-pre-thinkable being** <note>original German: *unvordenkliches Sein*. Thus, in all philosophies of the modern era, we have seen this striving for **monism** <note>The philosophical view that all of reality is made of one single substance or principle.</note> realized in one way or another, more or less completely. <meta>This page transitions from the historical analysis of Schelling’s "positive philosophy" to the author’s own systematic conclusion: that the Unconscious is the single, absolute essence behind all material and mental phenomena.</meta>

<page-num>461</page-num>

That which is not fully explained by the concepts of **Matter** and **Consciousness**—such as organic formation, instincts, and so on—had already (in sections A and B) proved to be the most immediate and most easily recognizable effects of the Unconscious.

With this, we have *understood* 1) **Matter**, 2) **Consciousness**, and 3) organic formation, instinct, etc., as three modes of operation or—for us—three *modes of appearance* of the Unconscious, with the latter being the *Essence* of the world. Once we had finally grasped the concept of *individuality* on the one hand, and the peculiar nature of the *Unconscious* on the other, the ultimate reason for assuming a multiplicity of essences within the Unconscious vanished from our hands. All multiplicity now belongs only to the realm of appearance, not to the *Essence* that posits it; rather, this Essence is the *One absolute Individual*, the *Single Being* that *is All*, while the *world* with all its glory is reduced to mere *appearance*. However, this is not a subjectively posited appearance, as in the works of Kant, Fichte, and Schopenhauer <note>The author distinguishes his view from "Subjective Idealism," where the world is just a product of the human mind. Instead, he argues the world is a real "appearance" created by the Unconscious.</note>, but an objectively (or as Schelling says [Works II. 3. p. 280] “divinely”) posited appearance—or, as Hegel expresses it (Works VI. p. 97), a “mere appearance not only for us, but *in itself* <note>original German: *an sich*. In philosophy, this refers to the true nature of a thing as it exists independently of human observation.</note>.” What appears to us as substance “is merely the expression of an equilibrium of opposing activities” (Schelling’s Works I. 3. p. 400), and what appears to us as consciousness is likewise the mere expression of a *conflict* of opposing activities. That piece of matter there is a conglomerate of *atomic forces*—that is, of *acts of will* of the Unconscious—which, from this point in space, pull with this much strength and, from that point, push with that much strength. Should the Unconscious interrupt and cancel these acts of will, that piece of matter would cease to exist at that very moment; should the Unconscious will them anew, the matter is there once more. Here, the *monstrous* nature of the creation of the material world dissolves into the everyday miracle of its *preservation*, which is renewed every moment and constitutes a *continuous creation*. The world is only a steady series of *sums* of uniquely combined acts of will of the Unconscious, for it exists only so long as it is steadily posited; should the Unconscious cease to "will" the world, this *play* of the Unconscious’s intersecting activities would cease to *be*.

It is an illusion that vanishes upon thorough examination—a sensory illusion in the broader sense—when we believe we possess something immediately real in the world, in the "Not-Self." It is an illusion of the egoistic instinct when we believe we possess something immediately real in ourselves, in that dear "Self." The world consists only of a sum of activities or acts of will of the Unconscious, and the Self consists of another sum of activities or acts of will of the Unconscious. Only insofar as the former activities intersect with the latter does the world become perceptible to me; only insofar as the latter intersect with the former, **do I become perceptible to myself**. (In this context, my body and even my brain are naturally counted as part of the Not-Self, the world.) Only through the fact that one act of will enters into opposition with another, and they offer mutual resistance and limit each other—only through this does that which we call **Reality** arise. This reality alone is accessible to the Will, because in the realm of representation <note>original German: *Vorstellung*. In 19th-century philosophy, this refers to the mental images, ideas, or "pictures" the mind has of things, as opposed to the things themselves or the active Will.</note>, ideal opposites exist peacefully side-by-side before the Will has seized them. Even this interaction of acts of will is only understandable if they are activities of one and the same Being.

Let the Unconscious change the combination of activities or acts of will that constitute me, and I have become someone else; let the Unconscious cease these activities, and I have ceased to be. I am a phenomenon like the rainbow in the cloud; like it, I am born from the convergence of circumstances, becoming someone else every second because these circumstances change every second, and I will dissolve when these circumstances dissipate. That which is *Essence* in me, *is not I*. At the same spot, another rainbow may one day appear that looks exactly like this one, yet it is not the same, for temporal continuity is lacking. Likewise, in my place, a Self completely identical to me may one day stand, but it will no longer be I. Only the sun shines eternally, which plays within this cloud; only the Unconscious reigns eternally, which also refracts within my brain.

## VIII.

# The Essence of Procreation from the Standpoint of the All-Unity of the Unconscious.
<term>All-Unity: The philosophical concept (All-Einheit) that all individual things in the universe are fundamentally part of one single, unified essence.</term>

---

We now wish to use our newly gained standpoint to illuminate several questions; some have occupied philosophers for millennia, while others have recently captured a particular interest among the public. It will be shown how the solutions, which flow from the principles we have established thus far, align perfectly with what the facts require and what an effortless critique leaves remaining from the various possible explanations.

The first of these questions concerns the nature of **procreation**. In the past, two views contended over procreation: **Creationism** and **Traducianism**. <note>These are theological terms regarding the origin of the human soul. Creationism (Creatianismus) argues God creates a new soul for every body; Traducianism (Traducianismus) argues the soul is passed down from parents to children.</note> The former assumed a new spiritual creation at every act of procreation; the latter assumed a transfer of parts of the parents' souls into the child. The first view therefore establishes a creation out of nothing—a new miracle—at every procreation, and for that reason alone it is unacceptable to the healthier perspectives of modern times. The latter view, however, contradicts the facts. For if a man, given a sufficient number of women, could easily father over a hundred children annually—and thus many thousands during the period of his virility—and yet notoriously suffers no decrease in his own soul, then the portion given to the child at each procreation must have been smaller than the many-thousandth part of that minimum decrease which would just barely be felt as a loss of soul. Clearly, however, the child could not remain satisfied with such a tiny sliver of a soul in the long run, much less his children and grandchildren, who in a decreasing progression would soon only

When **Ellis** (*Voyage to Hudson’s Bay, translated from the English p. 236* <note>Henry Ellis (1721–1806) was an explorer who searched for the Northwest Passage; his 1748 book described the extreme cold and its effects on wildlife.</note>) overwintered at the Nelson River on Hudson Bay, a completely frozen clump of black biting flies was found; brought near the fire, they revived. He reported that one frequently finds frogs on the shores of the lakes there that are frozen as solid as the ice itself, and yet, when thawed at a moderate temperature, they revived to such a degree that they crawled from one place to another.

Even entirely frozen trees can come back to life after slow thawing and sprout fresh leaves.

Hunter <note>John Hunter (1728–1793), a pioneering Scottish surgeon and scientist who performed early experiments on cryogenics.</note> found in his experiments, however, that a fish must only die *slowly* in the cold and then freeze for it to be impossible to call it back to life through thawing. For this reason, it is also not possible to let a whole warm-blooded animal freeze and be revived by thawing; we must abandon the hope of ever seeing one of those prehistoric elephants <note>The author refers to "mammoths of the primeval world" (original: "Elephanten der Vorwelt") often found preserved in Siberian permafrost.</note> preserved entirely unspoiled in the polar ice, or a rhinoceros from those regions, come back to life under favorable circumstances—just as toads have been found inside solid rock, in which they must have been enclosed for centuries, perhaps millennia, and which then, once freed, hopped about alive.

Even if more recent authorities dispute that frozen fish can ever come back to life under any circumstances (because the blood has already been decomposed by the frost), or that toads can remain viable without any trace of respiration through diffusion (though to me the case on both questions does not yet seem closed), the cited examples generally suffice to make plausible the self-evident <note>original: "*a priori*"</note> truth that every trace of life can have escaped from an organism, and yet it can still retain the capacity to begin a new vital activity under favorable circumstances—provided that no such changes have occurred within it that make the resumption of vital functions <term>vital functions|The basic processes (like breathing or circulation) necessary for an organism to stay alive.</term> anatomically or physiologically impossible after the restoration of normal conditions. To this...

For the reader who is not familiar with the interesting facts belonging to this subject, I am including a brief note on them.

**Aristotle** still believed that most lower animals arise through **spontaneous generation** <term>Urzeugung: the historical theory, also called abiogenesis, that living organisms could arise from non-living matter, such as mud or decaying meat</term>. Until a few decades ago, **spontaneous generation** was still assumed to be the cause of **intestinal worms** and **infusoria** <term>Infusoria: a historical term for a wide variety of microscopic organisms found in infusions of organic matter</term>, although voices had been raised for some time reminding us of the possible oversight of parental germs. First, the migration routes and various life stages of **intestinal worms** were scientifically established; then it was shown that boiled infusions, which only came into contact with heated air, did not allow any organisms to develop. However, proponents of spontaneous generation rightly argued that the heating of the air must also remove its capacity to generate organisms.

**Schröder** and **Dusch** first demonstrated that a twenty-inch-long cotton plug filters the air in such a way that it no longer allows organisms to arise. — **Pasteur** <note>Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), the French chemist and microbiologist whose experiments definitively disproved spontaneous generation and established the principles of vaccination and pasteurization.</note> investigated the germs floating in the air by catching them with gun-cotton <note>original: "Schiessbaumwolle," an early explosive material made from nitrocellulose, used here as a filter</note> and dissolving this in ether and alcohol. He found these germs to correspond in every respect to the otherwise known germs of the lowest animals. He also positively proved that they are the cause of the development of organisms in infusions by introducing a small cotton plug containing germs into the heated air; every time, organisms emerged just as if the air had had free access. **Pasteur** even compared, through an ingenious method, the relative amounts of germs contained in the air at various locations. With this, the assumption of spontaneous generation in infusions is scientifically settled once and for all.

I want to mention another case: the emergence of *Monas amyli* <note>original: "Monas amyli," a historical name for a microscopic organism observed in starch grains</note>. People saw a swarm of single-celled infusoria emerging in starch grains and believed they recognized spontaneous generation therein. However, as one followed the history of these beings further, one saw them become free upon the final decay of the starch grain, each of them seeking out a fresh starch grain and completely covering it, expanding in the manner of amoebas. This thin membrane on the surface of the grain—the animal which has, as it were, swallowed the grain and is now slowly digesting it layer by layer—was...

### IX.

# The Ascending Development of Organic Life on Earth.

---

In the previous chapter, we established the probability that **the Unconscious** <term>Das Unbewusste: In Hartmann’s philosophy, this is a creative, purposeful force that directs both the laws of nature and the development of life without being "conscious" in the human sense</term> only undertook the expenditure of force required for **spontaneous generation** <term>Urzeugung: the historical theory, widely debated in the 19th century, that living organisms could arise from non-living matter</term> for as long as it was absolutely necessary—that is, until **parental generation** <term>Elternzeugung: biological reproduction from existing parents (biogenesis)</term> could replace it. From the same general natural principle of the greatest possible **economy of force** <term>Kraftersparniss: a concept suggesting that nature always chooses the most efficient path to achieve its ends</term>, another proposition follows immediately—one that was assumed as self-evident in our previous considerations: that a spontaneous generation (that is, a direct creation from unorganized matter) can only apply to the very simplest forms of organic life. In contrast, to produce higher life forms, the Unconscious would by no means take the path of direct creation—which is already so difficult even for the simplest beings—but would instead adopt a mode of origin **mediated by intermediate stages**.

Not that I wish to claim the absolute impossibility of the direct spontaneous generation of a higher animal—on the contrary, I have always maintained that the Will can achieve what it wills, if it only wills strongly enough to overcome opposing acts of will. Nor do I wish to deny the theoretical possibility that, even within the laws of inorganic nature at certain moments of the Earth’s development, the Unconscious could have brought about a direct spontaneous generation of higher animals; to presume to judge such a thing would be folly. I only maintain this: that a direct spontaneous generation of higher organisms would have required a tremendous expenditure of force—an expenditure which [would exceed] that required for the spontaneous generation of the simplest **cell** <term>Zelle: the basic structural and functional unit of life; Hartmann argues here that even a single cell is difficult for nature to create from scratch</term> by infinitely many <note>The sentence ends abruptly here as the original German text "unendlich viel" is cut off at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Hartmann introduces the evolutionary principle that "the Unconscious" prefers gradual development through intermediate stages over the "expensive" process of creating complex organisms directly from non-living matter. This provides a philosophical basis for evolution driven by a purposive force rather than mere chance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the "special creation" theory by examining the biological requirements of eggs and embryos. It contrasts the idea of spontaneous generation with the author’s preference for the gradual modification of existing species through the Unconscious.</meta>

Agassiz <note>Louis Agassiz (1807–1873), a Swiss-American biologist who famously opposed Darwin’s theory of evolution in favor of "special creation."</note>, a leading proponent of the **separate creation of species**, concedes that this creation could only have occurred in the form of eggs. He further admits that for these parentlessly created eggs to develop, conditions similar to those under which parentally produced eggs develop today must have been created at the same time. This surely means, however, that for those eggs requiring parental care, foster parents—of other species, naturally—must have been employed.

But I ask: which idea is more monstrous? That an individual of a higher species develops from the egg of a lower species, or that the egg of the higher species was formed ready-made through **spontaneous generation** <term>Urzeugung: the hypothetical process by which living organisms develop from non-living matter</term>? And specifically, such an egg from which absolutely nothing but this higher species could emerge, and in which all the characteristics of that higher species were consequently already *implicitly* contained?

It should be noted that the eggs of the highest and lowest animals are morphologically and chemically so similar, and pass through the initial stages of embryonic development so uniformly, that they can hardly be distinguished—or only slightly, and even then usually only by incidental characteristics. It is of no use to rely on the claim that, usually, all the characters of a genus are truly contained *implicitly* in the fertilized egg of a species. No matter how correct this view may be (though it is, in fact, unprovable), an egg must always have already passed through a number of developmental stages before it reaches the point where it can exist independently and be hatched through the heat of the sun, the animal heat of foster parents, or the geothermal heat of that era. This does not even consider the fact that the eggs of live-bearing animals <note>original: "lebendig gebärenden Thiere"; referring to mammals</note> never attain this independence.

Where, then, was this development of the egg supposed to have taken place before it became independent? From where was it to have drawn the necessary quantity of **albumin** <term>Albumin: a group of proteins, such as egg white, essential for the nutrition and growth of an embryo</term> if not from a mother animal? From where was the first gathering focal point for the primitive **yolk cell** <term>Dotterzelle: the primary cell within an egg that contains the nutrients for the developing embryo</term> to have come, if it did not lie within an ovary? Albumin is truly not so common in inorganic nature that the spontaneous generation of a yolk cell would be an easy matter. In any case, it must have been infinitely more difficult for **the Unconscious** <note>original: "das Unbewusste"; the author’s term for the fundamental, creative force of nature</note> to [create] such an egg, endowed with all the characters of the new higher species to be created...

<meta>This page continues the argument that evolutionary progress does not occur through the most specialized species of an order, but through primitive, simpler ancestors that have managed to survive alongside their more advanced relatives.</meta>

However, those forms that resemble the ends of a branch are not the ones from which a new animal order <term>Thierordnung: a high-level taxonomic group, such as mammals or reptiles</term> emerges under the changed conditions of a later geological period. This is because they have, so to speak, run themselves into a dead end through an abundance of very specific characteristics. Instead, it is those imperfect, primitive stem-forms <term>Stammformen: ancestral or foundational species</term> of the order—the ones that have barely managed to hold their own through that period against their far superior descendant forms in the struggle for existence <note>This is a direct reference to Charles Darwin's "struggle for life," a central concept in the theory of natural selection.</note>—that are the source of progress. These "shy offshoots," standing closest to the main trunk of the branch, are the ones from which the new order later grows through the addition of new, previously non-existent primal characteristics. However incomplete our knowledge of these transitional stages may be—based on the forms preserved in today's fauna and the paleontological remains found so far—it is nonetheless fully sufficient to prove our claim.

After the crustaceans reached their peak in crabs, the arachnids <term>Arachniden: the class containing spiders, scorpions, and mites</term> began with the most imperfect mites; after these were perfected into the spider, a setback occurred in the insects, returning to the low-standing lice. The highest forms of the mollusks <term>Weichthiere: literally "soft animals," the group including snails, clams, and squid</term> are the cuttlefish, and of the arthropods <term>Gliederthiere: literally "jointed animals," a broad group including insects and crustaceans</term>, the Hymenoptera <term>Hautflügler: the order of insects including bees, wasps, and ants</term>. Both are far more highly organized than the lowest fish known to us, and both lived in a state of perfection equivalent to today's forms before there were any vertebrates <term>Wirbelthiere: animals with backbones</term> on the Earth. But they were too one-sided and too richly specialized to serve as the starting point for an order based on entirely different fundamental conditions of structure. Rather, fish developed from worms, slugs, and crustaceans. For easily understood reasons, the oldest fossil fish belong only to the transitional forms of the crustaceans, because the other two types were too soft to leave fossil remains; on the other hand, transitional forms from the latter two have survived in two species to this day. 

The lancelet <term>Lanzettfischen: a primitive, fish-like marine animal</term>, *the lancelet* <note>original: "Amphioxus lanceolatus Pall."; a species named by Peter Simon Pallas. It is a key specimen in biology because it represents a bridge between invertebrates and vertebrates.</note>, which lives on the coasts of the North Sea and the Mediterranean and is two inches long and almost transparent, does not yet possess a skull or a spinal column. Instead, it has only a simple, solid cartilaginous cord as a base for the spinal cord, no brain separate from the spinal cord, no heart, no spleen, and instead of a liver, it has only a simple pouch. It has no colored blood and no fin rays, but only a delicate, membrane-like (embryonic) tail fin.
