is a matter of mutual agreement how far one wishes to extend the <term>concept of species: the scientific definition (Artbegriff) used to classify groups of organisms that can interbreed and share common traits</term>; although we have, **on the whole**, agreed upon those anatomical and external markers that constitute a species distinction, differences of opinion regarding the application of the concept will naturally always persist at the boundaries. Furthermore, they must be superior to a higher degree the greater the distance between their respective levels of organization, since every new step in development yields a new increase in viability, and these increases are cumulative.

This aligns with the observation that the **struggle for existence** <note>original: "Kampf um's Dasein"</note>—the competition for the conditions of life—occurs more frequently, is more bitter, and more certainly ends with the total destruction of one party the more closely **related** the competing species or varieties are. Conversely, species live more peacefully alongside one another and support each other more in the preservation of life the further apart they stand on the genealogical tree of organization.

In every locality—setting aside the differences between land and sea—one finds all levels of organization represented, and all thrive excellently alongside one another. According to a strict interpretation of Darwinian theory, however, only **one** species, namely the highest, should ultimately remain in each **locality**, because this species would surpass all others in viability for those specific conditions. Yet, that is precisely what is wonderful and magnificent about nature: every final type of a class is so **perfect** in itself that one can indeed go beyond it, but only by adding new **anatomical-morphological** <note>original: "anatomisch-morphologische Voraussetzungen"; the structural and formal blueprints of a body's design</note> prerequisites of construction, not by simply increasing the existing form or its accommodation to the conditions of life; for both are already complete. But whether this struggle occurs or is absent in a specific case, a crossing of the species boundary will never result. Finally, a species will not easily encounter such a massive change in external conditions, nor will it migrate into such divergent circumstances, that the adaptability and capacity for acclimatization—which we have recognized as so considerable within species boundaries—would not suffice. <meta>This page continues the author’s argument that the struggle for existence cannot explain the leap from simple to complex biological types, transitioning now into a distinction between physiological and morphological changes.</meta>

If one finally asks in a positive sense what kind of useful adaptations arise through the **struggle for existence** <note>original: "Kampf um’s Dasein"</note>, the answer is: they are **exclusively physiological in nature**. Here, the true limit of the **Darwinian principle** is clearly visible: it is sufficient as long as we are dealing with the formation and transformation of an existing organ for a physiological function required by circumstances, but it fails us as soon as a **morphological change** <term>morphological change: a change in the physical structure, shape, or arrangement of an organism, rather than just how an organ functions</term> is to be explained. There is no doubt that morphological changes are also possible through the summation of individual variations, and Darwin proves this with many examples, notably in the skeletons of pigeons; but in all the cited cases, artificial breeding takes place. A few teeth, vertebrae, or a toe more or less, or a vertebra shaped one way or another, are entirely **indifferent** <note>original: "indifferent"; meaning they do not offer a survival advantage in the wild</note> to the struggle for existence, and yet these are precisely the characteristics by which the zoologist most reliably distinguishes **species**. 

In the **animal kingdom**, the universal recognition of the claim—that only physiological, and not morphological, changes are decisive for the degree of viability—encounters difficulties. This is because the occurrence of **sympathetic changes** <term>sympathetic changes: also known as "correlated variation," where a change in one part of the body (like a longer beak) leads to an unintentional change in another part (like the shape of the skull)</term>, which even Darwin acknowledged, often allows **morphological changes** to go hand in hand with the physiological change of an organ, often in entirely different parts of the body. This phenomenon, arising from the peculiar laws of the organic formative activity of the **Unconscious** <note>The author, likely Eduard von Hartmann, refers to his theory that a hidden, purposeful intelligence guides biological development</note>, is quite capable of confusing one's **judgment**. However, our assertion appears with complete clarity in the **plant kingdom**. The competent judgment of Prof. Dr. Nägeli (*The Origin and Concept of the Natural-Historical Species* <note>original: "Entstehung und Begriff der naturhistorischen Art"</note>, Munich, 1865, p. 26) regarding this is as follows: “The highest organization manifests itself in two aspects: in the most diverse morphological structure and in the most extensive division of labor. Both aspects usually coincide in the animal kingdom, since the same organ also possesses the same function. In plants, however, they are independent of each other; the same function can be performed by quite different organs, even in closely related plants...”

> „The purely morphological peculiarities of plants should, accordingly, be the easiest to change, while the organizational conditions dictated by a specific function should be the most difficult. Experience shows the opposite. The positional relationships and the arrangement of cells and organs are the most constant and persistent characteristics, both in nature and in cultivation. In a plant that has opposite leaves and flower parts in fours, one will sooner succeed in producing all possible functional changes in the leaves than in producing a spiral arrangement of them—even though this arrangement, being completely indifferent to the **struggle for existence** <note>original: "Kampf um das Dasein"</note>, could not have attained any constancy through **natural selection** <note>original: "natürliche Züchtung"; literally "natural breeding"</note>.“

Had Darwin borrowed his examples more from plants than from animals, he might have noticed for himself the natural limit to the effect of the struggle for existence. It is clear that this struggle can only alter the behavior of organisms toward external living conditions—that is, their functions, and the organs only insofar as the functions depend on them. However, it can have no influence on those properties of organisms whose modification brings neither advantage nor disadvantage to the relationship between the organism and the outside world. Among these latter properties in plants, and even in animals, are most of the **basic principles of the morphological type, such as, specifically, the numerical ratios chosen for it.** <note>The author refers here to "numerical ratios" such as the number of petals or the specific geometric patterns of leaf growth, which seem to follow mathematical rules regardless of survival needs.</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Darwinian evolution, specifically focusing on the limitations of natural selection in explaining the transition between different "levels of organization." It builds on the previous page's discussion of plants to argue for an internal, purposive force.</meta>

We have found here a confirmation of our above assertion that natural selection in the **struggle for existence** <note>original: "Kampf um's Dasein"</note> is indeed a highly valuable aid for the exhaustive **perfecting** of an already existing **type within** the same level of organization, but it cannot serve to explain the **transition** from a lower to a higher level of organization, since such a transition is always connected with an **elevation** of the morphological type. In his latest investigations (*Botanical Communications* 1868) regarding the behavior of individuals of one and the same plant species—on the one hand under identical conditions, and on the other under different external circumstances—Nägeli <note>Karl Wilhelm von Nägeli (1817–1891) was a Swiss botanist who studied cell division and pollination but was skeptical of Darwin's theory of natural selection as the sole driver of evolution.</note> reaches the result that the formation of unequal varieties occurs under identical conditions just as often as the formation of equal varieties occurs under unequal conditions. From this, the following is to be concluded: 1) external conditions are **insufficient** as the sole cause for the formation of varieties, but rather presuppose a second, cooperating condition: a property inherent in the plant, a "**tendency to vary**"; 2) this inner property of the plant alone can indeed suffice to bring about the formation of different varieties even under identical external conditions. This confirms our assumptions made above. —

If we briefly summarize the train of thought of this chapter once more, the following resulted from the principle of always reaching the intended goal with the smallest possible expenditure of force:

1) **The Unconscious** <term>The Unconscious: In this context, the author (Eduard von Hartmann) refers to a universal, creative force that directs nature toward specific goals without conscious awareness.</term>, in the presentation of higher levels of organization, renounces **spontaneous generation** <term>Urzeugung: the historical theory that living organisms could arise from non-living matter, which the author argues is avoided in favor of evolving existing forms.</term>; it rather builds upon the already existing forms of organization.
2) It does not directly transform the lower form into the higher, but rather develops the latter out of a favorably disposed **germ** of the lower species.
3) It takes the smallest possible steps and forms the larger differences through the **summation** of a multitude of small individual differences.
4) It uses the individual deviations that arise by chance during every reproduction, insofar as these exist in the directions that correspond to its purpose.

<summary>The author concludes that natural selection can only refine existing types, while the leap to higher biological levels requires an internal "tendency to vary" guided by the Unconscious. <meta>This page continues the author's summary of how the "Unconscious"—a guiding metaphysical force—interacts with biological evolution. 5) To preserve variations, regardless of how they arose, it utilizes **natural selection in the struggle for existence** <note>original: "Kampf um's Dasein"</note>, insofar as these variations **grant the organisms a greater viability** within that struggle.

6) The Unconscious must (aside from its continuous intervention in every organic formation, and thus in every act of procreation) exert a direct activity in the further development of the biological organization: on the one hand, to bring about variations in new germs that do *not* arise by chance but are nevertheless part of its plan; and on the other hand, to **protect from extinction through cross-breeding** those variations that have arisen and belong to its plan, even if they **do not grant the organisms an increased capacity for the struggle for existence**. —

Finally, it should be noted that for the same reason that <term>spontaneous generation</term> <note>original: "Urzeugung." The historical theory that living organisms could arise from non-living matter, which the author suggests ceases once biological reproduction is established.</note> no longer occurs once <term>parental reproduction</term> <note>original: "Elternzeugung." Reproduction through parents (biogenesis).</note> becomes possible, the development of a new species from lower ones **only takes place when the species does not yet exist, or at least does not exist in that specific location** <note>original: "Localität"</note>. Thus, the development of a new species should be understood as **a process occurring only once, or at most a few times**, in different locations under similar circumstances. In contrast, after the one-time emergence of the new species, its uniform or slightly modified reproduction is the normal, constantly repeated process, until the eventual extinction of the species. Even if one imagines the developmental process of a new species to be quite slow (taking perhaps several hundreds or thousands of years), it will still only be an insignificantly small part of the period of the **essentially unchanged persistence** of the finished species (some hundreds of thousands to hundreds of millions of years).

This is a **second reason**, in addition to others already mentioned above, why one finds so many more uniform fossil specimens of distinct **species characteristics** than those that represent **transitional stages** <note>original: "Uebergangsstufen"</note> between closely related species.

# X.

## Individuation.

---

If the essence that appears in the world is a single, indivisible one, then where does the multiplicity of appearing individuals come from? Where does the uniqueness of each individual come from, why does it exist, and how is it possible?

Answering these questions has always been a primary difficulty for any explicitly <term>monistic philosophy</term> <note>Monism is the philosophical view that all of reality is composed of one single substance or principle, as opposed to "dualism" (mind and matter) or "pluralism" (many substances).</note>. Dismissing or or providing an insufficient answer to these questions is what has always paved the way for the backlash against monism, leading back to a realistic <term>polyism</term> <note>A belief in many fundamental substances or "many-ness."</note> or pluralism (for example, Leibniz following Spinoza, or Herbart following Schelling and Hegel). Spinoza leaves the above questions as unaddressed as the ancient philosophers did; he dogmatically declares individuals to be <note>original Latin: "modi"</note> **modes** of the One Substance. However, he completely fails to provide an explanation for the development of the <note>original Latin: "modus"</note> **mode** from the substance, or a demonstration of why each mode differs from the others and forms an existence unique in its kind. <term>Subjective idealism</term> <note>The philosophical position held by Kant, Fichte, and Schopenhauer that the world we perceive is essentially a mental construct rather than an external reality.</note> (Kant, Fichte, Schopenhauer) believes it has done enough if it explains the multiplicity in the world as "subjective appearance," arising through the forms of subjective <term>intuition</term> <note>original: "Anschauung." In German philosophy, this refers to the mind's fundamental way of organizing sensory data—specifically through the frameworks of space and time.</note>: space and time. This ignores two things: first, that the difficulty has merely been shifted from the objective realm into the subjective realm, where it persists just as unresolved as it did before; and second, that the question remains unanswered as to how this **perceiving individual**—who is unique in its kind and distinct from every similar being—is even possible according to monistic principles.

Schelling certainly recognizes this latter side of the question (Works I. 3. p. 483):

Real multiplicity is *more* than the concept of multiplicity; it is a sum of individuals, none of whom resembles another, each of whom is a "This," a nameless, unique...

Anyone who has never felt the need or the difficulty of understanding individuation from the standpoint of **monism** <note>Monism is the belief that all of reality is made of one single substance or principle, making it difficult to explain why we all seem to be separate individuals.</note> may safely skip the first half of this chapter until the discussion of character; they would find no **interest** in it anyway.

Generally speaking, the answer is: "Individuals are objectively established phenomena; they are willed thoughts of the Unconscious or specific acts of its will; the unity of the **Essence** remains untouched by the multiplicity of individuals, which are merely activities or combinations of certain activities of the **One Essence.**" But precisely so that this general answer becomes plausible, one must go into detail and once again visualize through which combination of which activities an individual arises, and to what extent each individual must necessarily be different from every other—that is, be **unique.**

Individuals of a higher order arise, as we have seen (Ch. C. VI.), through the composition of individuals of a lower order with the addition of new activities of the Unconscious directed toward the result of that composition; one must, therefore, begin the understanding of individuation with the individuals of the lowest order—that is, the atoms. Here, according to the current state of scientific hypotheses, we have only two different types of individuals to distinguish: repulsive and attractive forces; within each of these groups, there is complete equality between individuals, with the sole **exception of location.**

It might seem to a superficial observer that this is the same as what Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a philosopher who argued that the world is fundamentally "Will" and that our perception of individual objects is an illusion created by our minds.</note> said, as he also claims space and time as the "principle of individuation" <note>original Latin: *principium individuationis*</note>. For him, therefore, the entire process of individuation is a mere subjective illusion, to which no reality corresponds outside of brain-consciousness.

<meta>This page continues the critique of how individual identity is formed within a monistic system. While the previous page discussed matter as the physical medium that allows for individuality, the author now challenges Arthur Schopenhauer’s metaphysical explanation of character, arguing that "individual character" cannot exist outside of time.</meta>

...seems more acceptable, then a remarkable case arises: nothing can be objected from a metaphysical standpoint against the view of the French naturalists. Conversely, the view held by the metaphysician Schopenhauer—who assumes that character is established by a timeless, once-and-for-all decision—can hardly withstand criticism based on his own principles.

Schopenhauer himself intends to be an absolute monist <note>Monism is the philosophical view that all of reality consists of one fundamental substance or principle. For Schopenhauer, this single "thing-in-itself" is the Will.</note>; if the Will of the world is essentially One, and if character is also, according to his own assertion, nothing but the peculiarity of the individual will, then clearly the **individuality** of character can only be conceived as an individualized activity of the general Will. It cannot be thought of as directly grounded in the essence of the general Will, since that essence always remains general. But how the activity of the Will, which produces character, is to be thought of as timeless, I have no concept of; I can think of a being as timeless, but not its activity, since activity immediately establishes time—unless one wants to assume an activity is possible in "zero-time," in which case it would vanish in an instant. Character, however, which is meant to last throughout the individual's lifetime, clearly requires an activity of the general Will that lasts just as long. In other words, the doctrine of the **intelligible individual character** <note>In Schopenhauer’s philosophy, the "intelligible character" is the underlying, unchanging essence of a person's will that exists outside of our sensory experience of time and space.</note> is a contradiction of the monistic principle, and also a contradiction of the transcendental ideality of space and time. For in the "intelligible" or spiritual realm, the <term>principle of individuation <note>original: "principium individuationis"; the philosophical rule that distinguishes one thing from another. Throughout all ages and among all peoples, the wisdom of the world-creator, the world-orderer, or the world-ruler has been admired and praised. This is a factual untruth, for from this proposition it would follow without further ado that I must prefer the combination of evil *a* with well-being *A* over the possession of the latter alone, since evil *a* is by no means absolute evil (i.e., zero-well-being), but only a lesser degree of well-being, and thus increases the degree of well-being contained in *A* by its own amount. The *pinnacle* <note>original: *non plus ultra*—the highest point or ultimate example</note> of madness according to this view, however, would be if someone, in order to avoid a great evil, renounced a good; and the person who endures all conceivable physical and mental torments simultaneously in the extreme measure would have to be praised as happy even in that moment compared to the insensible state of one under chloroform, not to mention compared to the peaceful slumber of death. A false hypothesis, invented for the sake of biased purposes, leads into such unnatural distortions.

But if we ask about the motive in which this hypothesis was formulated, it turns out remarkably to be an error, thus rendering the whole hypothesis superfluous.

It was believed, namely, that the existence of a real evil presented a contradiction to a perfect world. Much mischief has always been played with the word "perfect."

If it should now turn out that this existing world is *worse than none at all*, the Creator would face the accusation of why He created it in the first place, since it would have been more rational to create nothing. In that case, the creation as such—regardless of how it actually turned out—would owe its origin to an *irrational act*. One would then have only two choices: *either* to assume that the Creator's **reason** had no part in this original act, and that reason was only tasked with continuing and executing the existence (which was decided without its input) in the best possible way; *or* to admit that the Creator's wisdom—which is undeniable in its specific details—fell into a fundamental **error** as a whole and thus became completely unfaithful to itself. This second option applies if one maintains the claim that the totality of the Creator was involved in that original act, including His reason.

The *second assumption* is too monstrous; how could **All-Wisdom** be so unfaithful to itself as to commit the greatest stupidity at the most important moment? However, *Leibniz* could and would not accept the *first assumption* either, because he did not recognize a plurality of attributes within God <note>Leibniz adhered to the idea of divine simplicity, meaning God's Will and Reason are not separate "parts" that could act independently of one another.</note>. Consequently, his only remaining option was to secure himself *in advance* against the possibility that this world might turn out to be *worse than none*, and for this purpose, he invented the doctrine of the privative character of evil.

# XII.

# The Irrationality of Willing and the Misery of Existence.

---

### Orientation regarding the task.

The task of this chapter is to investigate whether the existence or the non-existence of this present world deserves preference. More than ever before, the reader's indulgence must be requested here, since a somewhat exhaustive treatment of the subject would require an entire volume. Nevertheless, only an episodic treatment can be permitted here—both for external reasons and especially because the result of this investigation, while important for clarifying the ultimate principles of philosophy, has no direct influence on the main subject promised in the title of the work: "the Unconscious." <note>The author, Eduard von Hartmann, is distinguishing between his core theory of the Unconscious and this specific detour into "Pessimism," for which he became very famous.</note> Nevertheless, I hope that in a brief reflection offering many new perspectives, I may also provide some stimulation to the opponents of the views presented here, which should compensate them to some extent for reading through this digression.

If we look at the personal judgments of the greatest minds of all time, those among them who took any opportunity to express their opinion on this point speak out decisively in a condemning sense.

Plato <note>Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC) and student of Socrates.</note> says in the *Apology*: 
> "Now, if death is without all sensation and like a sleep in which the sleeper sees no dream, it would indeed be a wonderful gain. For I believe that if someone were to pick out such a night in which he slept so soundly that he had no dream, and the" <note>original: "Apologie"; this is a famous passage from Socrates' defense speech before his execution, where he argues that even a dreamless sleep is better than most days of living.</note>

Now imagine Death stepping up to this man and saying: “Your lifetime has run out, and in this hour you fall victim to annihilation; yet it depends on your current decision of will whether, after a complete forgetting of everything that has happened before, you will live through your now-concluded life once more in exactly the same way. Now choose!”

I doubt that the man would prefer the repetition of the previous game to non-being, if he considers it with undaunted, calm reflection and is not simply foolish. How much more, then, must this man prefer non-being to a reentry into life which does not guarantee him the favorable conditions his previous life offered—which, on the contrary, would leave it entirely to chance into which new living conditions he would enter, and which therefore offers him, with a probability bordering on certainty, worse living conditions than those he just rejected.

Yet the Unconscious <note>A reference to "The Unconscious" as a metaphysical force, a central concept in the philosophy of Eduard von Hartmann, who synthesized Schopenhauer’s "Will" with Hegel’s "Reason."</note> would find itself in the position of this man at every moment of a new birth, if it truly had the possibility of making a choice.

But even in this example, the criticism leveled at the views of geniuses cannot be avoided: namely, that one has questioned an intelligence raised far above the average through education. However, since every single phenomenon <term>phenomenon: in this philosophical context, an "Erscheinung" or individual manifestation of life</term> must be judged by its own standard, the world as a whole can only be judged approximately correctly if the judgment is based on the average measure of all individual phenomena. Yet, from the example above—if it is correct in itself—it remains true that this high level of intelligence already condemns the very life that carries it. Regarding that specific life, the genius is undeniably the only competent court of judgment. The error lies only in the fact that the genius considers themselves competent to also condemn those beings standing below them, while those lower forms of life must likewise only be measured by their own standard.

This error is not surprising, for it occurs quite generally even where intelligence is not so high as to condemn its own existence. One might ask, for example, a woodcutter, or a "Hottentot," <note>original: "Hottentotten." This is an archaic and now offensive term used in the 19th century to refer to the Khoekhoe people of Southern Africa. The author uses it here as part of a common historical trope comparing different "levels" of human and animal life.</note> or an orangutan, whether they would prefer total annihilation or rebirth as a hippopotamus or a louse; they would all presumably prefer annihilation. Nevertheless, they would still prefer a repetition of their *own* life over annihilation, just as the hippopotamus and the louse would prefer a repetition of their own lives over annihilation.

This error arises because the person being asked, at the moment of decision, projects themselves with their current intelligence into the life of the lower stage. From that perspective, they naturally find such a life unbearable. They forget that at that lower stage, they would only have the intelligence of that lower stage at their disposal to judge it.

Thus, in truth, nothing remains but to judge every stage of manifestation of the **Unconscious** <term>the Unconscious: a central concept in this philosophy (likely Eduard von Hartmann's), referring to the fundamental, creative, but blind force that underlies all reality</term> by its own standard, and then to calculate the **algebraic sum** of all these specific judgments. Every judgment made from an external perspective yields useless results; for every being is exactly as happy as it feels itself to be, not as I would feel in its place with my intelligence, since that is an unrealistic assumption.

Page 536

Pain and pleasure exist only insofar as they **are felt**; they therefore have no reality at all except within the feeling subject. Consequently, they do not possess an objective reality directly, but only by means of the objective reality of the subject in which they exist. That is to say, their reality is immediately subjective, and only insofar as they have subjective reality do they also indirectly have objective reality. It follows from this that there is no other immediate standard for the reality of sensation than the subjective one, and that, accordingly, a deception or "untruth" of feeling as such is impossible.

A feeling can certainly be called "untrue" insofar as the representations <term>representations: the German "Vorstellungen" refers to the mental images or ideas we have of the outside world</term> that excite it are untrue, but in that case, the deception always lies only in the representation of the object. The feeling itself—regardless of whether it rests on a real basis or an illusion—is always equally true and equally entitled to be factored into the great sum of existence.

Now, if the difference between the judgment that the intelligence of a louse passes on its life, and the judgment that my intelligence passes on its life, rests solely on the fact that the louse is under illusions that I do not share, and that these illusions grant it a surplus of felt—and therefore real—happiness <note>The author is arguing that if a creature *feels* happy because of a mistake, that happiness is still a real addition to the world's "total" pleasure.</note> which makes it prefer its life over non-existence, then the louse would clearly be right and I would be wrong. However, the decision is not quite so simple. Aside from this source of error on my part, there remains another source of error in the response of the louse, which falsifies its judgment just as the former falsifies mine. For even though the value of every being's life can only be estimated according to its own subjective standard, and here every illusion counts the same as truth, this by no means says that every being draws the **correct** algebraic sum from the collective affections <term>affections: the various ways a subject is affected by pleasure, pain, or emotion</term> of its life. In other words, it does not mean that its **overall judgment** of its own life is a correct one in relation to its subjective experiences. Quite apart from the degree of intelligence necessary to pass such a summary judgment, there remains first the possibility of errors in memory and combination—

We cannot spare ourselves this investigation, because all progress in the world aims at the increase of conscious intelligence.

From this, one would have to conclude that it would have been more rational to hinder the development of the world—the earlier the better—and best of all to have suppressed its creation at the **moment of origin**.

### 1. Critique of Schopenhauer’s Theory of the Negativity of Pleasure.

In this analysis, I must assume the so-called Schopenhauerian pessimism is already known to the reader <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher famous for his view that the world is driven by a blind, irrational "Will" and that life is characterized by suffering.</note> (see: *The World as Will and Representation*, Vol. I. §. 56–59, Vol. II. Chap. 46, *Parerga and Paralipomena*, 2nd Ed. Vol. I. pp. 430–39 and Vol. II. Chap. XI and XII). I ask the reader to read through these cited sections in the order indicated; given Schopenhauer’s engaging style, this is a request for which the reader not yet acquainted with him will certainly be grateful. To what extent I depart from the views adopted there is largely evident from what I have said previously. 

The attempted proof (in *The World as Will and Representation*, 3rd Ed. Vol. II, pp. 667–668) that this world is the worst of all possible worlds is an obvious sophism <term>sophism: a clever but false argument, especially one used deliberately to deceive</term>; everywhere else, Schopenhauer himself intends to claim and prove nothing more than that the existence of this world is worse than its non-existence, and I consider this assertion to be correct. The word "pessimism" is thus an inappropriate imitation of the word "optimism" <note>The author suggests that "pessimism" shouldn't just be the opposite of Leibniz's "best world," but rather a specific judgment on whether being is better than non-being.</note>. 

Furthermore, just as I found the attempts of Leibniz <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) argued that we live in the "best of all possible worlds" because a perfect God would not create anything less.</note> to be useless—his efforts to explain away the world's misery through demonstrations in order to rescue the idea of divine all-wisdom—I can also not approve of how Schopenhauer overlooks the wisdom of the world's arrangement in favor of its misery. Even when he cannot deny this wisdom entirely, he ignores it as much as possible and treats it with contempt. 

Finally, I object to the concept of "guilt" which Schopenhauer injects into the creation of the world. I have already spoken out several times against the transcendent <term>transcendent: applying human concepts (like morality or guilt) to a realm beyond physical or human experience</term> use of ethical terms, because these only have meaning for conscious individuals in their interactions with other conscious individuals. I can only conclude, along with Schopenhauer, from the misery of existence that the creation of the world owes its primary origin to an irrational act,

<meta>This page continues the critique of Arthur Schopenhauer’s pessimistic philosophy. ...that is, to a will in which reason has not cooperated, thus to the mere groundless will. — Finally, however, I must highlight Schopenhauer's false use of the concept of **negativity**. Just as Leibniz attributes a negative character to displeasure <note>The German *Unlust* is a broad term for pain, suffering, or general "un-pleasure."</note>, so Schopenhauer wants to attribute an exclusively negative character to pleasure <note>original: *Lust*</note>—not quite in the privative sense used by Leibniz <note>Leibniz argued that evil and pain are simply a "privation" or lack of good, much like cold is a lack of heat.</note>, but in such a way that pain alone is the thing that arises directly, while pleasure is only possible indirectly, through the removal or reduction of pain. Now, I do not intend in the least to dispute that every removal or reduction of a pain is a pleasure, but not every pleasure is a removal or reduction of pain; and conversely, it holds just as well that the removal or reduction of pleasure is a displeasure.

However, a restriction already exists here that works in favor of pain. Namely, pleasure as well as pain attack the nervous system and thereby produce a kind of fatigue, which at the highest degrees of pleasure can become a **deadly exhaustion**. From this arises a need that grows with the duration and degree of the feeling—that is, a (conscious or unconscious) **will**—to let the cessation or lessening of the feeling occur; in the case of displeasure <note>pain</note>, this need arising from the attack on the nerves works together with the direct aversion to enduring a pain; in the case of pleasure, on the other hand, it works *against* the direct desire to hold onto the pleasure, and always diminishes it; indeed, it can ultimately outweigh it (think of the exhaustion in sexual enjoyment). Pain becomes (aside from complete numbing of the nerves through great pains) all the more painful, while pleasure becomes all the more indifferent and tedious, the longer it lasts.

Here lies the first hidden reason why, even if the scales for the measure of direct pleasure and displeasure in the world were perfectly balanced, the balance would be tipped in favor of pain by the added nervous affection. — Furthermore, because this additional need for subsiding applies to every enduring feeling, indirect displeasure (i.e., that arising from the cessation of a pleasure) is relatively diminished, whereas indirect <insert>pleasure</insert> (i.e., that arising from the cessation of a displeasure)...

pleasure is relatively increased, it shows already *a priori* <note>Latin: "from the former," referring to knowledge gained through theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note> that a proportionally much larger part of the pleasure in the world, compared to displeasure, points toward an *indirect* origin from the subsiding of its opposite. Consequently, for practical purposes, it amounts to nearly the same thing as what *Schopenhauer* claims (namely, that pleasure has an *indirect* origin, and only pain has a *direct* one); however, this must not alter the fundamental conception. The reconciliation and agreement are easily found if one looks more closely at the enjoyment of good taste <note>original: *Wohlgeschmack*, referring to the sensory pleasure of food or drink.</note> or an artistic pleasure and asks oneself where the Will might be hidden—that Will which, as long as it is unsatisfied, is displeasure. Here, in the Will that falls prey to the satisfaction destroying it the moment it arises, it is clearly shown that the pleasure of satisfaction is indeed something entirely positive—not something arising directly and solely from the reduction of pain. It deserves special attention that, regarding the entire plant kingdom and the lower stages of the animal kingdom, one cannot assume the degree of developed <term>consciousness</term> <note>original: *Bewusstsein*; here referring to the capacity for self-reflection and the ability to link cause and effect.</note> which is required to compare experiences and recognize their dependence on external causes. Consequently, one must also consider them incapable of any awareness of <term>will-satisfactions</term> <note>original: *Willensbefriedigungen*; the fulfillment of a desire, impulse, or biological drive.</note>, and thus incapable of <term>pleasurable sensations</term> <note>original: *Lustempfindungen*.</note>, whereas pain and displeasure force themselves upon even the dimmest consciousness with relentless necessity. But even higher animals might generally become aware of far fewer <term>will-satisfactions</term> than one is usually inclined to assume based on human analogy. As for humans themselves, because naturally not every person in every moment of a small will-satisfaction is forced to compare it with opposite experiences, generally only those will-satisfactions become conscious—that is, felt as pleasure—whose accompanying circumstances point the person toward the contrast with opposite experiences without any effort on their part; for example, those that are unusual or rare, whether by their nature or their degree, or those which, through the <term>association of ideas</term> <note>original: *Ideenassociation*; the mental process where one thought or sensation naturally triggers the memory of another.</note>, remind one of opposite experiences, whether those of others or one's own past experiences.

All will-satisfactions that have become habit and rule are felt less and less as such—that is, as pleasure—the less they allow the memory of opposite experiences to arise. It is clear that by far the greater part (not in intensity, but in number) of will-satisfactions are thereby lost to consciousness, while all non-satisfactions are felt in their entirety. Therefore, Schopenhauer says quite rightly in *The World as Will and Representation* <note>original: *Welt als W. und V.* (*Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung*), Schopenhauer's primary philosophical work.</note> (3rd ed. Vol. II. p. 657): 
> "We feel the wish as we feel hunger and thirst; but as soon as it has been fulfilled, it is like the morsel of food enjoyed, which ceases to exist for our feeling the moment it is swallowed."

We painfully miss enjoyments and joys as soon as they are absent; but pains, even if they cease after a long presence, are not immediately missed, but are at most intentionally thought of by means of <term>reflection</term> <note>original: *Reflexion*; the act of conscious, deliberate thinking.</note>.

Because of this very fact, however, the receptivity for suffering increases; for the loss of the habitual is *painfully felt*." (From the second edition of *Parerga and Paralipomena* <note>original: *Parerga, 2. Aufl. Bd. II. S. 312*; Schopenhauer's collection of shorter philosophical essays.</note>, Vol. II, p. 312): "Just as we do not feel the health of our whole body, but only the small spot where the shoe pinches, we do not think about our overall, perfectly successful affairs, but about some insignificant trifle that annoys us." However, it is incorrect when he adds: "Upon this rests the <term>negativity of well-being and happiness</term> <note>Schopenhauer’s theory that happiness is not a thing in itself, but merely the temporary removal of a desire or pain.</note> I have often emphasized, in contrast to the <term>positivity of pain</term>." To be sure, a certain analogy of these concepts *exists* for how we become conscious of pleasure and pain, insofar as pain is conscious on its own, whereas pleasure only becomes conscious in contrast to the representation of pain; certainly, the effects are often the same as if Schopenhauer’s conception of the negativity of pleasure were correct. Nevertheless, there is a world of difference between the two, and the principle remains that pleasure and pain generally differ like the mathematical positive and negative; that is, in such a way that it is indifferent which sign one gives to the one and which to the other.

It has once again been shown quite clearly how infinitely more fruitful it is to reflect on the reasons by which great men are led into false hypotheses than to engage in mere criticism. For, by finding the hypothesis of the negativity of pleasure to be just as incorrect as <term>Leibniz’s</term> <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a philosopher who argued that evil is merely a "privation" or lack of good, rather than a positive force.</note> hypothesis of the negativity of evil, we have simultaneously grasped three factors, each of which tips the scales in favor of pain, and which in their combination yield practically the same result as Schopenhauer’s theory. These are: 1) the excitation and fatigue of the nerves and the resulting need for the cessation of enjoyment as well as of pain; 2) the necessity of considering all pleasure as indirect, which arises only through the cessation or lessening of a displeasure, but not through the momentary satisfaction of a will at the moment of its excitation; 3) the difficulties which stand in the way of becoming conscious of <term>will-satisfaction</term>—

We must give some further consideration to the second point. If we seek examples of such sensations of pleasure which consist only in a cessation or easing of unpleasure, one must take care not to include cases where the pleasure is reinforced by an additional satisfaction of the Will coming from elsewhere—as, for example, when the satisfaction of hunger and thirst is joined by the pleasant taste of food and the cooling refreshment of drink, or when the satisfaction of longing for love is joined by physical sexual enjoyment. Pure examples are, for the sensory realm, a subsiding toothache; for the mental realm, the recovery of a friend from a fatal illness. As soon as one considers such pure examples, no one will doubt any longer that the pleasure arising from the cessation of unpleasure is much less than that unpleasure was—just as, conversely, the unpleasure arising from the cessation of a pleasure is much less than that pleasure was.

This phenomenon might at first seem surprising, since one usually considers the strength of a feeling to depend only on the degree of change, and not on the position of the starting or ending point of the change relative to the <term>point of indifference</term> <note>The neutral state where one feels neither pleasure nor pain.</note> of sensation. ...has occurred below the zero point of sensation, actually enters into consciousness. The less the consciousness of the person concerned perceives the movement as being below the zero point of sensation, the more the pleasure becomes factually equal in degree to the unpleasure in whose cessation it consists. This is least possible in the case of physical pain; therefore, no one will have themselves stretched on the rack <note>A historical reference to a torture device used to stretch the limbs.</note> just to enjoy the pleasure of the pain ceasing. In the mental realm, however, the struggle with necessity and the joy over every hard-won victory that secures the immediate future is proof of this. As soon as people realize that this joy relates to the preceding worry in no other way than the subsiding of pain relates to the agonies of the rack—and that this movement, like the other, falls entirely below the zero point of sensation—they will no longer **enjoy** those victories over necessity any more than the tortured person **enjoys** the slackening of the ropes.

What is called the specter of **mass poverty** <note>original: *Massenarmuth*</note> today is nothing but this emerging consciousness among the masses that the struggle with necessity, the worry, and its alleviation lie entirely on the negative (pain) side of the zero point of sensation. Previously, when mass poverty was ten times greater, this consciousness was lacking, and people bore their poverty as if by the grace of God. This is yet another proof of how advancing intelligence makes human beings unhappier. — This struggle of mankind against necessity is, however, only one example; if one looks around at the possible joys of the world, one will very soon perceive that—with the exception of physical-sensory, aesthetic, and scientific enjoyments—hardly any happiness can be found that is not based on liberation from a preceding unpleasure; this will apply most especially to great, lively joys. Voltaire says: *"there are no true pleasures except with true needs"* <note>original French: *„il n’est de vrais plaisirs qu’avec de vrais besoins.“*</note>.

This leads directly to the interesting question of whether pleasure can be a balancing equivalent for pain at all, and what coefficient or exponent must be assigned to a degree of pleasure in order to outweigh an equal degree of pain for the consciousness. Schopenhauer, citing Petrarch's verse: *"A thousand pleasures..."* <note>original Italian: *„Mille piacer’“* — from Petrarch's *Triumph of Death*: "A thousand pleasures are not worth one pain."</note>

If I have the choice either to hear nothing at all, or first to hear five minutes of discord and then five minutes of a beautiful piece of music; if I have the choice either to smell nothing, or first to smell a stench and then a fragrance; if I have the choice either to taste nothing, or first to taste something foul and then something delicious—in all these cases, I will decide in favor of hearing, smelling, and tasting nothing. This remains true even if the successive sensations of **unpleasure** <term>unpleasure: a technical term for *Unlust*, the opposite of pleasure (Lust), encompassing pain, discomfort, or distress</term> and pleasure seem to me to be of the same degree, although it would certainly be very difficult to prove an exact equality of degree. 

From this I conclude that pleasure must be noticeably greater in degree than a similar unpleasure if the two are to balance each other out for consciousness in such a way that their combination is equated to the zero point of sensation, and preferred to it only when there is a slight increase in pleasure or a decrease in unpleasure. Incidentally, this coefficient probably fluctuates between certain limits in different individuals, and its average magnitude is likely greater than 1.

I do not venture to propose any hypotheses regarding the causes underlying this remarkable phenomenon. This much is certain: if the fact is correct, this circumstance also speaks against the idea of a predominant happiness in the world. The world then resembles a **money lottery**: one must pay the full price of the pains staked, but the winnings are only paid out after a deduction. As **Schopenhauer** says (*Parerga and Paralipomena* II. 313): "This also agrees with the fact that, as a rule, we find pleasures far below, and pains far above, our expectations." ## 2. Health, Youth, Freedom, and a Sufficient Existence as Conditions for the Zero Point of Sensation, and Contentment.

The aforementioned states are usually claimed as the highest goods of life, and not without reason; nevertheless, they grant no positive pleasure whatsoever, except when they first arise through the transition from their opposite states of unpleasure. During their undisturbed existence, however, they represent nothing more than the **zero point of sensation** and by no means a positive elevation above it; they are the **building horizon** <note>original: *Bauhorizont*; a metaphor for the baseline or foundation level from which one starts building</note> upon which the expected enjoyments of life are first to be erected. This is consistent with the fact that the existence of these states arouses as little a feeling of pleasure as of unpleasure—since at the zero point there is nothing at all to be felt—but every descent from this building horizon into sickness, old age, lack of freedom, and necessity is felt painfully. These goods, therefore, actually have the purely **privative character** <note>privative character: a philosophical term meaning the state of being defined only by the absence of something else (like "cold" being the absence of "heat")</note> that Leibniz wanted to attribute to evil; they are the privation of old age, sickness, servitude, and necessity, and are by their nature incapable of rising above the zero point of sensation toward the side of pleasure...

Regarding health, all of this is quite self-evident; no one feels a limb unless they are sick; only the nerve patient feels that they have nerves, and only the eye patient that they have eyes; the healthy person, however, perceives that they have a body only through the senses of sight and touch. It is the same with freedom. Youth is, first, the stage of life in which alone perfect health and the unhindered use of body and mind are found, while with age, infirmities set in, which are felt painfully enough. Second, youth alone possesses—which actually follows from the unhindered use of body and mind—the full capacity for enjoyment, while in old age, all hardships, inconveniences, annoyance, adversities, and plagues become doubly palpable, while the capacity for enjoyment diminishes more and more. However, this capacity for enjoyment has only the value of a **foundational baseline** <note>original: *Bauhorizontes*, likely referring to a structural starting point or level</note>; it is only a capacity, i.e., a possibility (not the reality) of enjoyment; of what use are the best teeth to me, for example, if I have nothing to bite! 

Finally, a sufficient existence, or being secure from need and deprivation, cannot be regarded as a positive gain or enjoyment, but only as the **indispensable condition** <note>original: *conditio sine qua non*</note> for bare life, which only then awaits its pleasurable fulfillment. To endure hunger, thirst, frost, heat, or wetness is painful; protection from these evils through basic housing, clothing, and food cannot be called a positive good (the pleasure of eating does not belong to this consideration). For if bare life, secured in its conditions of existence, were already a positive good, then mere existence in itself would have to fulfill and satisfy us. If one truly possesses these four <term>privative goods</term> <note>These are "goods" defined by the absence of something negative, such as health (absence of illness) or freedom (absence of restraint).</note>, the external conditions for **contentment** are met. If the necessary internal condition is then added—**resignation**, the act of being **modest** and satisfied with what is necessary—then contentment will reign in the individual, so long as no significant misfortunes or pains afflict them. **Contentment requires no positive happiness**; it is precisely the **renunciation** of such things. It requires only the freedom from significant evils and pains—essentially, the "zero point" of sensation. Positive goods and positive happiness **can add nothing** to contentment; indeed, they can even endanger it. For the greater the positive goods and happiness one possesses, the greater the probability of suffering great pain through their loss, which temporarily abolishes contentment. Contentment, therefore, can so little be regarded as a sign of positive happiness that, on the contrary, the poorest and most modest person can most easily take permanent possession of it.

If, nonetheless, contentment is so frequently praised as a form of happiness—even as the highest attainable happiness—(Aristotle, *Eudemian Ethics* VII. 2: <note>original Greek: "ἡ εὐδαιμονία τῶν αὐτάρκων ἐστί"</note> "Happiness belongs to the self-sufficient"; Spinoza, *Ethics* Part 4, Proposition 52, Note: "Contentment with oneself is truly the highest thing we can hope for"), this can only be correct if the state of **painlessess** and voluntary **resignation** from all positive happiness deserves preference over the possession of positive happiness, which by its nature is fleeting. In general, if it is justified (as I believe it is) to call health, youth, freedom, and a care-free existence the highest goods, and contentment the highest happiness, then it is clear from the outset what a precarious state all positive goods and positive happiness must be in, that one may rightly place the privative ones—those consisting merely in **freedom from pain**—ahead of them. ### 3. Hunger and Love.

> "Until the structure of the world
> Is held together by philosophy,
> Its machinery is kept in motion
> Through hunger and through love,"
<note>This is a famous quote from the poem "The World-Sages" (Die Weltweisen) by Friedrich Schiller (1759–1805).</note>

as Schiller very rightly says. Both are almost the only active driving forces for progress and development in the **animal kingdom**, as well as for the early stages of human development and the cruder conditions that characterize it. If we must "break the staff" <note>A German idiom meaning to pass a final, negative judgment on something, originating from the custom of a judge breaking a staff over a condemned man.</note> over the value of these two factors for the individual, then there is already little prospect of saving the value of individual life for its own sake through other means.

Hunger is agonizing, which, of course, only those who have already felt it can know; its satisfaction—the **pleasure of satiety**—is for the brain merely the removal of pain. While for subordinate **nerve centers**, it may indeed involve a positive elevation above the zero point of sensation in the physical comfort of digestion, this will carry all the less weight for the "general feeling" or total well-being of the individual the more the subordinate nerve centers recede in importance relative to the brain. The brain receives only faint traces of the comfort of digestion, but feels all the more depressed in its mental mood and capacity for work by the state of satiety. For someone in the fortunate position of being able to satisfy hunger immediately whenever it first appears, and who is not inconvenienced by the dulling of the brain caused by satiety, there may indeed—

But this duping of conscious judgment by the drive does not last forever. The attained possession soon becomes habitual property; the mental image of the contrast with the difficulties of attainment fades more and more; the will for possession becomes latent, since no disturbance of possession threatens, and the satisfaction of this will is felt less and less as **pleasure**. Illusory pleasure and prevailing displeasure <note>original: *Unlust*; the opposite of *Lust*, often translated as "pain," "unpleasure," or "suffering."</note> even in the happiest case, mostly the obstruction of the will without reaching the goal amidst grief and despair, and the destruction of the future of so many female individuals through the loss of female honor—their only social support—these are the results we have found.

There could be no doubt that reason would only advise total abstinence from love, if only the torment of the indestructible drive, which thirsts to fill its void, were not an even **greater** evil than a moderate involvement with love. One must therefore give full credit to the saying of **Anacreon** <note>Anacreon was a Greek lyric poet (c. 582 – 485 BC) famous for his verses on love and wine.</note>, which reads:

->It is hard not to love,<- <note>original Greek: χαλεπὸν τὸ μὴ φιλῆσαι (chalepon to mē philēsai)</note>
->But it is also hard to love.<- <note>original Greek: χαλεπὸν δὲ καὶ φιλῆσαι (chalepon de kai philēsai)</note>

Once love is recognized as an evil and yet must be chosen as the lesser of two evils so long as the drive exists, then reason necessarily demands a third option, namely the **uprooting of the drive**, i.e., castration <note>original: *Verschneidung*; the act of becoming a eunuch, here discussed as a radical philosophical or ascetic solution to the "evil" of romantic drive.</note>, if an uprooting of the drive is achieved through it. (Compare **Matthew 19:11–12:** "All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given. For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother's womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the **kingdom of heaven's** sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it!")

#### 4. Compassion, Friendship, and Family Happiness.

Compassion, upon which—according to Aristotle (though not in my view)—the pleasure in tragedy is mainly based, and according to Schopenhauer all morality is founded, is a sensation mixed from displeasure <term>displeasure</term> <note>original: *Unlust*; a technical term in German philosophy referring to a state of dissatisfaction, pain, or psychological aversion.</note> and pleasure, as everyone knows. The reason for the displeasure is clear; it is precisely the "suffering-with" <term>suffering-with</term> <note>original: *Mit-Leiden*; the author highlights the literal meaning of the German word for compassion (*Mitleid*), which is to suffer alongside another.</note> another’s perceptibly visible pain, which can become so strong that it allows no trace of pleasure to arise in compassion, but rather transforms it entirely into heart-wrenching misery, the horror of which drives one to turn away. Imagine the sight of a battlefield after the battle, or a person lying in total convulsions.

But where the sensation of pleasure usually found in moderate compassion originates is harder to grasp. Of course, we are not speaking here of the satisfaction brought about by any potential assistance, for this lies beyond compassion itself. Malicious glee <term>malicious glee</term> <note>original: *Schadenfreude*; the experience of pleasure or self-satisfaction that comes from learning of or witnessing the troubles or failures of others.</note> is the only sensation of pleasure that the sight of another's suffering is capable of awakening directly; however, everyone knows very well how to distinguish this from the mild pleasure of compassion.

I see no other possibility for understanding the pleasure in compassion—nor have I found even the slightest attempt at another explanation—than this: that the contrast of another’s suffering with one’s own freedom from this suffering simultaneously arouses and satisfies a latent aversion toward enduring such pain, bringing that satisfaction to consciousness. Through this, the pleasure of compassion is admittedly declared to be purely egoistic; however, I do not see to what extent this

One must therefore use the vulgar masses only with caution when deciding whether pleasure or displeasure predominates in compassion as such. In my subjective judgment, the latter is decidedly the case; however others may judge, it is beyond doubt that the emotional coarseness of humanity is, on average, decreasing more and more, and that with this decreasing coarseness, the displeasure in compassion increasingly gains the upper hand over the pleasure.

Now, however, the ratio becomes even more unfavorable for pleasure when we take into account the immediate consequences of compassion within the soul. Specifically, compassion immediately awakens the desire to still the foreign suffering, and this is indeed the purpose of this instinct. This desire, however, finds a partial satisfaction only in very rare cases, and total satisfaction even more rarely; it will therefore arouse displeasure far more frequently than pleasure.

Thus, even if the instinct of compassion cannot be denied its justification as the "lesser of two evils"—acting as a corrective and limit to egoism and the injustice arising from it—it is nonetheless still an evil when considered in itself, for it brings more displeasure than pleasure.

Regarding **sociability and friendship**, the same cannot be proven, although it has been asserted many times—and for a certain **temperament** <term>temperament</term> <note>original: *Gemüthsart*; refers to one’s inherent disposition or character.</note>, quite rightly so. For example, **La Bruyère** says: “All our unhappiness comes from our inability to be alone.” <note>original: "*Tout notre mal vient de ne pouvoir être seuls.*"</note> (Compare also **Schopenhauer, Parerga I. 444–458.**)

However, it can be maintained that the drive for sociability is an instinctive need arising from the weakness and powerlessness of the individual. Its fulfillment—much like health and freedom—merely places the human being upon a foundation level <term>foundation level</term> <note>original: *Bauhorizont*; literally a "construction horizon," a technical term used here metaphorically to describe the baseline or ground level upon which further structures of happiness can be built.</note>. Only upon this social foundation is one then capable of erecting certain positive enjoyments. Furthermore, only a small part of true friendship, which is so rare anyway, represents a value that positively exceeds the zero point of sensation.

Just as there are herd animals in nature, man is a social animal; powerless and defenseless, abandoned to every power of nature and every enemy, his instinct directs him toward community with his own kind. Here, it is truly a felt deficiency that creates the need, and the pleasure <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: *Lust*</note> of this sociability is merely the cancellation of the displeasure <term>displeasure</term> <note>original: *Unlust*; the psychological state of pain or lack.</note> of that deficiency or need.

Secondly, beyond the defense against hardship and hostile attacks, social community enables the generation of positive achievements more effectively than solitude. Examples include economic labor, political-economic or artistic production, sexual love, the increase of education or knowledge through the exchange of ideas, or the gathering of interesting news. Social community enables all of this, but it does not *effect* it; it is simply the foundation level, which can remain unused or be used in the most diverse ways. In this regard, sociability is only the possibility of pleasure, but not the pleasure itself; rather, the pleasure belongs entirely to the buildings to be erected upon this foundation. It must be considered in those structures, not in sociability itself. Indeed, even the positive pleasure that can be established on its ground can, for the most part, be obtained in solitude in an unchanged or slightly modified manner.

To be sure, one seeks comfort, but if one considers it properly, what comfort can it truly provide to also spoil a friend's mood with one's own inconveniences and troubles?

Here, too, it comes down to the fact that the increase of mutual compassion in friendship is the lesser of two evils, the other of which appears as the greater only because of one's own weakness.

Therefore, when the highly praised happiness of friendship is subjected to a proper appraisal, it rests partly on human weakness in enduring suffering—just as very strong characters have the least need for friendship—and partly on the pursuit of a common goal; in a word, on the **alignment of interests**. This is why even the most seemingly inseparable friendships dissolve or wither away when the leading interests change in one party, so that they now diverge from those of the other. In the early years, the inconvenience and the hassle of care predominate; then comes the annoyance with neighbors and the anxiety over illnesses; then the worry of marrying off daughters and the grief over the foolish antics and debts of sons; added to all this is the worry of raising the necessary funds, which is greatest for the poor in the early years and for the educated classes in the later years. And despite all the labor and effort, all the grief and worry, and the constant fear of losing them, what is the actual happiness that children provide to the person who has them? Aside from the occasional satisfaction of vanity through the hypocritical flattery of a pleasant neighbor—it is *hope*, nothing but *hope* for the future.

And when the time comes to fulfill these hopes—provided the children have not died or gone astray beforehand—they leave the parental home and go their own way. Thus, insofar as that hope is selfish, it *always* deceives; but insofar as one merely hopes for the child’s sake, and not for one's own benefit, what then?

As we shall see, people eventually withdraw from everything in old age, except for that one illusion of the only instinct remaining to them: that they build their hopes for their children upon the same miserable existence <note>original: *erbärmliche Dasein*</note> whose vanity they have recognized in every other respect regarding themselves. If they live long enough to see their own children become old, they certainly withdraw from that hope as well, yet then they simply *start from the beginning* with their grandchildren and great-grandchildren; — man never learns his lesson <note>original: *der Mensch lernt nie aus*; a play on the German idiom meaning "one is never too old to learn," used here ironically to suggest that humans never learn to break the cycle of biological instinct.</note>.

### **5. Vanity, Sense of Honor, Ambition, Lust for Glory, and Lust for Power.**

Love, honor, and the drive for acquisition <note>original: "Erwerbstrieb"—the impulse to gain resources or wealth</note> are likely the three most powerful driving forces in the spiritual domain. Here we concern ourselves with the second. One can distinguish honor into objective and subjective honor. The objective honor of a person is, generally expressed, their **valuation** by others.
Objective honor can be classified as follows:

<margin>Positive Honor</margin>
- A. Honor of external value:
    - a. Honor of possession,
    - b. Honor of social standing <note>original: "Standes"</note>,
    - c. Honor of rank,
    - d. Honor of beauty.
- B. Honor of internal value:
    - a. Honor of labor,
    - b. Honor of intelligence and education,
    - c. Moral honor,
        - α) of neighborly love <term>Nächstenliebe: altruistic or charitable love for others</term>,
<margin>Negative Honor</margin>
        - β) of justice,
    - d. Civil honor,
    - e. Female (sexual) honor.

Everyone possesses negative honor by default until it is lost; positive honor must be acquired through circumstances (birth, actions, achievements). The former denotes only the zero point of value; the latter positively exceeds it. The honor of possession is based on power; that of social standing on power and achievements, though it easily ossifies into forms persisting from earlier times. The honor of rank—insofar as it exceeds the honor of the power and labor associated with that rank—is an artificial creation of the state, designed to allow for the payment of lower salaries <note>A cynical observation that the state grants titles and prestige as a cheap substitute for financial compensation</note>. The honor of beauty must be sought not among us, but among peoples who have a sense for beauty (such as the ancient Greeks); the honor of labor is proportional to the economic value of the work performed. Intelligence and education replace the honor of labor especially in cases where mental labor is not understood as "work" at all. Moral honor is positive only in active, charitable love; the honor of justice is merely negative, just like civil and sexual honor—the latter of which exists only for women <note>The author reflects the 19th-century view that "honor" for a woman was defined negatively by the absence of sexual scandal, rather than by positive achievements</note>.

<summary>This page categorizes "Honor" into external and internal types, distinguishing between "positive honor" (earned through merit) and "negative honor" (a baseline reputation lost through misconduct).</summary>
<keywords>honor, social standing, ethics, labor, positive honor, negative honor, social status, 19th-century philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 578 ---
<meta>Continuing from page 574, where the author categorized "objective honor" (how the world values an individual), this page explores "subjective honor"—how the individual perceives their own value and the value others place upon them. The text transitions from structural definitions to psychological analysis.</meta>

*Subjective honor* is of a twofold nature; the **direct** subjective honor of a human being is their valuation of themselves; the **indirect** is their valuation of the valuation of themselves by others, or their valuation of **objective honor**.

The former is called **self-valuation, self-respect, self-esteem, pride**; if the valuation is below the true value, it is called: **modesty, humility**; if it is above the true value: **self-overestimation, conceit, arrogance**; the latter, on the other hand, is called **vanity**; even if people may resist allowing this word in the context of nobler endeavors—in essence, it is the same whether a girl is vain about the reputation of her beauty, or a poet is vain about the reputation of his works. Both parts together, pride and vanity, constitute subjective honor, which is subject to the same classification according to the objects of valuation as objective honor. In relation to the negative part, it is called a sense of honor; in relation to the positive part, ambition <note>The author uses "sense of honor" (Ehrgefühl) here to mean the baseline drive to avoid shame, and "ambition" (Ehrgeiz) as the drive for positive distinction.</note>. The direct and indirect parts of subjective honor can exist in very different proportions of strength to one another, but as a rule, the latter will predominate—indeed, predominate so much that one frequently encounters the view that subjective honor consists only in this valuation of the valuation of oneself by others. However, this is pure vanity: to place value on another's judgment of one's worth while simultaneously denying oneself all worth, thus holding the foreign judgment to be false.

Pride, one's own high self-esteem, is an enviable quality, regardless of whether the estimation is true or false, as long as one simply considers it to be correct.

To be sure, an unshakable pride is rare; mostly it must endure alternating struggles with doubt or even despair in oneself, which cause more pain than the pride itself causes pleasure. Furthermore, pride increases one's sensitivity toward the outside world and is, for its part, forced to adopt the hypocritical mask of modesty if it does not wish to prepare unpleasantness for itself. Taken together, this likely outweighs the pleasure of high self-esteem. — Now, as for that sense of honor and ambition which are based largely or exclusively on vanity: however practical an instinct they may be for our current stage of development, one cannot deny that they are, firstly, vain

### 6. Religious Edification.

We have already mentioned in Chapter B. IX. that the elevation of religious feeling in devotion and edification—which is always of a more or less mystical nature—is capable of granting such high bliss that it transcends all earthly suffering. But firstly, these high degrees of elevation are rare; because they are essentially mystical in nature, they cannot be acquired through industry and effort, but rather presuppose a natural disposition or talent for it, just like the enjoyment of art. Secondly, like every pleasure, they are not without their own peculiar displeasure. This is best understood by looking at the lives of penitents and saints. The highest degrees of religious elevation are hardly conceivable without a long-continued <term>mortification of the flesh</term> <note>original: *Abtödtung des Fleisches*—the ascetic practice of subduing physical desires through self-denial or even pain to achieve spiritual growth.</note>, which refers not only to sensual desires but to all worldly pleasures in general. Seldom is this renunciation sustained by a consciousness of the illusory nature of earthly pleasure and the predominance of the displeasure that simultaneously arises from earthly longing...

### 7. Immorality.

Immoral action or wrongdoing arises from egoism, which is established as an inevitable consequence of individuation <note>The philosophical concept that individual existence is a separate, distinct state from the universal whole; this separation is seen here as the source of selfishness.</note>. It essentially consists in this: that I, in order to procure a pleasure for myself or to spare myself a pain—in short, to satisfy my individual will—inflict a greater pain on one or more other individuals. All other forms of wrongdoing are derived from this original one. It is therefore clear that the essence of injustice or immorality consists in changing the relationship between pleasure and displeasure <term>displeasure</term> <note>original: *Unlust*.</note> already existing in the world to the detriment of pleasure, since the pain of the victim of injustice is greater than the...

Regarding the badness, worthlessness, malice, and meanness of humanity, Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher famous for his pessimistic outlook, arguing that human life is driven by an insatiable and painful "Will."</note> indulges in vivid descriptions which could hardly be called exaggerated, and which I will spare myself from repeating here. But if wrongdoing increases the suffering of the world, doing what is right is by no means capable of reducing it; for it is nothing other than the maintenance of the *existing state of affairs* <note>original: *status quo*</note> before the first wrong was committed—it is thus no positive movement beyond the baseline of development <note>original: *Bauhorizont* — literally "construction horizon," referring here to the established level of moral or social order.</note>. No one who receives what is rightfully theirs will feel joy over it, unless the fear of being wronged has been taken away; and the person who allows another their due right has even less reason for pleasure, for he has curtailed his own individual will and yet done no more than his duty. True joy can only be granted by the exercise of positive morality—of active neighborly love <note>original: *Nächstenliebe* — often translated as "charity" or "altruism."</note> — yet even then, the giver will feel the displeasure of the sacrifice, while the receiver will feel the displeasure of shame over the benefit received. This increase in the world’s pleasure through active neighborly love is of no consequence compared to the vast mass of immorality.
