### 8. Scientific and Artistic Enjoyment.

Like the weary traveler who, after a long pilgrimage in the desert, finally encounters an oasis—that is how we feel now as we come upon art and science; finally, a friendly glimpse of sunlight in the night of striving and suffering. If Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher who argued that aesthetic experiences allow a person to temporarily escape the "Will"—the source of all human suffering—into a state of pure, painless contemplation.</note> could define the state of mind during artistic or scientific reception or production as mere painlessness, then he must never have known the state of ecstasy or rapture into which one can fall over a work of art or a newly opening sphere of science. But if he had recognized the positive nature of such a state of highest enjoyment, he could no longer have claimed that it was a state free from will and interest. Instead, he would have seen that it is a state of the highest and most perfect positive **satisfaction**—and the satisfaction of what, if not a will? Admittedly, not the satisfaction of common practical interests or the mundane will, but of the striving for knowledge <note>original: *Erkenntniss* — this refers to a deep, often intuitive grasp of truth or intellectual discovery.</note>, or rather for that harmony, that unconscious logic beneath the veil of sensory form—in short, for that "something" in which beauty consists, regardless of what that may be. That ecstatic delight (for example, over a musical performance, a painting, a poem, or a philosophical treatise) is, of course, something very rare; the very capacity for it is granted only to gifted natures, and even they will not be able to boast of too many such moments in their lives. This is, as it were, a compensation granted to such sensitive beings for the pains of life, which they must feel much more intensely than other people whose dullness makes many things easier for them.

Whether the latter <note>Referring to the "dull" or less sensitive individuals.</note> do not fare better on the whole is hardly a question. For since displeasure so greatly outweighs pleasure in life, a duller sensitivity toward it—even at the cost of forgoing a pleasure that is never missed, no matter how high it may be or how restricted to a few moments of life—would likely not be too high a price to pay. This is confirmed by the fact that, on average, people think the less of the **value** of life the more sensitive and intellectually elevated they are. What

Now, one might ask what percentage of the earth's inhabitants are receptive to artistic and scientific enjoyment to any noteworthy degree, and one will already find that the significance of art and science for the happiness of the world in general should not be estimated too highly. Furthermore, consider how small a percentage of those who are receptive are, in turn, capable of attaining the joy of self-creation—of artistic or scientific production—which stands considerably higher than that of merely receiving.

In assessing the receptivity of the common people, however, one must also not forget to filter out those reasons for interest that are not based on the art itself. For example, curiosity or a craving for the horrific or gruesome <note>original: *Graulichen* — referring to a morbid fascination with the macabre or terrifying in stories.</note> in the interest shown for folk singers or folk tales; the desire for dancing in the interest for folk music; the consideration of practical utility in the interest for scientific communications, and so forth. Among the "educated," however, many affect an interest—and thus a capacity for enjoyment—regarding art and science which they do not possess at all. Just think how many are enticed to become scholars or artists by the prospects of a career (which perhaps pleases them more because of its perceived freedom) without having an actual calling for it. If one wanted to weed out all those who are uncalled and untalented, the ranks of scholars and artists would melt away tremendously. To the scholarly career <note>original: *Gelehrtenlaufbahn*</note>, people are enticed more by the prospects of a future position and the ease of entry into the career (scholarships, etc.); to the artistic career <note>original: *Künstlerlaufbahn*</note>, people are drawn more by the lack of restraint in the profession and the nature of the work, which appears more like a cheerful game, but often also by the mere hope of earning a living; think of the unfortunate girls who train to be music teachers. ### 9. Sleep and Dreaming.

Insofar as sleep is dreamless, it represents a complete inactivity of the brain and brain-consciousness; for as soon as the brain is active in any way, it begins to play with images. Such an unconscious state also makes any sensation of pleasure or displeasure impossible. However, if a nervous excitation occurs that must stimulate pleasure or displeasure, it also interrupts the inactive state of the brain. Unconscious sleep is therefore equal to the **zero point** of sensation in relation to specifically human or brain-consciousness. This does not exclude the possibility that other nerve centers, such as the spinal cord and ganglia, continue their consciousness; this is even necessary for the continuation of breathing, digestion, blood movement, and so on. But this is merely a deeply animalistic consciousness, standing perhaps at the level of a lower fish or worm, which can have only a very slight positive significance in the calculation of human happiness. Yet, even in this animal consciousness of the lower nerve centers, pleasure and displeasure alternate; pleasure can only occur with the normal and undisturbed progress of the vegetative functions <note>The "vegetative functions" refer to the involuntary bodily processes like heart rate and digestion, managed by the autonomic nervous system.</note>, in the event that this ani-

As far as the dream is concerned, all the drudgeries of real life cross over with it into the state of sleep, except for the one thing that can somewhat reconcile the educated person with life: scientific and artistic enjoyment. Added to this is the fact that a joy in a dream is not easily expressed as anything other than a pleasant, joyful mood—for example, as a feeling of weightlessness, of hovering, flying, and the like—whereas unpleasure expresses itself not only as a mood, but also in all kinds of specific unpleasantnesses: anger, resentment, bickering and strife, the incomprehensible impossibility of achieving what is willed, or other chicanes and adversities. On average, the judgment on the value of the dream will therefore follow the judgment of real life, but will nonetheless turn out quite a bit worse. —

Falling asleep, if one can fall asleep quickly, is a pleasure, but only because fatigue had made staying awake a torment and falling asleep frees me from this torment. Waking up is also said to be a pleasure for some people; however, I have never been able to find this to be the case, and I believe that this claim rests on a confusion with that pleasure which consists in not having to get up while fatigue is still present, but rather being able to slumber on with half-consciousness. ### 10. The Acquisitive Drive and Comfort.

By acquisitive drive <note>original: "Erwerbstrieb." The impulse to earn, acquire, or accumulate property and wealth.</note> I mean here primarily the striving that goes beyond the essentials of possession—that is, beyond housing, food, and clothing for oneself and one's family. I will spare myself a reference to the small percentage of the population, even in civilized states <note>original: "Culturstaaten." Referring to the industrialized or "developed" nations of the 19th century.</note>, for whom a satisfaction of this drive becomes possible, as modern statistics have made this relationship terrifyingly clear. But if we ask ourselves what advantages a possession exceeding the necessary can offer, it is first of all that it protects us from future need through its capital value—or even better, through the interest earned on that capital—and removes the fear of future need. But this benefit is not yet a positive one; it merely secures us against future unpleasure and eliminates present unpleasure (fear and worry). Secondly, possession confers the power to attain positive enjoyments; it creates the honor of ownership, it grants power and dominion over those who expect advantages from my possession, it buys the pleasures of the palate and even the joys of love; in short, possession or its symbol, money, is the magic wand which all enjoyments

It can, quite obviously, only represent the zero point of sensation.

Consequently, regarding that which excites the greatest envy—wealth—we arrive, strangely enough, at the same negative result as we did with the bare maintenance of existence, with which we began. This is certainly significant and characteristic of the value of life.

It must be maintained that the acquisitive drive <term>Erwerbstrieb</term> can always only be a means for other purposes, and its value must be measured according to the value of these purposes; in no case may it claim a value in and of itself. If it does so, it immediately joins the ranks of those illusory drives that produce a preponderance of unpleasure. — Cf. <note>Compare</note> on this Luke 12:15: "Take heed and beware of greed, for even in abundance, no one's life comes from his external resources." <note>original German: "Sehet zu und hütet Euch vor der Habgier, denn auch im Ueberflusse kommt Keinem das Leben aus seinen äusseren Hülfsquellen."</note> And Matthew 6:19–21 and 24–34.

### 12. Hope.

> “And so, whatever he may bear,
> He does not despair of salvation,
> Fate leads him to the grave
> Upon the fool’s rope of hope!”
<note>Hartmann is likely quoting or paraphrasing a common poetic sentiment regarding the illusory nature of hope, often compared to a "fool's rope" (Narrenseil) that pulls one along.</note>

No matter how poorly a person is doing—as long as a tiny spark of life-force still flickers within him, he clings to the hope of future happiness. If hope were not in the world, despair would be the order of the day, and we would have to record countless suicides in defiance of the instinct for self-preservation and the fear of death.

Thus, hope is the necessary **auxiliary instinct** of the drive for self-preservation; it is hope that first makes the love of life possible for us poor fools, in mockery of our reason.

Hope is a **character trait**. There are people who always see the future darkly, and others who always see it rosily. It springs from a certain **elasticity** of the spirit, an abundance of life-force and life-drive that is not diminished by even the most palpable experiences, and which raises its head with its old courage after the heaviest blows of fate. No character trait is as dependent as this one upon the general physical constitution and the influences of the **vitality of the blood** <note>original: "Blutleben," referring to the physiological/circulatory state</note> on **neural and cerebral life**. However, no character trait is so important regarding the subjective influence on thinking when considering the question of the **value** and **worthlessness** of life. Since hope is clearly a useful **instinct** even when life has the greatest **worthlessness** (whereas on the other hand, if life really had a **value**, it would be impossible to see how **pessimism** <note>original: "Schwarzseherei," literally "black-seeing"</note> as a **character eccentricity** could benefit man), one must guard oneself to the utmost against a bribery and falsification of one’s judgment by the former instinct.

Without doubt, hope is a quite real pleasure. But what does one hope for then? Surely for finding happiness in life

<meta>This page continues Hartmann’s psychological and philosophical analysis of hope as a deceptive mechanism. He argues that hope exists solely to trick individuals into persevering through a life where suffering inevitably outweighs enjoyment.</meta>

to catch and hold onto. If, however, happiness is not to be found in life because—no matter how long one lives—pain always outweighs pleasure, then it surely follows that hope is perverse and void; it is essentially the illusion *pre-eminently* <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχήν" (kat' exochēn), meaning par excellence or in the highest sense</note>. It exists strictly to dupe us—that is, to make fools of us—so that we might endure in order to solve our other task, which we have not yet understood. 

But once someone has gained the conviction that hoping itself is as void and illusory as the thing being hoped for, the instinct of hope must very soon be weakened and suppressed by this intellectual insight. The only thing that remains possible for such a person as an object of hope is not the greatest possible happiness, but the smallest possible misfortune. Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics VII. 12) already expressed this: *“The prudent man pursues freedom from pain, not pleasure.”* <note>original Greek: "ὁ φρόνιμος τὸ ἄλυπον διώκει, οὐ τὸ ἡδύ" (ho phronimos to alypon diōkei, ou to hēdy)</note> With this realization, however, any positive significance is stripped away from hope.

But even those who never, or never fully, see through the illusory nature of hope might still be forced to admit—at least regarding their past (for instinct misleads them regarding the future)—that nine-tenths of all hopes, indeed far more, come to naught. They must admit that in the vast majority of cases, the bitterness of disappointment was greater than the sweetness of the hope itself. The correctness of this assertion is confirmed by the rules of common practical wisdom, which suggest that one should approach all things with the lowest possible expectations; only then is one able to enjoy whatever good may be found in things, whereas otherwise the immediate enjoyment of the present would be spoiled by deceived expectations. Consequently, the result for the instinct of hope is that it is both illusory and that, within the very illusions in which it operates, it brings more pain than pleasure.

a) **nerve fatigue** increases the resistance to suffering and decreases the effort to hold onto pleasure; thus, it increases the displeasure felt toward suffering and decreases the pleasure felt toward pleasure itself;

b) the pleasure that arises from the cessation or lessening of a **suffering** can never remotely outweigh that suffering;

c) suffering forces itself upon the **consciousness**, which is compelled to feel it; pleasure, however, does not. It must, so to speak, be discovered and unlocked by consciousness, and is therefore very often lost to consciousness when the motive for its discovery is lacking;

d) **satisfaction** is brief and fades quickly, while suffering—insofar as it is not limited by hope—lasts as long as the desire remains unsatisfied (and when would such a desire not exist?).

Through their cooperation, these four factors produce a result that is practically almost the same as if pleasure were—as **Schopenhauer** <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a philosopher famous for his pessimism, who argued that life is essentially suffering and that pleasure is merely the temporary absence of pain</note> maintains—something negative and unreal, and suffering the only positive and real thing.

a) those that bring only suffering or at least next to no pleasure (see No. 13);

b) those that represent only the **zero point** of sensation, or the **baseline of life** <note>original: "Bauhorizont," literally a construction horizon or foundation level</note>—the absence of certain types of suffering. These include health, youth, freedom, a sufficient existence, comfort, and, for the most part, community with one’s peers or sociability;

c) those that have a real significance only as **means** to ends lying outside themselves, whose value can therefore only be measured by the value of those ends, but which are illusory when considered as ends in themselves—for example, the pursuit of property, power, and honor, and partially also sociability and friendship;

This happiness of the "illusory daze" is particularly characteristic of youth. Every young man and young woman sees themselves more or less as the hero or heroine of a novel. They console themselves over present misfortunes or frustrations—much as one does while reading a novel—with the prospect of a brilliant conclusion. The only difference is that this conclusion never arrives, and they forget that behind the seemingly brilliant ending of a novel, only the common misery of daily life lies in wait.

However, from the rich selection of youthful hopes, one after another is recognized as illusory with increasing age and experience. The mature man already stands there relatively much poorer in illusions than the youth; usually, only ambition and the drive for acquisition <term>Erwerbstrieb: the impulse to accumulate wealth or property</term> remain for him.

Even these two are recognized as illusory by the old man—unless ambition has hardened into childish vanity, or the drive for acquisition into greed. Among sensible elders, one will indeed no longer find many illusions relating to the life of the individual, except, of course, for the instinctive love for their children and parents.

The result of an individual life, therefore, is that one eventually retreats from everything; that one realizes, like Koheleth <note>The Hebrew name for the author of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes.</note>: "All is utter vanity"—that is, illusory and worthless.

<meta>This page continues the author’s exploration of "illusions" that allow humanity to endure existence. Having previously discussed the "dazed" optimism of youth and the "poor in spirit," the author now shifts to a historical analysis of how ancient civilizations—specifically the Jewish, Greek, and Roman worlds—conceived of happiness as an attainable earthly goal.</meta>

In these spheres, the worldviews and ways of life that would later become distinct are still unclearly mixed together. Judaism expresses the belief in the reachability of individual earthly happiness in the most overt way, both in its promises and in its general optimistic worldview, which lacks a transcendent background <note>The author suggests that early Jewish thought focused on divine favor and prosperity within this life, rather than a focus on an afterlife.</note>. In Greek culture, this same striving manifests in a nobler fashion through the enjoyment of art and science and in what is, as it were, an aesthetic conception of life. Hellenism, too, is ultimately absorbed in a refined pursuit of individual earthly happiness, since the <term>politeia: the Greek term for the city-state or political community</term> is intended only to provide preservation and protection for the individual. Consider the statement of the dead Achilles in the *Odyssey* (XI. 488–491):

> “Speak not to me of comfort regarding death, noble Odysseus! 
> I would rather cultivate the field as a day-laborer 
> for a poor man without inheritance or wealth of his own, 
> than rule over the entire host of the departed dead.”

The Roman Republic certainly adds a new element: the pursuit of happiness in and through the elevation of the glory and power of one’s immediate fatherland. After this striving for world domination proves to be an illusion for the attainment of happiness, the Roman world also adopts the Greek worldview—though degraded into something common—in the form of the shallowest Epicureanism <note>A philosophy often associated in this period with the pursuit of simple sensory pleasure and the avoidance of pain.</note>, and the ancient world outlives itself until it reaches an utter disgust with life.

Aristotle stands on the same ground; in *On the Soul* (Book I, Ch. 4, 408a, 24 ff.), he denies the <term>active intellect</term> <note>original: "νοῦς ποιητικός" (nous poietikos). In Aristotelian thought, this is the part of the mind that acts upon information to create understanding; it is often described as eternal and separate from the individual.</note>—as he calls the immortal part of the soul—not only love and hate, but also memory and <term>discursive thinking</term> <note>original: "διανοεῖσθαι" (dianoeisthai). This refers to the step-by-step logical reasoning characteristic of human consciousness, as opposed to immediate, divine intuition.</note>. Elsewhere it is known that the active intellect (or productive understanding) is the eternal, universal, and unchanging element in humans, inaccessible to any external impressions; yet, it is utterly impossible to see how it could be considered individual.

Spinoza, who certainly starts from entirely different premises, reaches the same result: "The human mind cannot be absolutely destroyed with the body, but something of it remains which is eternal" (*Ethics*, Part 5, Proposition 23). This "something" is the idea that necessarily exists in God, which grasps the essence of the human body in question under the <term>form of eternity</term> <note>original Latin: "sub specie aeternitatis." To see things "under the form of eternity" is to see them not as they happen in time, but as they exist as eternal truths within the structure of the universe.</note> (Ibid., Proof); that is, with intuitive knowledge, which stands higher than the knowledge of the adequate ideas of the properties of things and is entirely identical to our intuitive knowledge of the Unconscious. (Compare Part 2, Proposition 40, Scholium 2.)

Eternity is nothing other than the essence of God, insofar as it includes a necessary existence (according to Part 1, Definition 8); therefore, the eternal existence of the human mind cannot be defined by time or explained through duration (Part 5, Prop. 23, Proof). — "The mind is subject to the movements of the soul <note>Referring to the "passions" or emotions that affect the mind.</note> that belong to passive states only as long as the body lasts" (Part 5, Prop. 34). "From this it follows that no love except <term>intellectual love</term> <note>original Latin: "amor intellectualis." For Spinoza, this is the rational, detached love for God/Nature that arises from true understanding.</note>" (with which God loves himself) "is eternal" (Ibid., Corollary). Memory and sensory representation likewise do not remain after death (Ibid., Scholium to Prop. 38 and Corollary to Prop. 40). "As soon as the uneducated person ceases to suffer, he also ceases to be" (Prop. 42, Scholium).

In Leibniz, at least this much is noteworthy: he can only conceive of that which constitutes the individual limitation of the <term>monad</term> <note>In Leibniz's philosophy, "monads" are the basic, indivisible building blocks of reality. Every soul is a monad, but its individuality is tied to its "point of view," which Leibniz connects to having a body.</note> as being the body itself. Therefore, he only dares to assert the immortality of the soul alongside the simultaneous immortality of a body that is peculiar and inseparable from it. Given the current standpoint of natural science, this latter assumption critiques itself <note>That is, the idea of an "indestructible" physical body accompanying the soul is seen as scientifically untenable by the author's time.</note>.

<summary>The author examines the views of Aristotle, Spinoza, and Leibniz to demonstrate that these philosophers do not support the idea of individual, personal immortality. They conclude that while an eternal "intellect" or "essence" may remain, the personal traits of memory, emotion, and discursive thought perish with the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of individual immortality by examining the German Idealists—Schelling, Fichte, and Hegel—as well as Schopenhauer. Schelling expresses himself exactly like Spinoza (I. 6, 60—61): “The eternal aspect of the soul is not eternal because of a beginning-less or endless duration, but because it has no relationship to time at all. Following these citations, we need not hesitate to declare the hope for an individual persistence of the soul to be likewise an illusion. With this, the "main nerve" of Christian promises is severed, for at heart, man is only concerned with his "dear ego"; "what use is the greatest future bliss to me if I do not feel and enjoy it!"

But how does it stand generally with that <term>eternal bliss</term> <note>original: "ewige Seligkeit." This refers to the state of ultimate happiness or salvation promised in religious and philosophical systems.</note> according to our premises? The <term>All-One Unconscious</term> <note>original: "All-Einige Unbewusste." This is the central concept of Eduard von Hartmann’s philosophy, describing a single, unconscious cosmic force that underlies all reality.</note> is all-knowing and all-wise; therefore, it can no longer become "smarter." It has, as Aristotle also says, no memory; thus, it can learn nothing through experiences it might have had in the world. Consequently, once the world has ceased to exist, it remains exactly the same as it was before the creation of the world. It is now as blissful as it was before—no more and no less. Never can the <term>world-process</term> <note>original: "Weltprocess." The unfolding of history and nature over time.</note> help it to a greater bliss than it possessed previously, unless it were to find its bliss within the process itself.

However, we are not considering this latter case here, for that would be the worldly life itself, whereas we are asking about the bliss of the state *outside* the world. If we therefore cannot gain anything in bliss through earthly life beyond that pre-worldly state, but rather reach exactly that state again after the conclusion of the world-process, then the question arises: what was the nature of that state? It is obvious that if a <term>Willing</term> <note>original: "Wollen."</note> had existed, then there would also have been an <term>Act</term> <note>original: "Actus." ...essence would be, and the Unconscious would not be world-less; the world-less state could only be that of non-willing.

Now, however, we have seen in Chapter C. I. that <term>Representation</term> <note>original: "Vorstellen." In 19th-century German philosophy, this refers to the mind's ability to form mental images, thoughts, or "ideas" of the world.</note> could only be driven from non-being into being through <term>Willing</term> <note>original: "Wollen." This describes a fundamental, blind urge or drive that brings the universe into existence.</note>, so long as the world did not yet exist. In itself, Representation had no drive and no interest in stepping from non-being into being; consequently, before the onset of Willing, no Representation was actual. Therefore, before the origin of the world, there was neither Willing nor Representation—that is, nothing at all. As long as Willing lasts, the <term>world-process</term> <note>The unfolding of history and nature as a continuous development.</note> and its appearance in consciousness—the world—will last. If, therefore, one day there is to be no more world, then there must also be no more Willing, and consequently no more Representation (since the unconscious representation only ever becomes actual to the extent that the interest of the Will demands it). That is to say, there will once again be Nothing. This is also the state that alone fits the assertions of the Apostles, that there will be no more time and no more knowledge. So long as the world exists, there is the world-process, including all the bliss or misery it contains; before the origin and after the cessation of the world and the world-process, there is—Nothing.

Where then remains the promised bliss? It should not and cannot be found within the world, and the Nothing after the world can only be relatively more blissful or miserable than a previous state, but not a positive bliss or misery. (Compare Aristotle, <note>original: "Eth. N."</note> *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book I, Chapter 11, 1100a 13). <note>Aristotle argues here about whether a person’s well-being can be affected after their death.</note> To be sure, if the world is the state of misery for the world-essence, then the "Nothing" will be a bliss in comparison to it.

This is how Buddhism intends it with <term>Nirvana</term>, and so does Schopenhauer, but not so Christianity. Such a reduction to the zero-point of sensation—to painlessness and joylessness—would, for the time being, serve the ordinary egoistic common sense very little. We see as the only result of this expectation the individual <term>denial of the will</term> <note>A core concept in Schopenhauer’s philosophy where one attempts to escape suffering by suppressing all desires.</note> and world-renunciation of the Indian penitents or Schopenhauerian asceticism—which is not only useless but even harmful to the world-process—rather than the "bliss of hope" found in the Gospel.

The Roman spirit had indeed possessed and practiced this self-denial, but only for the benefit of increasing the power of the closest tribal community. They had, so to speak, merely expanded individual egoism into a tribal egoism, and with this, they pursued the phantoms of ambition and the lust for power. Now, however, it is a matter of expanding the egoistic consciousness into a **cosmic** consciousness and striving—into the awareness that the individual, like the nation, is nothing but a wheel or a spring in the great machinery of the world, and has no task other than to do its duty as such, in order to promote the <term>world-process</term> <note>The overall development of the universe and history toward a specific end.</note>, which is all that truly matters.

Naturally, the ancient world was not yet ripe for such a thought or such self-denial. ### v. Hartmann, Philosophy of the Unconscious. 39

...from the second to the third stage, the progress toward truth consists in the attained insight that the path to <term>redemption</term> <note>original: "Erlösung." In Hartmann's philosophy, this refers to the liberation of the spirit from the suffering inherent in existence.</note> from the misery of the present must be sought, first, not within the individual but outside of it, and second, not outside the *world-process*, but lies within the *world-process* itself. Thus, the future redemption of the world is to be found not in *abstaining from life*, but in *surrender to life*. Yet, this *surrender to life*, which would be a perversity if pursued for its own sake, only has meaning for the sake of the future of the process of the whole.

This transition from the second to the third stage is, given human weakness, admittedly hardly conceivable except through a partial misunderstanding of this latter truth—that is, as a partial relapse into the first stage of illusion <note>The "first stage of illusion" is the pursuit of individual happiness in the present life, which Hartmann considers a childish but necessary phase of development.</note>. For how is man to reach a sufficiently strong faith in a future happiness on earth if he considers the current state to be miserable in every respect and regards all happiness attainable in present life as vanity?

Therefore, with the principle of free inquiry and criticism established by the Reformation, we see the progressive decomposition of Christian dogma and the destruction of its promises begin negatively. Yet, at the same time, we see the reawakening *love for the world* taking the place of the Christian "blessedness in the hope of the hereafter"—manifested through the rebirth of ancient art and science, the flourishing of urban wealth and commerce, the progress of technology, and the universal expansion of the intellectual horizon.

The giant strides in all directions after such long stagnation fired hope toward even greater expectations. Thus, as always in epochs of promising progress, a time of *optimism* arose, whose primary theoretical representative is *Leibniz* <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), famous for his "Theodicy," which argued that we live in the "best of all possible worlds."</note>. (Presently, as the formation of nation-states rushes toward its goal, a similar *optimism* prevails in political matters.) Only slowly and gradually can the power of an idea as immense as the Christian one be broken. This is particularly interesting to observe in the most recent philosophy. *Kant* <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804). ### Third Stage of Illusion.

#### Happiness is conceived as lying in the future of the world-process.

To this stage belongs, first of all, the concept of **immanent development**, its application to the world as a whole, and the belief in a **world-development**. In ancient philosophy, with the exception of Aristotle, not a trace of this is found; but even with him, the application of the concept is essentially limited to the natural development of the individual, and in any case, it exercised no epoch-making influence in a spiritual sense on his contemporaries or posterity.

Even **Spinoza's** rigid necessity—whose soul-lessness and aimlessness make the changing variety of the forms of existence appear as nothing more than an indifferent, I might almost say, whimsical and accidental game—still has no room for the concept of development. This concept lives and breathes most deeply in **Hegel**, for whom the entire world is nothing but a development and realization of the Idea.

In the individual, it is not difficult to convince oneself of the presence of development; one sees it daily in everything and everyone. It is all the more difficult, however, to take the thought of the development of a whole—consisting of many individuals—so much into one's "flesh and blood" that one gains an interest in it that transcends the egoistic; for nothing is harder to overcome than the instinct of egoism.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of late 19th-century philosophical movements, transitioning from the discussion of historical development in Leibniz and Lessing to a sharp critique of Max Stirner’s radical individualism. It examines Stirner's rejection of all abstract ideals in favor of the "I."</meta>

<page-num>612</page-num>

...interested in practical philosophy should leave unread. The work <note>This refers to Max Stirner’s 1844 book, *The Ego and Its Own* (*Der Einzige und sein Eigentum*), a foundational text for individualist anarchism.</note> subjects all ideas that influence practical life to a murderous critique and demonstrates them to be "idols" that only possess power over the "I" insofar as the "I" grants it to them in its own self-doubting weakness. In its witty and pungent manner, it uses striking arguments to crush the ideal aspirations of political, social, and humane liberalism; it shows how, upon the ruins of all these ideas—which have collapsed into the nothingness of their own impotence—only the "I" can remain as the laughing heir. 

If these considerations only intended to substantiate the theoretical claim that I can no more step out of the framework of my "I-ness" than I can jump out of my own skin, then nothing more would need to be added. However, because Stirner claims to have found in the *idea* of the "I" the absolute standpoint for all action, he falls into one of two traps. Either he commits the same error he fought against in other ideas—such as *honor, freedom, right*, and so on—and surrenders himself for better or worse to the tyranny of an *idea* whose absolute sovereignty he acknowledges, not for any specific reasons, but blindly and instinctively; or, he conceives of the "I" not as an *idea* but as a reality. In the latter case, he arrives at nothing more than a completely empty and meaningless tautology: that I can only will my own will, only think my own thoughts, and that only my thoughts can become the motives for my willing—a fact that is just as undeniable for the opponents he attacks as it is for himself. 

But if he means—and this is the only way his conclusion makes sense—that one should recognize the *idea* of the "I" as the sole ruler and allow all other ideas only insofar as they have value for the "I," then he should have first investigated the *idea* of the "I" itself. He would then have discovered, first and foremost, that just as all other ideas are catchwords for instincts pursuing specific goals, the "I" is the catchword of a universal instinct: *egoism*. This egoism relates to specific instincts much like an *all-access pass* <note>original: "passe-partout-Billet," a French term for a master key or universal ticket.</note> relates to daily tickets; many specific instincts are merely outgrowths of egoism in particular cases. While one can get along quite well using egoism alone after proscribing all other instincts, egoism itself can never be entirely dispensed with in life.

<meta>This page continues the critique of Max Stirner’s radical individualism, moving from a theoretical deconstruction of the "I" to the author’s argument that egoism is a source of perpetual suffering. It introduces the "Philosophy of the Unconscious" as the resolution to the problems posed by Stirner’s egoism.</meta>

<page-num>613</page-num>

It is, to be sure, more pardonable to grant this instinct an absolute sovereignty than any other; however, aside from the fact that the error is the same in both cases, the consequences are even worse when one offers exclusive homage to **egoism**. Specifically, other instincts—if they are strong enough—can frequently be satisfied, even if generally only at the cost of total happiness, which they do not make worthwhile; but **egoism**, according to our previous investigations, can never be satisfied, because it always produces a surplus of <term>unpleasure</term> <note>The original term *Unlust* refers to the psychological state of pain, dissatisfaction, or the opposite of pleasure.</note>.

This insight—that from the standpoint of the "I" or the individual, the <term>denial of the will</term> <note>A concept popularized by Arthur Schopenhauer, suggesting that true freedom is found in suppressing the biological urge to live and desire.</note> or renunciation of the world and the relinquishing of life is the only rational procedure—is entirely lacking in Stirner. Yet, it is the surest remedy against the **boastfulness** of the standpoint of the "I." Whoever has once understood the prevailing unpleasure that every individual must endure in life, whether consciously or unconsciously, will soon despise and scorn the standpoint of the "I" that wishes to preserve and enjoy itself—in a word, the "I" that affirms its own existence. Whoever first learns to disregard their own egoism and their "I" will hardly continue to insist upon it as the absolute standpoint by which everything must be governed. Such a person will value personal sacrifices less highly than before and will less reluctantly agree with the result of an investigation that presents the "I" as a mere appearance of a being that is one and the same for all individuals.

Contempt for the world and for life is the easiest path to self-denial; only in this way has a morality of self-denial, such as the Christian and Buddhist ones, become historically possible.

Had Stirner finally approached the direct philosophical investigation of the idea of the "I," he would have seen that this idea is an appearance as devoid of essence, arising in the brain, as perhaps the idea of honor or of right. He would have seen that the only essence which corresponds to the idea of the inner cause of my activity is something **non-individual**, the **All-One Unconscious**, which therefore corresponds just as well to Peter’s idea of his "I" as it does to Paul’s idea of his "I." Upon this very deepest foundation rests only the esoteric—

Once one has firmly and deeply made this insight their own—that one and the same Being feels my pain and yours, my pleasure and yours, only accidentally mediated through different brains—then, and only then, is exclusive egoism broken at its root. Previously, it was only shaken, though deeply so, by a contempt for the world and life. Only then is the Stirnerian standpoint <note>Referring to Max Stirner (1806–1856), a philosopher of radical "egoism" who argued the individual should be the sole center of their own world.</note> finally overcome—a standpoint to which one must have once entirely belonged in order to feel the greatness of this progress. Only then is egoism <term>sublated</term> <note>The German term *aufgehoben* implies that something is simultaneously canceled out, preserved, and lifted to a higher level of meaning.</note> as a moment in consciousness, forming a link in the <term>world-process</term> <note>A central concept in the author's philosophy, viewing history and nature as a singular, unfolding development of the Unconscious.</note> in which it finds its necessary place up to a certain degree.

Indeed, at the end of each of the previous stages of illusion, and before the discovery of the following stage, the voluntary abandonment of individual existence—**suicide**—emerges as a necessary consequence. Both the pagan, weary of life, and the Christian, despairing of both the world and their faith, must logically take their own lives; or, if they believe (as Schopenhauer did) that this means does not achieve the goal of abolishing individual existence <note>Arthur Schopenhauer argued that suicide was futile because it only destroyed the body, while the "Will to Live" remained untouched.</note>, they must at least turn their will away from life in total abstinence or even asceticism.

It is different, however, when an interest in the development of the Whole takes root in the heart and the individual feels themselves to be a member of the Whole—a member who fills a more or less valuable, but never entirely useless, position in the process of the Whole. Then, for the sake of filling this position, it becomes necessary to surrender oneself with a true sacrificial spirit to the life that, from the standpoint of the "I," was discarded not only as a useless good but as a true torment. Then the instinct of egoism is restored anew by **consciousness**, but now no longer as an absolute and sovereign power; rather, it is measured by its **purpose** **for the Whole** and limited by the recognition and respect for the strivings of other individuals who are equally necessary for the process.

Just as egoism is restored as a whole, so too are those drives restored by consciousness which—such as compassion or a sense of fairness—possess a value for the Whole, or which—such as love and honor—possess a...

...growing population of the earth, the number of millions living on the hunger line <note>original: *Hungergrenze* — the bare minimum level of subsistence required to avoid starvation</note> also grows! The increased nutritional yield of the earth, the increased comfort, and the increased luxury together represent the increased **national wealth** or rather **worldly wealth**; however, even this latter cannot be understood as a growth in positive happiness. To one extent, it causes nothing but an increase in population and thus in misery; to another extent, its high esteem is based on the illusion created by the **instinctive acquisitive drive**; to a third extent, its success is a reduction of displeasure and an approximation toward the **zero-point of sensation**, which can never be reached. The only positive benefit of the growth of prosperity is that it frees up forces, which were previously bound in the struggle with necessity, for **intellectual labor**, and that it thereby accelerates the <term>world-process</term> <note>original: *Weltprocess* — a philosophical concept, likely influenced by Eduard von Hartmann, suggesting history is a grand, unfolding movement toward a specific goal, often at the expense of individual happiness</note>. The last great advances of the world which remain for us to consider are the political and social ones. Let us assume the most perfect state were realized, and the population of the earth had solved its political task in a completed manner. What does one have then in this state formation? A snail shell without the snail, an empty form awaiting its fulfillment elsewhere! Humanity does not live to govern itself, but governs itself to be able to *live* (in the highest sense of the word). All the well-known tasks of the state are negative in nature; they are called *protection against*, *security from*, *defense against*, and so on. The achieved "perfect state" does nothing more than place a person where he can begin to live without fear of unauthorized interference—that is, to unfold his powers and abilities in all directions that do not violate the state-claimed rights of others. Thus, even the ideal of the state only places man upon the **construction horizon of his happiness**.

It is no different with **social ideals**. If the ideal goals were achieved, the **zero-point** or **point of indifference** <note>original: *Indifferenzpunct* — a neutral state where one feels neither pleasure nor pain</note> of sensation in relation to these directions of life would be reached; but since ideals remain eternally ideals, and the progress of reality may approach them but can never reach them, the world will never reach the height of the zero-point in this direction of life either, but will always remain stuck below it in a state of prevailing **displeasure** <note>original: *Unlust* — a central term in German pessimistic philosophy referring to a state of pain, discomfort, or general "un-pleasure" that outweighs any positive feeling</note>.

Someone who enters a better life situation will certainly feel *pleasure* during the transition from the worse to the better; but this *pleasure* disappears with astonishing speed. (The transition from the better to the worse, however, produces a much longer-lasting *displeasure*.) It is exactly the same with a nation, and exactly the same with humanity. Who feels better now than they did thirty years ago simply because there are now **railroads**, and back then there were none? And even if older people might still perceive the difference from back then, those born after the creation of the **railroads** certainly do not. <meta>This page continues the author’s argument that progress does not lead to happiness. <page-num>624</page-num>

...discussion, we have seen that **indigenous peoples** <note>original: *Naturvölker* — literally "nature-peoples," a 19th-century term for societies not yet shaped by industrial "civilization"</note> are not more wretched, but **happier** than civilized nations; that the poor, lowly, and unrefined classes are happier than the wealthy, noble, and educated; that the **foolish** are happier than the **clever**; and in general, that a being is all the happier the more dull its nervous system is. This is because the excess of displeasure <note>original: *Unlust* — a key term in this philosophy referring to a state of pain, dissatisfaction, or "un-pleasure" that outweighs any positive feeling</note> over pleasure becomes smaller, and the entrapment in illusion becomes greater. Now, however, with the progressive development of humanity, not only do wealth and needs grow, but also the sensitivity of the nervous system and the capacity and education of the mind. Consequently, there is also an increase in the excess of felt displeasure over felt pleasure and the destruction of illusion—that is, the consciousness of the wretchedness of life, the vanity of most pleasures and endeavors, and the feeling of misery. Thus, **both the misery and the consciousness of misery grow**, as experience shows; the frequently asserted increase in the world’s happiness through the progress of the world rests upon a completely superficial appearance.

(This is especially to be taken to heart by those who perhaps do not agree with me that the sum of displeasure in the world currently outweighs the sum of pleasure.)

Just as the suffering of the world has grown with the development of biological organization from the primordial cell to the emergence of man, so it will continue to grow with the progressive development of the human spirit, until the goal is one day reached. It was a childish shortsightedness when **Rousseau** <note>Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778), the philosopher who famously argued that humanity was happiest in a primitive "state of nature"</note> drew the conclusion from the recognition of growing suffering: the world must, if possible, turn back—back to its childhood! As if the childhood of humanity had not also been misery! No, if one must go backwards, then further, ever further, until before the creation of the world! But we have no choice; we must go **forward**, even if we do not wish to. But it is not the golden age that lies before us, but the iron one <note>In classical mythology, the "Iron Age" was the final, most difficult, and most corrupt era of humanity</note>, and the daydreams of a future golden age prove to be even more futile than those of the past. Just as a burden becomes heavier for its carrier the further he carries it, so too will the suffering of humanity and the consciousness of its misery grow and grow until it becomes unbearable. Just as the individual first lives for the moment as a child, then as a youth dreams of transcendent ideals, then as a man strives for fame and later for possession and practical science, until finally as an old man, recognizing the vanity of all striving, he lays his weary head, longing for peace, to rest—so too does humanity. For do we not see nations arise, ripen, and pass away? Do we not also find in humanity the clearest symptoms of growing older? Why should we doubt that after the vigorous activity of its manhood, an old age will not also one day come for it, where, consuming the practical and theoretical fruits of the past, it enters a period of mature contemplation; where it looks back upon the entirety of the suffering of its past life-course, through which it stormed so wildly, grasping it all at once with wistful mourning, and understands the complete vanity of the previously supposed goals of its striving.

Only one difference exists between it and the individual: elderly humanity will have no heir to whom it can leave its accumulated riches; no children or grandchildren whose love could disturb the clarity of its thinking. Then it will hover, in that sublime melancholy which one usually finds in geniuses or in mentally superior elders, as if it were a transfigured spirit over its own body; and like Oedipus at Colonus <note>In Sophocles' tragedy, the aged Oedipus finds a mystical, final peace and release from his lifelong suffering.</note> in the anticipated peace of non-being, it will feel the sufferings of existence only as something *foreign*, no longer a *suffering*, but only a *compassion* <note>original: *Mitleid* — literally "suffering with," here used to mean a detached pity for one's own former self.</note> with itself. ## XIII.

### The Goal of the World-Process and the Significance of Consciousness.

->**(Transition to Practical Philosophy.)**<-

We had already seen in Chapter C. XI. that the chain of finality <term>Finality (Finalität): The philosophical concept that things happen for a purpose or toward a specific end, rather than just being pushed by random causes.</term> cannot be thought of as infinite, unlike the chain of causality <term>Causality (Causalität): The law of cause and effect, where every event is the result of a prior event.</term>. This is because every purpose in the chain is **only** a means in relation to the following one; therefore, the goal-setting intellect must always have the entire future series of purposes present within it, and yet it is impossible for a completed infinity of purposes to be present there.

Accordingly, the series of goals must be finite—that is, it must have a last or **ultimate purpose** <note>original: "Endzweck." The final justification or destination for all of existence.</note>, which is the target of all intermediate purposes. We also saw in Chapter C. XI. that justice and morality, by their nature, cannot be ultimate purposes, but only intermediate ones; and the previous chapter has taught us that positive happiness <note>original: "Glückseligkeit." Often translated as "bliss" or "beatitude," referring to a state of supreme, lasting contentment.</note> also cannot be the goal of the world-process. This is because happiness is not only never reached at any stage of the process, but its opposite—misery and wretchedness—is reached at all times. Furthermore, this suffering grows throughout the process as illusions are destroyed and consciousness <note>original: "Bewusstsein." In this context, the author argues that as we become more aware and "conscious," we realize how much we are suffering, thus increasing our misery.</note> is heightened. It is entirely meaningless to regard the process as an **end in itself** <note>original: "Selbstzweck." Something that is valuable for its own sake rather than as a tool to reach something else.</note>—that is, to attribute an absolute value to it. After all, the process is only the sum of its moments, and if the individual moments are not only worthless but even reprehensible, then so is their sum: the process. Some might name **freedom** as the goal of the process. For me, freedom is nothing...

...positive, but something privative <note>original: "Privatives." ...impose the greatest sacrifices. Thus, the goal of the world-process must be sought along the path of the **development of consciousness**, and consciousness is undoubtedly the immediate purpose of nature and the world. The question remains open, however, whether consciousness is truly the **ultimate goal** <term>original: "Endzweck." The final, intended result of a process.</term>—and thus an **end in itself** <term>original: "Selbstzweck." Consciousness certainly cannot be an end in itself. It is born in pain, it ekes out its existence in pain, and it buys its own advancement with pain; and what does it offer in exchange for all this? A vain self-reflection! Were the world otherwise beautiful and valuable, one might perhaps tolerate its vain self-complacency in contemplating its own reflection in consciousness, though even then it would remain a weakness. But a world that is thoroughly miserable—one that can never take joy in its own sight but must condemn its existence as soon as it understands itself—should such a world find a rational ultimate goal and end-in-itself in the ideal, illusory doubling of itself in the mirror of consciousness?

Even less can one assume that the purely formal determination of action according to the laws of conscious **Reason** could be a rational ultimate goal. For what does Reason gain by determining action, or what does action gain by being determined by Reason, aside from the potential reduction of **displeasure** <note>original: "Unlust." A technical term in German pessimism referring to the state of dissatisfaction or pain that drives the Will.</note> brought about by it? If painful existence and willing did not exist at all, no Reason would need to be troubled with its determination! 

Therefore, consciousness and its continuous increase in the process of world development can in no way be an end in itself; it, too, can only be a **means to another purpose**. If it were not, it would hang aimlessly in the air—and by extension, the entire process would cease to be an "evolution," and the whole chain of natural purposes would hang aimlessly, their status as purposes effectively nullified...

Now, however, since consciousness is the immediate purpose of nature or the world; since we necessarily require a further purpose for consciousness and can absolutely conceive of no other ultimate end than the greatest possible happiness; since, on the other hand, all striving after **positive** happiness—which is identical with willing—is perverse because it only achieves misery, and the greatest possible attainable state of happiness is the absence of pain; and since, finally, it lies within the very concept of consciousness to have the emancipation of the intellect from the will, and the combatting and final destruction of willing as its result: should it then still be possible to doubt that the all-knowing Unconscious, which thinks of purpose and means as one, created consciousness for the sole purpose of **redeeming the Will from the misery of its willing,** from which it cannot redeem itself? Is it not clear that the **ultimate goal of the world-process, which consciousness serves as the final means, is to realize the greatest possible attainable state of happiness, namely that of the absence of pain?**

We have seen that in the existing world everything is arranged in the wisest and best way, and that it may be regarded as the best of all possible worlds; yet, despite this, it is thoroughly wretched and worse than no world at all. This can only be understood (compare the conclusion of Chapter C. This consideration is, moreover, merely the same principle applied to the world as a whole that we have long known when applied to the individual. The physical atom is a force of attraction; its "what and how"—that is, the attraction according to such and such a law—is representation <term>representation: (German: *Vorstellung*) the mental or logical blueprint of how a thing functions.</term>, while its "that," its existence, its reality, its force, is Will. Thus the world is also what it is and how it is as a representation of the Unconscious; and this unconscious representation, as the servant of the Will to which it owes its own actual existence and against which it has no independence, also has no counsel or voice regarding the "that" (the existence) of the world. The main difficulty lies in how the ultimate end of this struggle is to be conceived: the final redemption from the misery of willing and existence toward the painlessness of non-willing and non-being—in short, the complete <term>abolition: (*Aufhebung*) the negation or cessation</term> of willing through consciousness. The core of this theory consists in the assumption that the individual, by virtue of individual knowledge of the misery of existence and the irrationality of willing, is capable of causing their individual willing to cease, and thereby falling prey to *individual annihilation* after death, or, as Buddhism expresses it, no longer being reborn. It is obvious that this assumption is completely incompatible with Schopenhauer's fundamental principles—

<meta>This page continues the critique of Arthur Schopenhauer’s philosophy, specifically addressing his failure to account for "development" or evolution in his system. It follows the previous page's introduction of the problem: how can the conscious mind truly abolish the universal "Will to live"?</meta>

...is obvious, and only his pervasive inability to grasp the concept of development makes understandable the short-sightedness which made it impossible for him to overcome this blatant inconsistency in his system. This inconsistency must be briefly demonstrated here. To him, the Will is the <note>original: ἓν καὶ πᾶν</note> One and All, the All-One Essence of the world, and the individual is merely subjective appearance—not even an objectively real manifestation of this Essence. But even if it were the latter, how should the individual possess the possibility of denying his individual will as a whole—not merely theoretically, but also practically—given that his individual willing is, after all, only a ray of that All-One Will? Schopenhauer himself rightly explains that the negation of the Will is not achieved through suicide, but in *voluntary starvation* it is supposedly achieved to the highest conceivable degree. This sounds almost ridiculous when one considers his statement alongside it: “that the body is the Will itself, perceived objectively as a spatial appearance,” from which it follows directly that with the <term>abolition: (*Aufhebung*) the cessation or negation</term> of the individual will, its spatial appearance—the body—must also *disappear*. According to our view, at the very least, with the abolition of the individual will, all organic functions dependent on the unconscious will, such as heartbeat, breathing, and so on, would have to cease momentarily and the body would collapse as a corpse. No one will doubt that even this is empirically impossible; but whoever must first kill his body *through the refusal of food* proves by that very act that he *is not capable* of denying and *abolishing* his unconscious will to live.

But even setting the impossible as possible, what would be the consequence? One of the many rays of the One Will—the one relating to this individual—would be withdrawn from its actuality, and this person would have died. **This, however, is no more and no less than what happens in every case of death**, regardless of the cause from which it arose, and the All-One Will now finds itself in no different a situation than if a roof tile had struck that man dead; it continues as before to seize life wherever it finds it and can seize it; for it cannot, after all, gain experience and become wiser through experience. For if the goal lay at an infinite distance in time, then no matter how long the finite duration of the process lasted, it would not have come a single step closer to the goal, which would remain infinitely far away. The process would then no longer be a means to reach the goal; consequently, it would be pointless and aimless. Just as it would be incompatible with the concept of **development** to ascribe an infinite duration to the world-process in the past—because then every conceivable development would already have had to be completed, which is clearly not the case—we can just as little grant the process an infinite duration for the future. This much is certain: wherever the process may reach its conclusion, the goal of the process and the struggling forces will always be the same in this world. Schopenhauer does not hesitate to declare man equal to the task, but he is only so decisive because he conceives of the task **individually**, whereas we must conceive of it **universally**, where it naturally requires entirely different conditions which we shall soon consider more closely. Be that as it may, in the world known to us, we are the first-born of the spirit and must fight honestly; if the victory does not succeed, it is not our fault. But if we were capable of victory and failed to achieve it only out of sluggishness, then we—that is, the world-essence, which we also are—would have to bear the **torment of existence** for that much longer as an immanent punishment. Therefore, move briskly forward in the world-process as workers...

The **third** condition is a sufficient communication among the Earth’s population to allow for a simultaneous, collective decision. In this point, the fulfillment of which depends only on the perfection and more skillful application of technical inventions, the imagination has free rein.

Assuming these conditions are met, the possibility exists that the majority of the spirit active in the world will decide to negate <term>Negate: To nullify or cancel out. Hartmann uses the word "aufheben," a philosophical term for ending something while simultaneously transitioning to a new state.</term> its willing. The only remaining question is whether this decision can achieve the desired success. To decide this, we must return to our knowledge of the nature of willing and motivation. (Compare Chapter B. XI. beginning and section 4.)

There is no doubt that a specific act of willing in a human—a desire, affect, or passion—can, under certain circumstances, be negated for the specific case in question through the influence of conscious reason. If, for example, I strive for honor through a deed or a work, and reason tells me that those whose recognition I crave are fools and simpletons, then this insight—if it is convincing and powerful enough—will be able to negate my ambition, at least in this instance. However, all psychologists agree that such a negation should not be thought of as a direct influence of reason upon the desire to be negated. Instead, it works only indirectly through motivation or the arousal of an opposingly directed desire, which then enters into a collision with the first; the result is that both are paralyzed to zero.

The negation of the positive world-will, which Schopenhauer calls the **"will to live"** <note>original: "Wille zum Leben"</note>, can only be conceived in this same way. Conscious knowledge cannot diminish or negate the will directly; it can only arouse an opposingly directed—and thus **negative**—will, which reduces the positive will by the degree of its own strength. According to this, Schopenhauer’s doctrine of the **"quietive"** <term>Quietive: In Schopenhauer's philosophy, the "quietive of the will" is a state where deep insight into the suffering of existence causes the will to stop wanting anything at all.</term> of willing is entirely inadmissible. He claimed this quietive exists in an entirely different mode of knowledge, before which motives are supposed to become ineffective, and that it represents the only possible case of an intervention of **"transcendental freedom"** <note>original: "transcendente Freiheit"; refers to a freedom that exists beyond the physical world of cause and effect</note> of the will into the world of appearances.

# XIV.

## The Final Principles.

---

In our investigations so far, we have repeatedly encountered two principles, **Will** and **Representation**, without the assumption of which nothing at all can be explained. These are principles—that is, original elements—precisely because any attempt to decompose them into simpler elements appears hopeless to us from the outset. Furthermore, we have nowhere required any principles other than these two for our explanations; we have recognized those things that are otherwise often treated as principles—namely, feeling or sensation and consciousness—as consequential phenomena <note>original: *Folgeerscheinungen*; effects or secondary results that arise from primary causes.</note> of our two principles.

As for our concepts of these principles, we have proceeded here in a purely empirical and inductive manner. We initially assumed them in the way they are grasped by natural common sense, which is formed by the <term>Leading-strings of the German language: An idiom suggesting that our initial understanding of concepts is often guided or limited by the vocabulary and structures of our native tongue.</term>, and we then modified, expanded, and restricted them according to the requirements of the scientific explanation of facts. If, according to our results, these two principles are sufficient to explain the phenomena presented to us in the known world, then they form the apex of the **pyramid of inductive knowledge**. It only remains for us to take one last look at this climbed summit at the conclusion, whereby a comparison with the ultimate principles of existing philosophical systems should also be of interest. This chapter therefore forms the direct continuation of Chapters A. IV., C. I., and VII., the contents of which I ask the kind reader to first call to mind.

To the reader without philosophical training, perhaps

the reflections of this chapter may, in and of themselves, be the least interesting, because more than all the preceding ones, they lose themselves in the dissection of concepts <note>original: *Zergliederung von Begriffen*; the analytical breakdown of complex ideas into their simplest components.</note> that reach the ultimate limits of abstraction and of our understanding in general. However, on the one hand, the relationship of my standpoint to the systems of the most important philosophers—only briefly suggested here—and on the other hand, the stricter discussion of the concepts whose meaning and mutual relations have hitherto been largely assumed, should be attractive enough for the reader who has followed the preceding parts with interest. This is due to the light these discussions cast back upon many points previously left in darkness, making it worthwhile not to leave even this concluding chapter unread.

If one measures the value of scientific results solely by the degree of their certainty or security, then their value undoubtedly becomes smaller the further they move from the ground of the facts to be explained, because their probability becomes smaller; the value that the apex of the **pyramid of knowledge** <term>Pyramid of Knowledge: A metaphor for a logical structure where broad empirical facts form the base and the singular, most abstract governing principles form the peak.</term> could claim would then be the smallest. However, in determining value, other elements besides the mere degree of probability should probably be taken into account, which can be summarized as the degree of importance these results would have compared to other objects of knowledge, assuming they were all grasped with a probability of 1—that is, with absolute certainty. Regarding this factor, the value of the apex of the knowledge pyramid clearly rises above all other possible objects of knowledge. Therefore, I will not grow weary of contributing my mite <note>original: *Scherflein*; a reference to the "widow's mite," signifying a small but humble and sincere contribution to a larger cause.</note> toward a better determination of the final metaphysical principles, hoping that another will soon come who can take it further than I. On the other hand, I hope that my successors will find the foundation of the pyramid built by me well and firmly enough to continue building upon it, and will have no reason to tear it down in any essential parts.

Plato’s <note>See the exemplary presentation of Platonic principles in: Zeller, *Philosophy of the Greeks*, 2nd ed., Vol. II. 1., pp. 441 to 471.</note> best-known and most important principle is the **Platonic Idea**. This is why he also calls it **relatively non-being** <note>original: *μὴ ὄν* (me on)</note>. Yet, it is this principle that takes the Ideas into itself as its content and introduces them into the whirlpool of the process. While the Idea is the measured and self-contained, this second principle is the measureless and the **unlimited** <note>original: *ἄπειron* (apeiron)</note>. While the Idea (even as a Number) is determined only qualitatively, the second principle brings the quantitative into appearance; to it belongs "everything that is capable of more or less, stronger or weaker, and excess," which is why Plato also calls it the "**Great and the Small**."

While the Idea is the **Good**, and everything good in the world originates from it, that "unlimited" <note>original: *ἄπειron*</note> is **Evil**. <meta>This page continues the comparison between different philosophical systems, specifically contrasting Arthur Schopenhauer’s "blind Will" with G.W.F. Hegel’s "rational Idea." The previous page discussed how Plato’s philosophy mirrors the author’s own theories on the Unconscious.</meta>

It also requires a strange kind of limitation to find satisfaction in absolute *stupidity* and its poverty as a principle; hence the amateurish quality that *Schopenhauer’s philosophizing* possesses, despite all its wealth of spirit.

On the other hand, one cannot sufficiently admire and praise the *wisdom of the Unconscious* for creating such a *narrow-minded genius* to show posterity what can and cannot be done with that principle in its isolation. The one-sided development of this principle was just as necessary in the genetic developmental path of philosophy as the sharpening of the opposite extreme in *Hegel*.

How closely both philosophies are connected can be proven by the accidental circumstance that the main works of both philosophers appeared in the year 1818, especially if one simultaneously recalls the statement by Hegel (Vol. 15, p. 619):

> “Where several philosophies appear simultaneously, they are distinct sides that constitute a totality which underlies them.”

Just as certainly as Schopenhauer was unable to grasp Hegel, so must Hegel—if he knew of him at all—have shrugged his shoulders at Schopenhauer. Both stood so far apart that they lacked any point of contact for mutual appreciation.

While Kant’s criticism had to reject any attempt at a theoretical metaphysics and only *Fichte* began the positive metaphysical development of modern philosophy with the dialectical <note>referring to a method of argument that resolves contradictions between opposing ideas</note> treatment of self-consciousness, *Hegel* draws the sum total of this development up to the first third of the century. He did this by adopting the principle from *Schelling* that had, until then, been its more or less unconscious driving force: the Idea alone is the essence of the world. Logic is therefore *ontology* <note>the philosophical study of the nature of being or existence</note>; the dialectical self-movement of the concept is the *world-process*. Compared to the complete poverty of Schopenhauer’s principle, this principle is the absolutely rich one, for everything the world is, it is through the Idea. Something could actually be done with it, and it is no wonder that it produced four systems, while its counterpart exhausted itself in one.

> "Knowledge knows not only itself, but also the *negative* of *itself*, or its limit."

In the *Logic* <note>Referring to Hegel’s *Science of Logic*, a foundational text of his system.</note> Volume 2, page 400, he further states: "Because the pure Idea of knowing is, to that extent, enclosed within subjectivity, it is a **drive to abolish this.**" Here he even senses that the act of going beyond the Idea can only be a matter of the Will. However, the thought that this "willing of the Idea to step out of itself" could come from the Idea itself—from the eternal rest of its <term>Being-for-itself: a state of being where something is self-contained and self-aware</term>—is entirely impossible. Such a state must rather be equated with an absolutely self-sufficient **peace**, an unclouded, self-enclosed **satisfaction**.

Not only would it be **incomprehensible** how the Idea could, by its own impulse, come to plunge its eternal clarity into the whirlpool of the real process; it would be shockingly absurd if the Idea—which encompasses all knowledge—were to sacrifice its blessed peace of timeless, eternal silence without any external necessity, only to fall prey to the torment of the process, the misery of willing, and the wretchedness of real existence. No, absolute Reason itself cannot suddenly become unreasonable; rather, the "unreasonable" must be a **second** or **other** thing lying outside of Reason.

If it lay within the nature of the Logical to transition into the Unlogical by itself, then this occurrence would be a necessary and eternal one, and there could never be any talk of a conclusion to the process or of a "salvation" <note>In this context, "salvation" or "redemption" refers to the philosophical goal of resolving the conflict between the mind and the material world.</note>.

Furthermore, it is only the negative, relative definition of that "opposite of the Idea"—namely, its relation to the logical Idea—to be called "the Unlogical." Its positive definition, however, is to be the principle of change, the origin of reality: the **Will**. When Hegel suddenly throws in this definition of being a "drive" in the passage above, it is quite clear that he has fetched it purely from the empirical need to explain the reality of Nature.

This is indeed the only possible way to arrive at the knowledge of the Will. Through <term>prior reasoning: known as *a priori*, or knowledge gained independent of experience</term>, one can at most recognize the Idea and everything that follows from it; however, the existence of the Will can only be inferred <term>after the fact: known as *a posteriori*, or knowledge derived from observed experience</term>. For all *a priori*, purely logical, or purely rational philosophy can only recognize ideal relationships, but not real existen— <note>original: "existen-"; the text cuts off mid-word "existenzen" (existences) at the end of the page.</note>

This corresponds exactly to the relationship where the Idea determines only the "**What**" of things <note>The "What" refers to the essence or nature of a thing—its definition.</note>, while the Will determines their "**That**" <note>The "That" refers to the "facticity" or the sheer reality that a thing exists at all.</note>; thus, the Idea can only comprehend things insofar as it determines them, and therefore can never grasp their *real existence*.

This necessary step in philosophy, which Hegel was unable to take, was carried out by Schelling\*) in his final system. As already hinted at in Chapter C. VII., Schelling recognized the purely logical character of previous philosophy, declared it to be <term>Negative Philosophy: a system that deals with the realm of pure possibility and rational concepts but cannot prove existence</term>, and, in opposition to it, raised the demand for a <term>Positive Philosophy: a system that begins with actual existence and experience rather than pure reason</term> beginning from a "pre-reflective Being" that can only be recognized through experience (cf. Insofar as Schelling’s deductions are critical and preparatory, they are excellent; however, as soon as he begins to present his positive philosophy itself, he becomes weak. He wavers between an explanatory, reasoning-based procedure, a dialectical method, and a peculiar, unmotivated bursting forth with newly introduced primary concepts, only to soon lose himself in the shallows of a mystical <term>theogony: an account of the origin or genealogy of gods or divine principles</term> and the details of Christian theology. This is quite simply because, for the sake of his past and his habits, he becomes unfaithful to his own better insight: that the principle of positive philosophy can only be gained *a posteriori* <note>original: "a posteriori" — Latin for "from what comes after," meaning knowledge gained through observation and experience rather than through pure reason alone.</note> from experience, and thus **on an inductive path**.

[Because Schopenhauer proceeds mainly **inductively** in his principal works (e.g., *The World as Will and Representation*, Book 2, and *On the Will in Nature*), he achieves so much more in this task, even though he is not particularly clear about his own method and why it is the only correct one.]

<meta>This page continues the transition from the critique of Hegel to the appraisal of Schelling's later "Positive Philosophy." Nonetheless, Schelling's final system (the unity of positive and negative philosophy) possesses a high value in that it synthesizes the principle of Hegel (the Idea) and that of Schopenhauer (the Will) as coordinated, equally valid, and equally indispensable sides of a single Principle (cf.
