Schelling recognizes in that "extra-logical nature of existence" (II. 3, 95), in that "unfathomable basis of reality" (I. 7, 360), with full decisiveness, the **Will**. **That** something is can only be recognized by the resistance it offers, but the only thing capable of resistance is the **Will** (II. 3, 206). It is the **Will**, therefore, which lends to the entire world and to every individual thing its **existence** <note>original: "Dass" (literally "the that")—the fact that a thing exists at all, its reality.</note>; the Idea can only determine its **essence** <note>original: "Was" (literally "the what")—the nature or definition of the thing.</note>. Already in his treatise on the essence of human freedom, which appeared in 1809 (thus long before Schopenhauer’s writings), he said (Works I. 7. p. 350): "In the highest and final instance, there is no other Being at all than **Willing**. **Willing** is **Primal Being** <note>original: "Ursein"</note>, and all its predicates apply to this alone: groundlessness, eternity, independence from time, self-affirmation. All philosophy strives only toward finding this highest expression." And in his "anthropological schema" (I. 10. p. 289) one finds: "I. **Will**, the actual spiritual substance of man, the ground of everything, the original generator of matter, the **only thing** in man that **is the cause of Being.**"

In contrast to this, he explains in the same passage that the **Understanding** is "not the creator, but the **regulator**, the **limiter**, that which **gives measure** to the infinite, boundless will."

This corresponds exactly to the principles of the Pythagoreans: the unlimited <note>original: ἄπειρον (apeiron)</note>, and the limiting <note>original: περαῖνον (perainon)</note> or form-giving <note>original: εἰδοποιοῦν (eidopoion)</note> (I. 10, 243). However, the word of this longing is **Representation** <note>original: "Vorstellung"—the mental act of placing an object before the mind; the "What" of things</note>,—that representation which is simultaneously the understanding (I. 7, 361), or "the ideal principle" (I. 7, 395). <meta>This page continues the discussion of Schelling’s "Positive Philosophy," specifically focusing on how he defines the "Will" and the "Idea" as the two foundational principles of existence. In his later accounts, Schelling endeavors to derive these principles from the concept of "that which is" <note>original: "des Seienden"</note> as its necessary components—an undertaking that reveals its lack of productivity in that every actual progress is only gained by reinstating concrete definitions. Here, the <term>potential for existing</term> <note>original: "Seinkönnende" or *potentia existendi*—the capacity or power to transition into being.</note> corresponds to the **Will**, while the "purely Being" (that is, without potential, existing ideally) corresponds to the **Idea**. Regarding the potential for existing, he says (Volume II, Part 3, pp. 205—206):

> "But the potential for existing of which we speak here is not a conditioned one; it is the unconditional **potential for existing** <note>original: *potentia existendi*</note>; it is that which can pass **from potentiality to actuality** <note>original: *a potentia ad actum*</note> unconditionally and without further mediation. Now, however, we know of no other transition **from potentiality to actuality** than in the act of Willing. The Will in itself is the **pre-eminent** <note>original: *κατ' ἐξοχήν*</note> potential; Willing is the **pre-eminent** act. The transition **from potentiality to actuality** is everywhere only a transition from non-willing to willing. Thus, that which is immediately capable of being is that which, in order to be, requires nothing more than to pass from non-willing to willing. Its being consists precisely in willing; in its being, it is nothing other than willing. No actual being is thinkable without an actual willing, however specifically modified it may be." — The potential for existing is the Will in itself—the not-yet-objective, but rather the **primordial** <note>original: "urständliche"</note> Will, which can indeed will (otherwise it would not be Will), but simply does not yet will; the Will before its expression (II. 3, pp. 212 to 213).

If this Will "ignites" into active willing, it thereby surrenders its freedom—its ability to also *not* be—and falls into "blind being," much like Spinoza’s substance. As such, it becomes the "sinister," the "source of all indignation and displeasure" (II. 3, 226).

The "purely Being," or the Idea, is neither potential nor act, for "act" is only that which arises from potential; Schelling calls its state **pure act** <note>original: *actus purus*—a theological term for a being with no unrealized potential, traditionally applied to God.</note>. I note here that for the sake of the Christian **Trinity** <note>original: "Dreieinigkeit"</note>, Schelling endeavors to turn his principles and their substantial unity into Persons, and for that purpose ascribes a unique Will to each of the three, which is entirely wrong-headed. So that one may [understand] this wrong-headedness...

<meta>This page continues the argument that the "Real" is defined by "Willing." It builds on the previous page's comparison of metaphysical systems by applying these principles to the physical world and the nature of "matter."</meta>

...dead products can be associated with a clear concept; however, after substance has been recognized by us as a chimera <note>An illusion or fabrication of the mind.</note>, matter as a system of atomic forces, and the material world as an unstable, constantly changing *state of equilibrium* of many intersecting *volitional activities*, every reason to assume the existence of dead remains of earlier productivity disappears. We now recognize the real in every *moment* of the process as a present *volitional activity*, and thus the existence of the world as a continuous *act of creation*. This is likely also the meaning of the "second corollary" at the beginning of Schelling’s <note>Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854) was a central figure in German Idealism.</note> *Philosophy of Nature* (Works I. 3, p. 16):

> "Nature exists as a product nowhere; all individual products in nature are apparent products, not the absolute product, in which the absolute activity exhausts itself, and which is always becoming and never is."

This view by no means contradicts—as it might appear at first glance—the physical principle that the effect of a cause, once acting, persists; for the newly brought about state in which the physical effect consists (e.g., a movement of such and such direction and speed) does indeed persist, provided that the object persists whose state it is—that is, provided that this object is continuously <term>re-posited</term> <note>In this philosophical context, to "posit" (setzen) means to be actively brought into existence or established by a fundamental force or will.</note>.

It is connected to this view of the world’s existence as a continuous *act of creation* that we can no longer consider willing as separate from the *deed*; the willing is itself the *deed*.

This truth can be illustrated most clearly in the <term>atomic will</term> <note>The theory that even the smallest particles of matter possess a fundamental form of "will" or driving force.</note>, as explained in Chapters C. 2) Only willing that is directed toward the *present* is identical with the *deed*; willing directed toward the *future*, however, is not a true categorical willing at all, but only a hypothetical willing—a resolution or an intention.

3) In psychology, a *deed* is understood only as an action of the whole person, not as those movements of brain molecules caused by the will which are not strong enough in themselves to bring about an external action of the body, or which are prevented from doing so by other brain oscillations acting in the opposite direction.

Therefore, in psychology, it is indeed only the *entire* present willing of the individual—that is, the <term>resultant</term> <note>A term borrowed from physics, referring to a single force that is the equivalent of two or more individual forces acting together.</note> of all their simultaneous individual wills or desires—that is identical with the deed. Meanwhile, the simultaneous components exhaust their effectiveness against one another within the brain, insofar as they do not become a deed within that resultant. Strictly speaking, however, even the movement of brain molecules is an entry of the will into external effectiveness—that is, a deed. In this sense, every single desire within the individual is also a deed, though it may perhaps be hindered by other brain oscillations from realizing itself to its full potential extent. For example, hunger produces brain oscillations in a beggar that would compel him to stretch out his hand for the bread in the bakery; the fear of theft produces other brain oscillations which prevent the deed of this limb movement. Both, however—the positive as well as the negative desire—express themselves in the deed as brain oscillations.

> "The *Will* in itself is the *potentiality* par excellence, *Willing* is the *actuality* par excellence." <note>Original: "Der *Wille* an sich ist die *Potenz* κατ’ ἐξοχήν, das *Wollen* der *Actus* κατ’ ἐξοχήν." <meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the Will and the mind's internal images or "representations." ...determination; that is, that willing must have a representation <note>original: "Vorstellung"; the mental image or concept of something that the mind "places before" itself.</note> as its content.

On the other hand, we know from Chapter C. Thus, only the Will can grant the representation existence. Here, however, we find ourselves in a circle: willing is supposed to become existential only through the representation, and the representation only through the will. Surely no effect (action) can be exerted upon the representation by the will "in itself"—that is, insofar as it is mere potency and not "actual" <note>original: "actuell"; in the sense of being active or realized in the world.</note>. If, then, on one hand, the will as mere potency cannot act at all (and thus cannot act upon the representation), and if, on the other hand, willing as a true act <note>original: "Actus"</note> only becomes existential **through** the representation, and yet the representation cannot become existential of its own accord, only one assumption remains: that the will acts upon the representation in a middle state. This state behaves **already as an act** in relation to the potential will, but **still as potency** in relation to the true, actualized will; it is therefore not yet existential in the sense of that specific act. Such a middle state is **empty willing**.

The philosopher Friedrich Schelling also recognizes this **empty willing**; he says (Volume II. 1. Page 462): "But now a distinction forces itself upon us that is important for the entire sequence—the distinction between the willing that is essentially objectless, which only wills itself (= **craving** <note>original: "Sucht"; can also mean addiction or an obsessive drive.</note>), and the willing that now possesses itself and remains as the product of that first willing."

**Empty willing** does not yet "exist," for it still lies before that actuality and reality which we are accustomed to comprise under the predicate of "Being." However, it no longer merely "essences" <note>original: "weset"; a philosophical term meaning to exist in a latent, essential, or internal way without being fully manifested.</note> either, like the will "in itself" as pure potency, for it is already a consequence of that potency and thus relates to it as an act. If we wish to apply the correct predicate, we can only say: **empty willing becomes**. Here, "becoming" is used in that eminent sense where it signifies not a transition from one form to another, but from absolute **non-being** (**pure essence**) into **being**. **Empty willing** is the **struggle for existence**, which can only reach existence when...

If the Will in itself is the Will capable of willing (consequently also capable of not-willing, or <note>original Latin: "velle et nolle potens"</note> *capable of both willing and not-willing*), then the "empty willing" is the Will that has decided to will (thus it can no longer *not* will). It is the Will that wants to will, but now cannot will—more precisely: a Will unable to will (<note>original Latin: "velle volens, sed velle non potens"</note> *willing to will, but not capable of willing*) until the representation <note>The mental image or concept of an object.</note> is added, which it then can will.

The empty willing is therefore "actual" <note>In the sense of being active or in motion.</note> insofar as it struggles for its realization, but it is not actual insofar as it cannot achieve this realization through itself without the addition of an external circumstance. As a empty **Form**, it can only become truly existential once it has attained its **Fulfillment**; however, it cannot find this fulfillment within itself, because it is merely **Form** and nothing more. Thus, while the striving of a "specific willing" aims at the realization of its **Content** (asserting itself against opposing strivings), the striving of empty willing has no other goal than to realize itself—to realize itself as **Form**, to get **hold** of itself, to come to Being, or what is the same thing, to **Willing**; that is, **to come to itself**.

No other striving than this—in which the **pure form itself constitutes the content or the goal**—can even be imagined in the absolutely representation-less and mindless <note>original: "dummen," literally "stupid" or "dumb"; here referring to the Will's lack of intellectual direction.</note> Will. Thus, it remains a perpetual **run-up** without ever reaching the **leap**; it remains a **Becoming** from which nothing becomes, from which nothing results. This **willing-to-Will** yearns for **fulfillment**, and yet the form of willing cannot be realized until it has grasped a content; but as soon as it has done this, the willing is no longer **empty willing**, no longer **willing-to-Will**, but rather **specific willing**, a **willing-something**. The state of empty willing before its fulfillment is thus an eternal yearning for a fulfillment that can only be given to it through the representation; that is, it is absolute **misery** <note>original: "Unseligkeit"; a state of being "un-blessed" or in deep existential distress.</note>, torment without pleasure, even without pause. The reader should recall that, according to Chapter C. III., every non-satisfaction of a will *by that very fact* generates **consciousness**.

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical discussion regarding the "Potentiality" of the Will. The previous page ended by suggesting that because the Unconscious has no memory, the world-process could theoretically repeat itself, and the author was beginning to calculate the probability of such a recurrence.</meta>

absolute freedom is conceivable. Freedom and chance, as absolute concepts—that is, stripped of their relations—are identical. Schelling conceives of the relationship in a similar way when he says (II. 1, p. 464):

> “Willing, which for us is the beginning of another world set outside the Idea... is the primordial-contingent, the primordial chance itself.” <note>Original: "Das Wollen, das für uns der Anfang einer anderen, ausser der Idee gesetzten Welt ist .... ist das Urzufällige, der Urzufall selbst." Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling (1775–1854) was a major figure in German Idealism.</note>

If the <term>Potentiality|Potenz; the latent power or capacity of the Will to act before it actually does so.</term> were temporal, then, since time is infinite, the probability would be = 1—that is, it would be a certainty—that the Potentiality would eventually decide once again in favor of the <term>Act|Actus; the state of being active or realized, as opposed to mere potential.</term>. However, since Potentiality stands outside of time (which is only created by the Act), and since this extra-temporal eternity differs in nothing from a single moment when viewed in a temporal relation (just as large and small differ in nothing in regards to color), the probability that the Potentiality determines itself toward Willing in its extra-temporal eternity is equal to the probability that it determines itself to do so in a single moment: that is, 1/2. <note>The author is using a mathematical analogy: in the void before time, the "choice" to create a world or not is a 50/50 coin toss.</note> From this it follows that the redemption from Willing cannot be regarded as final; rather, it only reduces the torment of Willing and Being from a probability of 1 (which it possesses during the world-process) to a probability of 1/2. This nonetheless provides a gain that is not to be despised for practical purposes.

Naturally, the probability of what happens in the future cannot be influenced by the past; thus, the probability coefficient of 1/2 for the re-emergence of Willing from Potentiality is not diminished by the fact that it had already decided once before in favor of Willing. However, if one considers *a priori* <note>from theoretical deduction rather than from observation</note> the probability that the emergence of Willing from Potentiality repeats itself along with the entire <term>world-process|Weltprocess; the collective history and development of the universe.</term> *n* number of times, then this is obviously = 1/2^*n*, just like the *a priori* probability of tossing a coin "heads up" *n* times in a row.

Specifically, since time ceases with the end of a world-process, there has been no "pause" until the beginning of the next one; rather, the matter is exactly as if the Potentiality, at the moment of the annihilation of its previous Act, had anew externalized itself into an Act. It is clear, however, that the probability 1/2^*n* becomes so small as *n* increases that it is practically sufficient for one's peace of mind. —

<meta>This page continues the transition from discussing the "Will" and its potentiality to the second major aspect of the author's system: "Representation" (Vorstellung). Let us now move on to the other form of existence, **Representation**, and consider first of all its relationship to the Platonic Idea.

Aristotle calls the Platonic Ideas *essences* <note>original: "οὐσίαι" (ousiai). In Greek philosophy, this term refers to the fundamental substance or "being-ness" of a thing.</note>, an expression which Plato himself, to our knowledge, never used. In any case, for Aristotle it means something quite different from what we now understand by "substance," and would most likely be translated as "**essences**." For Plato himself, one can hardly claim more than that he conceived of the Ideas as objective existences, and denied that they existed only in the soul or that they were merely the knowledge of a person. He likely went no further in discussing their nature, but contented himself with setting them up—in contrast to the transient flux of the sensory world—as that which truly is <note>original: "ὄντως ὄν" (ontos on); the ultimate reality behind appearances.</note>, as that which is in and for itself <note>original: "ὄν αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτό" (on auto kath’ auto).</note>, and as the unchangeable, which "never in any way or manner admits of any change" <note>original: "οὐδέποτε οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς ἀλλοίωσιν οὐδεμίαν ἐνδεχόμενον" (oudepote oudamē oudamōs alloiōsin oudemian endechomenon). A famous definition of the eternal from Plato's *Phaedo*.</note>. While Aristotle defines this more closely by calling the Ideas *essences*, the later Platonists and the Neoplatonic school understood it to mean that the Ideas were **eternal thoughts of the Godhead**.

To Plato himself, both interpretations were likely equally close. For even if the eternal thoughts of the Godhead cannot be substances in the modern sense, it is by no means a contradiction to call them *essences* in the Aristotelian sense precisely because they are **eternal thoughts of the Godhead**, and thus possess an essence that remains eternally the same.

Admittedly, Plato would never have conceded that they were a form of **knowledge**, or that they were **conscious** thoughts of the Godhead, for that would have completely robbed them of their objectivity, which was the main point for him. When Plato identifies the Idea with divine reason, this can also be understood as him having—with a very understandable poetic license—identified the essence with its sole eternal activity.

It stands to reason, then, that one should understand the Platonic Ideas as **eternal, unconscious thoughts** (of an impersonal being), where "eternal" expresses not an infinite duration, but a state of being outside of time, sublime above all time. For us, too, the unconscious representation is an extra-temporal, unconscious, intuitive thought, which stands in opposition to consciousness—

We see here the two elements from which **causality** is composed. That the stone I now release falls is due to the continuation of the Willing beyond this moment; but that it falls, and specifically falls with such-and-such a speed, is because it is logical for it to be so, and would be illogical if it were otherwise. That anything happens at all—that the effect takes place—is due to the Will; that the effect, when it takes place, occurs with necessity as *this* specific effect and no other, is due to **the Logical**. <note>The author uses "the Logical" (*das Logische*) to refer to the rational, ideal structure that directs the raw energy of the Will.</note> That the cause is indirectly the determinant for the effect is quite clear, for only under these specific conditions, which we summarize under the term "cause," is it logical that this effect should follow.

Hereby, causality is understood as logical necessity which receives reality through the Will.

Now that we have recognized **purpose** as the positive side of the Logical, we may henceforth unconditionally subscribe to the proposition of Leibniz: "efficient causes depend on final causes..." <note>original Latin: "causae efficientes pendent a causis [finalibus]". That need is quite undeniable. If **will and representation** were separate substances, it would be much harder to believe in an **interaction** between them; it would no longer be clear how the one should enter into a relationship with the other, how the **will** could seize the **logical** as its content, or how the **logical** could find cause to react against an **unlogical** <note>original: "Unlogisches"</note> that is entirely foreign to it and does not concern it at all, and its irrational actions. Meanwhile, these relationships are understood quite naturally if it is one and the same **essence** which is both of these—that is, the essence of which and in which they are **attributes**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on metaphysical unity. The previous page explored how Hegel and Schelling define "Substance"—the core reality—and how the Idea (logic) relates to existence. The **monism** <note>The philosophical view that all of reality is made of one single substance or principle.</note> toward which, as we have seen, everything strives, would thereby be absolutely abolished and a pure **dualism** <note>A system that recognizes two independent principles, like good and evil or mind and body.</note> set in its place. VII.—set aside, in that we have recognized it as a **dualism** only of **attributes**, which does not impair the unity of the substance, but which is impossible to do without where a **process** <note>In this context, "process" refers to the dynamic unfolding of reality or history.</note> is to be explained; for the **process** requires, first, something that "ought not to be," and second, another thing which fights against this "not-ought-to-be."

As early as **Plato**, in the *Parmenides*, he seeks to demonstrate that the **One** is not thinkable without an **immanent multiplicity** and that **multiplicity** is not thinkable without a **One that encompasses it**. In exactly the same way as we do, **Schelling** conceives of **dualism** within **monism** (Works II. 3, p. 218):

> “The **identity** must rather be taken in the strictest sense as **substantial identity**. The meaning is not that the **being-able-to-be** <term>Being-able-to-be (Seinkönnende): Schelling’s term for pure potentiality or the power to exist.</term> and the **purely being** are each thought of as a being-for-itself, i.e., as **substance** (for **substance** is that which exists for itself outside of another). They are **not themselves substance, but only determinations of the One Over-actual**. The meaning is therefore not that the **being-able-to-be** is outside of the **purely being**, but the meaning is that precisely the same thing, i.e., precisely **the same substance** in its unity and without therefore becoming two, is the **being-able-to-be** and the **purely being**.”

One could call this **substance**—which is identical in **Will** and **Representation** <note>Will and Representation: The two primary aspects of reality in this system; the drive to exist and the logical form that existence takes.</note>, this individual being which first carries those abstract generalities—"the absolute Subject," as that "to which nothing else can relate, and to which everything else relates only as an attribute" (Schelling II. 1, 318); but unfortunately, the word **Subject** is so ambiguous that one could easily cause misunderstandings with it. On the other hand, if one is entitled to call anything original the **absolute spirit**, then it is certainly this unity of Will and Representation, this **One substance**, which here wills and there represents—as we have called it until now: the **Unconscious**. This unconscious spirit is "the **Over-being** <note>original: "Ueberseiende"; a term for a reality that sits above or transcends standard categories of existence.</note>, which is all being." To be sure, it must...

<summary>This page argues that reality is a "monism of substance" but a "dualism of attributes," meaning one single reality expresses itself through two different powers: Will and Representation. Drawing on Plato and Schelling, the author identifies this unified, underlying reality as "the Unconscious."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Substantial Identity" of the two fundamental attributes of reality: the Will and the Idea. It moves from a critique of Schelling's terminology to a comparison with Spinoza and Hegel, ultimately grounding the dual nature of reality in a single underlying Substance.</meta>

<page-num>673</page-num>
<meta>v. Hartmann, Philosophy of the Unconscious.</meta>
<sig>43</sig>

...one must not then be biased by Hegel’s arbitrary restriction of the word "Spirit" to its appearance in the form of consciousness.

It would be a great error to conceive the relationship of our Substance to our Attributes as if the Substance were the *potency* <note>original: "Potenz"; refers to a latent power or potential that has not yet been realized.</note> of the attributes, and the attributes were *actus* <note>original Latin: "actus"; meaning acts, activities, or the actualization of a potential.</note> or *activities*. We have long since moved past the concept of *potency*, for the *potency* of *being* or *willing* is itself *one* of the attributes, and the other we have explicitly defined as pure *Being*, which has emerged from *no* further potency. Therefore, the Substance cannot stand in the relation of potency to either of them, and neither of them is an *actus* emerging from a potency. This is a primary difference from Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher who argued there is only one substance, which he called "God or Nature."</note>, in whose work the Substance quite clearly appears as the potency of the attributes.

The second difference lies in the definition of the one attribute which Spinoza, following the example of Descartes <note>Latinized as "Cartesius."</note>, calls *extension*. However, thinking and extension are not opposites at all, because extension is also found *within thinking* <note>Hartmann means that we can have a mental idea or "thought" of a physical shape or space.</note>. Only thinking and *real* extension form an opposition, which is what Spinoza actually meant. Yet, in the concepts of thinking and real extension, the opposition is not between "thinking" and "extension," but rather between "thinking" and "real," or between the "**Ideal and the Real**"; it is not extension that creates *reality*; rather, extension itself must first be made real to form an opposition to thinking. Spinoza's second attribute would therefore have to be that which—and now not just extension, but everything else ideal—*makes it real*. This is nothing other than the *Will*. Only then, when one replaces extension with the *Will*, does Spinoza’s metaphysics become what it ought to be; but then, the peak of our pyramid also coincides with the *One* Substance mystically postulated by Spinoza. —

->**Conclusion**<-

With this, our path is concluded; but in closing, let us turn our attention to one more question: namely, whether and how ***metaphysical knowledge is possible* from the standpoint of the *Philosophy of the Unconscious***.

This question is not unimportant, for often the most significant metaphysical systems, which encompass the entire world...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of reality, transitioning from a discussion on the attributes of "Substance" to the metaphysical foundations of how we can know anything at all. It bridges the gap between the critique of previous philosophical systems and the "Identity of Thinking and Being" central to modern German Idealism.</meta>

<page-num>674</page-num>

...explain in a coherent and acceptable manner, standing helpless before the problem of how, according to their own premises, the knowledge of the metaphysical connection they claim is even possible. At this point, of course, a full epistemology <term>Erkenntnisslehre: the philosophical study of the nature, origin, and limits of human knowledge</term> cannot be expected, but only a sketch of the standpoint we occupy regarding that question.

Greco-Roman philosophy ended in *Skepticism* because it did not succeed in finding a criterion of truth, and consequently it despaired over the possibility of deciding whether knowledge is possible at all. The *Dogmatism* <note>In philosophy, "dogmatism" refers to systems that assume the mind can know things as they are in themselves without first examining the limits of human reason.</note> of modern philosophy was broken in a similar way by David Hume, whose relentless critique *Kant* carried out to an even greater extent and with greater depth.

At the same time, however, *Kant* was the genius on the other side who initiated the latest developmental phase of philosophy. While Greek philosophy had fruitlessly tormented itself with the impossible demand of finding a characteristic within knowledge itself that would stamp it with the seal of truth, Kant went to work hypothetically and asked: "Regardless of whether true knowledge exists, what kind of metaphysical conditions must exist if such knowledge is to be possible?" or, as he poses the question: "How are synthetic judgments *a priori* <note>original Latin: "a priori"; refers to knowledge that is known independently of experience, such as mathematical truths.</note> possible?"

<margin>|</margin> All recent philosophy, with the exception of Schelling's final system, stands more or less consciously on this standpoint: *the conditions for the possibility of knowledge constitute its metaphysics*. As the first and fundamental condition for the possibility of all knowledge, one can assert the homogeneity <note>meaning that thought and reality must be "of the same kind" or nature to interact.</note> of thought and its external object; for if thought and the "thing" were heterogeneous <note>meaning "of different or incompatible kinds."</note>, absolutely no agreement between the two—that is, truth—and even less a consciousness of this agreement—that is, knowledge—would be possible. The so-called *Identity of Thinking and Being* is therefore the fundamental principle of the latest philosophy, a concept of which the ancients had scarcely a glimmer.

Schelling (I. 6, 138) explicitly admits that this identity, which forms the starting point of his system, can only be proven indirectly, specifically by the fact that "under no other possible assumption is *knowledge thinkable*."

<vocab>Metaphysics, Epistemology, Skepticism, Dogmatism, Immanuel Kant, F.W.J. Schelling, synthetic judgments a priori, Identity of Thinking and Being, Knowledge</vocab>

<summary>This page outlines the historical shift from ancient skepticism to Kant's "Copernican Revolution," arguing that knowledge is only possible if there is a fundamental identity between human thought and objective reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from Kantian critique to the specific metaphysical framework of the "Philosophy of the Unconscious," addressing how the dualities of mind and matter are reconciled within the Unconscious. It follows the discussion on page 674 regarding the possibility of knowledge and the limits of reason.</meta>

<page-num>675</page-num>

First, we must summarize how the *Philosophy of the Unconscious* relates to that opposition between thought and thing, **mind** <note>original Latin: *mens*</note> and **being** <note>original Latin: *ens*</note>, **reason** <note>original Latin: *ratio*</note> and **matter** <note>original Latin: *res*</note>, spirit and nature, the ideal and the real, and the subjective and the objective. Never and nowhere can the identity of the ideal and the real be understood as if there were no longer any difference between the two—which would make one of the words redundant; rather, the identity refers only to the **content**, while everyone understands that the **form** of existence of both differs precisely in that one is ideal and the other is real.

We now know more precisely from what has come before that Being is a product of the unlogical and the logical—of Will and Representation <term>Vorstellung: In German philosophy, this refers to the mental image, idea, or "representation" of an object in the mind</term>. We know that its "existence" <note>original: "Dass" (literally "the that"); the fact that something exists</note> is established by the Will, but its "essence" <note>original: "Was" (literally "the what"); the nature or properties of a thing</note> is the representational content of that Will. Therefore, this essence is not merely similar to the Idea, but is itself the Idea—that is, it is **identical** in the strictest sense of the word. In this way, spirit and nature are no longer distinct, for the original unconscious spirit is, in its "being-in-itself" <note>original: "Ansichsein"; the state of a thing as it exists independently of our perception</note>, that which is "nature" in its active connection, and which becomes "conscious spirit" (or spirit in the narrower Hegelian <note>Refers to G.W.F. Hegel, who saw Spirit as something that realizes itself through a historical process of becoming conscious</note> sense of the word) as a result of the natural process. As for the subjective and the objective, these are entirely relative concepts that only arise with the **emergence of consciousness**. In unconscious willing and unconscious representation, these terms have no place; the Unconscious is sublime, standing above those opposites, since its thinking is by no means subjective. Rather, for **us**, it is objective, but in truth, it is transcendent-absolute. One cannot actually say that the Unconscious **is** the absolute subject, but only that it is the only thing that **could become** a subject, just as it is the only thing that can **become** an object, because there is nothing outside of the Unconscious. **Understood this way**, one can indeed call the Unconscious the absolute subject and the absolute object, without prejudice to the fact that, as the Unconscious, it remains elevated above the opposition of the subjective and objective.

We have seen that consciousness only occurs during a collision of different directions of the Will. Of these, each is then the objective one for the other, and each is the subjective one for itself in contrast to the other which is objective to it, provided that

...both directions of the will <term>Willensrichtungen: The orientations or tendencies of the Will as it manifests in different forms</term> find themselves under circumstances that do not prevent the emergence of consciousness by lying below the threshold of consciousness.

If, for example, one imagined atoms to be above the threshold of consciousness, then atomic force A would become objective to atomic force B and vice versa; atomic force A, on the other hand, would become subjective to itself in contrast to the objectivity of B, and vice versa. Thus, the Unconscious would be conscious in both A and B in a twofold manner—both objectively and subjectively.

Having seen that the unification of all the aforementioned opposites follows from our principles, we return to the question of the possibility of knowledge <term>Erkenntniss: Often translated as "cognition" or "knowledge," referring here to the philosophical possibility of truly understanding reality</term>. Recent philosophy <note>Likely referring to the German Idealist tradition following Kant, specifically Schelling and Hegel</note> had thus proven that a system based on the abolition of those opposites was the only correct one, *provided* that true knowledge existed at all; but whether such knowledge actually existed, it still lacked any proof. It was as dogmatic in its assumption of this as pre-Kantian dogmatism <note>A term for the era of philosophy before Immanuel Kant’s "Critique of Pure Reason," which assumed the mind could know the "thing-in-itself" without questioning the limits of the mind</note> could ever be. Indeed, it did not even consider the possibility that someone could—and must—rightly deny the possibility of absolute knowledge (Reason) until a proof for it was obtained (cf. *Schelling* II. 3, p. 74).

Its entire philosophizing thus rested on a condition that was suspended completely in mid-air; the whole endeavor had been a hypothetical philosophizing based on an unproven premise.

Consequently, recent philosophy could only dissolve into skepticism. That this skepticism is the prevailing force in the younger, philosophically educated world (insofar as it has overcome an immature dogmatism) can hardly be denied. That this skepticism has not received a scientifically consistent development (— *Aenesidemus* <note>Original: *Aenesidemus*; a reference to the 1792 work by Gottlob Ernst Schulze, which used the name of the ancient Greek skeptic to launch a skeptical critique of Kant’s system</note> only stands just behind *Kant* —) is merely due to the fact that the tangible results of the exact sciences and the now all-consuming practical interests are generally unfavorable to philosophy, distracting theoretical thought too much and preventing a consistent deepening. To move forward, there are clearly only two ways: either one would have to, in order to [verify] the hypothetical result of *Identity Philosophy* <note>The "Philosophy of Identity" (Identitätsphilosophie) is a system associated with Friedrich Schelling, asserting that the objective (nature) and subjective (mind) are ultimately one</note>...

<meta>This page continues the critique of previous philosophical systems that assumed the possibility of knowledge without proof. It moves from a critique of the "Identity Philosophy" mentioned on the previous page toward a new method of proving how our thoughts align with reality.</meta>

<page-num>677</page-num>

...to ensure, to directly prove that true knowledge <term>Erkenntniss: The capacity of the mind to reach a true understanding of reality</term> exists—yet with such an endeavor, one would only fall back into the efforts of the Greeks, which were by their very nature futile (cf. Kant’s Works Vol. II, pp. 62 to 63) <note>Hartmann refers here to Immanuel Kant’s critique of ancient Greek logic and its inability to bridge the gap between thought and the "thing-in-itself."</note>—or one must actually utilize the most recent progress and grasp the thing from the opposite end as the Greeks did. That is to say, one must directly prove the substantive identity of thinking and being in a completely different way than has been attempted thus far, via a path that is accessible and illuminating to everyone. This path can only be the one we have traversed: the successive inductive ascent from experience.

Now, of course, the proof conducted in this way must itself be an act of knowledge if it is to prove anything; one might therefore think that we have only apparently taken a step forward, but in reality, we are standing with our feet in the air just as before. However, this is not the case; rather, the relationship is as follows.

Previously, the saying was: “if knowledge exists, then there is a substantive identity of thinking and being”; one could not get beyond this simple conditional statement.

Now, it is said:
1) If knowledge exists, it must rest on the substantive identity of thinking and being, and thus must also be found in immediate experience (the affection of thinking by being <note>The way external reality "affects" or triggers our mental processes</note>) and the logically correct conclusions drawn from it;
2) The conclusions drawn from experience confirm the substantive identity of thinking and being;
3) From this identity follows the possibility of knowledge.

With this, we have a self-contained circle where each link conditions the others, regardless of which one we start with, whereas previously we had only a conditional statement without, so to speak, a back-rest or a chest-rest. There remains, therefore, even now the possibility that this entire circle of psychological and metaphysical conditions is a mere subjective illusion <note>original: "subjectiver Schein"</note> which consciousness is forced to form by an inexplicable necessity; that there is, in fact, no knowledge and no identity of thinking and being, and that the circle of mutually reinforcing relationships built upon both is a mere chimera. For, of course, the transcendent <note>Beyond the limits of possible experience</note> and not merely...

<summary>Hartmann proposes that the identity of thought and reality can be proven through "inductive experience" rather than abstract logic. He acknowledges that while this creates a self-reinforcing logical circle, a skeptic could still argue that this entire structure is a necessary psychological illusion.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the philosophical argument regarding the "circle" of knowledge—the idea that we must use knowledge to prove the possibility of knowledge. It transitions from a theoretical justification of skepticism to a practical rejection of it, before concluding the volume with a list of errata and printing details.</meta>

<page-num>678</page-num>

subjective existence of that circle <note>The "logical circle" refers to the problem that one cannot prove the validity of human knowledge without already using that knowledge to perform the proof.</note> cannot be strictly proven as absolute truth, because consciousness is imprisoned within this circle and can never take a standpoint outside of it from which it could judge the nature of that circle; for consciousness cannot recognize the possibility of knowledge without knowledge itself.

Therefore, even if the absolute impossibility of the opposite cannot be proven, the probability that there is both knowledge <term>Erkenntniss: The capacity of the mind to reach a true understanding of reality</term> and an identity of thinking and being has become much greater through that circle than it was previously with that simple conditional statement—which lacked any supporting hold at the front or back. This probability has become so great that the possibility of the opposite no longer comes into consideration in any practical sense. Skepticism is therefore not annihilated, but rather recognized as theoretically justified; yet its significance is reduced to such a minimal measure that it disappears for the practice of not only life, but also science.

If we consider this result regarding the possibility of knowledge in general, it aligns remarkably with what should probably by now be admitted on all sides regarding the knowledge of every specific truth (insofar as it is not of a formal-logical nature): that for us there is no truth—that is, a probability with the value of 1—but only more or less great probability which never reaches 1. We must be perfectly satisfied if, in our knowing, we reach a degree of probability that strips the possibility of the opposite of its practical significance (cf. also Introductory I. b.).

<meta>This page serves as a visual conclusion to the manuscript, following the philosophical discussion on the limits of knowledge on page 678. It represents the physical bookbinding, specifically the decorative endpapers used to finish the volume.</meta>

[Illustration of Marbled Paper]

This page features a decorative pattern typical of historical bookbinding. The design consists of large, dark, irregular cells or "blobs" separated by thin, light-colored veins. Within many of these dark cells are small, white, circular ring-like spots.

<note>This style is known as **shell marbling** or **agate marbling**. Marbled paper was created by floating pigments on a liquid bath, combing or chemically manipulating them into patterns, and then "printing" the design onto a sheet of paper. These papers were frequently used as endpapers—the pages pasted to the inner covers of a book—to hide the binding construction and provide a decorative transition into the text.</note>

<term>Agate pattern: A marbling style characterized by small, ringed spots within larger droplets of color, resembling the natural banding found in agate stones.</term>

<term>Endpaper: A leaf of paper at the beginning or end of a book, half of which is pasted to the cover board, serving both a structural and decorative purpose.</term>
